Title: Function over form: a longitudinal study of predictors and mediation pathways for disordered eating in elite athletes
Authors: Fatt, S.J., Hay, P., George, E., Jeacocke, N., Rogers, K., Mitchison, D.
Population subgroup: Males T1 N=47 Males T2 N=25 Males T3 N=22 Females T1 N=126 Females T2 N=83 Females T3 N=63 Other T1 N=1 Other T2 N=1
Inclusion criteria: Adult athletes who had competed at a national, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level
Sporting population: National, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level
Degree of relationship: Model controlling for gender T1 drive for leanness for performance-T2 disordered eating 𝛃=.20, p=.006 T1 drive for leanness for performance-T3 disordered eating 𝛃=.21, p=.025
Authors' conclusions: Disordered eating in elite athletes is predicted by sport-specific weight pressures and drive for leanness for performance, rather than societal pressures or body image concerns. This suggests that athlete-specific mechanisms differ from those in the general population
Limits: The study had a limited and somewhat biased sample (mainly female, Western athletes) and insufficient power to test moderating factors like gender. Measurement choices and attrition may also affect the robustness of findings
Perspectives: Future research should test these models in more diverse and younger athlete populations and explore additional factors like perfectionism. Interventions should focus on performance-related beliefs and sport environments rather than appearance-based concerns

Title: Effect of achievement goals on Female aesthetic athletes disordered eating attitudes
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Corrion, K., & d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
Inclusion criteria: French high-level Female athletes aged from 13 to 20 years old; practiced gymnastics or figure skating intensively with a minimum of five years of experience in national or international competition
Authors' conclusions: Performance approach goals were positive predictors of emerging disordered eating attitudes. Mastery avoidance goals were also positive predictors of disordered eating attitudes. Performance avoidance was a protective factor. A relationship between mastery approach and disturbed eating attitudes did not emerge in the structural equation model or the correlation table.
Limits: The data were self reported, suggesting the likelihood that social desirability was operative. The study was cross sectional, conclusions about causality cannot be inferred. The athletes scores on the eating psychopathology measure indicated relatively healthy attitudes, it is unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to athletes with more severe eating disorders. The generalization of the results is limited to the Female gender and an elite level. The participants ages and competition experience were not controlled.
Perspectives:
Future studies might investigate whether the relationships can be generalized to athletes in other types of sport or to other types of population, as well as the aforementioned variables that could play a moderation or mediation role in this relationship. Future studies could replicate with a sample of non-athletic controls, as well as a clinical sample in order to determine whether the mechanisms involved in the eating psychopathology of athletes are also operative in the general population and patients with eating disorders. The contextual and temporal dimensions could be considered, with future studies examining the current eating behavior, with a temporal control especially concerning the current goals. 
Programs could be adapted to encourage an orientation toward task mastery as a means to protect from disordered eating attitudes.

Title: Achievement goal theory and disordered eating: relationships of disordered eating with goal orientations and motivation climate in Female gymnasts and dancers
Authors: Karin de Bruin, A.P., Bakker, F.C., & Oudejans, R.R.D.
Inclusion criteria: Only high level aesthetic performers who did not participate in additional competitive sport activities were included.
Mean_Exercise frequency:
M=16.7 hours per week, SD=6.7
Gymnasts M=18.1, SD=7.8
Dancers M=14.4, SD=3.28
DEAB_measure: 9-point-scale running from 1(never) to 9(always) with the following item Are you trying yo lose weight ?
Related_Factor_measure: Task and Ego Orientation in Sport Questionnaire (TEOSQ)
Authors' conclusions: Ego orientation and performance climate were related to more frequent dieting, using more pathogenic weight control methods, greater perfectionism and perceiving more weight related peer pressure. Having a high ego orientation means that a Female aesthetic performer is sgnificantly more likely to report indices of disordered eating. Non-significant correlations were found between task orientation and DE. With respect to performance climate, significant relationships were found with all DE variables. The present study also shows that a mastery climate is negatively related to disordered eating. Mastery climate explained some of the variance of dieting frequency.
Limits: A limitation in the present study was that we used a relatively crude measure for pathogenic weight control with limited reliability. Another limitation was that we had to confine ourselves to self-reported height and weight because objective measurement of body composition was perceived as too threatening form some aesthetic performers. Self-report holds the risk of both under or overstimation. Another constraint in the present study was the composition of our sample. As the number of high level competitive gymnasts in the Netherlands is limited, we also investigated a group of high level Female dancers.
Perspectives: In future studes focusing exclusively on relationships between eating disorders or disordered eating with achievement motivation, full versions of general or sport specific measures could be administered such as the Eating Disorder Inventory-2 or the Female Athlete Screening Tool for disordered eating. Future studies should continue to making an effort to include objective measurements by the researchers or recent actual data provided by medical staff members. The observed relationships of this study should be replicated in future studies using larger samples of various athletes at risk for disordered eating. Roberts (2001) stated that a high ego orientation is particularly detrimental if it is accompanied by a low task orientation. Future research should further investigate if this is also true for disordered eating. To gain a more complete understanding of the relationship between ego orientation and disordered eating, future studies could also include the more recent 2 by 2 framework which not only distinguishes between ego and task orientation but also between approach and avoidance achievmalet goals. We therefore recommaled that coaches and teachers should create a mastery climate with its emphasis on personal development and interpersonal cooperation.

Title: Eating disorders in Taekwondo athletes: the contribution of coach behavior, body satisfaction, and goal orientation
Authors: Baric, R., Erdeljac, T.
Inclusion criteria: Active practice of Taekwondo for at least 6 months and being a competitor in one of three competities categories: cadets, junior athletes or senior athletes
Sporting population:
17.3% top elite athletes, members of national selection and elite athletes
25 elite male
33 elite female
107 non-elite male
170 non-elite female
DEAB_measure: Croatian version of the Eating Attitudes Test (EAT_26)
Related_Factor_measure: Croatian Task and Ego Orientation in Sport Questionnaire (CTEOSQ)
Authors' conclusions: Goal orientation, body dissatisfaction, and negative behavior and pressure from coaches significantly contribute to the risk of ED development in female and male cadet, junior and non-elite athletes, while body dissatisfaction seems to be the strongest predictor, especially in female athletes.
Limits: The sample size, although it is realistic in relation to the number of active taekwondo competitors in Croatia. Self reported questionnaires.
Perspectives: Including other measures, more adjusted to male ED symptoms. As the results showed the significance of the behavior of coaches in relation to athletes ED symptoms, it would be very interesting to investigate the transgenerational transfer of distorted values, beliefs and behaviors related to ED from coaches to athletes, i.e., to investigate coaches history of ED symptoms and their current behavior.

Title: Eating disordered behaviours in Portuguese athletes: the influence of personal, sport, and psychological variables
Authors: Gomes, A.R., Martins, C., & Silva, L.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between 14 and 30 year of age
Sport_name: Athletics; karate; swimming; taekwondo; basketball; handball; volleyball
Sporting population:
Top division (38.8%)
Regional or national levels
Related_Factor_measure: Task and Ego Orientation in Sport Questionnaire (TEOSQ)
Authors' conclusions: The EDE-Q global score was positively associated with weight-related coach pressure, anxiety, taske orientation, impression motivation and threat perception, and negatively associated with less satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance. Eating behaviour was predicted by lower satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance, and higher anxiety and impression motivation.
Limits: Data were based on athletes self-report, which could have resulted in under-reporting of eating disordered behaviours. A better discrimination between sports according to their requirements needs to be introduced in order to better differentiate the demands and soecific characteristics of each sport. It is vital to further explore the impact of psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours.
Perspectives: It is important to assess athletes reactions in competition, the way they perceive themselves, and the way they want others to perceive them. If there is a better comprehension of these factors, then prevention of eating problems and promotion of better experiences in sport becomes easier to achieve.

Title: Protective and risk factors in exercise addiction: a series of moderated mediation analyses
Authors: Gori, A., Topino, E., & Griffiths, M.D.
Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Inclusion criteria: Participants who engaged in regular exercise at leat three times per week for a minimum of 30 minutes each session
Mean_Exercise frequency: At least three per week for a minimum of 30 minutes each session
Authors' conclusions: The study focused on various risk factors for exercise addiction, and found relationships relating to drive for thinness, bulimia, body dissatisfaction, body image concerns, as well as an important protective role of self esteem.
Limits: A modestly sized convenience sample of regular exercisers was recruited utilizing a snowball sampling method. Only self-report measures were used to collect the data, and such data are known to include well-etablished methods biases, such as social desirability ad memory recall. The cross sectional design requires caution in interpreting causality.
Perspectives: Future research would need to implement longitudinal designs in order to determine the specific directions of the relationships examined. Replicate the study with larger more representative samples and utilizing different recruitmalet techniques.

Title: Body dissatisfaction, addiction to exercise and risk behaviour for eating disorders among exercise practitioners
Authors: Freire, G.L.M., da Silva Paulo, J.R., da Silva, A.A., Baptista, R.P.R., Alves, J.F.N., & do Nascimaleto Junior, J.R.A.
Inclusion criteria: To be at least 18 years old; to be a physical exercise practitioner for at least 3 months; to regularly attend the gym/crossfit box at least twice a week
Mean_Age:
M=26.58, SD=7.76
Fitness practitioners M=24.86, SD=7
Crossfit practitioners M=31.31, SD=7.98
Authors' conclusions: There is a positive association of body dissatisfaction with risk behaviour for eating disorders and addiction to exercise.
Limits:
Small number of participants and who were practitioners of only two modalities, which males impossible to generalize th results to practitioners of other exercises. 
The cross sectional design which does not allow to make inferences of causality between the variables.
Perspectives:
Future researches should extend the study with practitioners from other regions of Brazilian population and exercises. 
A longitudinal study will be able to point to the causal nature of the association between BD, addiction to exercise and risk behavior for ED. 
It is important that instructors and personal trainers analyse the real motives of the individuals to begin the practice of the exercise, always considering the chosen modality. Moreover, it is essential to emphasize the effects of long term training focusing on maintaining health and quality of life, always respecting the individuality and healthy evolution of training.

Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions
Authors: Olave, L., Estévez, A., Momene, J., Penacoba, C., Macia, P., Macia, L., Etxaburu, N., Muniz, J.A., Iruarrizaga, I.
Inclusion criteria: People who practice physical exercise at least one day a week
Authors' conclusions: The study highlights strong links between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia, and multiple addictions, with impulsivity playing a key mediating role. These findings emphasize the importance of targeting impulsivity and emotion regulation in prevention and treatment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and the use of a homogeneous convenience sample limits generalizability. Additionally, reliance on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses may affect accuracy.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify causal relationships and further explore specific dimensions of impulsivity. There is also a need to develop prevention and intervention strategies focusing on emotion regulation and impulsivity

Title: The relationship between exercise addiction, eating disorders, and insecure attachment styles among recreational exercisers
Authors: Lev Arey, D., Sagi, A., & Blatt, A.
Inclusion criteria: Recreational exercisers who engage in a minimum of 4h of exercise per week
Sport_name: Running, triathlon, gym workouts, swimming, aerobics, biking, yoga, boxing, basketball, crossfit
Authors' conclusions: An anxious attachment was linked to eating disorder.
Limits: The restricted sample that was included. This study relied on self-administered questionnaires, which may have introduced social desirability and recall biases. The evaluation tools used were screening tools with no diagnostic validity.
Perspectives: Future research should explore the bidirectional relationship between insecure attachment and eating disorders. It would be valuable for future research to investigate the directionality and underlying mechanisms of the relationship between insecure attachment and eating disorder.

Title: Weight and diet preoccupation and addictiveness: the role of exercise
Authors: Davis, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; for exercisers engaged in some physical activity at least 3 times a week for a minimum of 30 minutes per session; non exercisers for those who engaged in less or no physical activities
Mean_Age:
Exercisers M=25.98, SD=8.70 
Non-exercisers M=27.34, SD=8.98
Mean_Exercise frequency: 3 times a week for a minimum 30 min per session

Title: Eating disorders risk assessment and body esteem among elite polish contact karate athletes
Authors: Dobkowska-Szefer, D., Staskiewicz-Bartecka, W., Kiciak, A., Kardas, M.
Inclusion criteria: Consent from both the club and the athlete to participate in the study, active participation in training in contact karate clubs (defined as > 3 training sessions per week for at least the past 6 months), achievement of at least one medal-winning position in competitions at the level of the Polish championships or higher, organized by national or international sports federations, and absence of chronic diseases, including diagnosed mental health disorders, as confirmed in the demographic section of the questionnaire
Related_Factor_measure: Body Esteem Scale (BES) in the Polish adaptation by Lipowska and Lipowski
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Affective dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This study identifies elite karate athletes as a high-risk group for disordered eating and orthorexia, with body image—especially in women—and weight-related pressures playing a central role. It highlights the importance of psychological factors over BMI in shaping risk.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, small and selective sample, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference and generalizability. The use of BMI and omission of key psychosocial variables further constrain interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include larger samples, longitudinal designs, and objective body composition measures. Preventive interventions focusing on body image, nutrition education, and sport-specific pressures are essential in weight-category sport

Title: Disordered eating, perfectionism and body esteem on elite synchronized swimmers
Authors: Ferrand, C., Magnan, C., Rouveix, M., & Filaire, E.
Inclusion criteria: N.A.
DEAB_measure: The French Version of Dietary Restraint
Related_Factor_measure: The Canadian French Version of the Body Esteem Scale
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Affective dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Socially prescribed perfectionism did not explain variance in dietary restraint scores. Self esteem oriented perfectionism was associated with dietary restraint and was related to body dissatisfaction. The current findings show a mediating effect of body esteem weight satisfaction on the relationship between self-oriented perfectionism and dietary restraint. The perfectionist personality would be a contributing factor in dietary restraint required to maintin a low body weight.

Title: Psychosocial characteristics and eating attitudes in young elite figure skaters in Canada and France: Are there any country differences?

Title: Difficulties in emotion regulation, alexithymia, and social phobia are associated with disordered eating in male and Female undergraduate athletes
Authors: Benau, E.M., Wiatrowski, R., & Timko, C.A.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduates at a large Mid-Atlantic university, sample of undergraduate athletes and non-athletes.
Sporting population:
Among the athletes (N=183): 
Recreational and club level (64% - N=116)
Collegiate (35% - N=63)
Semi professional and professional levels (1% - N=2)
Related_Factor_measure: Toronto Alexithymia Scale Difficulty Identifying Feelings subscale (TAS-DIF)
Authors' conclusions: Many of the psychosocial and socioemotional risk factors for disordered eating in the general population are also present in the undergraduate athlete population. Risk factors between male and Female differ in terms of presentation, but not necessarily on severity.
Limits: The present study was cross-sectional, and data were self reported from a self-selected and predominantly Caucasian sample at one undergraduate university, which limits conclusion about causality and generalizability. The EDI-3 was developed primarily with Female, which may not capture eating behavior and body shape concerns of athletes of all genders. Although many of the included instruments used in the present study have been used amply within collegiate athletes samples, only the EDI has been independently validated for this population. We did not inquire or determine eating disorder diagnosis as we were interested in disordered eating risk more generally. Finally, because we were interested in the influence of team dynamics, our classification of non-athletes included those who engaged in personal exercise but not organized exercise, which may also convey similar eating disorder risk to those involved in organized sports. Given to observed differences between athletes and non-athletes, we do not believe that engagement in personal fitness influenced the results of this study.
Perspectives: The cross-sectional nature of this study precludes a conclusion about causality. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify this relation. Given a comparatively higher focus on restrictive eating in athletes, more work is needed to confirm and better understand why Female athletes may engage in binge eating. Future reseachers should consider including the RMET as a behavioral measure of recognizing emotional expression in others that may measure different components of emotion regulation than self-report. Future researchers would do well to collect data from multiple campuses.

Authors: Boyda, D., & Shevlin, M.

The study excluding those who had recorded they were currently experiencing a mental health illness, those who were attending a gymnasium less than three days per week as this was considered to represent casual membership. Those who recorded that gym attendance of less than four years were also excluded.
Authors' conclusions: Anxiety was significantly associated with muscle dysmorphia. Anxiety and depression do not both mediate the relationship between victimisation experiences and muscle dysmorphia, the unique mediating effect of anxiety represents a possible and plausible route from childhood victimisation to muscle dysmorphia. Victimisation during childhood increases anxiety levels, as a consequence, individuals negatively evaluate their self-image resulting in a body image distorsion and ultimately muscle dysmorphia. Children who are victimised by family or peers during childhood via physical, verbal or social means may have an increased risk of developing a pathological fixation with their body and this may have an impact or increase the risk for muscle dysmorphia later in adulthood.
Limits: The study was retrospective and cross-sectional and this as such limited conclusions regarding mediation. The study did not ascertain the temporal ordering of experiences which may limit analysis and interpretation, while childhood memories recalled during adulthood maybe subject to negative recall bias. In addition, it should not be discounted that the mediation model contained too few mediators to accurately predict an association between the childhood victimisation and muscle dysmorphia. Also the sample size was relatively small and this sample is not likely to be representative of the general population due to the sampling method. However, recruited participants through bodybuidling forum ensured adequate levels of variability in muscle dysmorphia scores: a general population sample likely have produced scores heavily positively skewed. Finally, low participation from the three large forums was unexpected.
Perspectives:
A more appropriate recruitmalet strategy should be considered as an increased sample size xould contribute to more stable estimation of the mediation model. 
The future direction for a follow-up study should consider if such early experiences and subsequent manifestation of muscle dysmorphia lead to a gateway for the use of performance-enhancing drugs wich may further magnify the effects of msucle dysmorphia on their psychological functioning. This could be considered an important extension to this study as indivdiuals who use performance-enhancing drugs can rapidly change aspects of their muscularity including fat distribution as after all, this is the holy grail for those who have muscle dysmorphia.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: The impact of critical comments from teammates on athletes eating and exercise psychopathology
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Adults aged 18 and over from local sport clubs
Mean_Age:
Critical comment M=23.27, SD=8.34
No critical group M=23.20, SD=8.67
Mean_BMI:
Critical comment M=22.70, SD=3.83
No critical comment M=22.56, SD=3.55
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Critical comment M=9.61h/week, SD=6.65
No critical comment M=8.29, SD=5.46
Mean_Years of experience:
Critical comment M=7.35, SD=6.41
No critical comment M=6.12, SD=5.58
Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

Title: Teammate influences, psychological well-being, and athletes eating and exercise psychopathology: a moderated mediation analysis
Authors: Scott, C.L., Plateau, C.R., & Haycraft, E.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competed with a university sports team or with their club or school
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Mean_Years of experience: Member of their current team M=1.99, SD=2.61
Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. Gender was not a significant moderator, meaning that the role of psychological wellbeing in the relationships between teammate influences and eating.
Limits: Although age and BMI were controlled for, it is acknowledged that there are a number of additional co-variates (e.g., perfectionism, athletic identity) that could have contributed to the findings of this study. The self report nature of the data collected and the context it was collected in (i.e., before/after a training session and in the company of teammates/coach) may potentially misrepresent athletes true behaviours. Items comprising the EDI-drive for thinness and body dissatsifaction subscales may not be an accurate reflection of male athletes experiences with disordered eating.
Perspectives: Identifying key risk factors and relevant moderators and mediators for eating psychopathology is important for effectively identifying those athletes at increased risk of eating and exercise psychopathology, and for developing appropriately tailored intervention and prevention strategies. Future research into the role of teammates would benefit from experimentally manipulating mechanisms of teammate influence on athletes actual food intake and should consider employing methodologies that are specifically tailored to male athletes. Employing modeeling analytic techniques to further our understanding of the complex, multi-factorial influences on athlete eating and exercise behaviours.

Title: mental skills as protective attributes against eating disorder risk in dancers
Authors: Estanol, E.
Inclusion criteria: The majority of participants were European American collegiate ballet dancers; however, collegiate modern and professional ballet dancers were also included in the sample. In order to ascertain a sample more less representative o the US population, the companies and universities were selected based on geographic location (east coast, midwest and western states). Selection of universities was also made by locating programs that had pre-professional or elite dance programs.
Authors' conclusions: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Negative affect partially mediated the relationship between weight pressures and ED symptoms. mental skills, specifically coping with adversity, freedom from worry, and confidence/achievement motivation, fully mediated the relationship between negative affect and ED symptoms. Total score for the athletic coping skill inventory was signficantly negatively correlated with weight pressure in dance, anxiety, depression and eating disorder risk.
Limits: One limitation of this study was that the sample was predominantly white and Female. Results from this study may therefore not be generalizable to a more ethnically diverse sample or to male dancers. Furthermore, this study lacked a comparison group of non-dancers, which would have enabled the researchers to more objectively compare the impact of the dance environment with a non-dance environment.
Perspectives: Additional studies are needed to explore how other protective factors (i.e., satisfaction with life, optimism, self-esteem, humor, and spirituality) may further explain variations in ED symptoms in dancers and contribute to this mediation model identified. Future research that looks at variables in the context of high-risk groups by providing profiles of resilient dancers vs at-risk dancers is also needed in order to further clarify the relationship between risk and resilience factors and ED outcomes. Furthermore, including demographic variables in the analyses would help us to better understand if certain subpopulations of dancers, may be more at risk or protected from pressures in the dance environment. Finally, studies should include the use of alternative methods in addition to self-report to more thoroughly explore variables relating to the dance environment.

Title: Eating disordered behaviours in Portuguese athletes: the influence of personal, sport, and psychological variables
Authors: Gomes, A.R., Martins, C., & Silva, L.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between 14 and 30 year of age
Sport_name: Athletics; karate; swimming; taekwondo; basketball; handball; volleyball
Sporting population:
Top division (38.8%)
Regional or national levels
Authors' conclusions: The EDE-Q global score was positively associated with weight-related coach pressure, anxiety, taske orientation, impression motivation and threat perception, and negatively associated with less satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance. Eating behaviour was predicted by lower satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance, and higher anxiety and impression motivation.
Limits: Data were based on athletes self-report, which could have resulted in under-reporting of eating disordered behaviours. A better discrimination between sports according to their requirements needs to be introduced in order to better differentiate the demands and soecific characteristics of each sport. It is vital to further explore the impact of psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours.
Perspectives: It is important to assess athletes reactions in competition, the way they perceive themselves, and the way they want others to perceive them. If there is a better comprehension of these factors, then prevention of eating problems and promotion of better experiences in sport becomes easier to achieve.

General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: The impact of critical comments from teammates on athletes eating and exercise psychopathology
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Adults aged 18 and over from local sport clubs
Mean_Age:
Critical comment M=23.27, SD=8.34
No critical group M=23.20, SD=8.67
Mean_BMI:
Critical comment M=22.70, SD=3.83
No critical comment M=22.56, SD=3.55
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Critical comment M=9.61h/week, SD=6.65
No critical comment M=8.29, SD=5.46
Mean_Years of experience:
Critical comment M=7.35, SD=6.41
No critical comment M=6.12, SD=5.58
Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

Title: Teammate influences, psychological well-being, and athletes eating and exercise psychopathology: a moderated mediation analysis
Authors: Scott, C.L., Plateau, C.R., & Haycraft, E.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competed with a university sports team or with their club or school
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Mean_Years of experience: Member of their current team M=1.99, SD=2.61
Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. Gender was not a significant moderator, meaning that the role of psychological wellbeing in the relationships between teammate influences and eating.
Limits: Although age and BMI were controlled for, it is acknowledged that there are a number of additional co-variates (e.g., perfectionism, athletic identity) that could have contributed to the findings of this study. The self report nature of the data collected and the context it was collected in (i.e., before/after a training session and in the company of teammates/coach) may potentially misrepresent athletes true behaviours. Items comprising the EDI-drive for thinness and body dissatsifaction subscales may not be an accurate reflection of male athletes experiences with disordered eating.
Perspectives: Identifying key risk factors and relevant moderators and mediators for eating psychopathology is important for effectively identifying those athletes at increased risk of eating and exercise psychopathology, and for developing appropriately tailored intervention and prevention strategies. Future research into the role of teammates would benefit from experimentally manipulating mechanisms of teammate influence on athletes actual food intake and should consider employing methodologies that are specifically tailored to male athletes. Employing modeeling analytic techniques to further our understanding of the complex, multi-factorial influences on athlete eating and exercise behaviours.

Title: An examination of psychosocial correlates of eating disorders among Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Reel, J.J., & Carter, J.E.

Sport_name: Basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; field hockey; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; sport shooting; rowing; soccer; softball; swimming; synchronized swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.71, SD=1.27
M=8.89, SD=4.80
Authors' conclusions: The pressures participants felt from general media (e.g., magazines, television/movies) rather than from sport-specific (e.g., teammates, judges) and interpersonal (e.g., boy/girlfriend, friends) sources most strongly discriminated among the three eating disorder categories. The correlations between internalization and the discriminant functin were significant but small. Athlete, relative to nonathletes, may be more satisfied with their bodies, this variable is related strongly to eating pathology. Body image, internalization, negative affect and pressures contributed similarly to the differentiation among the three eating disorder categories.
Limits: All data were self reported, which allowed for the possibility of socially desirable responding. The cross sectional design did not allow for determining temporal relationships among the variables and eating pathology.
Perspectives:
Future sudies may want to employ Petrie and Greenleaf's (2007) conceptual model using structural equation modeling and incorporate qualitative interviews to better determine how Female athletes experience and cope with the pressure from coaches, and whether these pressures change over the time they are involved in their sports. Future research should include measure of dietary restraint to determine if it assists in accurately classifying athletes into the three eating disorder groups. 
Professionals need to develop methods for screening athletes prior to each season to identify eating disorder and symptomatic groups and intervene as early as possible. Body image groups that focus on decreasing internalization and the effects of societal pressures may be an effective intervention strategy with Female athletes.

Title: The contribution of BMI, body image inflexibility, and generalized anxiety to symptoms of eating disorders and exercise dependence in exercisers

Non sport M=21.29, SD=3.10
Authors' conclusions: BMI and body image inflexibility are predictive of eating disorders symptoms.
Limits: All measures rely on self reports, they are somewhat prone to measurement error that arises from self report bias. BMI has some disadvantages; BMI is biased because this measure does not take into account the difference between muscle mass and fat mass. The participants comprise only universities students. This study focuses on body image distorsion as one of the predictors while other possible variables such as self compassion, perfectionism, and obsessive compulsive personality disorder were not considered. Perspectives: Our findings suggest that the prevention and treatment of exercise dependence symptoms should consider interventions to improve the indivdiuals attitude towards the perception of their own body by addressing body image inflexibility.

Title: Influence of perfectionism on variables associated to eating disorders in dance students
Authors: Arcelus, J., Garcia-Dantas, A., Sanchez-Martin, M., Del Rio, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 12-20; participation was voluntary; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Sport_name: Dance (e.g., ballet, contemporary, flamenco, spanish folk)
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Title: Difficulties in emotion regulation, alexithymia, and social phobia are associated with disordered eating in male and Female undergraduate athletes
Authors: Benau, E.M., Wiatrowski, R., & Timko, C.A.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduates at a large Mid-Atlantic university, sample of undergraduate athletes and non-athletes.
Sporting population:
Among the athletes (N=183): 
Recreational and club level (64% - N=116)
Collegiate (35% - N=63)
Semi professional and professional levels (1% - N=2)
Authors' conclusions: Many of the psychosocial and socioemotional risk factors for disordered eating in the general population are also present in the undergraduate athlete population. Risk factors between male and Female differ in terms of presentation, but not necessarily on severity.
Limits: The present study was cross-sectional, and data were self reported from a self-selected and predominantly Caucasian sample at one undergraduate university, which limits conclusion about causality and generalizability. The EDI-3 was developed primarily with Female, which may not capture eating behavior and body shape concerns of athletes of all genders. Although many of the included instruments used in the present study have been used amply within collegiate athletes samples, only the EDI has been independently validated for this population. We did not inquire or determine eating disorder diagnosis as we were interested in disordered eating risk more generally. Finally, because we were interested in the influence of team dynamics, our classification of non-athletes included those who engaged in personal exercise but not organized exercise, which may also convey similar eating disorder risk to those involved in organized sports. Given to observed differences between athletes and non-athletes, we do not believe that engagement in personal fitness influenced the results of this study.
Perspectives: The cross-sectional nature of this study precludes a conclusion about causality. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify this relation. Given a comparatively higher focus on restrictive eating in athletes, more work is needed to confirm and better understand why Female athletes may engage in binge eating. Future reseachers should consider including the RMET as a behavioral measure of recognizing emotional expression in others that may measure different components of emotion regulation than self-report. Future researchers would do well to collect data from multiple campuses.

Title: Bulimic symptomatology among male collegiate athletes: a test of an etiological model
Authors: Chatterton, J., Petrie, T.A., Schuler, K.L., & Ruggero, C.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.

Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)

Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.

Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. The cross sectional design of the study does not allow for the determination of the temporal nature of the relationships between psychosocial variables and bulimic symptoms.
Perspectives:
Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.

Authors' conclusions: SPA scores contributed to dieting and bulimia scores in individual athletes. SPA and sport type independently and in combination contribute to greater dieting and bulimic behavior, particularly in Female individual sport athletes.
Limits: Only athletes attending the training would have been approached about the study. Not all athletes from each sport at each institute were present at the time of data collection due to other commutmalets. Most athletes were tested at training sessions, rather than in settings which might heighten SPA. The testing of athletes in this manner may identify more consistent levels of SPA and disordered eating. This division by team and individual sport may be too simplisticc, not accounting for other psychological and confounding factors. These factors may affect disordered eating.
Perspectives:
Longitudinal and experimental designs may elucidate the directionality of the relationship, providing support for possible interventions. 
Female indivdiual sport athletes in particular may benefit from practical methods of reducing SPA and encouraging healthy eating within the sport setting by coaches and peers. 
Attention to other trigger factors may be necessary when dealing with Female athletes in individual sports, as this subgroup reported the highest levels of dieting and bulimic tendencies, along with high SPA. Different techniques and strategies for dealing with SPA and disordered eating may be required for different sport types.

Inclusion criteria: Males. The first group consisted of bodybuilders; minimum level of training twice a week for at least a year. The second group consisted of competitive weightlifters recruited from the state weightlifting associations in four states of Australia.
Mean_Age:
Bodybuilders M=28.89, SD=6.19
Weightlifters M=27.60, SD=8.70
Non-athletic control M=26.43, SD=8.15
Mean_BMI:
Weightlifters M=28.60, SD=6.90
Bodybuilders M=26.04, SD=3.08
Controls M=24.18, SD=2.80
Sport_name: Bodybuilding, Weightlifting, Soccer, football, running, martial arts, swimming
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.40 hours per week
Weightlifters M=12.12 hours per week 
Controls M=3.8 hours per week
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.14 years
Weightlifters M=9.06 years
Authors' conclusions: Bodybuilding may represent a practice that encourages male to become more self-conscious of their bodies, putting them at greater risk of experiencing greater levels of monitoring of body appearance and anxiety about physical appearance. This body self consciousness is associated with a greater risk of body dissatisfaction and drive for muscularity. Weightlifting does not appear to represent an objectifying climate.
Limits: The cross sectional nature makes it possible only to speculate on the directions of causality. Unequal sample sizes of groups in our analyses, particularly with respect to fewer competitive weightlifters. Unknown selection bias that may be operating in the bodybuilder and weightlifter groups, and any subsequent influence on the interpretation of our results. The weighlifting and bodybuilder groups differed not only in the nature of their sport, but also in competitive nature of this sport, which may introduce confound for differences found between the groups.
Perspectives: Health pursuits for male should emphasize achievement and function rather than appearance if they are to avoid deleterious consesquences.

Title: How the obsession to eat healthy food meets with the willingness to do sports: the motivational background of orthorexia nervosa
Authors: Kiss-Leizer, M., Toth-Jiraly, I., & Rigo, A.
Inclusion criteria: Participants aged between 18 to 72 years
Range_Exercise frequency:
37.2% 3-4 times per week
25.8% 1-2h weekly
25% 3-4h 
35.2% for 5 or more than 5h
Authors' conclusions: Health anxiety, mood modification are a strong predictor of orthorexia nervosa.
Limits: The results of the present study were based on online data gathering which questions the representative nature of the sample. Although participants were represented in a broad range of age and educational level, the highest proportion of participants were young and highly qualified Female. The participation in the research was voluntary thus the increased interest towards the topic of the examination might bias the results. The correlational desing of the present study does not allow causal inferences. The subject of the present study was the tendency to orthorexia nercosa, not orthorexia nervosa as a diagnosis, the results cannot be fully transposed into orthorexia nervosa since no orthorexia diagnosed patients are available yet.
Perspectives: A viable next step in orthorexia nervosa research could be the use of experience sampling method which could provide important information about the daily fluctuation of orthorexia nervosa and the related variables. It would be benefical to collect information about the type of the exercise as well, because some sport activities (category sports, aesthetic sport) can mean a higher vulnerability to orthorexia.

Title: Social physique anxiety and disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors in adolescents: moderating effects of sport, sport related characteristics, and gender
Authors: Lanfranchi, M.C., Maiano, C., Morin, A.J.S., & Therme, P.
Population subgroup:
Not involved in sport practice (n=431)
Involved in sport practice (n=335)
Inclusion criteria: Adolescents aged between 11 and 18 years.
Sport_name: 46 different sports categorized on (1) leanness, (2) nonleanness, (3) individual, (4) team, (5) organized or (6) not, (7) competitive or (8) not
Authors' conclusions: The results demonstrating a significant and positive relationship between social physique anxiety and DEAB (i.e., generic DEAB, vomiting-purging behaviors, eating related control). Higher levels of SPA tend to be more associated with high levels of eating related control for boys and girls, this relation is more pronounced for boys.
Limits: Cross-sectional design, precluding examination of the directionality of the associations between SPA and DEAB. This study focused on the use of DEAB as a coping strategy for physical self-presentational concerns related to thinness or leanness. The fact that this study fails to consider concerns specifically related to muscularity and their possible relation with DEAB is an important limitation. No distinction was made for sports where the main emphasis is on muscularity, weight gain, or even drastric weight control (e.g., body building, football, power lifting). Less than half of the adolescents were involved in competitive sports and most did so at a nonelite level. We cannot identify the moderating role of the type of competition on the relationship between SPA and DEAB. This study neglected to examine more pathogenic behaviors (i.e., fasting, use of laxatives and/or diuretics, enemas, appetite suppressants) that adolescents could use to their physique. We do not know whether SPA is associated with the pathogenic weight control behaviors that adolescents engage in or whether sport practice is a moderator of this relationship.
Perspectives:
Consideration of the potential impact on muscularity oriented and weight control sports in the relationships between SPA, gender and DEAB should be the object of future studies. 
Culture is known to play an important role in the definition of body shape ideals and thus may exert a significant impact on the relationships observed in the current study. 
To further extend the current results, it would be interesting for future research to focus more specifically on the role of (a) body related sport motives (i.e., weight and shape control, weight loss, improvement of ones appearance), (b) social comparison processes and/or social physique pressure, and (c) socio contextual factors (parents, peers, coaches) of sport practices in the relationships between SPA, gender, sport practice and DEAB. 
One strategy that clinicians could adopt to prevent or reduce the development of high levels of DEAB in adolescents would be to focus on the reduction of high levels of physical self-presentation concerns ; adopt healthy coping strategies for dealing with SPA levels.

Title: Does coping mediate the relationship between competitive anxiety and eating disorders in athletes ?
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., do Nascimaleto Junior, J.R.A., Freire, G.L.M., & Ferreira, M.E.C.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum training of eight hours per week; minimum participation in a competition of regional dimension in 2016; be available to answer questionnaires and participate in anthropometric evaluations. The criteria for athletes exclusion were: 1. to present physical or intellectual disability; 2. to have taken psychoactive medications in the six months prior ro the research.
Sport_name: Athletics; basketball; boxing; canoing; cycling; football; handball; jiu-jitsu; judo; olympic weightlifting; swimming; water polo; rowing; ornamental jumping; tae-kwon-do; tennis; triathlon; sailing; volleyball; and beach volleyball
Authors' conclusions: The structural equation model has pointed out a direct relationship between competitive anxiety and eating disorder. These findings indicated that stress perception during competitive events and negative thoughts about competitive performance were associated with the triggering of eating disorders in Brazilian male athletes.
Limits: Since we used self-reported instruments as assessment tools, the result may not reflect th context analyzed, because the responses were subjective. Portuguese is the langage spoken in Brazil and Portugal, but these countries have significant cultural differences and also small changes in their own writing. In this sense, the use of such a psychometric instrument in this study may have influenced the results obtained. Another limitation is that we used only the total score of the instruments, maling impossible the mediating role of ACSI-28 subscales in the association between anxiety and eating disorders. In addition, this study was restricted to the evaluation of psychological variables of athletes in just one moment, which does not characterize the real relationships of cause and effect between the variables.
Perspectives:
Future investigations should use a prospective approach with the athletes, besides crossing the previously described psychological variables with the performance levels during the season. 
We suggest further investigations with male Brazilian athletes to confirm the findings of this study. Furthermore, it is recommaleded the construction of an etiological model of eating disorder for Brazilian athletes of both sexes. The practical results of this study are in the possibility of sports professionals, more specifically, sports psychologists, to develop interventions that make it possible to decrease the level of competitive anxiety and/or enhance the development of coping strategies to reduce the triggering of eating disorders in Brazilian male athletes.

Title: Correlates of eating disorders risk among Female figure skates: a profile of adolescent competitors

Title: mental skills as protective attributes against eating disorder risk in dancers
Authors: Estanol, E.
Inclusion criteria: The majority of participants were European American collegiate ballet dancers; however, collegiate modern and professional ballet dancers were also included in the sample. In order to ascertain a sample more less representative o the US population, the companies and universities were selected based on geographic location (east coast, midwest and western states). Selection of universities was also made by locating programs that had pre-professional or elite dance programs.
Authors' conclusions: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Title: Eating disordered behaviours in Portuguese athletes: the influence of personal, sport, and psychological variables

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Members of various urban fitness centers aged between 18 and 60 years
Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. Using self report questionnaire by collecting data at the same time from the same individuals raises the bias of common method variance. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Title: The relationship between exercise addiction, eating disorders, and insecure attachment styles among recreational exercisers
Authors: Lev Arey, D., Sagi, A., & Blatt, A.

Authors' conclusions: An anxious attachment was linked to eating disorder.

Title: The relationship between perceived stress, body image and eating behaviors in athletes

Journal: Research in Sport Education and Sciences
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between the ages of 13-23 who volunteered to participate
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism in athletes is linked to higher stress, eating disturbances, and body perception issues, with women showing higher stress, emotional eating, and restrictive eating behaviors. Limits: Findings are partly inconsistent with previous studies (e.g., gender differences), and results may depend on specific sports or samples. The study also relies on self-reported measures, which may introduce bias
Perspectives: Future research should further explore emotional eating across different sports and genders, and develop targeted interventions. Integrating psychological support, education, and nutritional guidance could help improve athletes’ well-being and performance
