Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: Interpersonal difficulties as a risk factor for athletes eating psychopathology
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
Inclusion criteria: British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, judo, rugby, football, hockey
Authors' conclusions: Negative and positive aspects of the quality of the coach athlete and teammate athlete were related to athletes eating psychopathology after controlling for baseline eating psychopathology score. Conflict with the coach was found to be the only significant independent predictor of athletes eating psychopathology. The quality of the relationship with parents and attachmalet styles were not found to be related to athletes eating psychopathology 6 months later.
Limits: The present findings are essentially correlational, thus preventing definitive conclusions about causality. The present study only examined the direct role of interpersonal relationships in atletes eating psychopathology. Fairburn et al. (2003) noted that interpersonal difficulties interact with other core psychopathological processes (low self esteem, clinical perfectionism, and mood intolerance) to potentially elicit and maintain eating disorders.
Perspectives: Future studies should seek to examine how such processes as clinical perfectionism, self esteem, and mood intolerance interact with interpersonal difficulties to elicit eating psychopathology . And investigaite how these interpersonal variables interact with each other to predict athletes eating psychopathology.

Title: Bulimic symptomatology among male collegiate athletes: a test of an etiological model
Authors: Chatterton, J., Petrie, T.A., Schuler, K.L., & Ruggero, C.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor_measure: Scale for muscle building behaviors and muscularity oriented body image subscales
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Title: Understanding athletic and exercise identity in relation to disordered eating behaviors
Authors: Palermo, M., & Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate students self identifying as athletes
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, baseball, softball, football, field hockey, lacrosse, volleyball, swimming, track and field, cross country, cheerleading, dance, equestrian, gymnastics
Authors' conclusions:
Study 1 : athletic identity was not associated with global disordered eating behaviors. 
Study 2 : athletic identity appeared to be associated with less cognitive restraint and was not significantly associated with other measures of disordered eating. Only exercise identity was associated with disordered eating.
Limits: Different disordered eating measures were used across study 1 and 2. Neither study 1 nor study 2 collected data about level of sport participation. Both studies were cross-sectional. This study included a broad sample of university students and findings may not generalize to other populations.
Perspectives: Exercise identity may be an important risk factor to consider in future research related to disordered eating and exercise behaviors in college students.

Title: Athletic identity and disordered eating in obligatory and non-obligatory runners
Authors: Gapin, J.I., & Petruzzello, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Participants were recruited from running clubs, road races, and kinesiology classes at a large Midwestern university. The only inclusion criterion was that participant be over the age of 18.
Authors' conclusions: There is relationships among obligatory exercise and DE. Athletic identity had a significant positive correlation with disordered eating attitudes and behaviours. Athletic identity correlated with both drive for thinness and perfectionism. The negative affectivity correlated with all the disordered eating measures. The hypothesis that athletic identity would mediate the effect of obligatory running on disordered eating was not supported.
Limits: All measures were self-report in nature. Not all the subscales of the Eating Disorder Inventory have been validated in athletic samples and there is some concern that the Eating disorder Inventory may not be accurate in identiying those athletes at risk for an eating disorder.
Perspectives: Obligatory and non obligatory runners were dichotomized. It is likely, however, that this form of exercise occurs on a continuum and it would be valuable to assess this. Longitudinal research of those at risk form becoming obligatory runners could determine whether th shift towards obligatory running patterns occurs immediately after adopting an exercise regimen or whether the change occurs over time as they progress in training frequency, duration, and intensity. Further research using the Athletic Identity Measurement Scale in a variety of athletic population is necessary. Future studies should examine other mediating variables related to identity (motivation to exercise are variables associated with DE and obligatory exercise). When examining obligatory runners it may be helpful to look at Deci and Ryan's (1985, 2000) self-determination theory as an explanation for obligatory exercisers motivations to engage in exercise. It would be helpful to use the regulation in exercise questionnaire in conjunction with the obligatory exercise questionnaire and eating disorder measures to evaluate in more detail why certain individuals are more susceptible to unhealthy exercise attitudes and behaviours than others.

Title: Teammate influences, psychological well-being, and athletes eating and exercise psychopathology: a moderated mediation analysis
Authors: Scott, C.L., Plateau, C.R., & Haycraft, E.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competed with a university sports team or with their club or school
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Mean_Years of experience: Member of their current team M=1.99, SD=2.61
Related_Factor_measure: Bulimic Modelling Scale adapted for athletes (BMS-A)
Degree of relationship:
Bulimia modelling-anxiety 𝛃=1.40, p<.01
Anxiety-drive for thinness 𝛃=.15, p<.05
Bulimia modelling-drive for thinness total effect 𝛃=1.15, p<.01
Bulimia modelling-drive for thinness direct effect 𝛃=.94, p<.05
Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. Gender was not a significant moderator, meaning that the role of psychological wellbeing in the relationships between teammate influences and eating.
Limits: Although age and BMI were controlled for, it is acknowledged that there are a number of additional co-variates (e.g., perfectionism, athletic identity) that could have contributed to the findings of this study. The self report nature of the data collected and the context it was collected in (i.e., before/after a training session and in the company of teammates/coach) may potentially misrepresent athletes true behaviours. Items comprising the EDI-drive for thinness and body dissatsifaction subscales may not be an accurate reflection of male athletes experiences with disordered eating.
Perspectives: Identifying key risk factors and relevant moderators and mediators for eating psychopathology is important for effectively identifying those athletes at increased risk of eating and exercise psychopathology, and for developing appropriately tailored intervention and prevention strategies. Future research into the role of teammates would benefit from experimentally manipulating mechanisms of teammate influence on athletes actual food intake and should consider employing methodologies that are specifically tailored to male athletes. Employing modeeling analytic techniques to further our understanding of the complex, multi-factorial influences on athlete eating and exercise behaviours.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Body Talk, Athletic Identity, and Eating Disorder Symptoms in male
Authors: Ahlich, E., Choquette, E.M., Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18-35 years; recruited using convenience sampling from a large southeastern university's research; receiving research credit upon completion of the study; informed consent
Related_Factor_measure: Single item asking participants if they considered themselves to be an athlete
Authors' conclusions: The current findings support body talk and fat talk as a potential risk factor for eating disorders among male. Muscle-focused body talk may not a risk factor for diagnostic eating disorder symptoms. Muscle talk among male is related less to muscle dissatisfaction and more to male socioalization processes. Athletic identity did non emerge as a significant moderator of the association between body talk and eating disorder symptoms.
Limits: The study was limited to a single university campus in the southeastern United States, limiting generalizability of the findings. Few participants endorsed aesthetic or lean sports, potentially attenuating results.
Perspectives:
Future work may benefit from using a more objective of body composition. 
Future work should explore such associations among male in a clinical sample, examining whether fat or muscle talk is associated with eating disorder and/or muscle dysmorphia symptom severity. 
Fat talk may be an important prevention target amon male, regardless of athletic identity.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: An identity mis-match ? The impact of self-reported competition level on the association between athletic identity and disordered eating behaviors
Authors: Palermo, M., & Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate students; participate in DI, club or intramural sports; aged between 18 and 35 years
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, baseball/softball, football, field hockey, lacrosse, volleyball
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Male M=3.10h/week, SD=1.08
Female M=3.06h/week, SD=.86
Authors' conclusions: High athletic identity paired with low level of sport competition was associated with disordered eating. The combination of high athletic identity and high perceived level of competition was not associated with disordered eating.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. Physical activity and sport competition level were self reported. Mobile technology (e.g., fitbit) would provide more precise physical activity data, as well as other related variables, such as heartrate, to investigate if intensity of exercise activity in-and out-of sport has associations with athletic identity and disordered eating behaviors. This study used the AIMS-Plus, which as limited psychometric validity. This study used a collegiate sample and findings may not generalize to other populations.
Perspectives: Longitudinal investigations of athletic identity, sport competition level and disordered eating among broad populations of athletes (e.g., currently competitive, previously competitive, and recreational) at various stages of sport participation (high shcool, collegiate) are needed.

Perspectives: Exercise identity may be an important risk factor to consider in future research related to disordered eating and exercise behaviors in college students.

Title: The Mediating Role of Self-Criticism in the Relationship Between Coaches’ Leadership Styles and Disordered Eating in Athletes
Authors: Coelho, C., Oliveira, D., Branco, C., Rui Gomes, A., Conceiçao, E., Machado, P.P.P., Gonçalves, S.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competing at the senior level in Portugal
Related_Factor_measure: Multidimensional Scale of Leadership in Sport (MSLS)
Measure Mediator: Self-Criticism Subscales of the Forms of Self-Criticizing and Reassuring Scale (FSCRS), Portuguese version
Degree of relationship: Total effect coach style leadership negative feedback-disordered eating 𝛃=.21, p=.017 Direct effet coach leadership style-disordered eating 𝛃=.11, p=.152 Indirect effect coach leadership style-inadequate self-disordered eating 𝛃=.10, p=.039
Authors' conclusions: This study shows that negative coaching styles are associated with disordered eating through increased self-criticism, while positive leadership styles help reduce self-criticism. It highlights self-criticism as a key psychological mechanism linking coaching behaviors to eating pathology.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, small sample size, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference and generalizability. Lack of control for key variables (e.g., age, sport type) may also influence results.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and multi-informant designs to clarify causal pathways. Interventions targeting coaching styles, self-compassion, and support services are promising strategies to prevent disordered eating in athletes.

Sport_name: Long distance running (1500m, 3000m, 5000m, 10000m, half marathon, marathon, cross-country, ultramarathon, fell running and other)
Sporting population: National level or above (n=33), county level (n=51), club level (n=292), recreational (n=125)
Type of analysis: Partial correlation with BMI included as covariate
Authors' conclusions: There is no association between ED psychopathology and athletic identity.
Limits: Cross sectional nature.
Perspectives: It would be interesting to examine whether athletic identity and compulsive exercise could increase vulnerability for Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S).

Title: Prevalence and correlates of disordered eating in Female figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Gould, D., Reel, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged 12 to 25. Former skaters, basic skills skaters, and those in adult skating programs (e.g., age-based competitions following adult test equivalencies) were excluded
Sport_name: Figure skating (singles, multiple, synchronized, ice dancing, pairs)
Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. Body dissatisfaction explained an additional 5.7% of the variance in disordered eating. Sport related body dissatisfaction also emerged as a significant predictor. Positive perfectionism made a significant contribution, but negative perfectionism did not. Self esteem may not be strongly related to disordered eating. Athletic identity did not emerge as a significant variable in the final regression model, although the bivariate correlation indicated a significant positive relationship with disordered eating.
Limits: Societal weight pressures were not exmained. Self report nature of the surveys and the willingness of athletes to honestly and accurately respond to survey items. The results are also based on a conveniance sample of skaters limited to clubs in the Midwest and Northeast. Cross sectional design, causal relationships and change over time could not be determined.
Perspectives:
Sport psychology practiitioners should aid this effort by teaching skaters to appreciate body strengths and utilize psychological skills that may buffer the impact of negative weight pressures (e.g., utilizing positive self talk and realistic goal-setting). 
A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.

Title: Frequency and psychosocial correlates of eating disorder symptomatology in male figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Petrie, T.A., Reel, J.J., & Gould, D.
Inclusion criteria: Male figure skaters
Sport_name: Figure skating (singles skaters, ice dancers, synchronized, multiple disciplines)
Authors' conclusions: Negative perfectionism, self esteem, and athletic identity were unrelated to ED symptomatology.
Limits: Smaller sample. Weight pressures may be experienced differently according to discipline specific performance demands. Cross sectional design.
Perspectives:
Future research should incorporate longitudinal designs to identify true risk factors of ED symptomatology and use qualitative interviews to further examine the lived experience of sport-related weight pressures. 
Practitioners may collaborate with other professionals, such as sports dieteticians, to educate skating communities on weight-performance myths and improve communication between skaters, parents, and coaches about the body. Practitioners may also assist athletes in coping with weight pressures by focusing on body appreciation and function while reinforcing that healthy training approaches can have positive effects on eating, exercise, and body image.

Title: Disordered eating, eating attitudes and reasons for exercise among male high school cross country runners
Authors: Wadas, G.
Inclusion criteria: The runners were selected from 12 of the thirty two public high schools in the local school district sponsoring sports teams located in the USA. Participants were current members of a high shcool cross country teams, were in grades 9-12 and between the ages of 14-18.
Sporting population: Some playing time (24.2%), starter on team (29%), conference (4.8%), regional (35.5%), national (4.8%), other (1.6%)
Authors' conclusions: Factors that have a significant relationship with disordered eating are performance perfectionism and weight management. A desire to control weight is associated with disordered eating behaviors in male high school cross country runners as determined from the modest correlation coefficient for the weight management subscale and the EAT-26. There was no significant correlation for the physical appearance subscale of the EMI-2 and the EAT-26. No significant relationships were found between disordered eating behaviors and social pressure on body shape, social pressure on eating and athlete identity.
Limits: The results are generalizable only to school districts of similar size and demographic makeup. The questionnaire were completed on one occasion by runners during the sumer prior to the start of the season. The study was limited by a low number of participants relative to the number of runners on the teams and number of high schools in the school district.
Perspectives: The present study did not investigate the reasons for dissatisfaction with current weight status, future studies may seek more information relative to the reasons. For example, do male cross country runners feels a need to be more muscular ? Do the bodies of male cross country runners not fit the ideal ?

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Related_Factor: Athletes perceptions of power balances with their coach/training staff
Related_Factor_measure: Modified version of the Participative decision-making subscale of the Empowering Leadership Questionnaire (ELQ-PD)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Athletes perceptions of power balances with their coach/training staff
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Athletes perceptions of power balances with their coach/training staff
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Specific predictors of disordered eating among elite and non-elite gymnasts and ballet dancers
Authors: Francisco, R., Narciso, I., & Alarcao, M.
Inclusion criteria: Young ballet dancers and gymnasts of both sexes; living in different parts of Portugal including the Lisbon metropolitan area, the north, the center, the south of the country and the Madeira Islands
Mean_BMI:
Ballet elite male M=18.22, SD=1.68
Ballet elite Female M=18.12, SD=1.85
Ballet non elite Female M=19.04, SD=2.26
Gymnasts elite male M=21.83, SD=2.26
Gymnasts elite Female M=20.16, SD=1.99
Gymnasts non elite male M=21.43, SD=3.29
Gymnasts non elite Female M=19.94, SD=2.42
Sport_name: Ballet; acrobatics gymnastics; trampoline gymnastics; rhythmic gymnastics; artistic gymnastics
Sporting population:
Elite dancers (N=66)
Recreational dancers (N=47)
International competition gymnasts (N=69)
Non elite gymnasts (N=67)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Social pressure, social support, self esteem, body dissatisfaction was related to DE. Social support was not strongly related to DE.. Activity specific body image dissatisfaction is a better predictor of DE than general body image dissatisfaction. When the pressure to be thin was introduced into the model, the competitive level was no longer significant in predicting aesthetic performers DE. Our final model explained 61% of the variance in aesthetic performers disordered eating and also confirmed the role of low self esteem and specific body image dissatisfaction as partial mediators from pressure to be thin to DE.
Limits: Small size of the groups of male aesthetic performers, and the absence of a group of non elite male ballet dancers. The cross sectional design does not allow for full comprehension of the relationship between participation in these activities and the development of disordered eating. The use of self-report questionnaires and the fact that we have not taken into account the percentage of respondents and non respondents.
Perspectives: It is important to distinguish between pressure on Female and male aesthetic performers. Such preventative measures are essential in professional dancer schools and especially gymnastics clubs. These actions should focus on promoting young aesthetic performer's self-esteem and satisfaction with their activity specific body image, which is essential to reducing the impact of pressure to be thin on their eating and weight control behaviors. Coaches and teachers sould understand the impact of their behaviors and comments that lead aesthetic performers to adopt unhealthy practices and should try to adjust their demands to healthier ideal body requirements for the practice of classical dance or gymnastics.

Title: Parental influences on elite aesthetic athletes body image dissatisfaction and disordered eating
Authors: Francisco, R., Narciso, I., & Alarcao, M.
Journal: Journal of Child and Family Studies
Inclusion criteria: Adolescents of both sexes; elite aesthetic athletes gymnasts; participating in international competitions and profesional dance students
Mean_Age:
Girls athletes M=15.05, SD=2.40
Girls controls M=14.51, SD=1.81
Boys athletes M=16.08, SD=3.33

Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Adolescents sex and BMI were significant predictors of disordered eating for both athletes. Parental influences emerged as the only family variable that predicted athletes disordered eating.
Limits: The relatively small sample size of adolescents athletes presents challenges, especially for carrying out multiple regressions. These regression are potentially unstable. The cross-sectional design does not allow for causal inferences to be made with regard to the influence of family variables in the development of adolescents body image dissatisfaction and disordered eating.
Perspectives: Longitudinal studies are needed. Test these models in different samples of male and Female athletes.

Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes
Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.
Inclusion criteria: NCAA Divisions I Female collegiate athletes drawn from three universities located in the Midwest, Soutwest, and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: gymnastics; rowing; softball; synchronized swimming; tennis; alpine skiing; basketball; cross country; cheerleading; diving; golf; field hockey; lacrosse; soccer; swimming; track and field; volleyball
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. The cross sectional design of the study does not allow for the determination of the temporal nature of the relationships between psychosocial variables and bulimic symptoms.
Perspectives:
Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.

Title: Eating disorders in Taekwondo athletes: the contribution of coach behavior, body satisfaction, and goal orientation
Authors: Baric, R., Erdeljac, T.
Inclusion criteria: Active practice of Taekwondo for at least 6 months and being a competitor in one of three competities categories: cadets, junior athletes or senior athletes
Sporting population:
17.3% top elite athletes, members of national selection and elite athletes
25 elite male
33 elite female
107 non-elite male
170 non-elite female
DEAB_measure: Croatian version of the Eating Attitudes Test (EAT_26)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Goal orientation, body dissatisfaction, and negative behavior and pressure from coaches significantly contribute to the risk of ED development in female and male cadet, junior and non-elite athletes, while body dissatisfaction seems to be the strongest predictor, especially in female athletes.
Limits: The sample size, although it is realistic in relation to the number of active taekwondo competitors in Croatia. Self reported questionnaires.
Perspectives: Including other measures, more adjusted to male ED symptoms. As the results showed the significance of the behavior of coaches in relation to athletes ED symptoms, it would be very interesting to investigate the transgenerational transfer of distorted values, beliefs and behaviors related to ED from coaches to athletes, i.e., to investigate coaches history of ED symptoms and their current behavior.

Title: Investigation of the relationship between muscle dysmorphia disorder, orthorexia nervosa, and motivation in male individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports
Authors: Abraş, H., Erdag, D., Buran, A.
Journal: Cyprus Turkish Journal of Psychiatry & Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Volunteer male participants aged between 18 and 58 engaged in bodybuilding; registered in gyms in TRNC.
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: As muscle dysmorphia increases, orthorexia nervosa increases in individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports in the TRNC.
Limits: Since this study was conducted only on male bodybuilders, the findings cannot be generalized to Female bodybuilders.
Perspectives:
It is essential to provide education on muscle dysmorphia, orthorexia nervosa, and the use of ergogenic nutritional supplements in Physical Education and Sports Schools, as well as in coach training programs. Additionally, training on athlete nutrition and sports psychology in these institutions would equip them with knowledge about both athlete motivations and the mental health disorders frequently seen in athletes. Given the rise of these mental health issues in gyms, sports psychologists should be present in these environments, and mental health assessments should be conducted alongside medical evaluations for new memberships.
Conducting similar studies across different sports and with female participants could contribute valuable new insights to the literature.

Title: Body Talk, Athletic Identity, and Eating Disorder Symptoms in male
Authors: Ahlich, E., Choquette, E.M., Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18-49 years; recruited using convenience sampling from a large southeastern university's research; receiving research credit upon completion of the study; informed consent
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The current findings support body talk and fat talk as a potential risk factor for eating disorders among male. Muscle-focused body talk may not a risk factor for diagnostic eating disorder symptoms. Muscle talk among male is related less to muscle dissatisfaction and more to male socioalization processes. Athletic identity did non emerge as a significant moderator of the association between body talk and eating disorder symptoms.
Limits: The study was limited to a single university campus in the southeastern United States, limiting generalizability of the findings. Few participants endorsed aesthetic or lean sports, potentially attenuating results.
Perspectives:
Future work may benefit from using a more objective of body composition. 
Future work should explore such associations among male in a clinical sample, examining whether fat or muscle talk is associated with eating disorder and/or muscle dysmorphia symptom severity. 
Fat talk may be an important prevention target amon male, regardless of athletic identity.

Title: Eating attitudes and body image concerns among Female athletes from aesthetic sports
Authors: Aleksić Veljković, A., Durović, D., Biro, F., Stojanović, K., Ilić, P.

Mean_Age:

Mage non-aesthetic=20, SD=3 years old
Sport_name: Artistic and rythmic gymnastics, dance, synchronized swimming, volleyball, soccer, basketball

Mean_Years of experience:
Maesthetic=7.40, SD=7.41 years

Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The study confirm the relationship between body image dissatisfaction and pathological eating attitudes among Female aesthetic sport athletes.
Limits: Limitation include a small sample size from only one country where participants reported their height and weight and were at different levels of competition, from threee different aesthetic sports.
Perspectives: The regulation of body mass is a critical issue for the athletes and attention must be paid to their strategies for weight control.

Title: The tripartite influence model of body image and disordered eating among young adult athletes
Authors: Tonsberg, E.N., Dixit, U., Henderson, R., Larsen, J., Lusich, R., Hauff, C., Ahlich, E.
Inclusion criteria: Being 18-26 years old, fluency in English and self-reporting yes to the item do you identify as an athlete ?
Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. It highlights the continued importance of both general and sport-specific influences on athletes’ eating behaviors
Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Title: Influence of perfectionism on variables associated to eating disorders in dance students
Authors: Arcelus, J., Garcia-Dantas, A., Sanchez-Martin, M., Del Rio, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 12-20; participation was voluntary; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Sport_name: Dance (e.g., ballet, contemporary, flamenco, spanish folk)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Title: Emotional Regulation and Risk of Eating Disorders in Adolescent Athletes
Authors: Espinoza-Barron, S.P., Cantu-Berrueto, A., Castejon, M.A., Berengui, R.
Journal: European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education
Inclusion criteria: Active membership in a sports team, training at least three times per week, age between 10 and 25 years, encompassing early, middle, and late adolescence
Sport_name: Cheerleading, American football, basketball, dance, gymnastics, figure skating
Mean_Years of experience: 50.5% had more than 7 years 10.4% had between 4 and 6 years 16.8% had between 1 and 3 years 22.2% had less than 1 year
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Emotion regulation plays a significant role in eating disorder risk among young athletes, with emotional suppression acting as a risk factor and cognitive reappraisal as a protective factor. Adolescence appears to be a critical period for these associations.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, reliance on self-reported data, and limited sample representativeness restrict causal interpretation and generalizability.
Perspectives: Longitudinal studies with more diverse samples and additional psychological and contextual variables are needed to better understand the mechanisms underlying eating disorder risk in athletes.

Title: Individual differences in male body image: an examination of self-objectivation in recreational body builders
Authors: Hallsworth, L., Wade, T., Tiggemann, M.
Inclusion criteria: Males. The first group consisted of bodybuilders; minimum level of training twice a week for at least a year. The second group consisted of competitive weightlifters recruited from the state weightlifting associations in four states of Australia.
Mean_Age:
Bodybuilders M=28.89, SD=6.19
Weightlifters M=27.60, SD=8.70
Non-athletic control M=26.43, SD=8.15
Mean_BMI:
Weightlifters M=28.60, SD=6.90
Bodybuilders M=26.04, SD=3.08
Controls M=24.18, SD=2.80
Sport_name: Bodybuilding, Weightlifting, Soccer, football, running, martial arts, swimming
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.40 hours per week
Weightlifters M=12.12 hours per week 
Controls M=3.8 hours per week
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.14 years
Weightlifters M=9.06 years
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Bodybuilding may represent a practice that encourages male to become more self-conscious of their bodies, putting them at greater risk of experiencing greater levels of monitoring of body appearance and anxiety about physical appearance. This body self consciousness is associated with a greater risk of body dissatisfaction and drive for muscularity. Weightlifting does not appear to represent an objectifying climate.
Limits: The cross sectional nature makes it possible only to speculate on the directions of causality. Unequal sample sizes of groups in our analyses, particularly with respect to fewer competitive weightlifters. Unknown selection bias that may be operating in the bodybuilder and weightlifter groups, and any subsequent influence on the interpretation of our results. The weighlifting and bodybuilder groups differed not only in the nature of their sport, but also in competitive nature of this sport, which may introduce confound for differences found between the groups.
Perspectives: Health pursuits for male should emphasize achievement and function rather than appearance if they are to avoid deleterious consesquences.

Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Sport_name: Cross country/track and field, swimming and diving, volleyball, wrestling, soccer, golf, football, lacrosse, baseball, basketball, tennis
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Title: Childhood victimisation as a predictor of muscle dysmorphia in adult male bodybuilders
Authors: Boyda, D., & Shevlin, M.

Degree of relationship:
Path a1 (childhood victimization-anxiety) 𝛃=3.75, p<.001
path b1 (anxiety-muscle dismorphia) 𝛃=5.84, p<.01
Path a2 (childhood victimization-depression) 𝛃=4.83, p<.001

Title: A socio-sports model of disordered eating among Brazilian male athletes
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., Caputo Ferreira, M.E., Fernandes de Oliveira, S.M., Serpeloni Cyrino, E., & Sousa Almeida, S.
Inclusion criteria: Systematiccaly trained in a sport modality based on a training regimen of at least six hours of training per week (e.g., minimum of three days per week of two-hour sessions or six days per week of one hour sessions); participation in at least one regional competition in 2014 and; availability to respond to questionnaires and to participate in anthropometric evaluations.
Sport_name: Track and field; basketball; boxing; canoeing; cycling; equestrian; jiu-jitsu; judo; swimming; water polo; rowing; diving; surfing; tae-kwon-do; tennis; triathlon; sailing; volleyball
Sporting population:
30% international level
42% national level
28% regional level
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Only the sociocultural factors and body fat dissatisfaction adhered to etiological model of DE in Brazilian male athletes. Sociocultural factors (parents, friends and the media) exhibit a direct relationship to DE. The results of the structural equation model indicate that body fat dissatisfaction mediates the relationship between sociocultural factors and DE.
Limits: Because self-reporting instruments were used as evaluative tools, the results may not reflect the reality because the responses given were subjective. Perspectives: Sport professionals may use the present study findings to intervene in factors that promote disturbed eating in athletes. The construction of a socio-sports model for Female is recommaleded.

Title: Exercise addiction and disordered eating in young Lebanese regular sport practitioners: the indirect role of body appreciation and body dysmorphic concerns
Authors: Abi Karam, M., El Khoury, R., Hokayem, C., Akiki, N., Obeid, S., Fekih-Romdhane, F., Hallit, S., Hokayem, M.
Inclusion criteria: Lebanese older than 18, actively engaged in sports, who participate in structured sports training sessions at least three times per week from a range of sports, including endurance, strength-based and team sports
Sport_name: Range of sports, including endurance, strength-based and team sports
DEAB_measure: The Arabic validated version of the Eating Attitudes Test (EAT-7)
Related_Factor_measure: The Dysmorphic Concern Questionnaire (DCQ) validated in Arabic
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This study highlights a positive association between exercise addiction and disordered eating, with body dysmorphic concerns and body appreciation acting as key mediating factors. Title: Maladaptive perfectionism as mediator among psychological control, eating disorders, and exercise dependence symptoms in habitual exerciser
Authors: Costa, S., Hausenblas, H.A., Oliva, P., Cuzzocrea, F., & Larcan, R.
Inclusion criteria: Inclusion criteria were that exerciser had trained for at least 6 consecutive months, lived at home with both parents, and were at least 18 years of age.
DEAB_measure:
Eating Attitude Test (EAT-26)
Exercise Dependence Scale-Revised (EDS-R)
Degree of relationship:
Psychological control-maladaptive perfectionism 𝛃=.48, p<.01
Psychological control-eating disorders 𝛃=.11, p<.01
Psychological control-exercise dependence 𝛃=.11, p<.01
Maladaptive perfectionism-eating disorder 𝛃=.28, p<.01
Maladaptive perfectionism-exercise dependence 𝛃=.28, p<.01
Psychological control-maladaptive perfectionism-eating disorder 𝛃=.13, p=N.S.
Psychological control-maladaptive perfectionism-exercise dependence 𝛃=.13, p=N.S.
Authors' conclusions: There is a significant relationship between parental psychological control and both exercise dependence and eating disorder symptoms. Psychological control, both maternal and parternal, predicted maladaptive perfectionism, while maladaptive perfectionism, predicted ED symptoms and exercise dependence symptoms. Results confirmed the mediating role of maladaptive perfectionism as a full mediator for ED and exercise dependence symptoms for both male and Female habitual exercisers in the maternal data. In the paternal data, maladaptive perfectionism mediated the relationships between paternal psychological control and eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms as full mediator for the Female participants and as partial mediator for the male participants.
Limits: First, the data were collected at one time point and not across multiple time points as it should be done for a true mediational analysis. Because of the cross-sectional and self-report design of our study, we cannot etablish either the direction or causality of the effects. As weel, the self-report data may have intrinsic limitations such as social desirability, so the use of objective and multi-informant measures and experimental designs are encourages. Although, our sample consisted of habitual exercisers, this sample was deemed justified, as eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms are prevalent in this population and because psychological control is a risk factor for eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms in this population.
Perspectives: The deleterious effects of parental psychological control, both on eating disorder and on exercise dependence symptoms, require the implementation of targeted interventions to educate parents in using fewer instrusions and parental autonomy support, as opposed to psychological control. It is important to educate parents about psychological control being a universally negative parenting strategy and to help parents identify and reduce the use of such dysfunctional practices. Parent training could be used to help parents to get to practice autonomy supportive skills by taking part in various exercices from common situations in familial daily living. Results of the study suggest that the therapist and client could work together to identify and correct the client's maladaptive perfectionism thought processes that result in maladaptive eating or exercise behavior.

Authors: Espinoza-Barron, S.P., Cantu-Berrueto, A., Castejon, M.A., Berengui, R.
Journal: European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education
Inclusion criteria: Active membership in a sports team, training at least three times per week, age between 10 and 25 years, encompassing early, middle, and late adolescence
Sport_name: Cheerleading, American football, basketball, dance, gymnastics, figure skating
Mean_Years of experience: 50.5% had more than 7 years 10.4% had between 4 and 6 years 16.8% had between 1 and 3 years 22.2% had less than 1 year
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Emotion regulation plays a significant role in eating disorder risk among young athletes, with emotional suppression acting as a risk factor and cognitive reappraisal as a protective factor. Adolescence appears to be a critical period for these associations.

Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: There is a positive association of body dissatisfaction with risk behaviour for eating disorders and addiction to exercise.
Limits:
Small number of participants and who were practitioners of only two modalities, which males impossible to generalize th results to practitioners of other exercises. 
The cross sectional design which does not allow to make inferences of causality between the variables.
Perspectives:
Future researches should extend the study with practitioners from other regions of Brazilian population and exercises.

Title: Disordered eating behaviors among crossfit athletes
Authors: Franco da Cunha, M.C., Costa Pereira Junqueira, A., Berbert de Carvalho, P.H., & Laus, M.F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 40 years, and be enrolled in the crossfit modality in a specialized gym, with a minimum frequency of practice of 6 months. Individuals who practiced other sports that favor hypertrophy in addition to crossfit and belonging to special groups, such as pregnant or nursing Female, indidviuals with any medical condition tha could have direct or indirect influence on physical appearance, elite athletes, were excluded.
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.
Limits: First, the sample may not be representative of the Brazilian population, as it was carried out in a single city in a single state. Second, there is a need to study other constructs, such as body dissatisfaction, which can predict other aspects of disordered eating in this population. Third, reported weight en height may be a bias, depiste being a common finding in body image  and eating behavior studies? Finally, even though the EAT-26 is frequently used in Brazil, the measure is not validated for adults in the country. Moreover, the EAT-26 appears to be a more focused instrument for investigating the symptoms of disordered eating often seen in Female, while recent studies have shown that disordered eating among male has its own characteristics.
Perspectives: Performance is directly related to diet, some disordered nutritional strategies can impair this performance and increase the risk of eating disorders in athletes.

Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor_measure: Scale for muscle building behaviors and muscularity oriented body image subscales
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Weightlifters M=27.60, SD=8.70
Non-athletic control M=26.43, SD=8.15
Mean_BMI:
Weightlifters M=28.60, SD=6.90
Bodybuilders M=26.04, SD=3.08
Controls M=24.18, SD=2.80
Sport_name: Bodybuilding, Weightlifting, Soccer, football, running, martial arts, swimming
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.40 hours per week
Weightlifters M=12.12 hours per week 
Controls M=3.8 hours per week
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.14 years
Weightlifters M=9.06 years
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Bodybuilding may represent a practice that encourages male to become more self-conscious of their bodies, putting them at greater risk of experiencing greater levels of monitoring of body appearance and anxiety about physical appearance. This body self consciousness is associated with a greater risk of body dissatisfaction and drive for muscularity. Weightlifting does not appear to represent an objectifying climate.
Limits: The cross sectional nature makes it possible only to speculate on the directions of causality. Unequal sample sizes of groups in our analyses, particularly with respect to fewer competitive weightlifters. Unknown selection bias that may be operating in the bodybuilder and weightlifter groups, and any subsequent influence on the interpretation of our results. The weighlifting and bodybuilder groups differed not only in the nature of their sport, but also in competitive nature of this sport, which may introduce confound for differences found between the groups.
Perspectives: Health pursuits for male should emphasize achievement and function rather than appearance if they are to avoid deleterious consesquences.

Title: Eating disorder risk in adolescent and adult female athletes: the role of body satisfaction, sport type, BMI, level of competition, and training background
Authors: Borowiec, J., Banio-Krajnik, A., Malchrowicz-Mosko, E., & Kantanista, A.
Journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competing at the national and international levels.
Sport_name: Lean aesthetic sports (e.g., artistic swimming, gymnastics, dance), lean non-aesthetic sports (e.g., athletics, swimming, karate, taekwondo), ball sports (e.g., soccer, volleyball, basketball, rugby, field hockey and floorball)
Related_Factor_measure: Feelings and Attitudes toward Body Scale incorporated in the Body Investment Scale
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: There are different relationships between eating disorder risk and individual (body satisfaction and body mass index) and sport environment factors (sport type, level of competition, and training background) among adolescent and adult athletes.
Limits: Body satisfaction and eating disorder risk were assessed using a self-assessment method, therefore the participants subjective interpretation of the questions may have influenced the results. The EAT-26 is a screening tool biased toward the thin body ideal and may not detect the risk of some types of ED.
Perspectives: Coaches and specialists should foster a positive body image among athletes and pay special attention to the eating behaviors of adolescent athletes, particularlry those who practice lean non-aesthetic sports.

Title: Eating disordered behaviours in Portuguese athletes: the influence of personal, sport, and psychological variables
Authors: Gomes, A.R., Martins, C., & Silva, L.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between 14 and 30 year of age
Sport_name: Athletics; karate; swimming; taekwondo; basketball; handball; volleyball
Sporting population:
Top division (38.8%)
Regional or national levels
Related_Factor: Satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance
Authors' conclusions: The EDE-Q global score was positively associated with weight-related coach pressure, anxiety, taske orientation, impression motivation and threat perception, and negatively associated with less satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance. Eating behaviour was predicted by lower satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance, and higher anxiety and impression motivation.
Limits: Data were based on athletes self-report, which could have resulted in under-reporting of eating disordered behaviours. A better discrimination between sports according to their requirements needs to be introduced in order to better differentiate the demands and soecific characteristics of each sport. It is vital to further explore the impact of psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours.
Perspectives: It is important to assess athletes reactions in competition, the way they perceive themselves, and the way they want others to perceive them. If there is a better comprehension of these factors, then prevention of eating problems and promotion of better experiences in sport becomes easier to achieve.

Title: Eating pathology in Female gymnasts: potential risk and protective factors
Authors: Harriger, J.A., Witherington, D.C., & Bryan, A.D.
Inclusion criteria: Females athletes involved in competitive gymnastics at a non-collegiate or non-elite level; between the age of 10-15 years
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Gymnasts who report spending more time training seem to be protected from pathological eating disturbances and that high levels of self esteem may serve as a more direct protective mechanism.
Limits: The sample size was relatively small. It is not feasible to determine why 14% elected not to participate, and it is possible that they may have differed from those who participated in the research. The self-report nature nature of the study may have been problematic in that it was difficult to assess for accuracy and honesty in these measures. The cross sectional design does not allow for an actual test of the dynamic process between the study variables across time and is therefore limited in what it can conclude about actual risk and protective factors. While the onset of puberty is typically associated with a significant weight gain for Females, it may be that, due to training regimens, gymnasts in the current study had not gained a considerable amount of weight, even though they reported experiencing accompanying development changes such as breast developmale t and growth of body hair.
Perspectives: Future studies would benefit from the addition of a procedure that analyzes body fat or using a longitudinal design to assess for weight gain during puberty. Continued exploration of this population is vital in order ton increase understanding of these and additional factors that may predispose or protect gymnasts from body dissatisfaction and pathological eating disturbances.

Title: Running to win or to be thin ? An evaluation of body dissatisfaction and eating disorder symptoms among adult runners
Authors: Anderson, L.M., Reilly, E.E., Gorrell, S., Anderson, D.A.
Population subgroup:
Male Middle-Distance(MDD) n=60
Male Long-Distance (MLD) n=156
Female Middle-Distance (WMD) n=61
Female Long-Distance (WLD) n=123
Inclusion criteria: Completing one of four running events-5 kilometer (k), 10k, half-marathon, and full marathon races in the northeast United States; 18-71 years old.
Mean_Age:
Mage M=41.6, SD=12.1 years old
MageW=38.6, SD=10.9 years old
Mean_BMI:
MMMD=24.2, SD=4.4 kg/m²
MWMD=24.2, SD=5.2kg/m² 
MMLD=24.4, SD=2.9kg/m² 
MWLD=23.1, SD=3.0kg/m²
Sport_name: Running middle distance and long distance (e.g., 5 kilometer, 10k, half marathon, full marathon)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Appearance and performance related BD significantly relate to ED symptoms among Female but not male.
Limits: Generalization of findings to other populations may be limited (sample comprised predominantly healthy adult runners with low ED symptomatology). BD reported by runners may not generalize to other types of athletes, due to varying anthropometric ideals and demographic profiles.
Perspectives: Additional data is needed to validate the context-specific body dissatisfaction (BD) constructs. Eating disorder (ED) assessment and prevention efforts for athletes should address performance-related BD in addition to the more commonly assessed appearance-related BD. Future research should aim to identify the nuances of BD, explore how BD constructs vary across different athletic contexts, and define individual differences that may help improve the assessment of ED risk among athletes.

Title: Equation for eating disorder risk behaviors in Female athletes
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., Caputo Ferreira, M.E., de Oliveira, S.M.F., Fiorese, L., & Sousa Almeida, S.
Journal: Sociedade Brasileira de Medicina do Exercicio e do Esporte
Inclusion criteria: (a) present the informed consent form signed by the guardian (if she was under 18) and sign the assent form; (b) systematically train her respective modality with a minimum training regime of six hours per week (minimum frequency of three days per week and duration of two hours/training, or frequency of six days per week and duration of one hour/training; (c) have minimal participation in a regional competition in 2014; (d) be available to answer questionnaires and participate in anthropometric assessments. In addition, the following exclusion criteria were adopted (a) present a physical or intellectual disability and (b) use psychoactive medications in the last six months.
Sport_name: Athletics; Basketball; Boxing; Cycling; Football; Artistic gymnastics; Rythmic gymnastics; Handball; Jiu-Jitsu; Judo; Synchronized Swimming; Swimming; Figure skating; Water pole; Rowing; Diving; Surf; Tae-kwon-do; Tennis; Triathlon; Sailing; Volleyball and Beach volley
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The predictive equation is reliable to assess risk for ED in Brazilian Female athletes.
Limits: The use of questionnaires is pointed out, as researchers emphasize that athletes may omit some behaviors/feelings. In addition, another limitation was the use of a doubly indirect method to assess %F. According to some authors, using skinfolds can be limited to assess body composition.
Perspectives: The need to conduct new scientific investigations in order to assess the external validity of the created predictive equation is emphasized. In addition, it is necessary to create a risk predictive equation for eating disorders also regarding Brazilian male athletes

Title: The Body shape of pubertal rhythmic gymnasts: the association with BMI, eating disorder risks, and perfectionism
Authors: Marković, A., Veljković, A.A., Jurišić, M.V., Obradović, A., Đurović, D.
Inclusion criteria: Female rhythmic gymnasts, affiliated with different rhythmic gymnastics clubs in the Balkans
Sporting population: National level tournaments and international cups
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Body shape concerns in pubertal rhythmic gymnasts are associated with disordered eating attitudes and maladaptive perfectionism, increasing vulnerability to eating disorders.
Limits: The study is limited by a small, specific sample, self-reported data, and a cross-sectional design without a control group. These factors restrict generalizability and prevent causal conclusions
Perspectives: Future research should include larger and more diverse samples and use longitudinal designs, especially during puberty. Early interventions targeting body image and perfectionism could help reduce eating disorder risk

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.

Title: Perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting in athletes: the role of gender and sport type
Authors: Prnjak, K., Jukic, I., & Tufano, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged from 18 to 29 years from the faculty of Kinesiology
Sport_name: Soccer; basketball; gymnastics; figure skating; athletics; swimming
Related_Factor_measure: Body Image and Body Change Inventory
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism and body satisfaction explain dieting among Female athletes. For the male athletes, none of the predictors contributed to the understanding of their dieting behaviour. In addition, age, sport type and duration of sport participation did not contribute to dieting behaviour un case of male and Female. Adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism were associated with body satisfaction among Female athletes but not with dieting behaviour directly. Satisfaction with one's body was shown to be the largest independent predictor of dieting and their relationship was negative.
Limits: The data was based on self reported measures. Cross sectional design limits the causal inference between perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting. The sample consisted of athletes who were enrolled in a university program which might limit the generalizability. PANPS should not be used as a measure of perfectionism due to a questionable factor validity of the positive perfectionism subscale. EAT-26 was shown to have a low positive predictive value due to the rarity of targeted conditions while two out of three EAT-26 subscales demonstrated low internal consistency and omitting them while investigating eating disorder may not be the best approach. The number of Female participants was lower than males, which might have affected some of the analysis were gender-split was included.
Perspectives: It would be important to further etablish the relationship between perfectionism dimensions and body satisfaction in the area of disordered eating but also take a consideration the context in which athletes perceive their body.

Title: Body checking and avoidance among dancers

Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This study provided an initial foundation of data on body checking and body avoidance among dancers, aspects of ED pathology that feature prominenly in evidence-based assessments and treatments and that may be an important target in dancer-specific ED interventions.
Limits: Small sample size which may have attenuated findings and constrained analyses. Restrospective self-report data may have compromised accuracy in participant's reporting. Title: Disordered eating behaviors among crossfit athletes
Authors: Franco da Cunha, M.C., Costa Pereira Junqueira, A., Berbert de Carvalho, P.H., & Laus, M.F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 40 years, and be enrolled in the crossfit modality in a specialized gym, with a minimum frequency of practice of 6 months. Individuals who practiced other sports that favor hypertrophy in addition to crossfit and belonging to special groups, such as pregnant or nursing Female, indidviuals with any medical condition tha could have direct or indirect influence on physical appearance, elite athletes, were excluded.
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.
Limits: First, the sample may not be representative of the Brazilian population, as it was carried out in a single city in a single state. Second, there is a need to study other constructs, such as body dissatisfaction, which can predict other aspects of disordered eating in this population. Third, reported weight en height may be a bias, depiste being a common finding in body image  and eating behavior studies? Finally, even though the EAT-26 is frequently used in Brazil, the measure is not validated for adults in the country. Moreover, the EAT-26 appears to be a more focused instrument for investigating the symptoms of disordered eating often seen in Female, while recent studies have shown that disordered eating among male has its own characteristics.
Perspectives: Performance is directly related to diet, some disordered nutritional strategies can impair this performance and increase the risk of eating disorders in athletes.
