Title: The relationship between gender, type of sport, body dissatisfaction, self esteem and disordered eating behaviors in Division I athletes
Authors: Milligan, B., & Pritchard, M.
Journal: Athletic Insight The Online Journal of Sport Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Division I student-athletes from an intitution in the Western Athletic Conferences aged between 18 to 23 years.
Sport_name: Basketball, track, tennis, golf, gymnastics, soccer, skiing, wrestling
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Regression analyses for females revealed that body dissatisfaction was the most strongly related variable to disordered eating behaviors, followed by self esteem and type of sport. The regression analysis revealed that for males, body dissatisfaction was the only variable that related to disordered eating behavior.
Limits: Only athletes at one large public institution were examined. Only Division I athletes were examined. The athletes surveyed were primarily Caucasian and of traditional college age. This study is correlational in nature. Thus, the present study cannot say that being an athlete makes one prone to developing body dissatisfaction or eating disordered behaviors. It could be that individuals prone to those behaviors are more likely to be drawn to athletics in the first place.
Perspectives: For further research, researchers should take overall team/individual performance (wins/losses) into account for a factor associated with eating disorders because performance plays a role in self esteem, which has shown to correlate with both body dissatisfaction and disordered eating behavior.

Title: Disturbed eating in young, competitive gymnasts: differences between three gymnastics disciplines
Authors: Nordin, S., Harris, G., & Cumming, J.
Population subgroup:
Rhytmic gymnasts
Artistic gymnasts
Sport acrobats
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts who participated in one of three different forms of gymnastics: artistic, rhythmic, or sports acrobatics; training and competing for various clubs in the West Midlands, UK.
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Rhytmic gymnasts were considered to be at a greater risk for ED development than were artistic gymnasts or sport acrobats. This findings is probably due to sport-specific pressure in rhythmic gymnastics to obtain a very thin body rather than other variables such as age or perfectionist tendencies.
Limits: Sample small. Only 6 on the 9 coaches who were approached agreed to participate in the study. It is possible that only those coaches who were certain that their group was altogether healthy would be more likely to agree to take part, and vice versa. Secrecy, deception and denial are considered inherent to eating disorders, and it is generally agreed that self report measures for eating disorders tend to yield conservative estimates. Underreporting also constitues a possible limitation.
Perspectives:
The climate in training can be an important variable in eating disorder development. An investigation into motivational climates and perceived sport specific pressures would be a welcome addition to the eating disturbances literature. 
Qualitative research methologies may be used to gain a deeper insight into what pressures are present, as well as their sources, such as coaches, parents, teammates, judges, and others.

Title: Body Talk, Athletic Identity, and Eating Disorder Symptoms in male
Authors: Ahlich, E., Choquette, E.M., Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18-35 years; recruited using convenience sampling from a large southeastern university's research; receiving research credit upon completion of the study; informed consent
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The current findings support body talk and fat talk as a potential risk factor for eating disorders among male. Muscle-focused body talk may not a risk factor for diagnostic eating disorder symptoms. Muscle talk among male is related less to muscle dissatisfaction and more to male socioalization processes. Athletic identity did non emerge as a significant moderator of the association between body talk and eating disorder symptoms.
Limits: The study was limited to a single university campus in the southeastern United States, limiting generalizability of the findings. Few participants endorsed aesthetic or lean sports, potentially attenuating results.
Perspectives:
Future work may benefit from using a more objective of body composition. 
Future work should explore such associations among male in a clinical sample, examining whether fat or muscle talk is associated with eating disorder and/or muscle dysmorphia symptom severity. 
Fat talk may be an important prevention target amon male, regardless of athletic identity.

Title: General and sport-specific weight pressures as risk factors for body dissatisfaction and disordered eating among female collegiate athletes
Authors: Pallotto, I.K., Sockol, L.E., Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 competing in NCAA division I programs at four-year institutions of higher education in the United States
Sport_name: Basketball, cross-country, diving, gymnastics, lacrosse, soccer, swimming and track and field
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Weight pressures from parents, peers and the media were directly associated with body dissatisfaction; moreover these pressures were indirectly associated with disordered eating via their associations with thin and muscular ideal internalization. In the full model, weight pressures specific to the sport context were not associated with body dissatisfaction or disordered eating. The degree to which athletes internalized ideals for thinness and muscularity was associated with higher levels of disordered eating. Body dissatisfaction was not associated with disordered eating after other variables in the model were taken into account.
Limits: A comprehensive understanding of sociocultural influences on disordered eating among athletes require not only greater representation of participants from marginazlied racial and ethnic groups, but also consideration of the role of intersecting marginalized identities (e.g., sexual orientation) and integration of qualitative and mixed methodological approaches that may more effectively characterizz the lived experiences of these athletes. Cross sectional design ; it is not possible to determine whether these characteristics are risk factors for disordered eating or correlates of these behaviors.
Perspectives:
There is a clear need for high-quality studies of athletes assessing weight related pressures, appearance ideal internalization, body satisfaction, and disordered eating over time. in addition to clarifying the temporal relationships among these characteristics, longitudinal designs could also address whether these relationships are stable at different stages of athletes careers or different time points throughout the athletic season. Future research sould also consider how sociocultural influences might contribute to positive eating-related outcomes, both in the sport context and more broadly. 
Interventions that specifically address the sociocultural pressures and appearance ideals most relevant to athletes, such as the Female Athlete Body Project, reduce risk for subsequent disordered eating behaviors. 
In addition to pressures and appearance ideals specific to the sports environment, eating disorder prevention programs for Female athletes should address general sociocultural pressures related to weight and appearance. These interventions should also address internalization of cultural ideals for appearance beyond thinness; for example dissonance-based interventions could challenge internalization of fit and muscular ideals and sport specific ideals for weight and shape. Interventions could also be enhanced by strengths-based approaches that build on elements of sport participation that appear to be protective, such as the contribution of athletes positive evaluations of their physical abilities and condition to body esteem.

Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.

Body satisfaction and disordered eating should be investigated in a racially diverse sample for both generalizability and differential risk. Future studies should examine Female's wrestling and explore gender differences in body satisfaction and disordered eaating behaviors.

Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.

Title: Pinning down the problems and influences: disordered eating and body satisfaction in male wrestlers
Authors: Satterfield, N.A., & Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate wrestlers; at least 18 years of age; at a college in the United States; a current mumber of a NCAA Division I wrestling team; and identified as a man.
Related_Factor_measure: Body Parts Satisfaction Scale for male
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. While we did find an association between body satisfaction and restricting eating behavior, there was not a significant association among binge eating, purging, and body satisfaction. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.
Limits: The majority of participants identiied as white ; the present study sample is not representative of the racial makeup of this population. There was a relatively low response rate to the survey, which limits the generalizability of our sample. This study was cross sectional and only examined athletes in season, which limits the conclusions we can draw. The use of self report measures means it is possible that participants downplayed some of their behaviors or were unaware of the frequency of them. In addition, we did not ask specifically about frequency of binge eating.
Perspectives:
One possible intervention is by providing coaches and athletes a decision tree to plan a safe weight-cutting strategu such as consuming strategic level of carbohydrates and fluids. It is important that wrestlers evaluate their weight-cutting and recovery practices before and after competitions to assess what is working safely. 
Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies that assess these variables in season versus out of season. Body satisfaction and disordered eating should be investigated in a racially diverse sample for both generalizability and differential risk. Future studies should examine Female's wrestling and explore gender differences in body satisfaction and disordered eaating behaviors.

Title: Contextual body image and athletes' disordered eating: the contribution of athletic body image to disordered eating in high performance Female athletes
Authors: Karin de Bruin, A.P., Oudejans, R.R.D., Bakker, F.C., & Woertman, L.
Population subgroup:
19 athletes with eating disorders
33 without disordered eating
Inclusion criteria: High performance Female athletes with disordered eating ; competing on national or international levels ; control without disordered eating. Subjects with disordered eating meet two of the major criteria: amaleorrhoea, low BMI or low body fat, purging methods, and bulimic episodes, in addition to two of the following minor criteria: fear of weight gain, feelings of fatness, maintained low weight and increased importance of weight/shape. If participants did not meet these criteria, they were placed in the control group without disordered eating.
Mean_BMI:
Athletes with disordered eating M=20.69, SD=2.89
Athletes without disordered eating M=20.23, SD=2.23
Sport_name: Rythmic/acrobatic gymnastics and synchronized swimming, aerobic endurance training, middle and long distance running, swimming or long distance speed skating, tennis
Mean_Years of experience:
Athletes with disordered eating M=9, SD=4.27
Athletes without disordered eating M=8.36, SD=4.09
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The results showed that the athletic body image strongly contributed to eating disorder symptomatology. More specifically, the athletes self-evaluations about shape, weight and fat percentage and the perceived opinions of others on these aspects appeared to be only significant factors uniquely explaining 14 and 9% of the EDE-Q variance. On the other hand, although these athletic body image components were the only significant factors in the regression model, their contributions turned out to be rather limited. Moreover, thin-fat-self-evaluations in daily lifealso seemed to contribute to the equation although it did not reach significance. 64% of the variance was explained by the relevant body image components from daily life and sport.
Limits: Limitations of the present study were its sample size and consitution. Unfortunately, the number of Dutch high performance athletes is not that extensive.
Perspectives: Future studies should further explore athletes body comparisons in daliy life and sport, and possible differences between athletes with and without disordered eating in this respect. Future research should further explore body images in sport and daily life, particularly in athletes with disordered eating. We needed to extent the sample with a group of at-risk athletes who were not professionaly diagnosed in advance. Future investigation needs to take into account dynamic and contextual body image changes. It should also focus more closely on why certain athletes develop a more negative body image and how this could be prevented.

Title: An examination of psychosocial correlates of eating disorders among Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Reel, J.J., & Carter, J.E.
Journal: Research Quartely for Exercise and Sport
Inclusion criteria: Female collegiate athletes from three different NCAA Division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: Basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; field hockey; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; sport shooting; rowing; soccer; softball; swimming; synchronized swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.71, SD=1.27
M=8.89, SD=4.80
Related_Factor_measure: Multidimensional Body Self Relations Questionnaire-Appearance Evaluation (MBSRQ-AE)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The pressures participants felt from general media (e.g., magazines, television/movies) rather than from sport-specific (e.g., teammates, judges) and interpersonal (e.g., boy/girlfriend, friends) sources most strongly discriminated among the three eating disorder categories. The correlations between internalization and the discriminant functin were significant but small. Athlete, relative to nonathletes, may be more satisfied with their bodies, this variable is related strongly to eating pathology. Body image, internalization, negative affect and pressures contributed similarly to the differentiation among the three eating disorder categories.
Limits: All data were self reported, which allowed for the possibility of socially desirable responding. The cross sectional design did not allow for determining temporal relationships among the variables and eating pathology.
Perspectives:
Future sudies may want to employ Petrie and Greenleaf's (2007) conceptual model using structural equation modeling and incorporate qualitative interviews to better determine how Female athletes experience and cope with the pressure from coaches, and whether these pressures change over the time they are involved in their sports. Future research should include measure of dietary restraint to determine if it assists in accurately classifying athletes into the three eating disorder groups. 
Professionals need to develop methods for screening athletes prior to each season to identify eating disorder and symptomatic groups and intervene as early as possible. Body image groups that focus on decreasing internalization and the effects of societal pressures may be an effective intervention strategy with Female athletes.

Title: Symptoms of muscle dysmorphia, body dysmorphic disorder, and eating disorders in a nonclinical population of adulte male weightlifters in Australia
Authors: Nieuwoudt, J.E., Zhou, S., Coutts, R.A., & Booker, R.
Journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: Adult males at least 18 years of age; individuals who are working out with weights (i.e., free weight or machines) at least 3 times per week and currently residing in Australia
Mean_Exercise frequency: At least 3 days or more per week
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Significant correlation were found between muscle dysmorphia and body dysmorphic disorder symptoms. The correlational data suggested a relationship between the symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and eating disorders. Small but significant correlations were found between the substance use subscale of the MASS and the laxatives, diuretics behavioral question of the EAT-26, between the injury risk subscale of the MASS and the vomit and exercise behavioral questions of the EAT-26, and between the muscle satisfaction subscale and the binge eating and the lost > 9kg behavioral questions of the EAT-26.
Limits: The EAT-26 may not be sensitive to muscularity oriented disordered eating and body image concerns. The current research consisted of an online survey, therefore the possibility existed that participants might have interpreted the meanings of questions or statements differently to those intended or might have perceived some of the statements or questions as vague. Self selection bias is a limitation of internet surveys. The data were exclusively based on self report which can have tendencies toward social desirability bias.
Perspectives: A better understanding and awareness of the rates and symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and body dismorphic disorder and eating disorders may help strength and conditioning professionals to identify and refer at risk individuals for help from mental health professionals.

Title: Pinning down the problems and influences: disordered eating and body satisfaction in male wrestlers
Authors: Satterfield, N.A., & Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate wrestlers; at least 18 years of age; at a college in the United States; a current mumber of a NCAA Division I wrestling team; and identified as a man.
Related_Factor_measure: Body Parts Satisfaction Scale for male
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. While we did find an association between body satisfaction and restricting eating behavior, there was not a significant association among binge eating, purging, and body satisfaction. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.
Limits: The majority of participants identiied as white ; the present study sample is not representative of the racial makeup of this population. There was a relatively low response rate to the survey, which limits the generalizability of our sample. This study was cross sectional and only examined athletes in season, which limits the conclusions we can draw. The use of self report measures means it is possible that participants downplayed some of their behaviors or were unaware of the frequency of them. In addition, we did not ask specifically about frequency of binge eating.

Title: Prevalence and correlates of disordered eating in Female figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Gould, D., Reel, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged 12 to 25. Former skaters, basic skills skaters, and those in adult skating programs (e.g., age-based competitions following adult test equivalencies) were excluded
Sport_name: Figure skating (singles, multiple, synchronized, ice dancing, pairs)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. Body dissatisfaction explained an additional 5.7% of the variance in disordered eating. Sport related body dissatisfaction also emerged as a significant predictor. Positive perfectionism made a significant contribution, but negative perfectionism did not. Self esteem may not be strongly related to disordered eating. Athletic identity did not emerge as a significant variable in the final regression model, although the bivariate correlation indicated a significant positive relationship with disordered eating.
Limits: Societal weight pressures were not exmained. Self report nature of the surveys and the willingness of athletes to honestly and accurately respond to survey items. The results are also based on a conveniance sample of skaters limited to clubs in the Midwest and Northeast. Cross sectional design, causal relationships and change over time could not be determined.
Perspectives:
Sport psychology practiitioners should aid this effort by teaching skaters to appreciate body strengths and utilize psychological skills that may buffer the impact of negative weight pressures (e.g., utilizing positive self talk and realistic goal-setting). 
A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.

Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem

The number of Female participants was lower than males, which might have affected some of the analysis were gender-split was included.
Perspectives: It would be important to further etablish the relationship between perfectionism dimensions and body satisfaction in the area of disordered eating but also take a consideration the context in which athletes perceive their body.

Authors' conclusions: The pressures participants felt from general media (e.g., magazines, television/movies) rather than from sport-specific (e.g., teammates, judges) and interpersonal (e.g., boy/girlfriend, friends) sources most strongly discriminated among the three eating disorder categories. The correlations between internalization and the discriminant functin were significant but small. Athlete, relative to nonathletes, may be more satisfied with their bodies, this variable is related strongly to eating pathology. Body image, internalization, negative affect and pressures contributed similarly to the differentiation among the three eating disorder categories.
Limits: All data were self reported, which allowed for the possibility of socially desirable responding. The cross sectional design did not allow for determining temporal relationships among the variables and eating pathology.

Future research should include measure of dietary restraint to determine if it assists in accurately classifying athletes into the three eating disorder groups. 
Professionals need to develop methods for screening athletes prior to each season to identify eating disorder and symptomatic groups and intervene as early as possible. Body image groups that focus on decreasing internalization and the effects of societal pressures may be an effective intervention strategy with Female athletes.

Title: Eating disorders in Taekwondo athletes: the contribution of coach behavior, body satisfaction, and goal orientation
Authors: Baric, R., Erdeljac, T.
Inclusion criteria: Active practice of Taekwondo for at least 6 months and being a competitor in one of three competities categories: cadets, junior athletes or senior athletes
Sporting population:
17.3% top elite athletes, members of national selection and elite athletes
25 elite male
33 elite female
107 non-elite male
170 non-elite female
DEAB_measure: Croatian version of the Eating Attitudes Test (EAT_26)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Goal orientation, body dissatisfaction, and negative behavior and pressure from coaches significantly contribute to the risk of ED development in female and male cadet, junior and non-elite athletes, while body dissatisfaction seems to be the strongest predictor, especially in female athletes.

Title: Investigation of the relationship between muscle dysmorphia disorder, orthorexia nervosa, and motivation in male individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports
Authors: Abraş, H., Erdag, D., Buran, A.
Journal: Cyprus Turkish Journal of Psychiatry & Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Volunteer male participants aged between 18 and 58 engaged in bodybuilding; registered in gyms in TRNC.
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: As muscle dysmorphia increases, orthorexia nervosa increases in individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports in the TRNC.
Limits: Since this study was conducted only on male bodybuilders, the findings cannot be generalized to female bodybuilders.
Perspectives:
It is essential to provide education on muscle dysmorphia, orthorexia nervosa, and the use of ergogenic nutritional supplements in Physical Education and Sports Schools, as well as in coach training programs. Additionally, training on athlete nutrition and sports psychology in these institutions would equip them with knowledge about both athlete motivations and the mental health disorders frequently seen in athletes. Given the rise of these mental health issues in gyms, sports psychologists should be present in these environments, and mental health assessments should be conducted alongside medical evaluations for new memberships.
Conducting similar studies across different sports and with female participants could contribute valuable new insights to the literature.

Title: Influence of perfectionism on variables associated to eating disorders in dance students
Authors: Arcelus, J., Garcia-Dantas, A., Sanchez-Martin, M., Del Rio, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 12-20; participation was voluntary; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Sport_name: Dance (e.g., ballet, contemporary, flamenco, spanish folk)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Title: Disturbed eating in young, competitive gymnasts: differences between three gymnastics disciplines
Authors: Nordin, S., Harris, G., & Cumming, J.
Population subgroup:
Rhytmic gymnasts
Artistic gymnasts
Sport acrobats
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts who participated in one of three different forms of gymnastics: artistic, rhythmic, or sports acrobatics; training and competing for various clubs in the West Midlands, UK.
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Rhytmic gymnasts were considered to be at a greater risk for ED development than were artistic gymnasts or sport acrobats. This findings is probably due to sport-specific pressure in rhythmic gymnastics to obtain a very thin body rather than other variables such as age or perfectionist tendencies.
Limits: Sample small. Only 6 on the 9 coaches who were approached agreed to participate in the study. It is possible that only those coaches who were certain that their group was altogether healthy would be more likely to agree to take part, and vice versa. Secrecy, deception and denial are considered inherent to eating disorders, and it is generally agreed that self report measures for eating disorders tend to yield conservative estimates. Underreporting also constitues a possible limitation.
Perspectives:
The climate in training can be an important variable in eating disorder development. An investigation into motivational climates and perceived sport specific pressures would be a welcome addition to the eating disturbances literature. 
Qualitative research methologies may be used to gain a deeper insight into what pressures are present, as well as their sources, such as coaches, parents, teammates, judges, and others.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Related_Factor_measure: Athlete responded to two items using a 5-point Likert scale: the ideal body shape for my sport is similar to the ideal body shape in broader society and the ideal body weight for my sport is similar to the ideal body weight in broader society
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Attitudinal dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Compulsive exercise as a mediator between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology
Authors: Egan, S.J., Bodill, K., Watson, H.J., Valentine, E., Shu, C., & Hagger, M.S.
Inclusion criteria: The population was adults over the age of 18 years who participated in a diverse range of sport and exercise. The inclusion criteria of exercice twice or more per week was chosen to include people who exercised regularly but the criterion was relatively low as amount of exercise in not the defiing feature of compulsive exercise.
Sport_name: Running, triathlon, ball sports (volleyball, football, baseball, basketball, golf, rugby, squash, netball, cricket, hockey, tennis, badminton), gym, other (water polo, sailing, surf lifesaving, pilates, skateboarding, hula hooping, equestrian), cycling, dance, yoga, athletics, rowing, swimming
Authors' conclusions: there were direct effects of clinical perfectionism on avoidance/rule driven behavior, weight control exercise, and mood improvement. There was also a direct effect of the weight control exercise subscale on eating pathology and a negative effect of the mood improvement subscale on eating pathology.
Limits: Participant recruitmalet was not random or stratified which limits generalizability. The sample comprised mainly of individuals who are actively involved in one particular type of athletic poursuit: individual endurance sports and particularly running. The sample may, therefore, not be representative of individuals involved in sport and exercise in general. In addition, the study was cross-sectional, therefore the bidirectional relationship between eating pathology and compulsive exercise could not be assessed as this requires a longitudinal design. While we hypothesized that perfectionism would affect compulsive exercise, which would impact eating pathology, it could equally be argued that perfectionism influences eating pathology, which then influences compulsive exercise (i.e., compulsive exercise is a symptom of eating pathology, rather than an antecedent). Indeed, Meyer et al.’s (2011) model proposed bidirectional links between eating pathology and compulsive exercise. Meyer et al. (2011) argued that dieting and exercise reinforce one another due to social reinforcers which accompany the initial weight loss from regular exercise, which then intensifies eating, shape and weight concerns.
Perspectives: It would be useful to determine whether interventions for both perfectionism and compulsive exercise may help to improve the efficacy of standard treatments for eating disorders, above the gain already found in efficacious treatments such as CBT-E (Fairbunr et al., 2009) where clinical perfectionism is a focus if it is elevated. Future research could also examine the efficacy of specific stand-alone treatments for perfectionism (e.g., Egan et al., 2014) for compulsive exercise and perfectionism in eating disorders. Future research should measure perfectionism, compulsive exercise and eating pathology at two time points using a panel design and include a cross-lagged effects to determine the bidirectional relations between variables.

Title: Self-determination, restrictive eating, and psychological needs: challenges for young athletes
Authors: Clermont, C., Paquette, L., Lalande, D., & Dion, J.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to meet the following inclusion criteria: (1) at least 14 years old, (2) in grade 9 or 10, and (3) attending French or English high school
Sport_name: Endurance, power/technical, ball game, weight dependent, technical, aesthetic, high mass
Sporting population: No competition (n=88); local, regional and inter-regional (n=409); provincial (n=363); national and international (n=117)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 57.8% practiced 10 hours or less, 20.1% between 11 and 15 and 22.1% 16 or more
Mean_Years of experience: M=7.89, SD=3.641 (age since they engaged in sport)
DEAB_measure: The dietary restriction subscale of the validated short form of the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q)
Related_Factor_measure: The Basic Psychological Needs Satisfaction and Frustration Scale (BPNSFS)
Authors' conclusions: Satisfaction of psychological need in sport was positively and significantly related to restrictive eating. The results revealed a full mediation effect of self-determination for sport in the association between frustration of psychological need in sport and restrictive eating behaviors. There is a significant negative association between self-determination for sport and restrictive eating behaviors in adolescent athletes. Being an elite athlete did not predict restrictive eating behaviors in our sample. Psychological needs frustration in sport more strongly predicts restrictive eating behaviors in girls, compared with boys. No significant moderation effect of gender was found in the association between satisfaction of psychological need and restrictive eating behaviors.
Limits: First, the associations found between variables do not demonstrate any causal link because the cross-sectional design does not permit any inference about causality. This study used a large and diverse sample, it was not representative of all adolescents in the country, limiting the generalizability of the findings. In addition, problematic eating behaviors in this study refer to restrictive eating, measured by dietary restriction subscale of the EDE-Q. Therefore, the results cannot be extrapolated to other eating behavior problems, such as compulsive eating or binge eating. Moreover, since the instruments used to measure basic psychological needs in sport and self determination for sport were adapted slightly for the sport context by the research team, further studies should replicate these findings using other measures of these contructs. Lastly, constructs were tested with self-reported measures, and therefore, the results may have been influenced by social dsirability.
Perspectives: Profesionals who guide young athletes in the regulation of their eating behaviors may benefit from more thorough consideration of self-determination and psychological needs specifically in the sport context. Moreover, both frustration and satisfaction of psychological needs in sports should be investigated because restrictive eating was associate with greater satisfaction of psychological needs in the present study. Thus, frustration of psychological needs in sport may be a better indicator of restrictive eating behaviors, especially in girls.

Title: Social predictors of psychological need satisfaction and well being among Female adolescent gymnasts: a longitudinal analysis
Authors: Kipp, L.E., & Weiss, M.R.
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts; aged 10 to 18; trained 15.2hr per week; competed in US gymnastics sanctioned meets, and represented the full range of competitive levels
DEAB_measure: Dieting subscale of the Children's Eating Attitude Test
Related_Factor_measure: Six item scale developed by Hollembeak and Amorose (2005)
Authors' conclusions: Perceptions of mastery climate, autonomy-support, and performance climate at preseason predicted higher self esteem and lower disordered eating during competitive season, through mediation of perceived competence.
Limits: We included a purposeful sample of competitive gymnasts, so our results may not generalize to other youth sport contexts. It should be noted that after removing unreliable items, performance climate in our study only tapped the unequal recognition aspect. Participants reported low lecels of performance climate. We could not examine the effect of controlling behaviors because this construct showed a poor fit in the model.
Perspectives: More theory driven longitudinal studies can determine relationships and mediation over time and inform interventions to promote well-being among youth partcicipants. Future research should continue to consider indices of physical, social, emotional, and cognitive maturity with youth samples to control for developmental differences in well-being outcomes.

Title: Equation for eating disorder risk behaviors in Female athletes
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., Caputo Ferreira, M.E., de Oliveira, S.M.F., Fiorese, L., & Sousa Almeida, S.
Journal: Sociedade Brasileira de Medicina do Exercicio e do Esporte
Inclusion criteria: (a) present the informed consent form signed by the guardian (if she was under 18) and sign the assent form; (b) systematically train her respective modality with a minimum training regime of six hours per week (minimum frequency of three days per week and duration of two hours/training, or frequency of six days per week and duration of one hour/training; (c) have minimal participation in a regional competition in 2014; (d) be available to answer questionnaires and participate in anthropometric assessments. In addition, the following exclusion criteria were adopted (a) present a physical or intellectual disability and (b) use psychoactive medications in the last six months.
Sport_name: Athletics; Basketball; Boxing; Cycling; Football; Artistic gymnastics; Rythmic gymnastics; Handball; Jiu-Jitsu; Judo; Synchronized Swimming; Swimming; Figure skating; Water pole; Rowing; Diving; Surf; Tae-kwon-do; Tennis; Triathlon; Sailing; Volleyball and Beach volley
Authors' conclusions: The predictive equation is reliable to assess risk for ED in Brazilian Female athletes.
Limits: The use of questionnaires is pointed out, as researchers emphasize that athletes may omit some behaviors/feelings. In addition, another limitation was the use of a doubly indirect method to assess %F. According to some authors, using skinfolds can be limited to assess body composition.
Perspectives: The need to conduct new scientific investigations in order to assess the external validity of the created predictive equation is emphasized. In addition, it is necessary to create a risk predictive equation for eating disorders also regarding Brazilian male athletes

Title: Symptoms of muscle dysmorphia, body dysmorphic disorder, and eating disorders in a nonclinical population of adulte male weightlifters in Australia
Authors: Nieuwoudt, J.E., Zhou, S., Coutts, R.A., & Booker, R.
Journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: Adult males at least 18 years of age; individuals who are working out with weights (i.e., free weight or machines) at least 3 times per week and currently residing in Australia
Mean_Exercise frequency: At least 3 days or more per week
Authors' conclusions: Significant correlation were found between muscle dysmorphia and body dysmorphic disorder symptoms. The correlational data suggested a relationship between the symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and eating disorders. Small but significant correlations were found between the substance use subscale of the MASS and the laxatives, diuretics behavioral question of the EAT-26, between the injury risk subscale of the MASS and the vomit and exercise behavioral questions of the EAT-26, and between the muscle satisfaction subscale and the binge eating and the lost > 9kg behavioral questions of the EAT-26.
Limits: The EAT-26 may not be sensitive to muscularity oriented disordered eating and body image concerns. The current research consisted of an online survey, therefore the possibility existed that participants might have interpreted the meanings of questions or statements differently to those intended or might have perceived some of the statements or questions as vague. Self selection bias is a limitation of internet surveys. The data were exclusively based on self report which can have tendencies toward social desirability bias.
Perspectives: A better understanding and awareness of the rates and symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and body dismorphic disorder and eating disorders may help strength and conditioning professionals to identify and refer at risk individuals for help from mental health professionals.

Title: Understanding body dysmorphic disorder risk and exercise addiction in the Philippines
Authors: Payumo, L., Gengania, R. G., Lachica, M. A. G., Licupa, K. J., Mallare, J., Ocariza, V. A., Quinopez, J. P., Santos, D. C., Suyat, S. R., Versosa, M. J., & Padilla, R. J.
Inclusion criteria: Those who had exercised regularly for the past six months, dedicating 10 hours per week
Range_Age: Adolescents (12-18 years old) n=20 Early adult (19-40 years old) n=143 Middle adult (41-65 years old) n=16
Mean_Exercise frequency: < 4 sessions/week n=76 5-6 sessions/week n=99 > 7 sessions / week n=4
Authors' conclusions: BDDR and EA are positively but weakly associated, indicating they may co-occur but represent distinct and complex phenomena that cannot be explained by one another alone
Limits: The study is limited by a restricted gym sample, time constraints, and potential participation bias due to the sensitivity of BDDR and male-dominated settings. These factors may have affected sample balance and generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should explore tailored interventions addressing both BDDR and EA, particularly across different age groups and contexts. There is also a need for broader, more diverse samples and integrated mental health screening in fitness settings

Title: Emotional Regulation and Risk of Eating Disorders in Adolescent Athletes
Authors: Espinoza-Barron, S.P., Cantu-Berrueto, A., Castejon, M.A., Berengui, R.
Journal: European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education
Inclusion criteria: Active membership in a sports team, training at least three times per week, age between 10 and 25 years, encompassing early, middle, and late adolescence
Sport_name: Cheerleading, American football, basketball, dance, gymnastics, figure skating
Mean_Years of experience: 50.5% had more than 7 years 10.4% had between 4 and 6 years 16.8% had between 1 and 3 years 22.2% had less than 1 year
Authors' conclusions: Emotion regulation plays a significant role in eating disorder risk among young athletes, with emotional suppression acting as a risk factor and cognitive reappraisal as a protective factor. Adolescence appears to be a critical period for these associations.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, reliance on self-reported data, and limited sample representativeness restrict causal interpretation and generalizability.
Perspectives: Longitudinal studies with more diverse samples and additional psychological and contextual variables are needed to better understand the mechanisms underlying eating disorder risk in athletes.

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: The impact of critical comments from teammates on athletes eating and exercise psychopathology
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Adults aged 18 and over from local sport clubs
Mean_Age:
Critical comment M=23.27, SD=8.34
No critical group M=23.20, SD=8.67
Mean_BMI:
Critical comment M=22.70, SD=3.83
No critical comment M=22.56, SD=3.55
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Critical comment M=9.61h/week, SD=6.65
No critical comment M=8.29, SD=5.46
Mean_Years of experience:
Critical comment M=7.35, SD=6.41
No critical comment M=6.12, SD=5.58
Related_Factor_measure: Bulimic Modelling Scale adapted for athletes (BMS-A)
Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility).

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Inclusion criteria: Athletes competed with a university sports team or with their club or school
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Mean_Years of experience: Member of their current team M=1.99, SD=2.61
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Degree of relationship:
Teammate pressure-anxiety 𝛃=1.45, p<.01
Anxiety-drive for thinness 𝛃=.15, p<.05
Teammate pressure-drive for thinness total effect 𝛃=1.60, p<.001
Teammate pressure-drive for thinness direct effect 𝛃=1.38, p<.01
Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. Gender was not a significant moderator, meaning that the role of psychological wellbeing in the relationships between teammate influences and eating.
Limits: Although age and BMI were controlled for, it is acknowledged that there are a number of additional co-variates (e.g., perfectionism, athletic identity) that could have contributed to the findings of this study. The self report nature of the data collected and the context it was collected in (i.e., before/after a training session and in the company of teammates/coach) may potentially misrepresent athletes true behaviours. Items comprising the EDI-drive for thinness and body dissatsifaction subscales may not be an accurate reflection of male athletes experiences with disordered eating.
Perspectives: Identifying key risk factors and relevant moderators and mediators for eating psychopathology is important for effectively identifying those athletes at increased risk of eating and exercise psychopathology, and for developing appropriately tailored intervention and prevention strategies. Future research into the role of teammates would benefit from experimentally manipulating mechanisms of teammate influence on athletes actual food intake and should consider employing methodologies that are specifically tailored to male athletes. Employing modeeling analytic techniques to further our understanding of the complex, multi-factorial influences on athlete eating and exercise behaviours.

Title: Prevalence of disordered eating and its association with emotion regulation in Female college athletes
Authors: Shriver, L.H., Wollenberg, G., & Gates, G.E.
Journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
Inclusion criteria: Member of the university Female's athletic teams; 18 years old; injury-free at the time of study inclusion
Mean_Age:
M=19.5, SD=1.2
Weight sensitive M=19.6, SD=1.3
Less weight sensitive M=19.4, SD=1.1
Mean_BMI:
M=22.1, SD=32.8
Weight sensitive M=21.7, SD=2.9
Less weight sensitive M=22.7, SD=2.5
Sport_name: Soccer, cross country, track and field, basketball, cheer/pom, equestrian, tennis, golf and softball
Authors' conclusions: The current study identified athletes desire to lose weight as an independent predictor of disordered eating Our study has identified emotional regulation as a promising predictor of disordered eating.
Limits: We used a convenience sample of Female college athletes without nonathlete controls in the sample, the finding cannot be generalized. Geographical, cultural, ethnic and other differences were not accounted for in our study. Some eligible athletes mau have had a known eating disorder and thus might have opted out of study participation, thus influencing the final results. Disordered eating were self reported. Athletes may have underreported their actual eating behaviors due to social desirability or other influences.
Perspectives: Future studies should investigate indivdiual dimensions of emotional regulation and body dissatisfaction and their relationship to disordered eating symptoms in representative samples of college Female athletes, including further investigation of potential diffrences between weight sensitive and less weight sensitive sports.

Title: Childhood victimisation as a predictor of muscle dysmorphia in adult male bodybuilders
Authors: Boyda, D., & Shevlin, M.
Inclusion criteria: male who practicing bodybuiling. The study excluding those who had recorded they were currently experiencing a mental health illness, those who were attending a gymnasium less than three days per week as this was considered to represent casual membership. Those who recorded that gym attendance of less than four years were also excluded.
Authors' conclusions: Anxiety was significantly associated with muscle dysmorphia. Anxiety and depression do not both mediate the relationship between victimisation experiences and muscle dysmorphia, the unique mediating effect of anxiety represents a possible and plausible route from childhood victimisation to muscle dysmorphia. Victimisation during childhood increases anxiety levels, as a consequence, individuals negatively evaluate their self-image resulting in a body image distorsion and ultimately muscle dysmorphia. Children who are victimised by family or peers during childhood via physical, verbal or social means may have an increased risk of developing a pathological fixation with their body and this may have an impact or increase the risk for muscle dysmorphia later in adulthood.
Limits: The study was retrospective and cross-sectional and this as such limited conclusions regarding mediation. The study did not ascertain the temporal ordering of experiences which may limit analysis and interpretation, while childhood memories recalled during adulthood maybe subject to negative recall bias. In addition, it should not be discounted that the mediation model contained too few mediators to accurately predict an association between the childhood victimisation and muscle dysmorphia. Also the sample size was relatively small and this sample is not likely to be representative of the general population due to the sampling method. However, recruited participants through bodybuidling forum ensured adequate levels of variability in muscle dysmorphia scores: a general population sample likely have produced scores heavily positively skewed. Finally, low participation from the three large forums was unexpected.
Perspectives:
A more appropriate recruitmalet strategy should be considered as an increased sample size xould contribute to more stable estimation of the mediation model. 
The future direction for a follow-up study should consider if such early experiences and subsequent manifestation of muscle dysmorphia lead to a gateway for the use of performance-enhancing drugs wich may further magnify the effects of msucle dysmorphia on their psychological functioning. This could be considered an important extension to this study as indivdiuals who use performance-enhancing drugs can rapidly change aspects of their muscularity including fat distribution as after all, this is the holy grail for those who have muscle dysmorphia.

Title: The Mediating Role of Self-Criticism in the Relationship Between Coaches’ Leadership Styles and Disordered Eating in Athletes
Authors: Coelho, C., Oliveira, D., Branco, C., Rui Gomes, A., Conceiçao, E., Machado, P.P.P., Gonçalves, S.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competing at the senior level in Portugal
Related_Factor_measure: Multidimensional Scale of Leadership in Sport (MSLS)
Authors' conclusions: This study shows that negative coaching styles are associated with disordered eating through increased self-criticism, while positive leadership styles help reduce self-criticism. It highlights self-criticism as a key psychological mechanism linking coaching behaviors to eating pathology.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, small sample size, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference and generalizability. Lack of control for key variables (e.g., age, sport type) may also influence results.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and multi-informant designs to clarify causal pathways. Interventions targeting coaching styles, self-compassion, and support services are promising strategies to prevent disordered eating in athletes.

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Mediator:
Parent support
Coach support
Parent conflict
Coach conflict
Self critical perfectionism
Self esteem
Depression
Measure Mediator:
Sport-Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (S-SQRI)
Sport-Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (S-SQRI)
Sport-Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (S-SQRI)
Sport-Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (S-SQRI)
Dysfunctional Attitude Scale (DAS)
Rosenberg Self Esteem Scale (RSES)
Symptom Checklist 90R (SCL-90)
Degree of relationship:
χ2 = 1367.94, df = 693, p < .0001, RMSEA = 0.041(90% CI =_x000D_0.038–0.044), NNFI = 0.94, and CFI = 0.94
Avoidant attachmalet-parent support 𝛃=-.27, p<.05
Avoidant attachmalet-coach support 𝛃=-.21, p<.05
Parent support-parent conflict 𝛃=-.51, p<.05
Coach support-coach conflict 𝛃=-.24, p<.05
Parent conflict-self critical perfectionism 𝛃=.30, p<.05
Coach conflict-self critical perfectionism 𝛃=.22, p<.05
Self critical perfectionism-self esteem 𝛃=-.50, p<.05
Self esteem-depression 𝛃=-.65, p<.05
Depression-eating psychopathology 𝛃=.50, p<.05
Parent support partial R²=.07
Coach support partial R²=.04
Parent conflict partial R²=.26
Coach conflict partial R²=.06
Self critical perfectionism partial R²=.14
Self esteem partial R²=.25
Depression partial R²=.42
Eating psychopathology R²=.25
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: Eating disorders in Taekwondo athletes: the contribution of coach behavior, body satisfaction, and goal orientation
Authors: Baric, R., Erdeljac, T.
Inclusion criteria: Active practice of Taekwondo for at least 6 months and being a competitor in one of three competities categories: cadets, junior athletes or senior athletes
Sporting population:
17.3% top elite athletes, members of national selection and elite athletes
25 elite male
33 elite female
107 non-elite male
170 non-elite female
DEAB_measure: Croatian version of the Eating Attitudes Test (EAT_26)
Authors' conclusions: Goal orientation, body dissatisfaction, and negative behavior and pressure from coaches significantly contribute to the risk of ED development in female and male cadet, junior and non-elite athletes, while body dissatisfaction seems to be the strongest predictor, especially in female athletes.
Limits: The sample size, although it is realistic in relation to the number of active taekwondo competitors in Croatia. Self reported questionnaires.
Perspectives: Including other measures, more adjusted to male ED symptoms. As the results showed the significance of the behavior of coaches in relation to athletes ED symptoms, it would be very interesting to investigate the transgenerational transfer of distorted values, beliefs and behaviors related to ED from coaches to athletes, i.e., to investigate coaches history of ED symptoms and their current behavior.

Authors: Chaba, L., Scoffier-Mériaux, S., d'Arripe-Longueville, F., & Lentillon-Kaestner, V.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum of 16 years; minimum of 3 hours of physical training per week; and minimum of 3 years of bodybuilding or running.
Mean_Age:
Bodybuilders M=26.63, SD=7.38
Runners M=37.66, SD=12.20
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.73, SD=3.41
Runners M=6.44, SD=4.21
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.85, SD=6.71
Runners M=11.93, SD=10.12
Related_Factor: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass
Related_Factor_measure: Five items related to the perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass/leaning body mass were used
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass
Authors' conclusions: The TCM was partially supported in the context of eating disorders in the bodybuilders and runners. Both types of motivations for sport were direct or indirect risk factors for the development of deviant behaviors, but CM seemed to indicate greater risk than autonomous motivation for the development of eating disorders.
Limits: First, our sample was composed of young male with different numbers of years of practice, hours of practice per week, and types of practices (i.e., noncompetitors, future competitors, competitors), which might infuenced their motivation and engagement. Second, the runners were older than the bodybuilders, and younger people are more at risk of developing eating disorders than older people. Third, the data were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, no model/theory on body image in male was used, although body dissatisfaction was clearly present, and drive for muscularity was not considered. Fifth, our study was correlational. Sixth, it would be useful to determine a cutoff for eating disorders in male athletes because the EAT is not adapted to measure eating disorders in male athletes desiring to gain muscle mass. Finally, the motivational mechanisms explaining the development of eating disorders in male bodybuilders and runners who desire to gain muscle mass/lean body mass need to be further investigated in terms of motivational profiles.
Perspectives:
Include the level of competition in the analyses. Another model that also takes into account sociocognitive variables, such as the Health Action Process Approach might be applied in future research. Future studies could also specifically measure body satisfaction and analyze the link between this variable, behaviors to gain muscle mass/lean body mass, and the development of eating disorders.  It would be interesting to conduct a longitudinal study to more closely examine causality in the relationships. An intraindividual approach would be more useful than an interindividual approach. 
It appears necessary to limit the deleterious effects of controlled motivation. This might be accomplished by identifying the motivational orientations of athletes and promoting the development of coaching styles and climates that support autonomy and basic needs. Given the paradoxical role of autonomous motivation observed in the present study, it also appears necessary to encourage athletes to build reasoned and healthy sports parctices, limiting muscle mass gain at all costs.

Title: Bulimic symptomatology among male collegiate athletes: a test of an etiological model
Authors: Chatterton, J., Petrie, T.A., Schuler, K.L., & Ruggero, C.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Title: Drive for muscularity behaviors in male bodybuilders: a trans-contextual model of motivation
Authors: Chaba, L., d'Arripe-Longueville, F., Lentillon-Kaestner, V., & Scoffier-Mériaux, S.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum of 16 years; minimum of 3 hours of physical training per week; and minimum of 3 years of bodybuilding.
Related_Factor: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass
Related_Factor_measure: Four items related to the perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass were used
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass
Authors' conclusions: The study show that autonomous motivation for sport had a significant, indirect and positive association with drive for muscularity via perceived behavioral control and intention to gain muscle, and that contolled motivation for sports was related to drive for muscularity both directly and via attitude and intention to gain muscle mass. These results indicate that the trans contextual model was partially supported in the context of bodybuiling, suggesting a complex motivational model underlying drive for muscularity in male bodybuilders.
Limits: Our data are limited because our sample was composed only of young male with different levels of expertise (i.e., non-competitors, future competitors, competitors), which might have influenced their motivation and engagement in drive for muscularity. Second, subjective norm is a questionable variable as it might indicate a measurement issue in the sense that such variables reflect greater pressure and controlling rather than supportive forms of motivation. Third, the date were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, the internal consistency of some measures was quite low and this might have been linked to our heterogeneous sample or to the psychometric quality concerning the controlled motivation scale, or the inconsistency between the external regulation and the introjected regulation.
Perspectives:

Related_Factor: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass

Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived benefits of gaining muscle mass
Authors' conclusions: The TCM was partially supported in the context of eating disorders in the bodybuilders and runners. Both types of motivations for sport were direct or indirect risk factors for the development of deviant behaviors, but CM seemed to indicate greater risk than autonomous motivation for the development of eating disorders.
