Title: Disordered eating behaviors among crossfit athletes
Authors: Franco da Cunha, M.C., Costa Pereira Junqueira, A., Berbert de Carvalho, P.H., & Laus, M.F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 40 years, and be enrolled in the crossfit modality in a specialized gym, with a minimum frequency of practice of 6 months. Individuals who practiced other sports that favor hypertrophy in addition to crossfit and belonging to special groups, such as pregnant or nursing Female, indidviuals with any medical condition tha could have direct or indirect influence on physical appearance, elite athletes, were excluded.
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.
Limits: First, the sample may not be representative of the Brazilian population, as it was carried out in a single city in a single state. Second, there is a need to study other constructs, such as body dissatisfaction, which can predict other aspects of disordered eating in this population. Third, reported weight en height may be a bias, depiste being a common finding in body image  and eating behavior studies? Finally, even though the EAT-26 is frequently used in Brazil, the measure is not validated for adults in the country. Moreover, the EAT-26 appears to be a more focused instrument for investigating the symptoms of disordered eating often seen in Female, while recent studies have shown that disordered eating among male has its own characteristics.
Perspectives: Performance is directly related to diet, some disordered nutritional strategies can impair this performance and increase the risk of eating disorders in athletes.

Title: Bulimic symptomatology among male collegiate athletes: a test of an etiological model
Authors: Chatterton, J., Petrie, T.A., Schuler, K.L., & Ruggero, C.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes
Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.
Inclusion criteria: NCAA Divisions I Female collegiate athletes drawn from three universities located in the Midwest, Soutwest, and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: gymnastics; rowing; softball; synchronized swimming; tennis; alpine skiing; basketball; cross country; cheerleading; diving; golf; field hockey; lacrosse; soccer; swimming; track and field; volleyball
Related_Factor: Perceived importance of being attractive and Thin
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Perceived importance of being attractive and thin
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived importance of being attractive and thin
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. The cross sectional design of the study does not allow for the determination of the temporal nature of the relationships between psychosocial variables and bulimic symptoms.
Perspectives:
Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.

Title: Psychological risk indicators of disordered eating in athletes
Authors: Stoyel, H., Shanmuganathan-Felton, V., Meyer, C., & Serpell, L.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to be over 18; there was no upper cap on the age of potential participants. Participants had to consider themselves to be an athlete, and a minimum of 10 hours a week participating in their sport as well as have been actively competing, thus meaning that competitive sport-rather than zealous exercise was a significant part of their daily experience.
Sport_name: Swimming, tennis, football, basketball, volleyball, dancing, track and field, golf, boxing, equestrian, cycling, ping-pong, orienteering, rugby, rowing and race walking
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Societal pressures mediated by internalisation, are associated with binge eating and bulimia, while body dissatisfaction leads to bulimia and binge eating, mediated by negative affect.
Limits: Cross sectional nature. None of the measurements scale were specifically designed for athletes. The scale for social media usage and modelled behaviours were purpose-built. for this study and thus were not formally validated in previous research and so had lower Cronbach alpha coefficients than would normally be acceptable. This research is limited in its ability to make sound assumptions on clinical implications.
Perspectives: Future research should use a longitudinal design to determine whether the relevant factors are able to predict future disordered eating in an athlete sample. Repeated this research with athletes younger than 18 years old would also provide additional insight as it is a high risk population for the development of eating disorders. A qualitative investigation to further understand the differences between the original etiological model and the revised model will also be undertaken.

Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes
Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.
Inclusion criteria: NCAA Divisions I Female collegiate athletes drawn from three universities located in the Midwest, Soutwest, and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: gymnastics; rowing; softball; synchronized swimming; tennis; alpine skiing; basketball; cross country; cheerleading; diving; golf; field hockey; lacrosse; soccer; swimming; track and field; volleyball
Related_Factor: Perceived importance of being attractive and thin
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Perceived importance of being attractive and thin
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived importance of being attractive and thin
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. The cross sectional design of the study does not allow for the determination of the temporal nature of the relationships between psychosocial variables and bulimic symptoms.
Perspectives:
Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.

Title: Examining the influence of crossfit participation on body image, self-esteem, and eating behaviours among Female
Authors: Coyne, P., & Woodruff, S.J.
Journal: Journal of Physical Education and Sport
Inclusion criteria: Be member of one of the five CrossFit affiliates located in Southwestern Ontario (Canada) in two midsized cities
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The multiple linear regression revealed that length of time since beginning crossfit was a small, but significant predictor of Female's eating behaviours, with longer attendance predicting lower disordered scores.
Limits: First, only five crossfit affiliates were included in this study. As such, the results of this study may not be generalizable to the entire crossfit population. Additionally, although it would have been preferred to have crossfit variables objectively measured, for reasons of feasibility, these crossfit variables were self-reported. This study is aslo limited as demographic variables, such as race or ethnicity, were not taken into consideration, depiste being potentially influential. In addition, surveys were not completed in a randomized order, preventing the researchers from eliminating order bias and potentially relevant demographic covariates were not included in the analysis.
Perspectives: Future research could benefit from investigating if members of crossfit affiliates perceive nutrition-related recommaledations offered by crossfit to be healthy or whether they identify thems as encouraging disordered eating. Future studies may benefit from using a more domain-specific measure of self-esteem.

Title: Testing general sociocultural and coach-related appearance pressures as the factors associated with disordered eating in competitive female athletes participating in various sport
Authors: Jankauskiene, R., & Baceviene, M.
Inclusion criteria: Being an athlete that competed for at least two years in any competitive sport (participating in sports competitions of one sport) and being an official member of a sports school, sports club or national sports team
Sporting population: Sports school, sports clubs, national team
DEAB_measure: Lithuanian version of the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q)
Related_Factor_measure: Lithuanian version of the Sociocultural Attitudes Towards Appearance Questionnaire (SATAQ-4)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: General sociocultural pressures (parents, peers and media) are directly associated with disordered eating, and internalization of appearance ideals and overweight preoccupation mediate these associations in female competitive athletes. Controlling for general sociocultural pressures, perceived body weight and appearance-related pressures from coaches were associated with disordered eating through appearance internationalization and overweight preoccupation.
Limits: Cross sectional desing; a full SEM to test the associations between latent variables was not conducted, only a basic path analysis. We did not assess variables such as negative affect and restrained eating that are integral parts of the original model. We assessed the aspects of negative body image (overweight preoccupation) and disordered eating as possible outcome of the general sociocultural and coach-related pressures.
Perspectives: It is important to promote resistance to sociocultural pressures (parents, peers, media) and pressures from coaches in disordered eating prevention programmes for female athletes of all ages participating in sports irrespective of sport group WS or less. Choaches must be educated to understand and recognise the associations between athletes body image, disordered eating, and physical, mental health and sports performance, as weel as their personal influence on it and to promote positive body image in sports environments.

Title: General and sport-specific weight pressures as risk factors for body dissatisfaction and disordered eating among female collegiate athletes
Authors: Pallotto, I.K., Sockol, L.E., Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 competing in NCAA division I programs at four-year institutions of higher education in the United States
Sport_name: Basketball, cross-country, diving, gymnastics, lacrosse, soccer, swimming and track and field
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Weight pressures from parents, peers and the media were directly associated with body dissatisfaction; moreover these pressures were indirectly associated with disordered eating via their associations with thin and muscular ideal internalization. In the full model, weight pressures specific to the sport context were not associated with body dissatisfaction or disordered eating. The degree to which athletes internalized ideals for thinness and muscularity was associated with higher levels of disordered eating. Body dissatisfaction was not associated with disordered eating after other variables in the model were taken into account.
Limits: A comprehensive understanding of sociocultural influences on disordered eating among athletes require not only greater representation of participants from marginazlied racial and ethnic groups, but also consideration of the role of intersecting marginalized identities (e.g., sexual orientation) and integration of qualitative and mixed methodological approaches that may more effectively characterizz the lived experiences of these athletes. Cross sectional design ; it is not possible to determine whether these characteristics are risk factors for disordered eating or correlates of these behaviors.
Perspectives:
There is a clear need for high-quality studies of athletes assessing weight related pressures, appearance ideal internalization, body satisfaction, and disordered eating over time. in addition to clarifying the temporal relationships among these characteristics, longitudinal designs could also address whether these relationships are stable at different stages of athletes careers or different time points throughout the athletic season. Future research sould also consider how sociocultural influences might contribute to positive eating-related outcomes, both in the sport context and more broadly. 
Interventions that specifically address the sociocultural pressures and appearance ideals most relevant to athletes, such as the Female Athlete Body Project, reduce risk for subsequent disordered eating behaviors. 
In addition to pressures and appearance ideals specific to the sports environment, eating disorder prevention programs for Female athletes should address general sociocultural pressures related to weight and appearance. These interventions should also address internalization of cultural ideals for appearance beyond thinness; for example dissonance-based interventions could challenge internalization of fit and muscular ideals and sport specific ideals for weight and shape. Interventions could also be enhanced by strengths-based approaches that build on elements of sport participation that appear to be protective, such as the contribution of athletes positive evaluations of their physical abilities and condition to body esteem.

Title: Perfectionism and learning experiences in dance class as risk factors for eating disorders in dancers
Authors: Penniment, K.J., & Egan, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Being a Female aged between 18 and 30 years, currently studying classical and/or jazz ballet
Mean_BMI: 22.5% may be classified as underweight, with a BMI under 18.5kg/m²
Sporting population: 20.4% reported that they had danced semi professionally at one time, and 23.9% reported that they had danced at a professional level at one time.
Mean_Years of experience:
Dance tuition M=6.92, SD=22
Years studying dance M=14.5, SD=5.90
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The relation between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was partially mediated by thinness related learning. The hypothesis that the relationship between thinness related learning and eating disorders symptoms were partially mediated by thiness restricting expectancies was also supported. A direct relationship between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was found.
Limits: The data was cross sectional. Although the current model fit the data well, there are multiple other risk factors for ED and it is very likely that this risk is determined by multiple factors and is not simply a function of the emphasis on thinness in the dance environment, or perfectionism. The sample was too small to split into professional and non professional dancers to examine if the model was the same in these groups. Our view of perfectionism was aligned with the construct of clinical perfectionism, and as a result we examined a selected subset of scales from the FMPS and did not use relevant scales from the HMPS.
Perspectives:
It would be useful for future research to examine the efficacy of targeting young Female involved in dance with elevated levels of perfectionism for prevention programs, as preliminary findings are positive for the ability of programs targeting perfectionism to reduce eating disorders risk in Female adolescents. 
It would be useful for clinicians to consider directly targeting perfectionism through CBT programs for perfectionism in young Female involved in dance classes as it is likely to be a factor that puts them at higher risk of developing an eating disorders within this environment.

Title: The tripartite influence model of body image and disordered eating among young adult athletes
Authors: Tonsberg, E.N., Dixit, U., Henderson, R., Larsen, J., Lusich, R., Hauff, C., Ahlich, E.
Inclusion criteria: Being 18-26 years old, fluency in English and self-reporting yes to the item do you identify as an athlete ?
Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. It highlights the continued importance of both general and sport-specific influences on athletes’ eating behaviors
Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Title: A model of relationships of teammate relations, body image, and eating behaviors among athletes
Authors: Runquist, E., Cox, M., Meyer, A., & Rodgers, R.F.
Population subgroup:
63.5% Females
35.3% Males
0.64% Other
0.64% Opted not to say
Inclusion criteria: Being a varsity or club athlete 18 years or older
Related_Factor_measure: First ten items, and an additional adapted four items of the Sociocultural Attitudes Toward Appearance Questionnaire-4 (SATAQ-4)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Results support the importance of teammate body comparison, pressure, and relationships for muscularity oriented disordered eating and weight and shape concerns amongst collegiate athletes.
Limits: The study had varying rates of participation across varsity and club athlete groups that led to unequal representation in the final sample and inhibited group comparison. The study small sample size. The data were self-reported, cross-sectional and collecte from athletes from only one division I university.
Perspectives: Interventions such as educational programming amongst teams, compaings including on social media to promote positive repesentation of embodiment among athletes, as well as access to appropriate mental health resources are needed to protect athletes from disordered eating habits and negative body image comparisons. Future studies could utilize the model created to further explore the nunances of athlete-teammate relationships in larger, more diverse athlete populations and sporting environments.

Title: A comprehensive model of disordered eating among aesthetic athletic girls: exploring the role of body image related cognitive fusion and perfectionistic self presentation
Authors: Paixao, C., Oliveira, S., & Ferreira, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes; ages between 12 to 18 years old; Portuguese nationality; practice of an individual aesthetic sport.
Mean_BMI: 7 participants were underweight; 98 had a normal weight; 29 presented as overweight and 8 presented obesity
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Body image related cognitive fusion was strongly associated with ED. A strong relationship was found between image related perfectionist self presentation and higher levels of disordered eating. Path analysis results demonstraed that the proposed model presents an excellent fit to the empirical data, accounting for 71% of the variance of disordered eating attitudes and behaviours.
Limits: Cross sectional study limits any causal inferences. This study only focused on Female participants. Use of data exclusively based on self report measures. Considering that disordered eating is a multi determined phenomaleon, other emotional processes should be considered to explain this phenomaleon.
Perspectives:
Future prospective studies should be conducted to clarify the associations between these variables and propose causal inferences. Also future research is needed to compare the acceptability and impact of cognitive behavioural therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy based interventions to promote athletes adaptive ways to deal with their body image. 
Data highlights the relevance of education programmes that promote more adaptive emotional strategies focusing on body image, to increase athletes defusion skills and the acceptance of unpleasant thoughts and emotions related to their body image. Our data seems to indicate that intervention and prevention programs for aesthetic athletes, should focus on the development of more adpative strategies related to body image, through the cultivation of a balanced and acceptance relationship with one's own body characteristics rather than on the adoption of body image related perfectionist self presentation strategies.

Journal: Baltic Journal of Sport and Health Sciences
Population subgroup:
Athletes who aim at achieving results (28.9%)
Non-athletes or only exercising in their leisure time (71.1%)
Inclusion criteria: Students from sixteen randomly selected schools and gymnasiums of Kaunas; 11th grade classes from each school
Mean_BMI:
Non-athletes M=20.68, SD=2.61
Athletes M=21.00, SD=2.60
Sport_name: gymnastics, bodybuilding, figure skating, dancing, basketball, football, handball, volleyball, skiing, cycling, swimming, athletics, boxing, judo, wrestling
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Higher media influence were related with higher body dissatisfaction, unhealthy weight control behavior and risk of eating disorders. Body dissatisfaction was related directly to disordered eating. Appearance internalization in athletes directly correlated only with unhealthy weight loss behavior and disordered eating. Unhealthy weight loss practices had the strongest correlation with disordered eating.
Limits: N.A.
Perspectives: More research be undertaken to examine the role of coaches, teachers and teammates in the development of body dissatisfaction, weight control behavior and disordered eating. Adolescents trust body weight control techniques from media and have poor understanding about the dosage of physical activity and exercising behavior related to weight loss program. They need education in this area. Parents, coaches and shcool health educators should emphasize skill and talent instead of weight and body image and educate adolescents about the negative health effects of extreme weight loss.

Sport_name: Basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; field hockey; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; sport shooting; rowing; soccer; softball; swimming; synchronized swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.71, SD=1.27
M=8.89, SD=4.80
Related_Factor: Perceived importance of being physically fit and in-shape
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Perceived importance of being physically fit and in-shape
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived importance of being physically fit and in-shape
Authors' conclusions: The pressures participants felt from general media (e.g., magazines, television/movies) rather than from sport-specific (e.g., teammates, judges) and interpersonal (e.g., boy/girlfriend, friends) sources most strongly discriminated among the three eating disorder categories. The correlations between internalization and the discriminant functin were significant but small. Athlete, relative to nonathletes, may be more satisfied with their bodies, this variable is related strongly to eating pathology. Body image, internalization, negative affect and pressures contributed similarly to the differentiation among the three eating disorder categories.
Limits: All data were self reported, which allowed for the possibility of socially desirable responding. The cross sectional design did not allow for determining temporal relationships among the variables and eating pathology.
Perspectives:
Future sudies may want to employ Petrie and Greenleaf's (2007) conceptual model using structural equation modeling and incorporate qualitative interviews to better determine how Female athletes experience and cope with the pressure from coaches, and whether these pressures change over the time they are involved in their sports. Future research should include measure of dietary restraint to determine if it assists in accurately classifying athletes into the three eating disorder groups. 
Professionals need to develop methods for screening athletes prior to each season to identify eating disorder and symptomatic groups and intervene as early as possible. Body image groups that focus on decreasing internalization and the effects of societal pressures may be an effective intervention strategy with Female athletes.

Title: The tripartite influence model of body image and disordered eating among young adult athletes
Authors: Tonsberg, E.N., Dixit, U., Henderson, R., Larsen, J., Lusich, R., Hauff, C., Ahlich, E.
Inclusion criteria: Being 18-26 years old, fluency in English and self-reporting yes to the item do you identify as an athlete ?
Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. It highlights the continued importance of both general and sport-specific influences on athletes’ eating behaviors
Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Title: Psychological risk indicators of disordered eating in athletes
Authors: Stoyel, H., Shanmuganathan-Felton, V., Meyer, C., & Serpell, L.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to be over 18; there was no upper cap on the age of potential participants. Participants had to consider themselves to be an athlete, and a minimum of 10 hours a week participating in their sport as well as have been actively competing, thus meaning that competitive sport-rather than zealous exercise was a significant part of their daily experience.
Sport_name: Swimming, tennis, football, basketball, volleyball, dancing, track and field, golf, boxing, equestrian, cycling, ping-pong, orienteering, rugby, rowing and race walking
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Societal pressures mediated by internalisation, are associated with binge eating and bulimia, while body dissatisfaction leads to bulimia and binge eating, mediated by negative affect.
Limits: Cross sectional nature. None of the measurements scale were specifically designed for athletes. The scale for social media usage and modelled behaviours were purpose-built. for this study and thus were not formally validated in previous research and so had lower Cronbach alpha coefficients than would normally be acceptable. This research is limited in its ability to make sound assumptions on clinical implications.
Perspectives: Future research should use a longitudinal design to determine whether the relevant factors are able to predict future disordered eating in an athlete sample. Repeated this research with athletes younger than 18 years old would also provide additional insight as it is a high risk population for the development of eating disorders. A qualitative investigation to further understand the differences between the original etiological model and the revised model will also be undertaken.

Title: Dieting, disordered eating and perfectionism in weight-classified combat sports: a pilot study
Authors: Sørheim, A. K., Sandgren, S. S., & Øvretveit, K.
Population subgroup: Males kickboxing n=18 Females kickboxing n=13 Males Brazilian jiu-jitsu n=11 Females Brazilian jiu-jitsu n=4
Inclusion criteria: Currently active athletes with ≥ 1 year of training experience in either kickboxing or BJJ were eligible to participate
Mean_Age: Males kickboxing M=28.9, SD=6.5 Females kickboxing M=25.3, SD=5.7 Males Brazilian jiu-jitsu M=27.5, SD=4.6 Females Brazilian jiu-jitsu M=26.0, SD=5.8
Mean_BMI: Males kickboxing M=25.1, SD=2.1 Females kickboxing M=23, SD=1.7 Males Brazilian jiu-jitsu M=24.8, SD=2.6 Females Brazilian jiu-jitsu M=24.4, SD=2.6
Mean_Years of experience: Males kickboxing M=10, SD=6.4 Females kickboxing M=7.1, SD=4.1 Males Brazilian jiu-jitsu M=4.9, SD=3.6 Females Brazilian jiu-jitsu M=7, SD=5
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Despite engaging in dieting and rapid weight loss, athletes showed relatively low levels of disordered eating, though perfectionism especially maladaptive was associated with these symptoms. Coaches and peers played a key role in shaping weight management behaviors
Limits: The small, single-city sample and cross-sectional design limit generalizability and prevent causal conclusions. Additionally, some measures (e.g., translated scales) were not fully validated
Perspectives: Future research should use larger samples to better assess disordered eating prevalence in combat sports and explore the role of perfectionism and sport regulations. This could help improve athlete education and safer weight management practices

Title: Drive for muscularity and social physique anxiety mediate the perceived ideal physique muscle dysmorphia relationship
Authors: Thomas, A., Tod, D.A., Edwards, C.J., & McGuigan, M.R.
Journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: male engaged in weight training
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Perceptions about the ideal physique predict muscle dysmorphia symptoms both directly and indirectly through the drive for muscularity and SPA.Evidence for indirect pathways was found for the global measure of muscle dysmorphia, exercise dependence, size/symmetry, supplementation, and physique protection.
Limits: Causality cannot be inferred from a descriptive study without sound theoretical justification.
Perspectives: N.A.

Title: Perceived coach and teammate weight/shape-related beliefs and disordered eating in NCAA swimmers
Authors: Pinson, C.K., Fox, K.R., Frank, G.K.W., Hooley, J.M., Javaras, K.N.
Population subgroup: Division I n=82 Division II n=19 Division III n=89
Inclusion criteria: NCAA swimmers from Division I, II, III, > 18 years old, > 1 year on the team
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Perceived teammate weight/shape beliefs are strongly associated with eating disorder symptoms and thinness-related concerns in NCAA swimmers, while coach beliefs appear more specifically linked to drive for muscularity
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, the sample (especially males) is limited, and the measurement tools (e.g., CTWSBQ) require further validation, restricting generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal or experimental designs, include more diverse sports and samples, and refine measurement tools to better inform targeted prevention and intervention strategies

Title: Eating disorders in ballet dancing students: problems and risk factors
Authors: Toro, J., Guerrero, M., Sentis, J., Castro, J., & Puertolas, C.
Population subgroup:
76 Females dancers
453 Females from the general population
29 students who had competed their secondary studies but were continuing their artistic training at the same school
Inclusion criteria: Girls aged between 12 and 17 who combine intermediate level dance and normal secondary/pre-universities studies at the Barcelona Theatre institute's dance conservatoire.
Related_Factor_measure: Questionnaire on Influences on Body Shape Model
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Cognitive dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Eating attitudes and depressive symptoms were significantly associated. As for attitudes and behaviours related to physical appearance, only EAT scores suggestive of risk were significantly associated with giving up performing to avoid showing the body, feeling very affected comparing the body with others, believing that during performances the audience paid a lot of attention to their body and feeling very affected by it.
Limits: Our results may be biased by the lack of sincerity among informants or by a failure to report symptoms. The groups includes students of classical ballet and Spanish dance; these two disciplines are not excatly the same: classical ballet tends to underline thinness; this fact may have introduced a bias. We cannot obtain causal conclusions. Therefore we cannot state that particular pressures and school life events trigger risk eating behaviours. The lack of objective data supporting the existence of pressure from coaches.
Perspectives: Further studes should analyse whether these apparent differences in type of dance (classical ballet vs Spanish dance) represent different risks for ED.

Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions
Authors: Olave, L., Estévez, A., Momene, J., Penacoba, C., Macia, P., Macia, L., Etxaburu, N., Muniz, J.A., Iruarrizaga, I.

Title: Understanding athletic and exercise identity in relation to disordered eating behaviors
Authors: Palermo, M., & Rancourt, D.

Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, baseball, softball, football, field hockey, lacrosse, volleyball, swimming, track and field, cross country, cheerleading, dance, equestrian, gymnastics
Authors' conclusions:
Study 1 : athletic identity was not associated with global disordered eating behaviors.

Authors: Adam, M.E.K., Kowalski, K.C., Duckham, R.L., Ferguson, L.J., & Mosewich, A.D.

Title: Athlete identity and eating pathology in distance runners: when compulsive exercise matters
Authors: Gorell, S., & Anderson, D.A.
Inclusion criteria: Adult distance runners; registered for either a full or half marathon in the upstate region of New York
Mean_BMI:
Male M=24.11, SD=3.07
Female M=22.63, SD=2.81
Authors' conclusions: Regression analyses indicated that increased identity with exercise contributed to decreased eating pathology amongst half marathon runners. There was a significant interaction effect noted between exercise identity and compulsive exercise, such that the relation of exercise identity and eating disorders pathology was significant amongst those runners reporting either lower or higher compulsive exercise scores. The significant associations identified for half marathoners were not demonstrated in marathon runners.
Limits: It is possible that individuals registered for the half marathon were of a more elite running status. This study was also dependent on cross-sectional, self reported data collection methods. The runners assessed were all adults who were registered for competitive events in the northeastern United States, and results may not necessarily generalize to other age groups, or geographical areas, including internationally.
Perspectives:
Future work should investigate the relation between the study variables over time, allowing for investigation of the impact of athlete injury. Investigate variables amongst runners who are adolescent and young adult. 
Clinicians should increase screening for eating disorders and compulsive exercise across runners of less elite status, and integrate eating disorders prevention efforts amongst athletes who report low exercise identity and either lower or higher compulsive exercise.

Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Sport_name: Cross country/track and field, swimming and diving, volleyball, wrestling, soccer, golf, football, lacrosse, baseball, basketball, tennis
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: Prevalence of orthorexia nervosa and association with mental health among Palestinian physical education students - cross sectional study
Authors: Al-Amouri, F.M., Abualhaija, R., Al Atrash, M., Abu Alwafa, R., AlTamimi, M., Badrasawi, M.
Journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
Inclusion criteria: Students from the physical education department at An-Najah National University
Sport_name: Badminton, swimming, weightlifting, basketball, football, volleyball, other sport
Authors' conclusions: This study highlights a higher risk of orthorexia nervosa (OrNe) among male students, with strong associations with dieting behaviors and, in females, BMI. It emphasizes the multifactorial nature of OrNe and the importance of early identification in young athletes.
Limits: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and self-reported measures may introduce bias. Additionally, mental health assessment tools and limited comparability with prior studies restrict interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include longitudinal designs, more diverse populations, and more specific mental health measures. Preventive strategies targeting dietary behaviors and body-related factors in university and sports settings are needed.

Title: Self confiidence and disordered eating amongst martial artists: a cross sectional study
Authors: Mickelsson, T.B., Thylin, M., Hansson, E.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes practicing MMA or Jiu Jitsu; practiced at least four years and exercise a minimum of six hours per week. BJJ athletes had to have a blue belt and to participate in a minimum of four tournaments a year, while MMA athletes had to have completed at least four fights in total. Participants weight ranged from 52kg to 93 kg.
Mean_Age:
MMA M=31.49, SD=6.3
Jiu jitsu M=32.63, SD=6.2
Mean_Exercise frequency:
MMA M=12.87h/week, SD=4.13
Jiu jitsu M=9.64h/week, SD=3.78
Mean_Years of experience:
MMA M=8.85, SD=4.09
Jiu jitsu M=8.48, SD=3.83
Authors' conclusions: There were no significant correlations for either group between EDE-Q and sport specific self confidence.
Limits: The athletes eating behavior was measured 28 days before the competition, and therefore no conclusions about athletes relations to food beyond this time frame could be drawn.
Perspectives: Allow a certain percentage of the participants body mass to be dieted ahead of the competition. Include pre measuring of athletes usual weight and locate them into a natural weight class or for MMA organizations to adopt the weight in rules of jiu jitsu.

Title: Function over form: a longitudinal study of predictors and mediation pathways for disordered eating in elite athletes
Authors: Fatt, S.J., Hay, P., George, E., Jeacocke, N., Rogers, K., Mitchison, D.
Population subgroup: Males T1 N=47 Males T2 N=25 Males T3 N=22 Females T1 N=126 Females T2 N=83 Females T3 N=63 Other T1 N=1 Other T2 N=1
Inclusion criteria: Adult athletes who had competed at a national, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level
Sporting population: National, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level
Degree of relationship: Model controlling for gender T1 athletic identity-T2 disordered eating 𝛃=-.05, p=.375 T1 athletic identity-T3 disordered eating 𝛃=.02, p=.776
Authors' conclusions: Disordered eating in elite athletes is predicted by sport-specific weight pressures and drive for leanness for performance, rather than societal pressures or body image concerns. This suggests that athlete-specific mechanisms differ from those in the general population
Limits: The study had a limited and somewhat biased sample (mainly female, Western athletes) and insufficient power to test moderating factors like gender. Measurement choices and attrition may also affect the robustness of findings
Perspectives: Future research should test these models in more diverse and younger athlete populations and explore additional factors like perfectionism. Interventions should focus on performance-related beliefs and sport environments rather than appearance-based concerns

Title: Do self-compassion and body satisfaction protect women collegiate athletes from disordered eating ?
Authors: Kit, O., Petrie, T.A., Moore, E.W.

Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Sport_name: Cross country/track and field, swimming and diving, volleyball, wrestling, soccer, golf, football, lacrosse, baseball, basketball, tennis
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: Self confiidence and disordered eating amongst martial artists: a cross sectional study
Authors: Mickelsson, T.B., Thylin, M., Hansson, E.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes practicing MMA or Jiu Jitsu; practiced at least four years and exercise a minimum of six hours per week. BJJ athletes had to have a blue belt and to participate in a minimum of four tournaments a year, while MMA athletes had to have completed at least four fights in total. Participants weight ranged from 52kg to 93 kg.
Mean_Age:
MMA M=31.49, SD=6.3
Jiu jitsu M=32.63, SD=6.2
Mean_Exercise frequency:
MMA M=12.87h/week, SD=4.13
Jiu jitsu M=9.64h/week, SD=3.78
Mean_Years of experience:
MMA M=8.85, SD=4.09
Jiu jitsu M=8.48, SD=3.83
Authors' conclusions: There were no significant correlations for either group between EDE-Q and sport specific self confidence.
Limits: The athletes eating behavior was measured 28 days before the competition, and therefore no conclusions about athletes relations to food beyond this time frame could be drawn.
Perspectives: Allow a certain percentage of the participants body mass to be dieted ahead of the competition. Include pre measuring of athletes usual weight and locate them into a natural weight class or for MMA organizations to adopt the weight in rules of jiu jitsu.

Title: Disordered eating, eating attitudes and reasons for exercise among male high school cross country runners
Authors: Wadas, G.
Inclusion criteria: The runners were selected from 12 of the thirty two public high schools in the local school district sponsoring sports teams located in the USA. Participants were current members of a high shcool cross country teams, were in grades 9-12 and between the ages of 14-18.
Sporting population: Some playing time (24.2%), starter on team (29%), conference (4.8%), regional (35.5%), national (4.8%), other (1.6%)
Authors' conclusions: Factors that have a significant relationship with disordered eating are performance perfectionism and weight management. A desire to control weight is associated with disordered eating behaviors in male high school cross country runners as determined from the modest correlation coefficient for the weight management subscale and the EAT-26. There was no significant correlation for the physical appearance subscale of the EMI-2 and the EAT-26. No significant relationships were found between disordered eating behaviors and social pressure on body shape, social pressure on eating and athlete identity.
Limits: The results are generalizable only to school districts of similar size and demographic makeup. The questionnaire were completed on one occasion by runners during the sumer prior to the start of the season. The study was limited by a low number of participants relative to the number of runners on the teams and number of high schools in the school district.
Perspectives: The present study did not investigate the reasons for dissatisfaction with current weight status, future studies may seek more information relative to the reasons. For example, do male cross country runners feels a need to be more muscular ? Do the bodies of male cross country runners not fit the ideal ?

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (SSQRI)
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (SSQRI)
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: Interpersonal difficulties as a risk factor for athletes eating psychopathology
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
Inclusion criteria: British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, judo, rugby, football, hockey
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (SSQRI)
Authors' conclusions: Negative and positive aspects of the quality of the coach athlete and teammate athlete were related to athletes eating psychopathology after controlling for baseline eating psychopathology score. Conflict with the coach was found to be the only significant independent predictor of athletes eating psychopathology. The quality of the relationship with parents and attachmalet styles were not found to be related to athletes eating psychopathology 6 months later.
Limits: The present findings are essentially correlational, thus preventing definitive conclusions about causality. The present study only examined the direct role of interpersonal relationships in atletes eating psychopathology. Fairburn et al. (2003) noted that interpersonal difficulties interact with other core psychopathological processes (low self esteem, clinical perfectionism, and mood intolerance) to potentially elicit and maintain eating disorders.
Perspectives: Future studies should seek to examine how such processes as clinical perfectionism, self esteem, and mood intolerance interact with interpersonal difficulties to elicit eating psychopathology . And investigaite how these interpersonal variables interact with each other to predict athletes eating psychopathology.

Title: Does coping mediate the relationship between competitive anxiety and eating disorders in athletes ?
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., do Nascimaleto Junior, J.R.A., Freire, G.L.M., & Ferreira, M.E.C.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum training of eight hours per week; minimum participation in a competition of regional dimension in 2016; be available to answer questionnaires and participate in anthropometric evaluations. The criteria for athletes exclusion were: 1. to present physical or intellectual disability; 2. to have taken psychoactive medications in the six months prior ro the research.
Sport_name: Athletics; basketball; boxing; canoing; cycling; football; handball; jiu-jitsu; judo; olympic weightlifting; swimming; water polo; rowing; ornamental jumping; tae-kwon-do; tennis; triathlon; sailing; volleyball; and beach volleyball
Authors' conclusions: The structural equation model has pointed out a direct relationship between competitive anxiety and eating disorder. These findings indicated that stress perception during competitive events and negative thoughts about competitive performance were associated with the triggering of eating disorders in Brazilian male athletes.
Limits: Since we used self-reported instruments as assessment tools, the result may not reflect th context analyzed, because the responses were subjective. Portuguese is the langage spoken in Brazil and Portugal, but these countries have significant cultural differences and also small changes in their own writing. In this sense, the use of such a psychometric instrument in this study may have influenced the results obtained. Another limitation is that we used only the total score of the instruments, maling impossible the mediating role of ACSI-28 subscales in the association between anxiety and eating disorders. In addition, this study was restricted to the evaluation of psychological variables of athletes in just one moment, which does not characterize the real relationships of cause and effect between the variables.
Perspectives:
Future investigations should use a prospective approach with the athletes, besides crossing the previously described psychological variables with the performance levels during the season. 
We suggest further investigations with male Brazilian athletes to confirm the findings of this study. Furthermore, it is recommaleded the construction of an etiological model of eating disorder for Brazilian athletes of both sexes. The practical results of this study are in the possibility of sports professionals, more specifically, sports psychologists, to develop interventions that make it possible to decrease the level of competitive anxiety and/or enhance the development of coping strategies to reduce the triggering of eating disorders in Brazilian male athletes.

Title: mental skills as protective attributes against eating disorder risk in dancers
Authors: Estanol, E.
Inclusion criteria: The majority of participants were European American collegiate ballet dancers; however, collegiate modern and professional ballet dancers were also included in the sample. In order to ascertain a sample more less representative o the US population, the companies and universities were selected based on geographic location (east coast, midwest and western states). Selection of universities was also made by locating programs that had pre-professional or elite dance programs.
Authors' conclusions: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Negative affect partially mediated the relationship between weight pressures and ED symptoms. mental skills, specifically coping with adversity, freedom from worry, and confidence/achievement motivation, fully mediated the relationship between negative affect and ED symptoms. Total score for the athletic coping skill inventory was signficantly negatively correlated with weight pressure in dance, anxiety, depression and eating disorder risk.
Limits: One limitation of this study was that the sample was predominantly white and Female. Results from this study may therefore not be generalizable to a more ethnically diverse sample or to male dancers. Furthermore, this study lacked a comparison group of non-dancers, which would have enabled the researchers to more objectively compare the impact of the dance environment with a non-dance environment.
Perspectives: Additional studies are needed to explore how other protective factors (i.e., satisfaction with life, optimism, self-esteem, humor, and spirituality) may further explain variations in ED symptoms in dancers and contribute to this mediation model identified. Future research that looks at variables in the context of high-risk groups by providing profiles of resilient dancers vs at-risk dancers is also needed in order to further clarify the relationship between risk and resilience factors and ED outcomes. Furthermore, including demographic variables in the analyses would help us to better understand if certain subpopulations of dancers, may be more at risk or protected from pressures in the dance environment. Finally, studies should include the use of alternative methods in addition to self-report to more thoroughly explore variables relating to the dance environment.

Title: Actions speak louder than coaches: eating disorder behaviour among student-athletes
Authors: Button, T.A.J., Ouellette, G.P.
Population subgroup:
130 Females
70 Males
129 Lean sport
71 Non-lean sport
Inclusion criteria: Individuals had to compete on one of the university's athletic sports teams
Sport_name: Swimming, cross country, dance, soccer, volleyball, field hockey, badminton, frisbee, basketball, football, rugby, lacrosse
Authors' conclusions: Athletes are susceptible to negative mental-health outcomes, better support systems are warranted to protect them from the harmful effects of eating disorders, and to support those who may already be sttruggling.
Limits: Athletes were aware of the nature of this research as they were informed about what we were studying prior to participation. Participation was voluntary and this may provoked individuals with personal experience with eating disorder behaviours to participate in the research, and discouraged those who were uninterested in the topic from completing the survey. This could change the perceptage and number of participant's concerning results.
Perspectives: Receive professional education centred around other areas (including sexual violence and substance use), may benefit from increased training around eating behaviours, body image, and mental health. Universities can inregrate student resources within athletics to ensure that athletics are a positive activity for those who participate.

Title: Influence of perfectionism on variables associated to eating disorders in dance students
Authors: Arcelus, J., Garcia-Dantas, A., Sanchez-Martin, M., Del Rio, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 12-20; participation was voluntary; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Sport_name: Dance (e.g., ballet, contemporary, flamenco, spanish folk)
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 12-20; participation was voluntary; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Sport_name: Dance (e.g., ballet, contemporary, flamenco, spanish folk)
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Title: Childhood victimisation as a predictor of muscle dysmorphia in adult male bodybuilders
Authors: Boyda, D., & Shevlin, M.
Inclusion criteria: male who practicing bodybuiling. The study excluding those who had recorded they were currently experiencing a mental health illness, those who were attending a gymnasium less than three days per week as this was considered to represent casual membership. Those who recorded that gym attendance of less than four years were also excluded.
Authors' conclusions: Anxiety was significantly associated with muscle dysmorphia. Anxiety and depression do not both mediate the relationship between victimisation experiences and muscle dysmorphia, the unique mediating effect of anxiety represents a possible and plausible route from childhood victimisation to muscle dysmorphia. Victimisation during childhood increases anxiety levels, as a consequence, individuals negatively evaluate their self-image resulting in a body image distorsion and ultimately muscle dysmorphia. Children who are victimised by family or peers during childhood via physical, verbal or social means may have an increased risk of developing a pathological fixation with their body and this may have an impact or increase the risk for muscle dysmorphia later in adulthood.
Limits: The study was retrospective and cross-sectional and this as such limited conclusions regarding mediation. The study did not ascertain the temporal ordering of experiences which may limit analysis and interpretation, while childhood memories recalled during adulthood maybe subject to negative recall bias. In addition, it should not be discounted that the mediation model contained too few mediators to accurately predict an association between the childhood victimisation and muscle dysmorphia. Also the sample size was relatively small and this sample is not likely to be representative of the general population due to the sampling method. However, recruited participants through bodybuidling forum ensured adequate levels of variability in muscle dysmorphia scores: a general population sample likely have produced scores heavily positively skewed. Finally, low participation from the three large forums was unexpected.
Perspectives:
A more appropriate recruitmalet strategy should be considered as an increased sample size xould contribute to more stable estimation of the mediation model. 
The future direction for a follow-up study should consider if such early experiences and subsequent manifestation of muscle dysmorphia lead to a gateway for the use of performance-enhancing drugs wich may further magnify the effects of msucle dysmorphia on their psychological functioning. This could be considered an important extension to this study as indivdiuals who use performance-enhancing drugs can rapidly change aspects of their muscularity including fat distribution as after all, this is the holy grail for those who have muscle dysmorphia.

Title: Muscle dysmorphia and its associated psychological features in three groups of recreational athletes
Authors: Cerea, S., Bottesi, G., Pacelli, Q.F., Paoli, A., & Ghisi, M.
Population subgroup:
42 Bodybuilders (BB group) 
61 Strenght athletes (SA group)
22 Fitness practitioners (FP group)
Inclusion criteria: At least 18 years of age; absence of severe neurological or medical conditions; no current or past psychothic disorders; no evidence of intellectual disabilities; Italian athletes who trained regularly for recreational purposes: bodybuilders, strenght training athletes, and fitness practitioners.
Authors' conclusions: Self esteem is significaltly related to muscle dysmorphia. Perfectionism is non-significantly related to MD. Perfectionism socially prescribed is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Social phobia is significantly related to MD. Orthorexia is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Depression is significantly related to MD.
Limits: First the sample size was relativelly small which likely reduces the generalizability of our conclusions. Related to this issue, the statisticcal power of the employed regression design could not guarantee a reliable detection of MD predictors. Secondly, the online recruitmalet strategy we adopted under-sampled those without internet capability and prevented the opportunity of conducting face-to-face interviews of participants self-identified as recreational bodybuilders and recreational strength athletess. Lastly, the absence of psychometric information for the MPS is another limitation.
Perspectives: Improving the identification of predictors and risk factors for MD, as well as its associated psychological features, might facilitate the identification of at-risk trainers, as well as the development of prevention strategies and interventions. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of MD manifestation among athletes may help to distinguishing individuals participating in a healthy manner versus those participating in an unhealthy manner.
