Title: Eating attitudes, perfectionism and body-esteem of elite male judoists and cyclists
Authors: Filaire, E., Rouveix, M., Pannafieux, C., & Ferrand, C.
Journal: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
Inclusion criteria: N.A.
Mean_Age:
Controls M=21.8, SD=1.8
Judoists M=19.5, SD=.5
Cyclists M=21.2, SD=2.8
Mean_BMI:
Controls M=22.1, SD=1.8
Judoists M=21.9, SD=2.21
Cyclists M=20.8, SD=1.4
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Judoists M=15h par week
Cyclists 600/700km per week
Controls 2h per week
Mean_Years of experience:
Judoists M=9.6, SD=2.4
Cyclists M=8.5, SD=1.4
DEAB_measure: The French Version of Eating Attitudes Test (EAT-26)
Related_Factor_measure: The French version of the Profile of Mood States (POMS)
Authors' conclusions: Depression mood accounted for a significant proportion of the variance of global EAT scores as well as of dieting and bulimia scores. Feelings about appearance accounted for a significant amount of variance in dieting scores among athletes. Perfectionism dimensions were not relevant in predicting eating disorders symptoms in this sample.
Limits: First, as with any study using self-reported measures, findings may be susceptible to selective or erroneous reporting. Self reported measures always carry risks, especially with athletes who might not be forthcoming in their answers for fear of being eliminated from the team if they appear to be eating disordered. Second, the EAT-26 alone does not yield a specific diagnosis of an eating disorder. However, the use of a self-administered questionnaire, which incorporates Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders, as we used in our study, increases the advantages of using this questionnaire, which has been used in many epidemiological or screening studies, even if each subscale sould be interpreted independently. Finally, the number of participants was small.
Perspectives: Further research is needed to more firmly etablish the prevalence eating disorders in the male athletes and further, extend the line of inquiry examining relationships among measures of eating disorders, mood, and personality of athletes.

Title: Individual differences in male body image: an examination of self-objectivation in recreational body builders
Authors: Hallsworth, L., Wade, T., Tiggemann, M.
Inclusion criteria: Males. The first group consisted of bodybuilders; minimum level of training twice a week for at least a year. The second group consisted of competitive weightlifters recruited from the state weightlifting associations in four states of Australia.
Mean_Age:
Bodybuilders M=28.89, SD=6.19
Weightlifters M=27.60, SD=8.70
Non-athletic control M=26.43, SD=8.15
Mean_BMI:
Weightlifters M=28.60, SD=6.90
Bodybuilders M=26.04, SD=3.08
Controls M=24.18, SD=2.80
Sport_name: Bodybuilding, Weightlifting, Soccer, football, running, martial arts, swimming
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.40 hours per week
Weightlifters M=12.12 hours per week 
Controls M=3.8 hours per week
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.14 years
Weightlifters M=9.06 years
Related_Factor_measure: Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D)
Authors' conclusions: Bodybuilding may represent a practice that encourages male to become more self-conscious of their bodies, putting them at greater risk of experiencing greater levels of monitoring of body appearance and anxiety about physical appearance. This body self consciousness is associated with a greater risk of body dissatisfaction and drive for muscularity. Weightlifting does not appear to represent an objectifying climate.
Limits: The cross sectional nature makes it possible only to speculate on the directions of causality. Unequal sample sizes of groups in our analyses, particularly with respect to fewer competitive weightlifters. Unknown selection bias that may be operating in the bodybuilder and weightlifter groups, and any subsequent influence on the interpretation of our results. The weighlifting and bodybuilder groups differed not only in the nature of their sport, but also in competitive nature of this sport, which may introduce confound for differences found between the groups.
Perspectives: Health pursuits for male should emphasize achievement and function rather than appearance if they are to avoid deleterious consesquences.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: The impact of critical comments from teammates on athletes eating and exercise psychopathology
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Adults aged 18 and over from local sport clubs
Mean_Age:
Critical comment M=23.27, SD=8.34
No critical group M=23.20, SD=8.67
Mean_BMI:
Critical comment M=22.70, SD=3.83
No critical comment M=22.56, SD=3.55
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Critical comment M=9.61h/week, SD=6.65
No critical comment M=8.29, SD=5.46
Mean_Years of experience:
Critical comment M=7.35, SD=6.41
No critical comment M=6.12, SD=5.58
Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

Title: Teammate influences, psychological well-being, and athletes eating and exercise psychopathology: a moderated mediation analysis
Authors: Scott, C.L., Plateau, C.R., & Haycraft, E.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competed with a university sports team or with their club or school
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Mean_Years of experience: Member of their current team M=1.99, SD=2.61
Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. Gender was not a significant moderator, meaning that the role of psychological wellbeing in the relationships between teammate influences and eating.
Limits: Although age and BMI were controlled for, it is acknowledged that there are a number of additional co-variates (e.g., perfectionism, athletic identity) that could have contributed to the findings of this study. The self report nature of the data collected and the context it was collected in (i.e., before/after a training session and in the company of teammates/coach) may potentially misrepresent athletes true behaviours. Title: Correlations among symptoms of depression and problematic eating patterns in intercollegiate athletes
Authors: Bravata, E.A., Storch, E.A., & Storch, J.B.
Inclusion criteria: Division I varsity intercollegiate athletes from a large public university in the southeastern United States participated; aged 18 to 26 years.
Authors' conclusions: Problematic eating behaviors in athletes were low, but meaningfully correlated with self-reported depression for both Female and male. Title: mental skills as protective attributes against eating disorder risk in dancers
Authors: Estanol, E.
Inclusion criteria: The majority of participants were European American collegiate ballet dancers; however, collegiate modern and professional ballet dancers were also included in the sample. Selection of universities was also made by locating programs that had pre-professional or elite dance programs.
Authors' conclusions: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes

Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)

Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Critical comment M=23.27, SD=8.34
No critical group M=23.20, SD=8.67
Mean_BMI:

Critical comment M=9.61h/week, SD=6.65
No critical comment M=8.29, SD=5.46
Mean_Years of experience:
Critical comment M=7.35, SD=6.41
No critical comment M=6.12, SD=5.58
Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: Eating psychopathology as a risk factor for depressive symptoms in a sample of British athletes
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: British nationality; aged 16-45; participating in sport; not receiving treatment for any medical or mental illness and not pregnant.
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, judo, rugby, football, hockey
Authors' conclusions: Depressive symptoms did not predict athletes eating psychopathology. The present stuy did not find direct prospective relations from depressive symptoms to eating disordered symptoms.
Limits: Methodological issues pertaining to the use of self report measures, a small sample composed largely of Caucasian Female athletes and the use of parametric methods to analyse nonparametric data. Athletes scores on both measures were relatively healthy. It is not possible to make definitive conclusions about causality, as the findings are essentially correlational.
Perspectives:
Future studies should aim to replicate and confirm the present findings using experimental designs as this is considered the next step in identifying true causal risk factors. 
Studies should seek to explore the prevalence of eating disordered, depressive and comorbidity symptoms in athletes as well as determine the factors that are unique to eating disorders and depression and those that are shared by both disorders.

Title: An examination of psychosocial correlates of eating disorders among Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Reel, J.J., & Carter, J.E.
Journal: Research Quartely for Exercise and Sport
Inclusion criteria: Female collegiate athletes from three different NCAA Division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: Basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; field hockey; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; sport shooting; rowing; soccer; softball; swimming; synchronized swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.71, SD=1.27
M=8.89, SD=4.80
Authors' conclusions: The pressures participants felt from general media (e.g., magazines, television/movies) rather than from sport-specific (e.g., teammates, judges) and interpersonal (e.g., boy/girlfriend, friends) sources most strongly discriminated among the three eating disorder categories. The correlations between internalization and the discriminant functin were significant but small. Athlete, relative to nonathletes, may be more satisfied with their bodies, this variable is related strongly to eating pathology. Body image, internalization, negative affect and pressures contributed similarly to the differentiation among the three eating disorder categories.
Limits: All data were self reported, which allowed for the possibility of socially desirable responding. The cross sectional design did not allow for determining temporal relationships among the variables and eating pathology.
Perspectives:
Future sudies may want to employ Petrie and Greenleaf's (2007) conceptual model using structural equation modeling and incorporate qualitative interviews to better determine how Female athletes experience and cope with the pressure from coaches, and whether these pressures change over the time they are involved in their sports. Future research should include measure of dietary restraint to determine if it assists in accurately classifying athletes into the three eating disorder groups. 
Professionals need to develop methods for screening athletes prior to each season to identify eating disorder and symptomatic groups and intervene as early as possible. Body image groups that focus on decreasing internalization and the effects of societal pressures may be an effective intervention strategy with Female athletes.

Title: Eating disorders in ballet dancing students: problems and risk factors
Authors: Toro, J., Guerrero, M., Sentis, J., Castro, J., & Puertolas, C.
Population subgroup:
76 Females dancers
453 Females from the general population
29 students who had competed their secondary studies but were continuing their artistic training at the same school
Inclusion criteria: Girls aged between 12 and 17 who combine intermediate level dance and normal secondary/pre-universities studies at the Barcelona Theatre institute's dance conservatoire.
Authors' conclusions: Eating attitudes and depressive symptoms were significantly associated. As for attitudes and behaviours related to physical appearance, only EAT scores suggestive of risk were significantly associated with giving up performing to avoid showing the body, feeling very affected comparing the body with others, believing that during performances the audience paid a lot of attention to their body and feeling very affected by it.
Limits: Our results may be biased by the lack of sincerity among informants or by a failure to report symptoms. The groups includes students of classical ballet and Spanish dance; these two disciplines are not excatly the same: classical ballet tends to underline thinness; this fact may have introduced a bias. We cannot obtain causal conclusions. Therefore we cannot state that particular pressures and school life events trigger risk eating behaviours. The lack of objective data supporting the existence of pressure from coaches.
Perspectives: Further studes should analyse whether these apparent differences in type of dance (classical ballet vs Spanish dance) represent different risks for ED.

Title: Prevalence of orthorexia nervosa and association with mental health among Palestinian physical education students - cross sectional study
Authors: Al-Amouri, F.M., Abualhaija, R., Al Atrash, M., Abu Alwafa, R., AlTamimi, M., Badrasawi, M.
Journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
Inclusion criteria: Students from the physical education department at An-Najah National University
Sport_name: Badminton, swimming, weightlifting, basketball, football, volleyball, other sport
Authors' conclusions: This study highlights a higher risk of orthorexia nervosa (OrNe) among male students, with strong associations with dieting behaviors and, in females, BMI. It emphasizes the multifactorial nature of OrNe and the importance of early identification in young athletes.
Limits: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and self-reported measures may introduce bias. Additionally, mental health assessment tools and limited comparability with prior studies restrict interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include longitudinal designs, more diverse populations, and more specific mental health measures. Preventive strategies targeting dietary behaviors and body-related factors in university and sports settings are needed.

Title: Effects of Sport Pressures on Female Collegiate Athletes: A Preliminary Longitudinal Investigation
Authors: Anderson, C.M., Petrie, T.A., Neumann, C.S.
Population subgroup:
Time 1: begin of the fall season (September)
Time 2: end of the season (February)
Inclusion criteria: Student athletes from 26 universities located within all regions of the United States
Authors' conclusions: Sport pressures and dietary restraint were highly stable over the course of a competitive season. Pressures gymnasts and swimmers/divers experienced regarding body weight, size, and appearance from their coaches and teammates predicted decreases in their body satisfaction over a 5-month period; this change occurred even though the athletes’ body mass index did not change significantly over that time.
Limits: Included only NCAA Division I Female gymnasts and swimmers.divers, who also happened to primarily be Caucasien. The authors examined the variables over only a 5-month period, which represented one competitive collegiate season for these athletes. They examined the relationships among only sport pressures, body dissatisfaction and dietary restraint, additional research is needed to examine other variables such as general sociatail pressures, internalization, and negative affect. The validity of self-report measures of dietary restraint as predictors of actual reductions in food intake has been challenged. Self report measures of dietary restraint are risk factors in the prediction of disordered eating attitudes and behaviors, the measures are poor predictors of behaviorally observed, acute dietary restriction. BMI did not vary over the course of the 5-month season, we were not able to obtain more sensitive measures of body composition due to the study's design.
Perspectives:
Health care personnel can help coaches and teammates become more aware of how, through their behaviors and comments, they create an environment that pressures athletes about their body, weight, and appearance. Sport health care professionals can target sport administrators and sport-governing bodies because they have the power to male policy changes that can improve the sport environment, maling it less toxic for athletes. Such entities, could make revealing uniforms less so, adjust judging criteria so there is less focus on aesthetic/appearance-based aspects of the performance, expand or raise weight classifications, and/or set up strict requirements regarding acceptable weight loss over specific periods of time. Preventive programming, sport health care profesionals can work directly with athletes to help them counter these sport pressures and reduce their likelihood of engaging in caloric restriction of feeling dissatisfied with their bodies. 
Future reseach should examine whether our findings are supported in other groups of Female athletes (e.g., different sports, different competitive levels, more diverse racial/ethnic groups); male athletes should also be studied and such research should include measures of drive for muscularity. Other longitudinal studies may want to examine eating disorders and other potential risk factors over a longer period of time, or a different period (e.g., from the end of the competitive season to the start of the next one).

Authors: Shriver, L.H., Wollenberg, G., & Gates, G.E.
Journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
Inclusion criteria: Member of the university Female's athletic teams; 18 years old; injury-free at the time of study inclusion
Mean_Age:
M=19.5, SD=1.2
Weight sensitive M=19.6, SD=1.3

Mean_BMI:
M=22.1, SD=32.8

Sport_name: Soccer, cross country, track and field, basketball, cheer/pom, equestrian, tennis, golf and softball
Authors' conclusions: The current study identified athletes desire to lose weight as an independent predictor of disordered eating Our study has identified emotional regulation as a promising predictor of disordered eating.
Limits: We used a convenience sample of Female college athletes without nonathlete controls in the sample, the finding cannot be generalized. Geographical, cultural, ethnic and other differences were not accounted for in our study. Authors' conclusions: SPA scores contributed to dieting and bulimia scores in individual athletes. SPA and sport type independently and in combination contribute to greater dieting and bulimic behavior, particularly in female individual sport athletes.
Limits: Only athletes attending the training would have been approached about the study. Not all athletes from each sport at each institute were present at the time of data collection due to other commutments. Most athletes were tested at training sessions, rather than in settings which might heighten SPA. The testing of athletes in this manner may identify more consistent levels of SPA and disordered eating. Perspectives:

Attention to other trigger factors may be necessary when dealing with female athletes in individual sports, as this subgroup reported the highest levels of dieting and bulimic tendencies, along with high SPA. Different techniques and strategies for dealing with SPA and disordered eating may be required for different sport types.

Title: Eating attitudes, body appreciation, perfectionism, and the risk of exercise addiction in physically active adults: a cluster analysis
Authors: Piko, B.F., Berki, T.L., Kun, O., Mellor, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years of age and have an active lifestyle with regular physical activity (at least once a week, for a minimum of 30min)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 1h or less/week n=72 1-2h/week n=114 3-5h/week n=16 >5h/week n=3
Mean_Years of experience: 1 year or less n=40 2-3 years n=24 3-5 years n=17 5-10 years n=37 >10 years n=87
DEAB_measure: The Hungarian validated version of the Exercise Addiction Inventory-Revised (EAI-R)
Related_Factor_measure: Validated Hungarian version of the Eating Attitude Test-26 (EAT-26)
Authors' conclusions: Exercise addiction (EA) can also occur in regular exercisers, not just athletes, and is often linked with disordered eating (DE) when body image concerns and perfectionism are present. These factors interact in complex ways, meaning EA is not always pathological but can signal risk when combined with unhealthy eating attitudes and excessive performance pressure
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and reliance on self-reports, a relatively small and female-biased sample, and heterogeneous sport types limit generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal designs, while exploring additional psychological variables and protective factors to better understand and prevent EA and DE

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Related_Factor: Discouragement/sabotage from friends to eat healthy
Related_Factor_measure: Social Support for Healthy Eating Habits Scale (SSES)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Discouragement/sabotage from friends to eat healthy
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Discouragement/sabotage from friends to eat healthy
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Pinning down the problems and influences: disordered eating and body satisfaction in male wrestlers
Authors: Satterfield, N.A., & Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate wrestlers; at least 18 years of age; at a college in the United States; a current mumber of a NCAA Division I wrestling team; and identified as a man.
Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. While we did find an association between body satisfaction and restricting eating behavior, there was not a significant association among binge eating, purging, and body satisfaction. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.
Limits: The majority of participants identiied as white ; the present study sample is not representative of the racial makeup of this population. There was a relatively low response rate to the survey, which limits the generalizability of our sample. This study was cross sectional and only examined athletes in season, which limits the conclusions we can draw. The use of self report measures means it is possible that participants downplayed some of their behaviors or were unaware of the frequency of them. In addition, we did not ask specifically about frequency of binge eating.
Perspectives:
One possible intervention is by providing coaches and athletes a decision tree to plan a safe weight-cutting strategu such as consuming strategic level of carbohydrates and fluids. It is important that wrestlers evaluate their weight-cutting and recovery practices before and after competitions to assess what is working safely. 
Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies that assess these variables in season versus out of season. Body satisfaction and disordered eating should be investigated in a racially diverse sample for both generalizability and differential risk. Future studies should examine Female's wrestling and explore gender differences in body satisfaction and disordered eaating behaviors.

Title: Disordered eating behaviors among crossfit athletes
Authors: Franco da Cunha, M.C., Costa Pereira Junqueira, A., Berbert de Carvalho, P.H., & Laus, M.F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 40 years, and be enrolled in the crossfit modality in a specialized gym, with a minimum frequency of practice of 6 months. Individuals who practiced other sports that favor hypertrophy in addition to crossfit and belonging to special groups, such as pregnant or nursing Female, indidviuals with any medical condition tha could have direct or indirect influence on physical appearance, elite athletes, were excluded.
Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.
Limits: First, the sample may not be representative of the Brazilian population, as it was carried out in a single city in a single state. Second, there is a need to study other constructs, such as body dissatisfaction, which can predict other aspects of disordered eating in this population. Third, reported weight en height may be a bias, depiste being a common finding in body image  and eating behavior studies? Finally, even though the EAT-26 is frequently used in Brazil, the measure is not validated for adults in the country. Moreover, the EAT-26 appears to be a more focused instrument for investigating the symptoms of disordered eating often seen in Female, while recent studies have shown that disordered eating among male has its own characteristics.
Perspectives: Performance is directly related to diet, some disordered nutritional strategies can impair this performance and increase the risk of eating disorders in athletes.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Disordered eating behaviors among crossfit athletes
Authors: Franco da Cunha, M.C., Costa Pereira Junqueira, A., Berbert de Carvalho, P.H., & Laus, M.F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 40 years, and be enrolled in the crossfit modality in a specialized gym, with a minimum frequency of practice of 6 months. Individuals who practiced other sports that favor hypertrophy in addition to crossfit and belonging to special groups, such as pregnant or nursing Female, indidviuals with any medical condition tha could have direct or indirect influence on physical appearance, elite athletes, were excluded.
Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.
Limits: First, the sample may not be representative of the Brazilian population, as it was carried out in a single city in a single state. Second, there is a need to study other constructs, such as body dissatisfaction, which can predict other aspects of disordered eating in this population. Third, reported weight en height may be a bias, depiste being a common finding in body image  and eating behavior studies? Finally, even though the EAT-26 is frequently used in Brazil, the measure is not validated for adults in the country. Moreover, the EAT-26 appears to be a more focused instrument for investigating the symptoms of disordered eating often seen in Female, while recent studies have shown that disordered eating among male has its own characteristics.
Perspectives: Performance is directly related to diet, some disordered nutritional strategies can impair this performance and increase the risk of eating disorders in athletes.

Title: Pinning down the problems and influences: disordered eating and body satisfaction in male wrestlers
Authors: Satterfield, N.A., & Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate wrestlers; at least 18 years of age; at a college in the United States; a current mumber of a NCAA Division I wrestling team; and identified as a man.
Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. While we did find an association between body satisfaction and restricting eating behavior, there was not a significant association among binge eating, purging, and body satisfaction. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.
Limits: The majority of participants identiied as white ; the present study sample is not representative of the racial makeup of this population. There was a relatively low response rate to the survey, which limits the generalizability of our sample. This study was cross sectional and only examined athletes in season, which limits the conclusions we can draw. The use of self report measures means it is possible that participants downplayed some of their behaviors or were unaware of the frequency of them. In addition, we did not ask specifically about frequency of binge eating.
Perspectives:
One possible intervention is by providing coaches and athletes a decision tree to plan a safe weight-cutting strategu such as consuming strategic level of carbohydrates and fluids. It is important that wrestlers evaluate their weight-cutting and recovery practices before and after competitions to assess what is working safely. 
Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies that assess these variables in season versus out of season. Body satisfaction and disordered eating should be investigated in a racially diverse sample for both generalizability and differential risk. Future studies should examine Female's wrestling and explore gender differences in body satisfaction and disordered eaating behaviors.

Title: Investigation of the relationship between muscle dysmorphia disorder, orthorexia nervosa, and motivation in male individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports
Authors: Abraş, H., Erdag, D., Buran, A.
Journal: Cyprus Turkish Journal of Psychiatry & Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Volunteer male participants aged between 18 and 58 engaged in bodybuilding; registered in gyms in TRNC.
Authors' conclusions: As muscle dysmorphia increases, orthorexia nervosa increases in individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports in the TRNC.
Limits: Since this study was conducted only on male bodybuilders, the findings cannot be generalized to Female bodybuilders.
Perspectives:
It is essential to provide education on muscle dysmorphia, orthorexia nervosa, and the use of ergogenic nutritional supplements in Physical Education and Sports Schools, as well as in coach training programs. Additionally, training on athlete nutrition and sports psychology in these institutions would equip them with knowledge about both athlete motivations and the mental health disorders frequently seen in athletes. Given the rise of these mental health issues in gyms, sports psychologists should be present in these environments, and mental health assessments should be conducted alongside medical evaluations for new memberships.
Conducting similar studies across different sports and with female participants could contribute valuable new insights to the literature.

Title: Body image and muscle dysmorphia in competitive weightlifters: relationships across variables
Authors: Tokay, B.
Inclusion criteria: Age between 15 and 35 years, no health issues or injuries within the past six months, at least 2 years of active, licensed participation in the Olympic weightlifting discipline, participation in a minimum of three official weightlifting competitions (domestic or international) and voluntary agreement to participate in the study
Mean_Age: Females M=16.04, SD=2.22 Males M=17.53, SD=3.26
Mean_BMI: Underweight N=17 Normal weight N=124 Overweight N=41 Obese N=21
Authors' conclusions: Higher body image (BI) was associated with lower muscle dysmorphia (MD), suggesting a protective role of positive body perception in weightlifters. While overall BI and MD did not vary by most demographics, BMI and age influenced specific MD symptoms, highlighting nuanced risk patterns
Limits: The study’s cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and some findings (e.g., lack of gender differences) may be sample-specific. Additionally, focusing on total scores may overlook important variations within subdimensions

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Difficulties in emotion regulation, alexithymia, and social phobia are associated with disordered eating in male and Female undergraduate athletes
Authors: Benau, E.M., Wiatrowski, R., & Timko, C.A.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduates at a large Mid-Atlantic university, sample of undergraduate athletes and non-athletes.
Sporting population:
Among the athletes (N=183): 
Recreational and club level (64% - N=116)
Collegiate (35% - N=63)
Semi professional and professional levels (1% - N=2)
Authors' conclusions: Many of the psychosocial and socioemotional risk factors for disordered eating in the general population are also present in the undergraduate athlete population. Risk factors between male and Female differ in terms of presentation, but not necessarily on severity.
Limits: The present study was cross-sectional, and data were self reported from a self-selected and predominantly Caucasian sample at one undergraduate university, which limits conclusion about causality and generalizability. The EDI-3 was developed primarily with Female, which may not capture eating behavior and body shape concerns of athletes of all genders. Although many of the included instruments used in the present study have been used amply within collegiate athletes samples, only the EDI has been independently validated for this population. We did not inquire or determine eating disorder diagnosis as we were interested in disordered eating risk more generally. Finally, because we were interested in the influence of team dynamics, our classification of non-athletes included those who engaged in personal exercise but not organized exercise, which may also convey similar eating disorder risk to those involved in organized sports. Given to observed differences between athletes and non-athletes, we do not believe that engagement in personal fitness influenced the results of this study.
Perspectives: The cross-sectional nature of this study precludes a conclusion about causality. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify this relation. Given a comparatively higher focus on restrictive eating in athletes, more work is needed to confirm and better understand why Female athletes may engage in binge eating. Future reseachers should consider including the RMET as a behavioral measure of recognizing emotional expression in others that may measure different components of emotion regulation than self-report. Future researchers would do well to collect data from multiple campuses.

Title: Comparison of disordered eating symptoms and emotion regulation difficulties between Female college athletes and non-athletes
Authors: Wollenberg, G., Shriver, L.H., & Gates, G.E.
Inclusion criteria: Being a member of an official university Female's athletic team; being 18 or older and participating in regular team practices and activities at the time of the study (i.e., no injuries or illness)
Sport_name: Soccer, cross-country, track and field, basketball, cheer/pom/dance, equestrian, tennis, golf and softball
Authors' conclusions: Emotion regulation difficulty was positively associated with disorder eating pattern in our study. The non accept dimension was identified as a significant predictor of EAT-26. Emotion regulation did partially mediate the link between athletic status and disordered eating.
Limits: We utilized a convenience sample of Female college students ; no representative of the national population of Female college students as geographical, ethnic and other differences. Data were self reported and some participants may not have disclosed truthful information for different reasons (i.e., denial of eating disturbances, social bias). Athletes with high relative prevalence of DE were not represented in our sample because the university did not have such teams at the time of the study.
Perspectives: Independent of family history of eating disorders and emotion regulation difficulties, characteristics of Female college athletes should be examined further to identify potential mediators through which athletic status serves as a protective measure from DE risks. Further investigate potential correlates and predictors of DE with large and representative samples of Female athletes that would allow for comparison by types of sport.

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Members of various urban fitness centers aged between 18 and 60 years
Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. Using self report questionnaire by collecting data at the same time from the same individuals raises the bias of common method variance. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Title: Difficulties in emotion regulation, alexithymia, and social phobia are associated with disordered eating in male and Female undergraduate athletes
Authors: Benau, E.M., Wiatrowski, R., & Timko, C.A.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduates at a large Mid-Atlantic university, sample of undergraduate athletes and non-athletes.
Sporting population:
Among the athletes (N=183): 
Recreational and club level (64% - N=116)
Collegiate (35% - N=63)
Semi professional and professional levels (1% - N=2)
Related_Factor_measure: Reading Mind in the Eyes Task (RMET)
Authors' conclusions: Many of the psychosocial and socioemotional risk factors for disordered eating in the general population are also present in the undergraduate athlete population. Risk factors between male and Female differ in terms of presentation, but not necessarily on severity.
Limits: The present study was cross-sectional, and data were self reported from a self-selected and predominantly Caucasian sample at one undergraduate university, which limits conclusion about causality and generalizability. The EDI-3 was developed primarily with Female, which may not capture eating behavior and body shape concerns of athletes of all genders. Although many of the included instruments used in the present study have been used amply within collegiate athletes samples, only the EDI has been independently validated for this population. We did not inquire or determine eating disorder diagnosis as we were interested in disordered eating risk more generally. Finally, because we were interested in the influence of team dynamics, our classification of non-athletes included those who engaged in personal exercise but not organized exercise, which may also convey similar eating disorder risk to those involved in organized sports. Given to observed differences between athletes and non-athletes, we do not believe that engagement in personal fitness influenced the results of this study.
Perspectives: The cross-sectional nature of this study precludes a conclusion about causality. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify this relation. Given a comparatively higher focus on restrictive eating in athletes, more work is needed to confirm and better understand why Female athletes may engage in binge eating. Future reseachers should consider including the RMET as a behavioral measure of recognizing emotional expression in others that may measure different components of emotion regulation than self-report. Future researchers would do well to collect data from multiple campuses.

Title: Emotional Regulation and Risk of Eating Disorders in Adolescent Athletes
Authors: Espinoza-Barron, S.P., Cantu-Berrueto, A., Castejon, M.A., Berengui, R.
Journal: European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education
Inclusion criteria: Active membership in a sports team, training at least three times per week, age between 10 and 25 years, encompassing early, middle, and late adolescence
Sport_name: Cheerleading, American football, basketball, dance, gymnastics, figure skating
Mean_Years of experience: 50.5% had more than 7 years 10.4% had between 4 and 6 years 16.8% had between 1 and 3 years 22.2% had less than 1 year
Related_Factor_measure: Emotion Regulation Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents (ERQ-CA)
Authors' conclusions: Emotion regulation plays a significant role in eating disorder risk among young athletes, with emotional suppression acting as a risk factor and cognitive reappraisal as a protective factor. Adolescence appears to be a critical period for these associations.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, reliance on self-reported data, and limited sample representativeness restrict causal interpretation and generalizability.
Perspectives: Longitudinal studies with more diverse samples and additional psychological and contextual variables are needed to better understand the mechanisms underlying eating disorder risk in athletes.

Title: Parental relationships, emotion regulation and orthorexia: a study on adolescent athletes
Authors: D'Urso, G., Maynard, A., Lionetti, F., Spinelli, M., & Fasolo, M.
Population subgroup:
139 Athletes (competitive sport that involves practice at least 3 or 4 days per week and at least 2-3 hours per practice)
164 Non-athletes
Inclusion criteria: Italian adolescents attending high school during the 2020–2021 school year
Authors' conclusions: The mediation analysis suggests that inadequate relational styles with parents can invaludate the emotional regulation of adolescents and encourage orthorexia behaviours.
Limits: First, the use of self-report questionnaires could provide information that is not pure because answers might be affected by social desirability. Another limitation is the cross-sectional nature of the current study.
Perspectives:
Coach and practicioners could incorporate aspects of emotional regulation interventions into practices or as supplemental activities to the season. For example, the coach could incorporate lunches with a sport psychologist, who could discuss emotional regulation tactics with the athletes. Similarly, the coach could incorporate goal-setting activities throughout the season, with a focus on how to set smart goals, and then how to regulate emotions through the challenges of achieving such goals. 
Future research could verify this model in a multi-time perspective as well as including personality and social variables that can be configured as risk and/or protective factors for the etiology of orthorexia. Finally, a longitudinal persceptive would enable a better exploration, through adolescent development, of the indivdiual differences in terms of both emotional and family variables, mainly in adolescents at risk of compulsive behaviours.

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Members of various urban fitness centers aged between 18 and 60 years
Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. Using self report questionnaire by collecting data at the same time from the same individuals raises the bias of common method variance. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Title: Bulimic symptomatology among male collegiate athletes: a test of an etiological model
Authors: Chatterton, J., Petrie, T.A., Schuler, K.L., & Ruggero, C.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes
Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.
Inclusion criteria: NCAA Divisions I Female collegiate athletes drawn from three universities located in the Midwest, Soutwest, and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: gymnastics; rowing; softball; synchronized swimming; tennis; alpine skiing; basketball; cross country; cheerleading; diving; golf; field hockey; lacrosse; soccer; swimming; track and field; volleyball
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. The cross sectional design of the study does not allow for the determination of the temporal nature of the relationships between psychosocial variables and bulimic symptoms.
Perspectives:
Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Sport_name: gymnastics; rowing; softball; synchronized swimming; tennis; alpine skiing; basketball; cross country; cheerleading; diving; golf; field hockey; lacrosse; soccer; swimming; track and field; volleyball
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. Perspectives:
Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.
