Title: The relationship between social and disordered eating in college-aged Female gymnasts
Authors: Ausmus, J.C., Blom, L.C., Bowman, S., Lebeau, J.C.
Inclusion criteria: Participants were recruited from club gyms and colleges throughout the united states via email, social media, and word of mouth to coaches, support staff and directly to athletes; Females between 18-25 years; self identify as competitive gymnasts; must have competed within the last three years
Sporting population: 87.67% competed in varsity level gymnastics, 6.85% stated that they participated in recreational gymnastics, 5.48% competed in clubs gymnastics
Related_Factor: Emotional reaction to critical comments about physical appearance
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Emotional reaction to critical comments about physical appearance
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Emotional reaction to critical comments about physical appearance
Authors' conclusions: This study did not find significant correlations between criticism received on social media and disordered eating behaviors in college gymnasts. Combining variables related to social hassles, body satisfaction, usage of certain social media outlets, and years of participation could perdict disordered eating. No relationship were found between social media variables and disordered eating behaviors.
Limits: The main limitation of this study was the sample size of the participants. Although measures were exhausted in the recruitmalet of participants; it may have been beneficial to have sent the recruitmalet materials out earlier in the off season as opposed to a month before the college gymnastics season started. Another limitation was the limited reliability data for the Social Hassles Questionnaire, as it is relatively new instrument and has not been extensively tested. Furthermore this study did not account for mental health status beyond possible disordered eating behaviors.
Perspectives:
Since depression and anxiety have been linked to disordered eating patterns, future studies should also consider these pathologies, along with self-esteem. Research should aim to better understand the relationship between social media criticism and disordered eating behaviors in athletic populations. Athletes from different sports may respond differently to criticism than gymnasts, so it could be valuable to study these variables in other aesthetic sports, such as figure skating, diving, cheerleading, or even non-aesthetic sports like softball or basketball. Additionally, exploring these factors in males involved in aesthetic sports and the overall impact of social media on athletes' mental health could provide important insights.

It would also be beneficial for athletes, parents, and other significant figures in athletes' lives to be trained in recognizing the signs of disordered eating behaviors. Such training could help raise awareness of the potential dangers of social media platforms like Snapchat and offer guidance on how to support athletes if disordered eating behaviors arise.

To counter the effects of social media criticism on athletes, education initiatives should target coaches, families, friends, and athletes themselves to prevent the development of harmful eating behaviors and patterns, both now and in the future.

Title: Social predictors of psychological need satisfaction and well being among Female adolescent gymnasts: a longitudinal analysis
Authors: Kipp, L.E., & Weiss, M.R.
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts; aged 10 to 18; trained 15.2hr per week; competed in US gymnastics sanctioned meets, and represented the full range of competitive levels
DEAB_measure: Dieting subscale of the Children's Eating Attitude Test
Related_Factor_measure: Modified version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule
Authors' conclusions: Perceptions of mastery climate, autonomy-support, and performance climate at preseason predicted higher self esteem and lower disordered eating during competitive season, through mediation of perceived competence.
Limits: We included a purposeful sample of competitive gymnasts, so our results may not generalize to other youth sport contexts. It should be noted that after removing unreliable items, performance climate in our study only tapped the unequal recognition aspect. Participants reported low lecels of performance climate. We could not examine the effect of controlling behaviors because this construct showed a poor fit in the model.
Perspectives: More theory driven longitudinal studies can determine relationships and mediation over time and inform interventions to promote well-being among youth partcicipants. Future research should continue to consider indices of physical, social, emotional, and cognitive maturity with youth samples to control for developmental differences in well-being outcomes.

Title: Does coping mediate the relationship between competitive anxiety and eating disorders in athletes ?
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., do Nascimaleto Junior, J.R.A., Freire, G.L.M., & Ferreira, M.E.C.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum training of eight hours per week; minimum participation in a competition of regional dimension in 2016; be available to answer questionnaires and participate in anthropometric evaluations. The criteria for athletes exclusion were: 1. to present physical or intellectual disability; 2. to have taken psychoactive medications in the six months prior ro the research.
Sport_name: Athletics; basketball; boxing; canoing; cycling; football; handball; jiu-jitsu; judo; olympic weightlifting; swimming; water polo; rowing; ornamental jumping; tae-kwon-do; tennis; triathlon; sailing; volleyball; and beach volleyball
Degree of relationship:
SEM = .007; GFI = .90; AGFI = .92; TLI = .93; CR = 2.56 / F(3, 736) = 56.08; p = .01
Coping-Eating disorder behaviors 𝛃=.37, p<.05
Competitive anxiety-Eating disorder behaviors 𝛃=.49, p<.05
Competitive anxiety-coping 𝛃=.71, p<.05
R²(eating disorder behaviors)=.42, p=.01
Authors' conclusions: The structural equation model has pointed out a direct relationship between competitive anxiety and eating disorder. These findings indicated that stress perception during competitive events and negative thoughts about competitive performance were associated with the triggering of eating disorders in Brazilian male athletes.
Limits: Since we used self-reported instruments as assessment tools, the result may not reflect th context analyzed, because the responses were subjective. Portuguese is the langage spoken in Brazil and Portugal, but these countries have significant cultural differences and also small changes in their own writing. In this sense, the use of such a psychometric instrument in this study may have influenced the results obtained. Another limitation is that we used only the total score of the instruments, maling impossible the mediating role of ACSI-28 subscales in the association between anxiety and eating disorders. In addition, this study was restricted to the evaluation of psychological variables of athletes in just one moment, which does not characterize the real relationships of cause and effect between the variables.
Perspectives:
Future investigations should use a prospective approach with the athletes, besides crossing the previously described psychological variables with the performance levels during the season. 
We suggest further investigations with male Brazilian athletes to confirm the findings of this study. Furthermore, it is recommaleded the construction of an etiological model of eating disorder for Brazilian athletes of both sexes. The practical results of this study are in the possibility of sports professionals, more specifically, sports psychologists, to develop interventions that make it possible to decrease the level of competitive anxiety and/or enhance the development of coping strategies to reduce the triggering of eating disorders in Brazilian male athletes.

Title: How the obsession to eat healthy food meets with the willingness to do sports: the motivational background of orthorexia nervosa
Authors: Kiss-Leizer, M., Toth-Jiraly, I., & Rigo, A.
Inclusion criteria: Participants aged between 18 to 72 years
Range_Exercise frequency:
37.2% 3-4 times per week
25.8% 1-2h weekly
25% 3-4h 
35.2% for 5 or more than 5h
Related_Factor_measure: Motivation for Healthy Behaviors in Orthorexia Nervosa Qyestionnaire (MHBONQ)
Authors' conclusions: Health anxiety, mood modification are a strong predictor of orthorexia nervosa.
Limits: The results of the present study were based on online data gathering which questions the representative nature of the sample. Although participants were represented in a broad range of age and educational level, the highest proportion of participants were young and highly qualified Female. The participation in the research was voluntary thus the increased interest towards the topic of the examination might bias the results. The correlational desing of the present study does not allow causal inferences. The subject of the present study was the tendency to orthorexia nercosa, not orthorexia nervosa as a diagnosis, the results cannot be fully transposed into orthorexia nervosa since no orthorexia diagnosed patients are available yet.
Perspectives: A viable next step in orthorexia nervosa research could be the use of experience sampling method which could provide important information about the daily fluctuation of orthorexia nervosa and the related variables. It would be benefical to collect information about the type of the exercise as well, because some sport activities (category sports, aesthetic sport) can mean a higher vulnerability to orthorexia.

Title: Social and individual factors associaated with eating disorders in young athletes: effects on concentration and fatigue
Authors: Checa Olmos, J.C., Montserrat Hernandez, M., Belmonte Garcia, T., Jiminez Rodriguez, D., Rodriguez Martinez, A., Berenguel Martinez, P., & Berrio Lopez, A.M.
Inclusion criteria: The sample was selected voluntarily from the participants of a sports injury prevention and medical examination program by MasqSano for sports clubs in he Province of Almeria.
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, handball, swimming, rugby, volleyball
Related_Factor_measure: Do you filed tired in the training session
Authors' conclusions: kipp
Limits: First, the sampling is not random and therefore does not offer representative data for each group of athletes. Second, there may be non-observational errors due to the impossibility of obtaining all the influencial variables, such as psychological variables. Third, although the survey were short, they were adiministered while medical examinations were conducted, meaning the subjects attitudes and cooperation could be rushed or hasty. Fourth, BMI is not a completely objective tool for diagnosing normal weight, underweight or overweight, particularly in the athletic population, since this value only considers weight and height, discarding other helpful information such as muscle mass and its ratio to fat mass. Fifht, we consider age to be a limiting factor since the subjects surveyed are at a stage in which numerous changes in body composition occur due to growth and social influence. In the absence of a longitudinal study, it is not possible to speak of a direct influence. Finally, sixth comprises the need for a non-athlete control group to compare the significance level of the variables in both populations.
Perspectives:
Its necessary and interesting for prevention to be carried out before the adolescent stage (before the age of 12 or 13). 
Implement health promotion programs where aspects of body image are also addressed in addition to working on eating and sport habits. Design interventions based on age, in addition to gender, since the data are increasingly similar between male and Female in terms of body image dissatisfaction and danger of ED. In the design of interventions, pay differentiated attention to the athlete and non-athlete population. Even within the group of athletes, it is recommaleded to differentiate according to modality for diagnosis, prevention and intervention. Finally, we would like to point out, two issues: First the young people participating in the study were not diagnosed, which shows that ecessive concern about physical appearance can lead to behavior or attitudes that affect health before the disease in diagnosed. Secondly, the results suggest the need for the development of longitudinal studies in which the variability of the different dimensions analized and their degree of influence on the risk of developing ED can be observed.

Title: Muscularity oriented disordered eating: investigating body image concerns and the moderating role of emotion dysregulation in cyclists
Authors: Mazaraki, J., Bussey, K., Cunningham, M., Jewell, T., & Trompeter, N.
Inclusion criteria: Australian cyslists over the age of 18 years
Related_Factor_measure: Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale-Short Form
Authors' conclusions: These findings highlight how body dissatisfaction and the pursuit of a lean body may lead to engagement in muscularity-oriented disordered eating.
Limits: The global indicator of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale was utilized and not the sub-scales. The smaller sample may have lacked the statistical power needed to detect significant effects that were evident in the combined analysis.
Perspectives: Future studies should incorporate interaction terms between gender and key predictors and consider using gender-specific models.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Members of various urban fitness centers aged between 18 and 60 years
Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. Using self report questionnaire by collecting data at the same time from the same individuals raises the bias of common method variance. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Title: Moral emotions in motion: a cross-sectional study of shame, guilt, and disordered eating in UK university athletes
Authors: Zasiekina, L., Dunn, M., Miller, L., Tattersall, I., Vidaurre, V.
Population subgroup: Males N=51 Females N=76 Other n=3
Inclusion criteria: Had a current membership in the university of Exeter Sports Society, was aged between 18 and 25 years, and had no personal history of diagnosed eating disorders or related mental health conditions
Sport_name: Weight sensitive sport, non-weight sensitive sport
Mean_Years of experience: Less than 6 months n=20 6-12 months n=25 13-24 months n=36 25-36 months n=41 More than 36 months n=8
Authors' conclusions: Weight-sensitive sports and higher levels of shame and guilt were associated with greater eating pathology symptoms (EPS), while non-weight-sensitive sports may have a protective effect. Title: The tripartite influence model of body image and disordered eating among young adult athletes
Authors: Tonsberg, E.N., Dixit, U., Henderson, R., Larsen, J., Lusich, R., Hauff, C., Ahlich, E.
Inclusion criteria: Being 18-26 years old, fluency in English and self-reporting yes to the item do you identify as an athlete ?
Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. It highlights the continued importance of both general and sport-specific influences on athletes’ eating behaviors
Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Title: Maladaptive perfectionism as mediator among psychological control, eating disorders, and exercise dependence symptoms in habitual exerciser
Authors: Costa, S., Hausenblas, H.A., Oliva, P., Cuzzocrea, F., & Larcan, R.
Inclusion criteria: Inclusion criteria were that exerciser had trained for at least 6 consecutive months, lived at home with both parents, and were at least 18 years of age.
Authors' conclusions: There is a significant relationship between parental psychological control and both exercise dependence and eating disorder symptoms. Psychological control, both maternal and parternal, predicted maladaptive perfectionism, while maladaptive perfectionism, predicted ED symptoms and exercise dependence symptoms. Results confirmed the mediating role of maladaptive perfectionism as a full mediator for ED and exercise dependence symptoms for both male and Female habitual exercisers in the maternal data. In the paternal data, maladaptive perfectionism mediated the relationships between paternal psychological control and eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms as full mediator for the Female participants and as partial mediator for the male participants.
Limits: First, the data were collected at one time point and not across multiple time points as it should be done for a true mediational analysis. Because of the cross-sectional and self-report design of our study, we cannot etablish either the direction or causality of the effects. As weel, the self-report data may have intrinsic limitations such as social desirability, so the use of objective and multi-informant measures and experimental designs are encourages. Although, our sample consisted of habitual exercisers, this sample was deemed justified, as eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms are prevalent in this population and because psychological control is a risk factor for eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms in this population.
Perspectives: The deleterious effects of parental psychological control, both on eating disorder and on exercise dependence symptoms, require the implementation of targeted interventions to educate parents in using fewer instrusions and parental autonomy support, as opposed to psychological control. It is important to educate parents about psychological control being a universally negative parenting strategy and to help parents identify and reduce the use of such dysfunctional practices. Parent training could be used to help parents to get to practice autonomy supportive skills by taking part in various exercices from common situations in familial daily living. Results of the study suggest that the therapist and client could work together to identify and correct the client's maladaptive perfectionism thought processes that result in maladaptive eating or exercise behavior.

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Members of various urban fitness centers aged between 18 and 60 years
Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. Using self report questionnaire by collecting data at the same time from the same individuals raises the bias of common method variance. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Authors' conclusions: Only the personality traits conscientiousness, emotional stability and agreeableness are significantly associated with disordered eating. Our mediation analyses revealed the relationship between conscientiousness and disordered eating was completely mediated via the path of exercise dependence and obsessive compulsive symptoms, while the relationship of emotional stability and disordered eating was partly mediated via exercise dependence symptoms and obsessive compulsive symptoms. The multiple mediation model of the effects of emotiona stability on disordered eating demonstrated an indirect effect of emotional stability via exercise dependence and obsessive compulsive symptoms. Considering the single mediation model of agreeableness on disordered eating, our results showed that the relationship between agreeableness and disordered eating can be explained through obsessive compulsive symptoms.

However, given that personality traits (e.g., perfectionism) were also identified as core characteristics among these disorders
Perspectives: Other personality dimensions or mechanisms should be examined in future studies to allow for more robust and nuanced conclusions.

Title: Effect of locus of control on disordered eating in athletes: the mediational role of self regulation of eating attitudes
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Paquet, Y., & d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
Inclusion criteria: University students who regularly (i.e., 6h per week) practised a sport in regional and national competitions
Related_Factor_measure: Multidimensional Health Locus of Control Scale (MHLCS)
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: External locus related to powerful others
Authors' conclusions: We observed a negative influence of the locus of control attributed to the coach on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and lack of anticipation of consequences on performance. The coach and sports firends contribute to maladaptive patterns of accomplishment and function as negative predictors of the self regulation of eating attitudes in several contexts. The results showed the positive influence of an internal locus of control on the self regulation of eating attitudes in the context of social interaction. We observed a negative influence of self regulatory eating attitudes on disordered eating in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and the absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. This study demonstrated the influence of an internal locus of control on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in a context of social interaction and the influence of an external locus of control, attributed to the coach and sports friends on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in context of negative affect, social interaction and an absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. This study did not reveal a significant influence of a locus of control attributed to the family or luck on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of temptation or negative affect. The self regulation subscales were not significant in the contexts of food temptation and a lack of compensatory strategies.
Limits: The data were self reported, which suggests that social desirability may have been a bias. The study used correlational and cross sectional methods, which limits the generalization of the relationships.
Perspectives:
The social environment has a powerful impact on the development of disordered eating in athletes; the influence of these social relationship on athletes self regulatory eating attitudes merits further study, through an emphasis on locus of control and/or relationship quality. A longitudinal study would determine the stability of this impact and an experimental study would help to etablish the direction of the causality. 
The use of locus of control and self regulatory eating attitudes as concurrent variables may be useful to sports psychology practitioners in their work with athletes. Title: Effect of locus of control on disordered eating in athletes: the mediational role of self regulation of eating attitudes
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Paquet, Y., & d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
Inclusion criteria: University students who regularly (i.e., 6h per week) practised a sport in regional and national competitions
Related_Factor_measure: Multidimensional Health Locus of Control Scale (MHLCS)

Authors' conclusions: We observed a negative influence of the locus of control attributed to the coach on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and lack of anticipation of consequences on performance. Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions
Authors: Olave, L., Estévez, A., Momene, J., Penacoba, C., Macia, P., Macia, L., Etxaburu, N., Muniz, J.A., Iruarrizaga, I.
Inclusion criteria: People who practice physical exercise at least one day a week
Authors' conclusions: The study highlights strong links between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia, and multiple addictions, with impulsivity playing a key mediating role. These findings emphasize the importance of targeting impulsivity and emotion regulation in prevention and treatment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and the use of a homogeneous convenience sample limits generalizability. Additionally, reliance on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses may affect accuracy.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify causal relationships and further explore specific dimensions of impulsivity. There is also a need to develop prevention and intervention strategies focusing on emotion regulation and impulsivity

Title: Food and alcohol disturbance by athlete status: the roles of drive for thinness, drive for muscularity and sex
Authors: Palermo, M., Choquette, E.M., Ahlich, E., & Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate male and female aged between 18 to 30 years old
DEAB_measure: Drive for Thinness subscale from the Eating Disorder Inventory
Related_Factor_measure: Compensatory Eating and Behaviors in Response to Alcohol Consumption Scale (CEBRACS)
Authors' conclusions: Results related to DEAB not discussed
Limits: Cross sectional nature of the data, limited information about sport participation and the utilization of self identified athlete status. Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Related_Factor: Frequency of receipt of anti-dieting advice
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Frequency of receipt of anti-dieting advice
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Frequency of receipt of anti-dieting advice
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: Investigation of the relationship between muscle dysmorphia disorder, orthorexia nervosa, and motivation in male individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports
Authors: Abraş, H., Erdag, D., Buran, A.
Journal: Cyprus Turkish Journal of Psychiatry & Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Volunteer male participants aged between 18 and 58 engaged in bodybuilding; registered in gyms in TRNC.
Authors' conclusions: As muscle dysmorphia increases, orthorexia nervosa increases in individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports in the TRNC.
Limits: Since this study was conducted only on male bodybuilders, the findings cannot be generalized to Female bodybuilders.
Perspectives:
It is essential to provide education on muscle dysmorphia, orthorexia nervosa, and the use of ergogenic nutritional supplements in Physical Education and Sports Schools, as well as in coach training programs. Additionally, training on athlete nutrition and sports psychology in these institutions would equip them with knowledge about both athlete motivations and the mental health disorders frequently seen in athletes. Given the rise of these mental health issues in gyms, sports psychologists should be present in these environments, and mental health assessments should be conducted alongside medical evaluations for new memberships.
Conducting similar studies across different sports and with female participants could contribute valuable new insights to the literature.

Perspectives: Future research should use larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal designs, while exploring additional psychological variables and protective factors to better understand and prevent EA and DE

Title: Pinning down the problems and influences: disordered eating and body satisfaction in male wrestlers
Authors: Satterfield, N.A., & Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate wrestlers; at least 18 years of age; at a college in the United States; a current mumber of a NCAA Division I wrestling team; and identified as a man.
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. While we did find an association between body satisfaction and restricting eating behavior, there was not a significant association among binge eating, purging, and body satisfaction. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.
Limits: The majority of participants identiied as white ; the present study sample is not representative of the racial makeup of this population. There was a relatively low response rate to the survey, which limits the generalizability of our sample. This study was cross sectional and only examined athletes in season, which limits the conclusions we can draw. The use of self report measures means it is possible that participants downplayed some of their behaviors or were unaware of the frequency of them. In addition, we did not ask specifically about frequency of binge eating.
Perspectives:
One possible intervention is by providing coaches and athletes a decision tree to plan a safe weight-cutting strategu such as consuming strategic level of carbohydrates and fluids. It is important that wrestlers evaluate their weight-cutting and recovery practices before and after competitions to assess what is working safely. 
Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies that assess these variables in season versus out of season. Body satisfaction and disordered eating should be investigated in a racially diverse sample for both generalizability and differential risk. Future studies should examine Female's wrestling and explore gender differences in body satisfaction and disordered eaating behaviors.

Title: Muscle dysmorphia and its associated psychological features in three groups of recreational athletes
Authors: Cerea, S., Bottesi, G., Pacelli, Q.F., Paoli, A., & Ghisi, M.
Population subgroup:
42 Bodybuilders (BB group) 
61 Strenght athletes (SA group)
22 Fitness practitioners (FP group)
Inclusion criteria: At least 18 years of age; absence of severe neurological or medical conditions; no current or past psychothic disorders; no evidence of intellectual disabilities; Italian athletes who trained regularly for recreational purposes: bodybuilders, strenght training athletes, and fitness practitioners.
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Self esteem is significaltly related to muscle dysmorphia. Perfectionism is non-significantly related to MD. Perfectionism socially prescribed is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Social phobia is significantly related to MD. Orthorexia is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Depression is significantly related to MD.
Limits: First the sample size was relativelly small which likely reduces the generalizability of our conclusions. Related to this issue, the statisticcal power of the employed regression design could not guarantee a reliable detection of MD predictors. Secondly, the online recruitmalet strategy we adopted under-sampled those without internet capability and prevented the opportunity of conducting face-to-face interviews of participants self-identified as recreational bodybuilders and recreational strength athletess. Lastly, the absence of psychometric information for the MPS is another limitation.
Perspectives: Improving the identification of predictors and risk factors for MD, as well as its associated psychological features, might facilitate the identification of at-risk trainers, as well as the development of prevention strategies and interventions. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of MD manifestation among athletes may help to distinguishing individuals participating in a healthy manner versus those participating in an unhealthy manner.

Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Population subgroup:
40 Athletes competing in rhythmic gymnastics
40 Athletes competing in football
40 Non-athletes
Inclusion criteria: Membership in Spanish sport clubs or rhythmic gymnastics, or footballers with a background > 4 years of systematic training and competitive experience, training a minimum of 8h per week, with absence of severe injuries
Mean_Age:
Gymnasts M=16.6, SD=2.62
Footballers M=17.98, SD=3.42
Mean_BMI:
M=20.§3, SD=2.77
Gymnasts M=18.72, SD=1.54
Footballers M=22.45, SD=2.93
Sporting population: Gymnasts group consisted of 5 elite competing internationally and 35 at the national level
Range_Exercise frequency:
Elites : 20-35h per week
National gymnasts : 12-20h per week
Footballers : 4 training sessions plus a competitive match per week
Range_Years of experience: Minimum 4 years of training and competitive experience
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Correlation obtained between anxiety (both trait and state) and the EAT-40 was positively and statistically significant. In the multiple regression analysis that was performed with SCOFF scores as a dependent variable, the most predictive variable was socially prescribed perfectionism. It showed negative correlation with EAT-40 and self esteem. Self esteem is probably a protective factor to develop an eating disorder despite perfectionism, which is the most predictive variable as the multiple linear regression showed, and this variable was high in athletes.
Limits: Small sample size. No precise clinical diagnostic data were available to validate ED screening in the current study.
Perspectives:

Title: Teammate influences, psychological well-being, and athletes eating and exercise psychopathology: a moderated mediation analysis

Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. Gender was not a significant moderator, meaning that the role of psychological wellbeing in the relationships between teammate influences and eating.

Authors' conclusions: Peer and romantic pressure collectively predicted Females body image, disordered eating behaviors, and self esteem, romantic pressure did not significantly contribute independently. Peer pressure positively predicted disordered eating behaviors.
Limits: The sample was primarily Hispanic, which is representative of the population where the data were collected, but reduces the generalizability of these findings. Authors' conclusions: General sociocultural pressures (parents, peers and media) are directly associated with disordered eating, and internalization of appearance ideals and overweight preoccupation mediate these associations in female competitive athletes. Controlling for general sociocultural pressures, perceived body weight and appearance-related pressures from coaches were associated with disordered eating through appearance internationalization and overweight preoccupation.

Title: General and sport-specific weight pressures as risk factors for body dissatisfaction and disordered eating among female collegiate athletes
Authors: Pallotto, I.K., Sockol, L.E., Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 competing in NCAA division I programs at four-year institutions of higher education in the United States
Sport_name: Basketball, cross-country, diving, gymnastics, lacrosse, soccer, swimming and track and field
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Weight pressures from parents, peers and the media were directly associated with body dissatisfaction; moreover these pressures were indirectly associated with disordered eating via their associations with thin and muscular ideal internalization. In the full model, weight pressures specific to the sport context were not associated with body dissatisfaction or disordered eating. The degree to which athletes internalized ideals for thinness and muscularity was associated with higher levels of disordered eating. Body dissatisfaction was not associated with disordered eating after other variables in the model were taken into account.
Limits: A comprehensive understanding of sociocultural influences on disordered eating among athletes require not only greater representation of participants from marginazlied racial and ethnic groups, but also consideration of the role of intersecting marginalized identities (e.g., sexual orientation) and integration of qualitative and mixed methodological approaches that may more effectively characterizz the lived experiences of these athletes. Cross sectional design ; it is not possible to determine whether these characteristics are risk factors for disordered eating or correlates of these behaviors.
Perspectives:
There is a clear need for high-quality studies of athletes assessing weight related pressures, appearance ideal internalization, body satisfaction, and disordered eating over time. in addition to clarifying the temporal relationships among these characteristics, longitudinal designs could also address whether these relationships are stable at different stages of athletes careers or different time points throughout the athletic season. Future research sould also consider how sociocultural influences might contribute to positive eating-related outcomes, both in the sport context and more broadly. 
Interventions that specifically address the sociocultural pressures and appearance ideals most relevant to athletes, such as the Female Athlete Body Project, reduce risk for subsequent disordered eating behaviors. 
In addition to pressures and appearance ideals specific to the sports environment, eating disorder prevention programs for Female athletes should address general sociocultural pressures related to weight and appearance. These interventions should also address internalization of cultural ideals for appearance beyond thinness; for example dissonance-based interventions could challenge internalization of fit and muscular ideals and sport specific ideals for weight and shape. Interventions could also be enhanced by strengths-based approaches that build on elements of sport participation that appear to be protective, such as the contribution of athletes positive evaluations of their physical abilities and condition to body esteem.

Eating Attitude Test (EAT-26)

Authors' conclusions: There is a positive association of body dissatisfaction with risk behaviour for eating disorders and addiction to exercise.

Small number of participants and who were practitioners of only two modalities, which males impossible to generalize th results to practitioners of other exercises.

Title: The tripartite influence model of body image and disordered eating among young adult athletes
Authors: Tonsberg, E.N., Dixit, U., Henderson, R., Larsen, J., Lusich, R., Hauff, C., Ahlich, E.
Inclusion criteria: Being 18-26 years old, fluency in English and self-reporting yes to the item do you identify as an athlete ?
Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. It highlights the continued importance of both general and sport-specific influences on athletes’ eating behaviors
Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Title: Perfectionism and eating psychopathology among dancers: the role of high standards and self-criticism
Authors: Goodwin, H., Arcelus, J., Geach, N., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 18 years or older; current member of a university recreational dance club; clubs comprised ballet, modern, tap, jazz, and/or hi hop disciplines. The participants were not screened for previous or current eating disorder treatment.
Sport_name: Dance (ballet, jazz/modern, contemporary dance, hip hop, tap, other)
Degree of relationship:
Restraint-self evaluative perfectionism 𝛃=.30, p<.001, R²=.09
Eating concern-self evaluative perfectionism 𝛃=.31, p<.001, R²=.10
Weight concern-self evaluative perfectionism 𝛃=.39, p<.001, R²=.15
Shape concern-self evaluative perfectionism 𝛃=.43, p<.001, R²=.17
Authors' conclusions: High standards and self criticism are positively associated with eating restraint, eating concern, weight concern and shape concern. The associations between self-criticism and eating pathology were not moderated by high standards. Self criticism fully mediated the relationships between high standards and restraint, eating concern, weight concern and shape concern.
Limits: The self report nature of the data means reports may be unreliable and subject to social desirability bias. The method of participants recruitlent precluded any analysis of response rate, and it was not known whether or not there was a bias to those who chose to participate versus those who did not participate. The heterogeneous nature of the sample means that underlying group differences (between dance style, competency level and hours of dance practice) may have been missed.
Perspectives: The relationships between high standards, self-criticism and eating disorder risk requires examination in more homogenous sub-groups of dancers, to further identify the risk environments for eating psychopathology.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Pinning down the problems and influences: disordered eating and body satisfaction in male wrestlers
Authors: Satterfield, N.A., & Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate wrestlers; at least 18 years of age; at a college in the United States; a current mumber of a NCAA Division I wrestling team; and identified as a man.
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. While we did find an association between body satisfaction and restricting eating behavior, there was not a significant association among binge eating, purging, and body satisfaction. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.
Limits: The majority of participants identiied as white ; the present study sample is not representative of the racial makeup of this population. There was a relatively low response rate to the survey, which limits the generalizability of our sample. This study was cross sectional and only examined athletes in season, which limits the conclusions we can draw. The use of self report measures means it is possible that participants downplayed some of their behaviors or were unaware of the frequency of them. In addition, we did not ask specifically about frequency of binge eating.
Perspectives:
One possible intervention is by providing coaches and athletes a decision tree to plan a safe weight-cutting strategu such as consuming strategic level of carbohydrates and fluids. It is important that wrestlers evaluate their weight-cutting and recovery practices before and after competitions to assess what is working safely. 
Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies that assess these variables in season versus out of season. Body satisfaction and disordered eating should be investigated in a racially diverse sample for both generalizability and differential risk. Future studies should examine Female's wrestling and explore gender differences in body satisfaction and disordered eaating behaviors.

Title: The impact of critical comments from teammates on athletes eating and exercise psychopathology
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Adults aged 18 and over from local sport clubs
Mean_Age:
Critical comment M=23.27, SD=8.34
No critical group M=23.20, SD=8.67
Mean_BMI:
Critical comment M=22.70, SD=3.83
No critical comment M=22.56, SD=3.55
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Critical comment M=9.61h/week, SD=6.65
No critical comment M=8.29, SD=5.46
Mean_Years of experience:
Critical comment M=7.35, SD=6.41
No critical comment M=6.12, SD=5.58
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

Title: Teammate influences, psychological well-being, and athletes eating and exercise psychopathology: a moderated mediation analysis

Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Employing modeeling analytic techniques to further our understanding of the complex, multi-factorial influences on athlete eating and exercise behaviours.

Title: An examination of psychosocial correlates of eating disorders among Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Reel, J.J., & Carter, J.E.
Journal: Research Quartely for Exercise and Sport
Inclusion criteria: Female collegiate athletes from three different NCAA Division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: Basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; field hockey; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; sport shooting; rowing; soccer; softball; swimming; synchronized swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.71, SD=1.27
M=8.89, SD=4.80
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: The pressures participants felt from general media (e.g., magazines, television/movies) rather than from sport-specific (e.g., teammates, judges) and interpersonal (e.g., boy/girlfriend, friends) sources most strongly discriminated among the three eating disorder categories. The correlations between internalization and the discriminant functin were significant but small. Athlete, relative to nonathletes, may be more satisfied with their bodies, this variable is related strongly to eating pathology. Body image, internalization, negative affect and pressures contributed similarly to the differentiation among the three eating disorder categories.
Limits: All data were self reported, which allowed for the possibility of socially desirable responding. The cross sectional design did not allow for determining temporal relationships among the variables and eating pathology.
Perspectives:
Future sudies may want to employ Petrie and Greenleaf's (2007) conceptual model using structural equation modeling and incorporate qualitative interviews to better determine how Female athletes experience and cope with the pressure from coaches, and whether these pressures change over the time they are involved in their sports. Future research should include measure of dietary restraint to determine if it assists in accurately classifying athletes into the three eating disorder groups. 
Professionals need to develop methods for screening athletes prior to each season to identify eating disorder and symptomatic groups and intervene as early as possible. Body image groups that focus on decreasing internalization and the effects of societal pressures may be an effective intervention strategy with Female athletes.

Title: Perfectionism, disordered eating and well-being in aesthetic sports: the mediating role of passion

Sporting population:

this research and further extend our understanding of the psychological
processes involved in disordered eating and physical and psychological
well-being in a broader set of sports and participants.

Title: Psychological risk indicators of disordered eating in athletes
Authors: Stoyel, H., Shanmuganathan-Felton, V., Meyer, C., & Serpell, L.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to be over 18; there was no upper cap on the age of potential participants. Participants had to consider themselves to be an athlete, and a minimum of 10 hours a week participating in their sport as well as have been actively competing, thus meaning that competitive sport-rather than zealous exercise was a significant part of their daily experience.
Sport_name: Swimming, tennis, football, basketball, volleyball, dancing, track and field, golf, boxing, equestrian, cycling, ping-pong, orienteering, rugby, rowing and race walking
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Societal pressures mediated by internalisation, are associated with binge eating and bulimia, while body dissatisfaction leads to bulimia and binge eating, mediated by negative affect.
Limits: Cross sectional nature. None of the measurements scale were specifically designed for athletes. The scale for social media usage and modelled behaviours were purpose-built. for this study and thus were not formally validated in previous research and so had lower Cronbach alpha coefficients than would normally be acceptable. This research is limited in its ability to make sound assumptions on clinical implications.
Perspectives: Future research should use a longitudinal design to determine whether the relevant factors are able to predict future disordered eating in an athlete sample. Repeated this research with athletes younger than 18 years old would also provide additional insight as it is a high risk population for the development of eating disorders. A qualitative investigation to further understand the differences between the original etiological model and the revised model will also be undertaken.

Title: Muscle dysmorphia and its associated psychological features in three groups of recreational athletes
Authors: Cerea, S., Bottesi, G., Pacelli, Q.F., Paoli, A., & Ghisi, M.
Population subgroup:
42 Bodybuilders (BB group) 
61 Strenght athletes (SA group)
22 Fitness practitioners (FP group)
Inclusion criteria: At least 18 years of age; absence of severe neurological or medical conditions; no current or past psychothic disorders; no evidence of intellectual disabilities; Italian athletes who trained regularly for recreational purposes: bodybuilders, strenght training athletes, and fitness practitioners.
Authors' conclusions: Self esteem is significaltly related to muscle dysmorphia. Perfectionism is non-significantly related to MD. Perfectionism socially prescribed is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Social phobia is significantly related to MD. Orthorexia is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Depression is significantly related to MD.
Limits: First the sample size was relativelly small which likely reduces the generalizability of our conclusions. Related to this issue, the statisticcal power of the employed regression design could not guarantee a reliable detection of MD predictors. Secondly, the online recruitmalet strategy we adopted under-sampled those without internet capability and prevented the opportunity of conducting face-to-face interviews of participants self-identified as recreational bodybuilders and recreational strength athletess. Lastly, the absence of psychometric information for the MPS is another limitation.
Perspectives: Improving the identification of predictors and risk factors for MD, as well as its associated psychological features, might facilitate the identification of at-risk trainers, as well as the development of prevention strategies and interventions. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of MD manifestation among athletes may help to distinguishing individuals participating in a healthy manner versus those participating in an unhealthy manner.

Title: Protective and risk factors in exercise addiction: a series of moderated mediation analyses
Authors: Gori, A., Topino, E., & Griffiths, M.D.
Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Inclusion criteria: Participants who engaged in regular exercise at leat three times per week for a minimum of 30 minutes each session
Mean_Exercise frequency: At least three per week for a minimum of 30 minutes each session
Authors' conclusions: The study focused on various risk factors for exercise addiction, and found relationships relating to drive for thinness, bulimia, body dissatisfaction, body image concerns, as well as an important protective role of self esteem.
Limits: A modestly sized convenience sample of regular exercisers was recruited utilizing a snowball sampling method. Only self-report measures were used to collect the data, and such data are known to include well-etablished methods biases, such as social desirability ad memory recall. The cross sectional design requires caution in interpreting causality.
Perspectives: Future research would need to implement longitudinal designs in order to determine the specific directions of the relationships examined. Replicate the study with larger more representative samples and utilizing different recruitmalet techniques.

Title: Correlates of eating disorders risk among Female figure skates: a profile of adolescent competitors
Authors: Monsma, E.V., & Malina, R.M.
Population subgroup:
Skaters solo
Skaters dance
Skaters pairs
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged between 12 and 22 years old; participants in four United States Figure Skating Association cluns and seven Canadian Figure Skating Association clubs
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for age and the BMI, social physique anxiety was related to the EDI accounting for 4% to 13% of the variance in five of the eight subscales. There is a positive correlation between SPA and maturity fears, bulimia and two EDI social adjustement. There is negative correlations between the EDI subscales and physical self perceptions indicated that skaters less satisfied with their physical characteristics reported higher EDI scores. Physical self perception explained a significant portion of the variance in each EDI subscale after controlling for age and body size. Satisfaction with body fat predicted both drive for thinness and body dissatisfaction.
Limits: N.A.
Perspectives: Future investigations should consider information on male partners and the potential mediating effects of SPA and self concept in the development of disordered eating. Maintaining or improving physical self perceptions may be an important foundation in the prevention of eating disorders, especially with skaters who skate with male partners.

Title: Disordered eating attitudes, anxiety, self esteem and perfectionism in young athletes and non athletes
Authors: Petisco-Rodriguez, C., Sanchez-Sanchez, L.C., Fernandez-Garcia, R., Sanchez-Sanchez, J., & Garcia-Montes, J.M.
Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Population subgroup:
40 Athletes competing in rhythmic gymnastics
40 Athletes competing in football
40 Non-athletes
Inclusion criteria: Membership in Spanish sport clubs or rhythmic gymnastics, or footballers with a background > 4 years of systematic training and competitive experience, training a minimum of 8h per week, with absence of severe injuries
Mean_Age:
Gymnasts M=16.6, SD=2.62
Footballers M=17.98, SD=3.42
Mean_BMI:
M=20.§3, SD=2.77
Gymnasts M=18.72, SD=1.54
Footballers M=22.45, SD=2.93
Sporting population: Gymnasts group consisted of 5 elite competing internationally and 35 at the national level
Range_Exercise frequency:
Elites : 20-35h per week
National gymnasts : 12-20h per week
Footballers : 4 training sessions plus a competitive match per week
Range_Years of experience: Minimum 4 years of training and competitive experience
Authors' conclusions: Correlation obtained between anxiety (both trait and state) and the EAT-40 was positively and statistically significant. In the multiple regression analysis that was performed with SCOFF scores as a dependent variable, the most predictive variable was socially prescribed perfectionism. It showed negative correlation with EAT-40 and self esteem. Self esteem is probably a protective factor to develop an eating disorder despite perfectionism, which is the most predictive variable as the multiple linear regression showed, and this variable was high in athletes.
Limits: Small sample size. No precise clinical diagnostic data were available to validate ED screening in the current study.
Perspectives:
In the future, the use of other kinds of measurements, less subjected to the desirability bias, would help to discriminate whether the improvements in self-esteem and eating disorders in elite gymnasts are due to this bias or to preventing psychological treatments and trainings by coaches.
 In addition, it is important to further explore the impact of other psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours such as body image, mood, depression or motivation, among others; due to the fact that they imply multifactorial aetiology of disorders.

Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes
Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.
Inclusion criteria: NCAA Divisions I Female collegiate athletes drawn from three universities located in the Midwest, Soutwest, and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: gymnastics; rowing; softball; synchronized swimming; tennis; alpine skiing; basketball; cross country; cheerleading; diving; golf; field hockey; lacrosse; soccer; swimming; track and field; volleyball
Related_Factor_measure: Marlowe-Crowne Social Desirability Scale Form B
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Only higher levels of body dissatifaction, a greater focus on diet and restricting food intake, and stronger feelings of guilt were related significantly to BULIT-R scores.
Limits: All the data collected were self reported and susceptible to socially desirable responding. The racial/ethnic makeup of the sample; our sample was predominantly Caucasian, thus limiting the generalizability to similar samples of Female college athletes. The cross sectional design of the study does not allow for the determination of the temporal nature of the relationships between psychosocial variables and bulimic symptoms.
Perspectives:
Use prospective design.

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: The relationship between perceived stress, body image and eating behaviors in athletes
Authors: Şentürk, G., Deliceoğlu, G., Atasoy, M., & Yıldırım, İ.G.
Journal: Research in Sport Education and Sciences
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between the ages of 13-23 who volunteered to participate
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism in athletes is linked to higher stress, eating disturbances, and body perception issues, with women showing higher stress, emotional eating, and restrictive eating behaviors. Emotional states significantly influence eating patterns, highlighting the need for psychological and nutritional support in sports contexts
Limits: Findings are partly inconsistent with previous studies (e.g., gender differences), and results may depend on specific sports or samples. The study also relies on self-reported measures, which may introduce bias
Perspectives: Future research should further explore emotional eating across different sports and genders, and develop targeted interventions. Integrating psychological support, education, and nutritional guidance could help improve athletes’ well-being and performance

Title: The impact of critical comments from teammates on athletes eating and exercise psychopathology

Critical comment M=9.61h/week, SD=6.65
No critical comment M=8.29, SD=5.46
Mean_Years of experience:
Critical comment M=7.35, SD=6.41
No critical comment M=6.12, SD=5.58
Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

Title: Protective and risk factors in exercise addiction: a series of moderated mediation analyses
Authors: Gori, A., Topino, E., & Griffiths, M.D.
Journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Inclusion criteria: Participants who engaged in regular exercise at leat three times per week for a minimum of 30 minutes each session
Mean_Exercise frequency: At least three per week for a minimum of 30 minutes each session
Authors' conclusions: The study focused on various risk factors for exercise addiction, and found relationships relating to drive for thinness, bulimia, body dissatisfaction, body image concerns, as well as an important protective role of self esteem.
Limits: A modestly sized convenience sample of regular exercisers was recruited utilizing a snowball sampling method.
