Title: Eating pathology in Female gymnasts: potential risk and protective factors
Authors: Harriger, J.A., Witherington, D.C., & Bryan, A.D.
Inclusion criteria: Females athletes involved in competitive gymnastics at a non-collegiate or non-elite level; between the age of 10-15 years
Authors' conclusions: Gymnasts who report spending more time training seem to be protected from pathological eating disturbances and that high levels of self esteem may serve as a more direct protective mechanism.
Limits: The sample size was relatively small. It is not feasible to determine why 14% elected not to participate, and it is possible that they may have differed from those who participated in the research. The self-report nature nature of the study may have been problematic in that it was difficult to assess for accuracy and honesty in these measures. The cross sectional design does not allow for an actual test of the dynamic process between the study variables across time and is therefore limited in what it can conclude about actual risk and protective factors. While the onset of puberty is typically associated with a significant weight gain for Females, it may be that, due to training regimens, gymnasts in the current study had not gained a considerable amount of weight, even though they reported experiencing accompanying development changes such as breast developmale t and growth of body hair.
Perspectives: Future studies would benefit from the addition of a procedure that analyzes body fat or using a longitudinal design to assess for weight gain during puberty. Continued exploration of this population is vital in order ton increase understanding of these and additional factors that may predispose or protect gymnasts from body dissatisfaction and pathological eating disturbances.

Title: Social predictors of psychological need satisfaction and well being among Female adolescent gymnasts: a longitudinal analysis
Authors: Kipp, L.E., & Weiss, M.R.
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts; aged 10 to 18; trained 15.2hr per week; competed in US gymnastics sanctioned meets, and represented the full range of competitive levels
DEAB_measure: Dieting subscale of the Children's Eating Attitude Test
Authors' conclusions: Perceptions of mastery climate, autonomy-support, and performance climate at preseason predicted higher self esteem and lower disordered eating during competitive season, through mediation of perceived competence.
Limits: We included a purposeful sample of competitive gymnasts, so our results may not generalize to other youth sport contexts. It should be noted that after removing unreliable items, performance climate in our study only tapped the unequal recognition aspect. Participants reported low lecels of performance climate. We could not examine the effect of controlling behaviors because this construct showed a poor fit in the model.
Perspectives: More theory driven longitudinal studies can determine relationships and mediation over time and inform interventions to promote well-being among youth partcicipants. Future research should continue to consider indices of physical, social, emotional, and cognitive maturity with youth samples to control for developmental differences in well-being outcomes.

Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes
Authors: Greenleaf, C., Petrie, T., Reel, J., & Carter, J.
Inclusion criteria: NCAA Divisions I Female collegiate athletes drawn from three universities located in the Midwest, Soutwest, and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: gymnastics; rowing; softball; synchronized swimming; tennis; alpine skiing; basketball; cross country; cheerleading; diving; golf; field hockey; lacrosse; soccer; swimming; track and field; volleyball
Related_Factor_measure: Marlowe-Crowne Social Desirability Scale Form B
Authors' conclusions: The inclusion of each set of variables (internalization, body dissatisfaction, dietary intent, and negative affect) contributed significantly to the prediction of bulimic symptomatology, accounting for 42% of the variance. Perspectives:
Use prospective design. 
Research can be advanced by improving measurement of affect, to capture temporal ebb and flow of mood as it relates to eating attitudes and behaviors.

Title: Perfectionism and eating attitudes in competitive rowers: moderating effects of body mass, weight classification and gender
Authors: Haase, A.M., Prapavessis, H., & Owens, G.
Inclusion criteria: National level heavyweight and lightweight rowers from New Zealand and Australia
Mean_Age:
Female M=20.08, SD=4.23
Male M=21.49, SD=4.67
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for social desirability effects, negative perfectionism scores were found to correlate positively with disturbed eating attitudes scores, whereas positive perfectionism scores were found to be unrelated to disturbed eating attitude scores.
Limits: Focus only on rowing sample.
Perspectives:
This would suggest that resiliency against unhealthy eating could be increased by teaching athletes how to develop and maintain high levels of positive perfectionism. Intervention with goal in mind is a worthy topic for future research. 
Do these perfectionistic tendencies change throughout an athlete's career ? How and why do these changes occur ? What implications do these changes have on eating attitude ?

Title: Correlates of eating disorders risk among Female figure skates: a profile of adolescent competitors
Authors: Monsma, E.V., & Malina, R.M.
Population subgroup:
Skaters solo
Skaters dance
Skaters pairs
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged between 12 and 22 years old; participants in four United States Figure Skating Association cluns and seven Canadian Figure Skating Association clubs
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for age and the BMI, social physique anxiety was related to the EDI accounting for 4% to 13% of the variance in five of the eight subscales. Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Inclusion criteria: Dancers aged 10-18 years
Mean_Age:

Authors' conclusions: Correlates of DE that may be used as halth warnings for young dancers include perfectionism and, for Females, excessives exercising outside of dance, sleep disturbances, and malestrual dysfunction.

Title: How the obsession to eat healthy food meets with the willingness to do sports: the motivational background of orthorexia nervosa
Authors: Kiss-Leizer, M., Toth-Jiraly, I., & Rigo, A.
Inclusion criteria: Participants aged between 18 to 72 years
Range_Exercise frequency:
37.2% 3-4 times per week
25.8% 1-2h weekly
25% 3-4h 
35.2% for 5 or more than 5h
Related_Factor_measure: Motivation for Healthy Behaviors in Orthorexia Nervosa Qyestionnaire (MHBONQ)
Authors' conclusions: Health anxiety, mood modification are a strong predictor of orthorexia nervosa.
Limits: The results of the present study were based on online data gathering which questions the representative nature of the sample. Although participants were represented in a broad range of age and educational level, the highest proportion of participants were young and highly qualified Female. The participation in the research was voluntary thus the increased interest towards the topic of the examination might bias the results. The correlational desing of the present study does not allow causal inferences. The subject of the present study was the tendency to orthorexia nercosa, not orthorexia nervosa as a diagnosis, the results cannot be fully transposed into orthorexia nervosa since no orthorexia diagnosed patients are available yet.
Perspectives: A viable next step in orthorexia nervosa research could be the use of experience sampling method which could provide important information about the daily fluctuation of orthorexia nervosa and the related variables. It would be benefical to collect information about the type of the exercise as well, because some sport activities (category sports, aesthetic sport) can mean a higher vulnerability to orthorexia.

Title: The impact of critical comments from teammates on athletes eating and exercise psychopathology
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Adults aged 18 and over from local sport clubs
Mean_Age:
Critical comment M=23.27, SD=8.34
No critical group M=23.20, SD=8.67
Mean_BMI:
Critical comment M=22.70, SD=3.83
No critical comment M=22.56, SD=3.55
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Critical comment M=9.61h/week, SD=6.65
No critical comment M=8.29, SD=5.46
Mean_Years of experience:
Critical comment M=7.35, SD=6.41
No critical comment M=6.12, SD=5.58
Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

There is negative correlations between the EDI subscales and physical self perceptions indicated that skaters less satisfied with their physical characteristics reported higher EDI scores. Title: Teammate influences, psychological well-being, and athletes eating and exercise psychopathology: a moderated mediation analysis
Authors: Scott, C.L., Plateau, C.R., & Haycraft, E.

Mean_Years of experience: Member of their current team M=1.99, SD=2.61
Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. Gender was not a significant moderator, meaning that the role of psychological wellbeing in the relationships between teammate influences and eating.
Limits: Although age and BMI were controlled for, it is acknowledged that there are a number of additional co-variates (e.g., perfectionism, athletic identity) that could have contributed to the findings of this study. The self report nature of the data collected and the context it was collected in (i.e., before/after a training session and in the company of teammates/coach) may potentially misrepresent athletes true behaviours. Items comprising the EDI-drive for thinness and body dissatsifaction subscales may not be an accurate reflection of male athletes experiences with disordered eating.
Perspectives: Identifying key risk factors and relevant moderators and mediators for eating psychopathology is important for effectively identifying those athletes at increased risk of eating and exercise psychopathology, and for developing appropriately tailored intervention and prevention strategies. Future research into the role of teammates would benefit from experimentally manipulating mechanisms of teammate influence on athletes actual food intake and should consider employing methodologies that are specifically tailored to male athletes. Employing modeeling analytic techniques to further our understanding of the complex, multi-factorial influences on athlete eating and exercise behaviours.

Authors' conclusions: Self concept subdomains are indirectly related to disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors through their relations with global and physical self worth in non-elite athlete adolescent girls competing in different types of sports.

Perspectives: It would be interesting to investigate similar relations in a sample of elite basketball players for whom reliance on these more extreme stretagies would likely prove counter-productive in the long term.

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: Eating disordered behaviours in Portuguese athletes: the influence of personal, sport, and psychological variables
Authors: Gomes, A.R., Martins, C., & Silva, L.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between 14 and 30 year of age
Sport_name: Athletics; karate; swimming; taekwondo; basketball; handball; volleyball
Sporting population:
Top division (38.8%)
Regional or national levels
Authors' conclusions: The EDE-Q global score was positively associated with weight-related coach pressure, anxiety, taske orientation, impression motivation and threat perception, and negatively associated with less satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance. Eating behaviour was predicted by lower satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance, and higher anxiety and impression motivation.
Limits: Data were based on athletes self-report, which could have resulted in under-reporting of eating disordered behaviours. A better discrimination between sports according to their requirements needs to be introduced in order to better differentiate the demands and soecific characteristics of each sport. It is vital to further explore the impact of psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours.
Perspectives: It is important to assess athletes reactions in competition, the way they perceive themselves, and the way they want others to perceive them. If there is a better comprehension of these factors, then prevention of eating problems and promotion of better experiences in sport becomes easier to achieve.

Title: Prevalence and correlates of disordered eating in Female figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Gould, D., Reel, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged 12 to 25. Former skaters, basic skills skaters, and those in adult skating programs (e.g., age-based competitions following adult test equivalencies) were excluded
Sport_name: Figure skating (singles, multiple, synchronized, ice dancing, pairs)
Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. Body dissatisfaction explained an additional 5.7% of the variance in disordered eating. Sport related body dissatisfaction also emerged as a significant predictor. Positive perfectionism made a significant contribution, but negative perfectionism did not. Self esteem may not be strongly related to disordered eating. Athletic identity did not emerge as a significant variable in the final regression model, although the bivariate correlation indicated a significant positive relationship with disordered eating.
Limits: Societal weight pressures were not exmained. Self report nature of the surveys and the willingness of athletes to honestly and accurately respond to survey items. The results are also based on a conveniance sample of skaters limited to clubs in the Midwest and Northeast. Cross sectional design, causal relationships and change over time could not be determined.
Perspectives:
Sport psychology practiitioners should aid this effort by teaching skaters to appreciate body strengths and utilize psychological skills that may buffer the impact of negative weight pressures (e.g., utilizing positive self talk and realistic goal-setting). 
A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.

Title: Muscle dysmorphia and its associated psychological features in three groups of recreational athletes
Authors: Cerea, S., Bottesi, G., Pacelli, Q.F., Paoli, A., & Ghisi, M.

42 Bodybuilders (BB group) 
61 Strenght athletes (SA group)
22 Fitness practitioners (FP group)
Inclusion criteria: At least 18 years of age; absence of severe neurological or medical conditions; no current or past psychothic disorders; no evidence of intellectual disabilities; Italian athletes who trained regularly for recreational purposes: bodybuilders, strenght training athletes, and fitness practitioners.
Authors' conclusions: Self esteem is significaltly related to muscle dysmorphia. Perfectionism is non-significantly related to MD. Perfectionism socially prescribed is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Social phobia is significantly related to MD. Orthorexia is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Depression is significantly related to MD.
Limits: First the sample size was relativelly small which likely reduces the generalizability of our conclusions. Related to this issue, the statisticcal power of the employed regression design could not guarantee a reliable detection of MD predictors. Secondly, the online recruitmalet strategy we adopted under-sampled those without internet capability and prevented the opportunity of conducting face-to-face interviews of participants self-identified as recreational bodybuilders and recreational strength athletess. Lastly, the absence of psychometric information for the MPS is another limitation.
Perspectives: Improving the identification of predictors and risk factors for MD, as well as its associated psychological features, might facilitate the identification of at-risk trainers, as well as the development of prevention strategies and interventions. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of MD manifestation among athletes may help to distinguishing individuals participating in a healthy manner versus those participating in an unhealthy manner.

Title: Protective and risk factors in exercise addiction: a series of moderated mediation analyses

Authors' conclusions: The study focused on various risk factors for exercise addiction, and found relationships relating to drive for thinness, bulimia, body dissatisfaction, body image concerns, as well as an important protective role of self esteem.
Limits: A modestly sized convenience sample of regular exercisers was recruited utilizing a snowball sampling method. Only self-report measures were used to collect the data, and such data are known to include well-etablished methods biases, such as social desirability ad memory recall. The cross sectional design requires caution in interpreting causality.
Perspectives: Future research would need to implement longitudinal designs in order to determine the specific directions of the relationships examined. Replicate the study with larger more representative samples and utilizing different recruitmalet techniques.

Title: Examining the influence of crossfit participation on body image, self-esteem, and eating behaviours among Female
Authors: Coyne, P., & Woodruff, S.J.
Journal: Journal of Physical Education and Sport
Inclusion criteria: Be member of one of the five CrossFit affiliates located in Southwestern Ontario (Canada) in two midsized cities
Authors' conclusions: The multiple linear regression revealed that length of time since beginning crossfit was a small, but significant predictor of Female's eating behaviours, with longer attendance predicting lower disordered scores.
Limits: First, only five crossfit affiliates were included in this study. As such, the results of this study may not be generalizable to the entire crossfit population. Additionally, although it would have been preferred to have crossfit variables objectively measured, for reasons of feasibility, these crossfit variables were self-reported. This study is aslo limited as demographic variables, such as race or ethnicity, were not taken into consideration, depiste being potentially influential. In addition, surveys were not completed in a randomized order, preventing the researchers from eliminating order bias and potentially relevant demographic covariates were not included in the analysis.
Perspectives: Future research could benefit from investigating if members of crossfit affiliates perceive nutrition-related recommaledations offered by crossfit to be healthy or whether they identify thems as encouraging disordered eating. Future studies may benefit from using a more domain-specific measure of self-esteem.

Title: The Mediating Role of Self-Criticism in the Relationship Between Coaches’ Leadership Styles and Disordered Eating in Athletes
Authors: Coelho, C., Oliveira, D., Branco, C., Rui Gomes, A., Conceiçao, E., Machado, P.P.P., Gonçalves, S.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competing at the senior level in Portugal
Related_Factor_measure: Self-Criticism Subscales of the Forms of Self-Criticizing and Reassuring Scale (FSCRS), Portuguese version
Authors' conclusions: This study shows that negative coaching styles are associated with disordered eating through increased self-criticism, while positive leadership styles help reduce self-criticism. It highlights self-criticism as a key psychological mechanism linking coaching behaviors to eating pathology.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, small sample size, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference and generalizability. Lack of control for key variables (e.g., age, sport type) may also influence results.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and multi-informant designs to clarify causal pathways. Interventions targeting coaching styles, self-compassion, and support services are promising strategies to prevent disordered eating in athletes.

Rhythmic gymnasts M=18.3, SD=1.2

DEAB_measure: The French Version of Eating Attitudes Test (EAT-26)
Related_Factor_measure: The French version of self-esteem scale
Authors' conclusions: Actual weight and low self esteem were not predictive of DE; no significant relationship was found between body esteem for appearance and eating attitudes scores. Only body esteem for weight and body esteem attribution emerged as statistically significant. There were correlations between self-esteem and body self-esteem in the three groups, components of body esteem appear to be better predictors of EAT scores.
Limits: First the sample involved 152 Female adolescents. Their consent was obtained after an informational session regarding the study, so some Female with eating issues may have chosen not to participate. Second, the relatively small number of participants in each group can suggest the caution should be applied in generalizing results. It should be noted that the problem of an important heteroscedasticity of the EAT-26 scores which cannot be solved by data transformation dissuaded us from using a global model. Third, it should be noted that the data collected for this study were self-reported. The self-report method can result in under-reporting of disordered eating symptoms in Female athletes.
Perspectives: Further research should involve a larger sample of aesthetic athletes and provide access to a wider variety of aesthetic sports. However, it would also be interesting to differentiate the role of direct and indirect social pressure in aesthetic sports and to understand how Female athletes interpret and react differently to them to achieve the perceived ideal body image. It would be interesting not to focus just on the pressures exerced by the coach but also to question the influence of peers. A clearer understanding og how these different pressures operate and interact may provide crucial information for the perceptions of the role of others and guide the content of specific intervention programmes.

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

There is a positive correlation between SPA and maturity fears, bulimia and two EDI social adjustement. There is negative correlations between the EDI subscales and physical self perceptions indicated that skaters less satisfied with their physical characteristics reported higher EDI scores. Physical self perception explained a significant portion of the variance in each EDI subscale after controlling for age and body size. Satisfaction with body fat predicted both drive for thinness and body dissatisfaction.
Limits: N.A.
Perspectives: Future investigations should consider information on male partners and the potential mediating effects of SPA and self concept in the development of disordered eating. Maintaining or improving physical self perceptions may be an important foundation in the prevention of eating disorders, especially with skaters who skate with male partners.

Title: Health-Related Quality of Life in Adolescent Athletes: Correlations With Energy Availability, Disordered Eating, and Compulsive Exercise Behaviors
Authors: Armento, A.M., Brna, M., Seehusen, C., Hagman, J., McCarthy, A., VanBaak, K.D., Howell, D.R.
Inclusion criteria: Males and females of ages 13 to 18 years, who were participating in at least 1 organized sports team
Mean_Age: Males M=15.3, SD=1.3 Females M=15.6, SD=1.6
Mean_BMI: Males M=20.7, SD=3.7 Females M=20.4, SD=2.9
Sport_name: Soccer, Football, Swimming, diving, baseball, basketball, lacrosse, track and field, cross country, volleyball, dance, track and field, softball, tennis, ice hockey
Authors' conclusions: This study shows that disordered eating is significantly associated with lower HRQOL in adolescent athletes, even at subclinical levels, particularly affecting psychosocial functioning. Female athletes appear more vulnerable to reduced HRQOL.
Limits: Methodological challenges in measuring energy availability, reliance on self-reported data, and limited generalizability (single region, sport dominance, no control group) may affect the findings.
Perspectives: Future studies should explore mediating factors and better assess energy availability and symptoms. Early screening and targeted interventions are essential to improve HRQOL in young athletes.

Title: The relationship between social and disordered eating in college-aged Female gymnasts
Authors: Ausmus, J.C., Blom, L.C., Bowman, S., Lebeau, J.C.
Inclusion criteria: Participants were recruited from club gyms and colleges throughout the united states via email, social media, and word of mouth to coaches, support staff and directly to athletes; Females between 18-25 years; self identify as competitive gymnasts; must have competed within the last three years
Sporting population: 87.67% competed in varsity level gymnastics, 6.85% stated that they participated in recreational gymnastics, 5.48% competed in clubs gymnastics
Related_Factor_measure: Two questions developed by Sidani, Shensa, Hoffman, Hanmer, and Primack (2015) were used to estimate how often participants used social media in a 24-hour period
Authors' conclusions: This study did not find significant correlations between criticism received on social media and disordered eating behaviors in college gymnasts. Combining variables related to social hassles, body satisfaction, usage of certain social media outlets, and years of participation could perdict disordered eating. No relationship were found between social media variables and disordered eating behaviors.
Limits: The main limitation of this study was the sample size of the participants. Although measures were exhausted in the recruitmalet of participants; it may have been beneficial to have sent the recruitmalet materials out earlier in the off season as opposed to a month before the college gymnastics season started. Another limitation was the limited reliability data for the Social Hassles Questionnaire, as it is relatively new instrument and has not been extensively tested. Furthermore this study did not account for mental health status beyond possible disordered eating behaviors.
Perspectives:
Since depression and anxiety have been linked to disordered eating patterns, future studies should also consider these pathologies, along with self-esteem. Research should aim to better understand the relationship between social media criticism and disordered eating behaviors in athletic populations. Athletes from different sports may respond differently to criticism than gymnasts, so it could be valuable to study these variables in other aesthetic sports, such as figure skating, diving, cheerleading, or even non-aesthetic sports like softball or basketball. Additionally, exploring these factors in males involved in aesthetic sports and the overall impact of social media on athletes' mental health could provide important insights.

It would also be beneficial for athletes, parents, and other significant figures in athletes' lives to be trained in recognizing the signs of disordered eating behaviors. Such training could help raise awareness of the potential dangers of social media platforms like Snapchat and offer guidance on how to support athletes if disordered eating behaviors arise.

To counter the effects of social media criticism on athletes, education initiatives should target coaches, families, friends, and athletes themselves to prevent the development of harmful eating behaviors and patterns, both now and in the future.

Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions
Authors: Olave, L., Estévez, A., Momene, J., Penacoba, C., Macia, P., Macia, L., Etxaburu, N., Muniz, J.A., Iruarrizaga, I.
Inclusion criteria: People who practice physical exercise at least one day a week
Authors' conclusions: The study highlights strong links between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia, and multiple addictions, with impulsivity playing a key mediating role. These findings emphasize the importance of targeting impulsivity and emotion regulation in prevention and treatment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and the use of a homogeneous convenience sample limits generalizability. Additionally, reliance on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses may affect accuracy.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify causal relationships and further explore specific dimensions of impulsivity. There is also a need to develop prevention and intervention strategies focusing on emotion regulation and impulsivity

Title: Prevalence and correlates of disordered eating in Female figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Gould, D., Reel, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged 12 to 25. Former skaters, basic skills skaters, and those in adult skating programs (e.g., age-based competitions following adult test equivalencies) were excluded
Sport_name: Figure skating (singles, multiple, synchronized, ice dancing, pairs)
Related_Factor: Importance of weight and appearance to family and friends
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Related Weight Pressures in Sport Scale-Females (WPS-F)
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: External eating and Weight related concerns
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Importance of weight and appearance to family and friends
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Importance of weight and appearance to family and friends
Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. Body dissatisfaction explained an additional 5.7% of the variance in disordered eating. Sport related body dissatisfaction also emerged as a significant predictor. Positive perfectionism made a significant contribution, but negative perfectionism did not. Self esteem may not be strongly related to disordered eating. Athletic identity did not emerge as a significant variable in the final regression model, although the bivariate correlation indicated a significant positive relationship with disordered eating.
Limits: Societal weight pressures were not exmained. Self report nature of the surveys and the willingness of athletes to honestly and accurately respond to survey items. The results are also based on a conveniance sample of skaters limited to clubs in the Midwest and Northeast. Cross sectional design, causal relationships and change over time could not be determined.
Perspectives:
Sport psychology practiitioners should aid this effort by teaching skaters to appreciate body strengths and utilize psychological skills that may buffer the impact of negative weight pressures (e.g., utilizing positive self talk and realistic goal-setting). 
A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.

Title: Parental relationships, emotion regulation and orthorexia: a study on adolescent athletes
Authors: D'Urso, G., Maynard, A., Lionetti, F., Spinelli, M., & Fasolo, M.
Population subgroup:
139 Athletes (competitive sport that involves practice at least 3 or 4 days per week and at least 2-3 hours per practice)
164 Non-athletes
Inclusion criteria: Italian adolescents attending high school during the 2020–2021 school year
Related_Factor_measure: Inventory of Parent and Peer Attachment (IPPA)
Authors' conclusions: The mediation analysis suggests that inadequate relational styles with parents can invaludate the emotional regulation of adolescents and encourage orthorexia behaviours.
Limits: First, the use of self-report questionnaires could provide information that is not pure because answers might be affected by social desirability. Another limitation is the cross-sectional nature of the current study.
Perspectives:
Coach and practicioners could incorporate aspects of emotional regulation interventions into practices or as supplemental activities to the season. For example, the coach could incorporate lunches with a sport psychologist, who could discuss emotional regulation tactics with the athletes. Similarly, the coach could incorporate goal-setting activities throughout the season, with a focus on how to set smart goals, and then how to regulate emotions through the challenges of achieving such goals. 
Future research could verify this model in a multi-time perspective as well as including personality and social variables that can be configured as risk and/or protective factors for the etiology of orthorexia. Finally, a longitudinal persceptive would enable a better exploration, through adolescent development, of the indivdiual differences in terms of both emotional and family variables, mainly in adolescents at risk of compulsive behaviours.

Title: Maladaptive perfectionism as mediator among psychological control, eating disorders, and exercise dependence symptoms in habitual exerciser
Authors: Costa, S., Hausenblas, H.A., Oliva, P., Cuzzocrea, F., & Larcan, R.
Inclusion criteria: Inclusion criteria were that exerciser had trained for at least 6 consecutive months, lived at home with both parents, and were at least 18 years of age.
Authors' conclusions: There is a significant relationship between parental psychological control and both exercise dependence and eating disorder symptoms. Psychological control, both maternal and parternal, predicted maladaptive perfectionism, while maladaptive perfectionism, predicted ED symptoms and exercise dependence symptoms. Results confirmed the mediating role of maladaptive perfectionism as a full mediator for ED and exercise dependence symptoms for both male and Female habitual exercisers in the maternal data. In the paternal data, maladaptive perfectionism mediated the relationships between paternal psychological control and eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms as full mediator for the Female participants and as partial mediator for the male participants.
Limits: First, the data were collected at one time point and not across multiple time points as it should be done for a true mediational analysis. Because of the cross-sectional and self-report design of our study, we cannot etablish either the direction or causality of the effects. As weel, the self-report data may have intrinsic limitations such as social desirability, so the use of objective and multi-informant measures and experimental designs are encourages. Although, our sample consisted of habitual exercisers, this sample was deemed justified, as eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms are prevalent in this population and because psychological control is a risk factor for eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms in this population.
Perspectives: The deleterious effects of parental psychological control, both on eating disorder and on exercise dependence symptoms, require the implementation of targeted interventions to educate parents in using fewer instrusions and parental autonomy support, as opposed to psychological control. It is important to educate parents about psychological control being a universally negative parenting strategy and to help parents identify and reduce the use of such dysfunctional practices. Parent training could be used to help parents to get to practice autonomy supportive skills by taking part in various exercices from common situations in familial daily living. Results of the study suggest that the therapist and client could work together to identify and correct the client's maladaptive perfectionism thought processes that result in maladaptive eating or exercise behavior.

Title: The relationship between exercise addiction, eating disorders, and insecure attachment styles among recreational exercisers
Authors: Lev Arey, D., Sagi, A., & Blatt, A.
Inclusion criteria: Recreational exercisers who engage in a minimum of 4h of exercise per week
Sport_name: Running, triathlon, gym workouts, swimming, aerobics, biking, yoga, boxing, basketball, crossfit
Authors' conclusions: An anxious attachment was linked to eating disorder.
Limits: The restricted sample that was included. This study relied on self-administered questionnaires, which may have introduced social desirability and recall biases. The evaluation tools used were screening tools with no diagnostic validity.
Perspectives: Future research should explore the bidirectional relationship between insecure attachment and eating disorders. It would be valuable for future research to investigate the directionality and underlying mechanisms of the relationship between insecure attachment and eating disorder.

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: Interpersonal difficulties as a risk factor for athletes eating psychopathology
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
Inclusion criteria: British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, judo, rugby, football, hockey
Authors' conclusions: Negative and positive aspects of the quality of the coach athlete and teammate athlete were related to athletes eating psychopathology after controlling for baseline eating psychopathology score. Conflict with the coach was found to be the only significant independent predictor of athletes eating psychopathology. The quality of the relationship with parents and attachmalet styles were not found to be related to athletes eating psychopathology 6 months later.
Limits: The present findings are essentially correlational, thus preventing definitive conclusions about causality. The present study only examined the direct role of interpersonal relationships in atletes eating psychopathology. Fairburn et al. (2003) noted that interpersonal difficulties interact with other core psychopathological processes (low self esteem, clinical perfectionism, and mood intolerance) to potentially elicit and maintain eating disorders.
Perspectives: Future studies should seek to examine how such processes as clinical perfectionism, self esteem, and mood intolerance interact with interpersonal difficulties to elicit eating psychopathology . And investigaite how these interpersonal variables interact with each other to predict athletes eating psychopathology.

Title: Eating disorders in Taekwondo athletes: the contribution of coach behavior, body satisfaction, and goal orientation
Authors: Baric, R., Erdeljac, T.
Inclusion criteria: Active practice of Taekwondo for at least 6 months and being a competitor in one of three competities categories: cadets, junior athletes or senior athletes
Sporting population:
17.3% top elite athletes, members of national selection and elite athletes
25 elite male
33 elite female
107 non-elite male
170 non-elite female
DEAB_measure: Croatian version of the Eating Attitudes Test (EAT_26)
Authors' conclusions: Goal orientation, body dissatisfaction, and negative behavior and pressure from coaches significantly contribute to the risk of ED development in female and male cadet, junior and non-elite athletes, while body dissatisfaction seems to be the strongest predictor, especially in female athletes.
Limits: The sample size, although it is realistic in relation to the number of active taekwondo competitors in Croatia. Self reported questionnaires.
Perspectives: Including other measures, more adjusted to male ED symptoms. As the results showed the significance of the behavior of coaches in relation to athletes ED symptoms, it would be very interesting to investigate the transgenerational transfer of distorted values, beliefs and behaviors related to ED from coaches to athletes, i.e., to investigate coaches history of ED symptoms and their current behavior.

Title: Effect of locus of control on disordered eating in athletes: the mediational role of self regulation of eating attitudes
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Paquet, Y., & d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
Inclusion criteria: University students who regularly (i.e., 6h per week) practised a sport in regional and national competitions
Related_Factor_measure: Multidimensional Health Locus of Control Scale (MHLCS)
Authors' conclusions: We observed a negative influence of the locus of control attributed to the coach on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and lack of anticipation of consequences on performance. The coach and sports firends contribute to maladaptive patterns of accomplishment and function as negative predictors of the self regulation of eating attitudes in several contexts. The results showed the positive influence of an internal locus of control on the self regulation of eating attitudes in the context of social interaction. We observed a negative influence of self regulatory eating attitudes on disordered eating in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and the absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. This study demonstrated the influence of an internal locus of control on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in a context of social interaction and the influence of an external locus of control, attributed to the coach and sports friends on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in context of negative affect, social interaction and an absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. This study did not reveal a significant influence of a locus of control attributed to the family or luck on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of temptation or negative affect. The self regulation subscales were not significant in the contexts of food temptation and a lack of compensatory strategies.
Limits: The data were self reported, which suggests that social desirability may have been a bias. The study used correlational and cross sectional methods, which limits the generalization of the relationships.
Perspectives:
The social environment has a powerful impact on the development of disordered eating in athletes; the influence of these social relationship on athletes self regulatory eating attitudes merits further study, through an emphasis on locus of control and/or relationship quality. A longitudinal study would determine the stability of this impact and an experimental study would help to etablish the direction of the causality. 
The use of locus of control and self regulatory eating attitudes as concurrent variables may be useful to sports psychology practitioners in their work with athletes. They might also be used to evaluate an athlete ability to engage in new and better adapted eating strategies and to determine whether the development of new eating attitudes would benefit performance outcomes.

Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions
Authors: Olave, L., Estévez, A., Momene, J., Penacoba, C., Macia, P., Macia, L., Etxaburu, N., Muniz, J.A., Iruarrizaga, I.
Inclusion criteria: People who practice physical exercise at least one day a week
Authors' conclusions: The study highlights strong links between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia, and multiple addictions, with impulsivity playing a key mediating role. These findings emphasize the importance of targeting impulsivity and emotion regulation in prevention and treatment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and the use of a homogeneous convenience sample limits generalizability. Additionally, reliance on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses may affect accuracy.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify causal relationships and further explore specific dimensions of impulsivity. There is also a need to develop prevention and intervention strategies focusing on emotion regulation and impulsivity

Title: Symptoms of muscle dysmorphia, body dysmorphic disorder, and eating disorders in a nonclinical population of adulte male weightlifters in Australia
Authors: Nieuwoudt, J.E., Zhou, S., Coutts, R.A., & Booker, R.
Journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: Adult males at least 18 years of age; individuals who are working out with weights (i.e., free weight or machines) at least 3 times per week and currently residing in Australia
Mean_Exercise frequency: At least 3 days or more per week
Authors' conclusions: Significant correlation were found between muscle dysmorphia and body dysmorphic disorder symptoms. The correlational data suggested a relationship between the symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and eating disorders. Small but significant correlations were found between the substance use subscale of the MASS and the laxatives, diuretics behavioral question of the EAT-26, between the injury risk subscale of the MASS and the vomit and exercise behavioral questions of the EAT-26, and between the muscle satisfaction subscale and the binge eating and the lost > 9kg behavioral questions of the EAT-26.
Limits: The EAT-26 may not be sensitive to muscularity oriented disordered eating and body image concerns. The current research consisted of an online survey, therefore the possibility existed that participants might have interpreted the meanings of questions or statements differently to those intended or might have perceived some of the statements or questions as vague. Self selection bias is a limitation of internet surveys. The data were exclusively based on self report which can have tendencies toward social desirability bias.
Perspectives: A better understanding and awareness of the rates and symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and body dismorphic disorder and eating disorders may help strength and conditioning professionals to identify and refer at risk individuals for help from mental health professionals.

Title: A longitudinal investigation of performance and injury outcomes associated with disordered eating in elite athletes
Authors: Fatt, S.J., Hay, P., George, E., Jeacocke, N., Rogers, K., Mitchison, D.
Population subgroup: Males T1 n=47 Males T2 n=25 Males T3 n=22 Females T1 n=126 Females T2 n=83 Females T3 n=63
Inclusion criteria: Current elite athletes who participated in the baseline (T1), 6 month follow-up (T2), and 12-month follow-up (T3) surveys
Sport_name: Lean sport, endurance sport, weight-class sport, aesthetic sport, anti-gravitational sports
Sporting population: Elite athletes (i.e., national, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level)
Related_Factor_measure: Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q)
Authors' conclusions: Disordered eating did not improve performance over time but was associated with poorer performance and increased injury-related absence, particularly over 6 months. This highlights its negative impact on athletes’ health and participation
Limits: The study relied on self-reported measures of performance and injury, which may be biased, and used a specific sample with limited diversity, affecting generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use more objective performance and injury measures, examine longer timeframes, and include more diverse athlete populations to better understand underlying mechanisms

Authors: Lantz, C.D., Rhea, D.J., & Mesnier, K.
Journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
Inclusion criteria: Participants from the 80-km race must have previously completed at least 1 competitive ultramarathon and participants from the 160-km race must have completed a 100-km race in less than 13h or a 160-km race in fewer than 24h, depending on age.
Mean_Exercise frequency:
M=37.74mi/week, SD=25.57
Males M=48.38mi/week, SD=25.15
Females M=34.58mi/week, SD=28.88
Authors' conclusions: Exercise identity had a significant positive correlation with eating attitudes and injury tolerance. The EAT scores positively correlated with injury tolerance, but not the other 2 dimensions

Population subgroup: Males T1 n=47 Males T2 n=25 Males T3 n=22 Females T1 n=126 Females T2 n=83 Females T3 n=63
Inclusion criteria: Current elite athletes who participated in the baseline (T1), 6 month follow-up (T2), and 12-month follow-up (T3) surveys
Sport_name: Lean sport, endurance sport, weight-class sport, aesthetic sport, anti-gravitational sports
Sporting population: Elite athletes (i.e., national, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level)
Related_Factor_measure: Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q)
Authors' conclusions: Disordered eating did not improve performance over time but was associated with poorer performance and increased injury-related absence, particularly over 6 months. This highlights its negative impact on athletes’ health and participation
Limits: The study relied on self-reported measures of performance and injury, which may be biased, and used a specific sample with limited diversity, affecting generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use more objective performance and injury measures, examine longer timeframes, and include more diverse athlete populations to better understand underlying mechanisms

Title: Achievement goal theory and disordered eating: relationships of disordered eating with goal orientations and motivation climate in Female gymnasts and dancers
Authors: Karin de Bruin, A.P., Bakker, F.C., & Oudejans, R.R.D.
Inclusion criteria: Only high level aesthetic performers who did not participate in additional competitive sport activities were included.
Mean_Exercise frequency:
M=16.7 hours per week, SD=6.7
Gymnasts M=18.1, SD=7.8
Dancers M=14.4, SD=3.28
DEAB_measure: 9-point-scale running from 1(never) to 9(always) with the following item Are you trying yo lose weight ?
Related_Factor_measure: Perceived Motivational Climate in Sport Questionnaire (PMCSQ)
Authors' conclusions: Ego orientation and performance climate were related to more frequent dieting, using more pathogenic weight control methods, greater perfectionism and perceiving more weight related peer pressure. Having a high ego orientation means that a Female aesthetic performer is sgnificantly more likely to report indices of disordered eating. Non-significant correlations were found between task orientation and DE. With respect to performance climate, significant relationships were found with all DE variables. The present study also shows that a mastery climate is negatively related to disordered eating. Mastery climate explained some of the variance of dieting frequency.
Limits: A limitation in the present study was that we used a relatively crude measure for pathogenic weight control with limited reliability. Another limitation was that we had to confine ourselves to self-reported height and weight because objective measurement of body composition was perceived as too threatening form some aesthetic performers. Self-report holds the risk of both under or overstimation. Another constraint in the present study was the composition of our sample. As the number of high level competitive gymnasts in the Netherlands is limited, we also investigated a group of high level Female dancers.
Perspectives: In future studes focusing exclusively on relationships between eating disorders or disordered eating with achievement motivation, full versions of general or sport specific measures could be administered such as the Eating Disorder Inventory-2 or the Female Athlete Screening Tool for disordered eating. Future studies should continue to making an effort to include objective measurements by the researchers or recent actual data provided by medical staff members. The observed relationships of this study should be replicated in future studies using larger samples of various athletes at risk for disordered eating. Roberts (2001) stated that a high ego orientation is particularly detrimental if it is accompanied by a low task orientation. Future research should further investigate if this is also true for disordered eating. To gain a more complete understanding of the relationship between ego orientation and disordered eating, future studies could also include the more recent 2 by 2 framework which not only distinguishes between ego and task orientation but also between approach and avoidance achievmalet goals. We therefore recommaled that coaches and teachers should create a mastery climate with its emphasis on personal development and interpersonal cooperation.

Title: Disordered eating behaviors among crossfit athletes
Authors: Franco da Cunha, M.C., Costa Pereira Junqueira, A., Berbert de Carvalho, P.H., & Laus, M.F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 40 years, and be enrolled in the crossfit modality in a specialized gym, with a minimum frequency of practice of 6 months. Individuals who practiced other sports that favor hypertrophy in addition to crossfit and belonging to special groups, such as pregnant or nursing Female, indidviuals with any medical condition tha could have direct or indirect influence on physical appearance, elite athletes, were excluded.
Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.
Limits: First, the sample may not be representative of the Brazilian population, as it was carried out in a single city in a single state. Second, there is a need to study other constructs, such as body dissatisfaction, which can predict other aspects of disordered eating in this population. Third, reported weight en height may be a bias, depiste being a common finding in body image  and eating behavior studies? Finally, even though the EAT-26 is frequently used in Brazil, the measure is not validated for adults in the country. Moreover, the EAT-26 appears to be a more focused instrument for investigating the symptoms of disordered eating often seen in Female, while recent studies have shown that disordered eating among male has its own characteristics.
Perspectives: Performance is directly related to diet, some disordered nutritional strategies can impair this performance and increase the risk of eating disorders in athletes.

Title: Prevalence of orthorexia nervosa and association with mental health among Palestinian physical education students - cross sectional study
Authors: Al-Amouri, F.M., Abualhaija, R., Al Atrash, M., Abu Alwafa, R., AlTamimi, M., Badrasawi, M.
Journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
Inclusion criteria: Students from the physical education department at An-Najah National University
Sport_name: Badminton, swimming, weightlifting, basketball, football, volleyball, other sport
Authors' conclusions: This study highlights a higher risk of orthorexia nervosa (OrNe) among male students, with strong associations with dieting behaviors and, in females, BMI. It emphasizes the multifactorial nature of OrNe and the importance of early identification in young athletes.
Limits: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and self-reported measures may introduce bias. Additionally, mental health assessment tools and limited comparability with prior studies restrict interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include longitudinal designs, more diverse populations, and more specific mental health measures. Preventive strategies targeting dietary behaviors and body-related factors in university and sports settings are needed.

Title: Mental health, eating disorder risk, and disordered eating patterns among Lebanese national taekwondo players: A cross-sectional study
Authors: Hoteit, M., Karaki, H., Haidar, A., Baroud, R., Zarifeh, H., Saidi, A., Kibbeh, F., Jbeily, N., Sadek, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Individuals aged 11-64 years, Lebanese nationals, holding a black belt in taekwondo (including both coaches and players of both genders), only black belt Taekwondo athletes
Authors' conclusions: Eating disorders and disordered eating in Taekwondo athletes are influenced by a complex interplay of mental health issues, socioeconomic factors, and sport-specific pressures, highlighting the need for integrated psychological and nutritional support
Limits: The cross-sectional design, self-reported data, small and specific sample (black belt athletes), and lack of clinical diagnoses limit causal inference and generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs, larger and more diverse samples, and include clinical assessments to better understand mechanisms and improve targeted interventions

Authors: Stoyel, H., Shanmuganathan-Felton, V., Meyer, C., & Serpell, L.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to be over 18; there was no upper cap on the age of potential participants. Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Sport_name: Cross country/track and field, swimming and diving, volleyball, wrestling, soccer, golf, football, lacrosse, baseball, basketball, tennis
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: Disordered eating behaviors among crossfit athletes
Authors: Franco da Cunha, M.C., Costa Pereira Junqueira, A., Berbert de Carvalho, P.H., & Laus, M.F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 40 years, and be enrolled in the crossfit modality in a specialized gym, with a minimum frequency of practice of 6 months. Individuals who practiced other sports that favor hypertrophy in addition to crossfit and belonging to special groups, such as pregnant or nursing Female, indidviuals with any medical condition tha could have direct or indirect influence on physical appearance, elite athletes, were excluded.
Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.
Limits: First, the sample may not be representative of the Brazilian population, as it was carried out in a single city in a single state. Second, there is a need to study other constructs, such as body dissatisfaction, which can predict other aspects of disordered eating in this population. Third, reported weight en height may be a bias, depiste being a common finding in body image  and eating behavior studies? Finally, even though the EAT-26 is frequently used in Brazil, the measure is not validated for adults in the country. Moreover, the EAT-26 appears to be a more focused instrument for investigating the symptoms of disordered eating often seen in Female, while recent studies have shown that disordered eating among male has its own characteristics.
Perspectives: Performance is directly related to diet, some disordered nutritional strategies can impair this performance and increase the risk of eating disorders in athletes.

Title: Contextual body image and athletes' disordered eating: the contribution of athletic body image to disordered eating in high performance Female athletes
Authors: Karin de Bruin, A.P., Oudejans, R.R.D., Bakker, F.C., & Woertman, L.
Population subgroup:
19 athletes with eating disorders
33 without disordered eating
Inclusion criteria: High performance Female athletes with disordered eating ; competing on national or international levels ; control without disordered eating. Subjects with disordered eating meet two of the major criteria: amaleorrhoea, low BMI or low body fat, purging methods, and bulimic episodes, in addition to two of the following minor criteria: fear of weight gain, feelings of fatness, maintained low weight and increased importance of weight/shape. If participants did not meet these criteria, they were placed in the control group without disordered eating.
Mean_BMI:
Athletes with disordered eating M=20.69, SD=2.89
Athletes without disordered eating M=20.23, SD=2.23
Sport_name: Rythmic/acrobatic gymnastics and synchronized swimming, aerobic endurance training, middle and long distance running, swimming or long distance speed skating, tennis
Mean_Years of experience:
Athletes with disordered eating M=9, SD=4.27
Athletes without disordered eating M=8.36, SD=4.09
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Authors' conclusions: The athletic body image strongly contributed to ED. The athletes self-evaluations about shape, weight and fat percentage and the perceived opinions of others on these aspects appeared to be only significant factors uniquely explaining 14 and 9% of the EDE-Q variance. 64% of the variance was explained by the relevant body image components from daily life and sport.
Limits: Limitations of the present study were its sample size and consitution. Unfortunately, the number of Dutch high performance athletes is not that extensive.
Perspectives: Future studies should further explore athletes body comparisons in daliy life and sport, and possible differences between athletes with and without disordered eating in this respect. Future research should further explore body images in sport and daily life, particularly in athletes with disordered eating. We needed to extent the sample with a group of at-risk athletes who were not professionaly diagnosed in advance. Future investigation needs to take into account dynamic and contextual body image changes. It should also focus more closely on why certain athletes develop a more negative body image and how this could be prevented.

Title: Psychometric properties of the contextual body image questionnaire for athletes: a replication and extension study in Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Stewart, T., Kilpela, L., Wesley, K., & Becker, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes at each university within the ages of 17-27 years
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Authors' conclusions: Daily life thin-fat others correlated with EDE-Q global scores. Sport muscularity did not correlated with EDE-Q. All dimensions except muscularity correlated with all subscales in both contexts. Appearance dimension (perceiving others opinions of yourself) was related to higher levels of ED pathology in both daily life and sport contexts. Self evaluation and perceived other evaluation as fatter were also related to more ED pathology. Muscularity in daily life was not related to ED symptomatology. CBIQA scores related to appearance may predict future ED pathology.
Limits: Reliance on self-report data, attrition at follow-up, and that the CBIQA was delivered to participants 12 months into the FAB program as opposed to the beginning of the parent trial.
Perspectives: Further research on cntextual body images is needed to evaluate the impact of these dual body images with Female athletes not only while in sport, but while away or retiring from sport, inclusding periods of injury, between seasons and when completing sport.

Title: Excessive health behaviors in sports: links of orthorexia nervosa and exercise addiction with well-being, exercise activity in sports categories, and gender effects
Authors: Wachten, H., Wurst, R., Paganini, S., & Strahler, J.
Population subgroup:
Females N=783
Males N=281
Study 1: N=387
Study 2: N=677
Inclusion criteria: Minimum age of 18 and the self-assignment ton male or female gender.
Sport_name: Endurance, resistance and fitness, health, ball and team, antigravitation, technical, aesthetical, rehabilitation, martial arts
Related_Factor_measure: Sport and exercise activity subscale of the Physical Activity, Exercise, and Sport Questionnaire
Authors' conclusions: Although pthological orthorexic eating and exercise addiction may co-occur and correlate moderately, their link can neither be explained by restriction in well-being nor participation in specific sports categories. A non-pathological interest in healthyeating may slightly enhance well-being in men, but orthorexia nervosa may be detrimental to women's well-being only.
Limits: Reliance on self-reported exercise activity and conveniance sampling may have introduced biases, such as self-selection and social desirability, which limit the validity of our results. Recruitment tool place in different locations, we cannot completely exclude overlap of participants across samples. The unequal gender distribution and small sample size who practiced martial arts and rehabilitation sports constrain generalizability. Without measuring disordered eating, we could not differentiate betweenn instrumental exercise aimed at improvng appearance and exercise addiction.
Perspectives: Prevention and treatment strategies for excessive health behaviors should focus on helping women maintain a balanced approach to healthy eating and assisting men in regulating their exercise activities.
