Title: Muscle dysmorphia and its associated psychological features in three groups of recreational athletes
Authors: Cerea, S., Bottesi, G., Pacelli, Q.F., Paoli, A., & Ghisi, M.
Population subgroup:
42 Bodybuilders (BB group) 
61 Strenght athletes (SA group)
22 Fitness practitioners (FP group)
Inclusion criteria: At least 18 years of age; absence of severe neurological or medical conditions; no current or past psychothic disorders; no evidence of intellectual disabilities; Italian athletes who trained regularly for recreational purposes: bodybuilders, strenght training athletes, and fitness practitioners.
Authors' conclusions: Self esteem is significaltly related to muscle dysmorphia. Perfectionism is non-significantly related to MD. Perfectionism socially prescribed is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Social phobia is significantly related to MD. Orthorexia is significantly related to MD among bodybuilders. Depression is significantly related to MD.
Limits: First the sample size was relativelly small which likely reduces the generalizability of our conclusions. Related to this issue, the statisticcal power of the employed regression design could not guarantee a reliable detection of MD predictors. Secondly, the online recruitmalet strategy we adopted under-sampled those without internet capability and prevented the opportunity of conducting face-to-face interviews of participants self-identified as recreational bodybuilders and recreational strength athletess. Lastly, the absence of psychometric information for the MPS is another limitation.
Perspectives: Improving the identification of predictors and risk factors for MD, as well as its associated psychological features, might facilitate the identification of at-risk trainers, as well as the development of prevention strategies and interventions. Furthermore, a deeper understanding of MD manifestation among athletes may help to distinguishing individuals participating in a healthy manner versus those participating in an unhealthy manner.

Title: Disturbed eating in young, competitive gymnasts: differences between three gymnastics disciplines
Authors: Nordin, S., Harris, G., & Cumming, J.
Population subgroup:
Rhytmic gymnasts
Artistic gymnasts
Sport acrobats
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts who participated in one of three different forms of gymnastics: artistic, rhythmic, or sports acrobatics; training and competing for various clubs in the West Midlands, UK.
Authors' conclusions: Rhytmic gymnasts were considered to be at a greater risk for ED development than were artistic gymnasts or sport acrobats. This findings is probably due to sport-specific pressure in rhythmic gymnastics to obtain a very thin body rather than other variables such as age or perfectionist tendencies.
Limits: Sample small. Only 6 on the 9 coaches who were approached agreed to participate in the study. It is possible that only those coaches who were certain that their group was altogether healthy would be more likely to agree to take part, and vice versa. Secrecy, deception and denial are considered inherent to eating disorders, and it is generally agreed that self report measures for eating disorders tend to yield conservative estimates. Underreporting also constitues a possible limitation.
Perspectives:
The climate in training can be an important variable in eating disorder development. An investigation into motivational climates and perceived sport specific pressures would be a welcome addition to the eating disturbances literature. 
Qualitative research methologies may be used to gain a deeper insight into what pressures are present, as well as their sources, such as coaches, parents, teammates, judges, and others.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: A longitudinal investigation of performance and injury outcomes associated with disordered eating in elite athletes
Authors: Fatt, S.J., Hay, P., George, E., Jeacocke, N., Rogers, K., Mitchison, D.
Population subgroup: Males T1 n=47 Males T2 n=25 Males T3 n=22 Females T1 n=126 Females T2 n=83 Females T3 n=63
Inclusion criteria: Current elite athletes who participated in the baseline (T1), 6 month follow-up (T2), and 12-month follow-up (T3) surveys
Sport_name: Lean sport, endurance sport, weight-class sport, aesthetic sport, anti-gravitational sports
Sporting population: Elite athletes (i.e., national, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level)
Authors' conclusions: Disordered eating did not improve performance over time but was associated with poorer performance and increased injury-related absence, particularly over 6 months. This highlights its negative impact on athletes’ health and participation
Limits: The study relied on self-reported measures of performance and injury, which may be biased, and used a specific sample with limited diversity, affecting generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use more objective performance and injury measures, examine longer timeframes, and include more diverse athlete populations to better understand underlying mechanisms

Authors: Burgon, R.H., Waller, G.

400 Females
108 Males
One non-binary
One declined to say

Inclusion criteria: Adults aged 18+ who were fluent in English
Sport_name: Running, cycling, swimming, hiking, gymgoer HIIT, gymgoer weights, gymnastics, dance, crossfit
Sporting population:
117 competitive sports engagers
276 non-competitive sport engager
117 sports non-engagers
Authors' conclusions: This longitudinal study contributes to understanding of the relationship between poor body image and eating psychopathology over time, and across sporting sub-samples (competitive, non-competitive and sports non-engagers). Limits: The longitudinal analysis were under-powered and could not be conducted separately for each group. Perspectives: Futures studies could recruit different samples to explain the body image-eating psychopathology link, such as all genders and gender identities and other sports types. Ethnicity should also be considered, given the fact that the thin-ideal is differently experienced in different groups.

Title: Interpersonal difficulties as a risk factor for athletes eating psychopathology
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
Inclusion criteria: British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, judo, rugby, football, hockey
Authors' conclusions: Negative and positive aspects of the quality of the coach athlete and teammate athlete were related to athletes eating psychopathology after controlling for baseline eating psychopathology score. Conflict with the coach was found to be the only significant independent predictor of athletes eating psychopathology. The quality of the relationship with parents and attachmalet styles were not found to be related to athletes eating psychopathology 6 months later.
Limits: The present findings are essentially correlational, thus preventing definitive conclusions about causality. The present study only examined the direct role of interpersonal relationships in atletes eating psychopathology. Fairburn et al. (2003) noted that interpersonal difficulties interact with other core psychopathological processes (low self esteem, clinical perfectionism, and mood intolerance) to potentially elicit and maintain eating disorders.
Perspectives: Future studies should seek to examine how such processes as clinical perfectionism, self esteem, and mood intolerance interact with interpersonal difficulties to elicit eating psychopathology . And investigaite how these interpersonal variables interact with each other to predict athletes eating psychopathology.

Title: A longitudinal investigation of performance and injury outcomes associated with disordered eating in elite athletes
Authors: Fatt, S.J., Hay, P., George, E., Jeacocke, N., Rogers, K., Mitchison, D.
Population subgroup: Males T1 n=47 Males T2 n=25 Males T3 n=22 Females T1 n=126 Females T2 n=83 Females T3 n=63
Inclusion criteria: Current elite athletes who participated in the baseline (T1), 6 month follow-up (T2), and 12-month follow-up (T3) surveys
Sport_name: Lean sport, endurance sport, weight-class sport, aesthetic sport, anti-gravitational sports
Sporting population: Elite athletes (i.e., national, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level)
Related_Factor_measure: Two questions developed by the authors
Authors' conclusions: Disordered eating did not improve performance over time but was associated with poorer performance and increased injury-related absence, particularly over 6 months. This highlights its negative impact on athletes’ health and participation
Limits: The study relied on self-reported measures of performance and injury, which may be biased, and used a specific sample with limited diversity, affecting generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use more objective performance and injury measures, examine longer timeframes, and include more diverse athlete populations to better understand underlying mechanisms

Title: Food and alcohol disturbance by athlete status: the roles of drive for thinness, drive for muscularity and sex
Authors: Palermo, M., Choquette, E.M., Ahlich, E., & Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate male and female aged between 18 to 30 years old
DEAB_measure: Drive for Thinness subscale from the Eating Disorder Inventory
Related_Factor_measure: Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test of Consumption (AUDIT-C)
Authors' conclusions: Results related to DEAB not discussed
Limits: Cross sectional nature of the data, limited information about sport participation and the utilization of self identified athlete status. No information was collected about level of competition, sport type, intensity or commitment to sport, or actual frequency and intensity of physical activity/sport participation. The use of a single item measure of athlete status may have attenuated effect sizes.
Perspectives: Findings suggest the utility of incorporating athlete status and societal body ideals into preventive intervention and full intervention approaches. Initial research on programs that take athlete status into account, such as the Female Athlete Body Project, show success in reducing eating disorder symptomatology in Female athletes.

Title: Eating disorders risk assessment and body esteem among elite polish contact karate athletes
Authors: Dobkowska-Szefer, D., Staskiewicz-Bartecka, W., Kiciak, A., Kardas, M.
Inclusion criteria: Consent from both the club and the athlete to participate in the study, active participation in training in contact karate clubs (defined as > 3 training sessions per week for at least the past 6 months), achievement of at least one medal-winning position in competitions at the level of the Polish championships or higher, organized by national or international sports federations, and absence of chronic diseases, including diagnosed mental health disorders, as confirmed in the demographic section of the questionnaire
Authors' conclusions: This study identifies elite karate athletes as a high-risk group for disordered eating and orthorexia, with body image—especially in women—and weight-related pressures playing a central role. It highlights the importance of psychological factors over BMI in shaping risk.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, small and selective sample, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference and generalizability. The use of BMI and omission of key psychosocial variables further constrain interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include larger samples, longitudinal designs, and objective body composition measures. Preventive interventions focusing on body image, nutrition education, and sport-specific pressures are essential in weight-category sport

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.

Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions
Authors: Olave, L., Estévez, A., Momene, J., Penacoba, C., Macia, P., Macia, L., Etxaburu, N., Muniz, J.A., Iruarrizaga, I.
Inclusion criteria: People who practice physical exercise at least one day a week
Authors' conclusions: The study highlights strong links between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia, and multiple addictions, with impulsivity playing a key mediating role. These findings emphasize the importance of targeting impulsivity and emotion regulation in prevention and treatment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and the use of a homogeneous convenience sample limits generalizability. Additionally, reliance on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses may affect accuracy.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify causal relationships and further explore specific dimensions of impulsivity. There is also a need to develop prevention and intervention strategies focusing on emotion regulation and impulsivity

Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Sport_name: Cross country/track and field, swimming and diving, volleyball, wrestling, soccer, golf, football, lacrosse, baseball, basketball, tennis
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions
Authors: Olave, L., Estévez, A., Momene, J., Penacoba, C., Macia, P., Macia, L., Etxaburu, N., Muniz, J.A., Iruarrizaga, I.
Inclusion criteria: People who practice physical exercise at least one day a week
Authors' conclusions: The study highlights strong links between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia, and multiple addictions, with impulsivity playing a key mediating role. These findings emphasize the importance of targeting impulsivity and emotion regulation in prevention and treatment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and the use of a homogeneous convenience sample limits generalizability. Additionally, reliance on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses may affect accuracy.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify causal relationships and further explore specific dimensions of impulsivity. There is also a need to develop prevention and intervention strategies focusing on emotion regulation and impulsivity

Title: Eating behaviors among male bodybuilders and runners: application of the Trans-Contextual Model of Motivation
Authors: Chaba, L., Scoffier-Mériaux, S., d'Arripe-Longueville, F., & Lentillon-Kaestner, V.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum of 16 years; minimum of 3 hours of physical training per week; and minimum of 3 years of bodybuilding or running.
Mean_Age:
Bodybuilders M=26.63, SD=7.38
Runners M=37.66, SD=12.20
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.73, SD=3.41
Runners M=6.44, SD=4.21
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.85, SD=6.71
Runners M=11.93, SD=10.12
Related_Factor: Perceived behavioral control related to gain muscle mass
Related_Factor_measure: Five items assessing the perceived behavioral control related to gaining muscle mass/lean body mass were used
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceived behavioral control related to gain muscle mass
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived behavioral control related to gain muscle mass
Authors' conclusions: The TCM was partially supported in the context of eating disorders in the bodybuilders and runners. Both types of motivations for sport were direct or indirect risk factors for the development of deviant behaviors, but CM seemed to indicate greater risk than autonomous motivation for the development of eating disorders.
Limits: First, our sample was composed of young male with different numbers of years of practice, hours of practice per week, and types of practices (i.e., noncompetitors, future competitors, competitors), which might infuenced their motivation and engagement. Second, the runners were older than the bodybuilders, and younger people are more at risk of developing eating disorders than older people. Third, the data were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, no model/theory on body image in male was used, although body dissatisfaction was clearly present, and drive for muscularity was not considered. Fifth, our study was correlational. Sixth, it would be useful to determine a cutoff for eating disorders in male athletes because the EAT is not adapted to measure eating disorders in male athletes desiring to gain muscle mass. Finally, the motivational mechanisms explaining the development of eating disorders in male bodybuilders and runners who desire to gain muscle mass/lean body mass need to be further investigated in terms of motivational profiles.
Perspectives:
Include the level of competition in the analyses. Another model that also takes into account sociocognitive variables, such as the Health Action Process Approach might be applied in future research. Future studies could also specifically measure body satisfaction and analyze the link between this variable, behaviors to gain muscle mass/lean body mass, and the development of eating disorders.  It would be interesting to conduct a longitudinal study to more closely examine causality in the relationships. An intraindividual approach would be more useful than an interindividual approach. 
It appears necessary to limit the deleterious effects of controlled motivation. This might be accomplished by identifying the motivational orientations of athletes and promoting the development of coaching styles and climates that support autonomy and basic needs. Given the paradoxical role of autonomous motivation observed in the present study, it also appears necessary to encourage athletes to build reasoned and healthy sports parctices, limiting muscle mass gain at all costs.

Title: Drive for muscularity behaviors in male bodybuilders: a trans-contextual model of motivation
Authors: Chaba, L., d'Arripe-Longueville, F., Lentillon-Kaestner, V., & Scoffier-Mériaux, S.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum of 16 years; minimum of 3 hours of physical training per week; and minimum of 3 years of bodybuilding.
Related_Factor: Perceived behavioral control related to gain muscle mass
Related_Factor_measure: Five items related to perceived behavioral control related to gaining muscle mass were used
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceived behavioral control related to gain muscle mass
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived behavioral control related to gain muscle mass
Authors' conclusions: The study show that autonomous motivation for sport had a significant, indirect and positive association with drive for muscularity via perceived behavioral control and intention to gain muscle, and that contolled motivation for sports was related to drive for muscularity both directly and via attitude and intention to gain muscle mass. These results indicate that the trans contextual model was partially supported in the context of bodybuiling, suggesting a complex motivational model underlying drive for muscularity in male bodybuilders.
Limits: Our data are limited because our sample was composed only of young male with different levels of expertise (i.e., non-competitors, future competitors, competitors), which might have influenced their motivation and engagement in drive for muscularity. Second, subjective norm is a questionable variable as it might indicate a measurement issue in the sense that such variables reflect greater pressure and controlling rather than supportive forms of motivation. Third, the date were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, the internal consistency of some measures was quite low and this might have been linked to our heterogeneous sample or to the psychometric quality concerning the controlled motivation scale, or the inconsistency between the external regulation and the introjected regulation.
Perspectives:
It would be interesting to conduct a longitudinal study to more closely examine the causal relationship between variables. Methodologically, an important perspective for the future would be to determine a cutoff for drive for muscularity, which might then function as a reference when using drive for muscularity as a screening instrument for disordered eating. Moreover, eating disorders are very common on male bodybuilders and it might be of value to examine the relationships between motivation for sport, drive for muscularity and other specified feeding or eating disorders such as food restriction or night eating syndrome, or binge eating. 
Preventive actions may be important for male bodybuilders, who focus on gaining muscle mass. Specifically, such actions should be directed toward helping them to avoid developing controlled motivation because, although motivation for sport of any kind can be a direct or indirect risk factor for the development of deviant behavior, controlled motivation seems to put them at greater risk. It may therefore be important to carefully keep track of the development of motivation for sport to be sure that controlled motivation stays low, with moderate and healthy practice of bodybuilding. Moreover, the motivational mechanisms explaining the development of drive for muscularity could be deepened by complementary analysis in terms of motivational profiles.

Title: Perceived coach and teammate weight/shape-related beliefs and disordered eating in NCAA swimmers
Authors: Pinson, C.K., Fox, K.R., Frank, G.K.W., Hooley, J.M., Javaras, K.N.
Population subgroup: Division I n=82 Division II n=19 Division III n=89
Inclusion criteria: NCAA swimmers from Division I, II, III, > 18 years old, > 1 year on the team
Related_Factor_measure: Coach and Teammate Weight/Shape Beliefs Questionnaire (CTWSBQ)
Authors' conclusions: Perceived teammate weight/shape beliefs are strongly associated with eating disorder symptoms and thinness-related concerns in NCAA swimmers, while coach beliefs appear more specifically linked to drive for muscularity
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, the sample (especially males) is limited, and the measurement tools (e.g., CTWSBQ) require further validation, restricting generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal or experimental designs, include more diverse sports and samples, and refine measurement tools to better inform targeted prevention and intervention strategies

Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Related_Factor: Perceived encouragement for healthy eating habit
Related_Factor_measure: Social Support for Healthy Eating Habits Scale (SSES)
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: External eating and weight related concerns
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceived encouragement for healthy eating habit
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived encouragement for healthy eating habit
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: The tripartite influence model of body image and disordered eating among young adult athletes
Authors: Tonsberg, E.N., Dixit, U., Henderson, R., Larsen, J., Lusich, R., Hauff, C., Ahlich, E.
Inclusion criteria: Being 18-26 years old, fluency in English and self-reporting yes to the item do you identify as an athlete ?
Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and sport pressure related to significant others
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of social and sport pressure from other
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. It highlights the continued importance of both general and sport-specific influences on athletes’ eating behaviors
Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Title: Disordered eating, eating attitudes and reasons for exercise among male high school cross country runners
Authors: Wadas, G.
Inclusion criteria: The runners were selected from 12 of the thirty two public high schools in the local school district sponsoring sports teams located in the USA. Participants were current members of a high shcool cross country teams, were in grades 9-12 and between the ages of 14-18.
Sporting population: Some playing time (24.2%), starter on team (29%), conference (4.8%), regional (35.5%), national (4.8%), other (1.6%)
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and sport pressure related to significant others
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of social and sport pressure from other
Authors' conclusions: Factors that have a significant relationship with disordered eating are performance perfectionism and weight management. A desire to control weight is associated with disordered eating behaviors in male high school cross country runners as determined from the modest correlation coefficient for the weight management subscale and the EAT-26. There was no significant correlation for the physical appearance subscale of the EMI-2 and the EAT-26. No significant relationships were found between disordered eating behaviors and social pressure on body shape, social pressure on eating and athlete identity.
Limits: The results are generalizable only to school districts of similar size and demographic makeup. The questionnaire were completed on one occasion by runners during the sumer prior to the start of the season. The study was limited by a low number of participants relative to the number of runners on the teams and number of high schools in the school district.
Perspectives: The present study did not investigate the reasons for dissatisfaction with current weight status, future studies may seek more information relative to the reasons. For example, do male cross country runners feels a need to be more muscular ? Do the bodies of male cross country runners not fit the ideal ?

Title: Impact of perfectionism on the risk of the female athlete triad in collegiate athletes
Authors: Brooks, S.G., Peach, H.D., Howden, R., Lowrie, J., Marino, J.S.
Journal: The Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: NCAA female student-athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 years at a Division I university
Sport_name: Cross country, soccer, softball, tennis, track throws, track sprints
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and sport pressure related to significant others
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of social and sport pressure from other
Authors' conclusions: This study found significant correlations between LEA risk, DE, triad risk, perfectionism and time spent in a program for female NCAA division I athletes
Limits: Sample size of the study. The athletes came from the same institutions. Study did not collect detailed dietary information, such as macronutrient composition, we did use validated methods of interpreting athletes eating attitudes and behaviors. No causal relationship between perfectionism and our outcomes could be established because this was a cross-sectional study.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate possible interventions to hemp athletes manifest their perfectionistic tendencies in adaptive dimensions rather than maladaptive dimensions associated with an increased risk. Other psychological variables (drive for thinness, self esteem) should also benefit explored to further our understanding of the role of mental health in athletes risk for adverse health conditions.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Related_Factor: Perceived appearance based pressures from family
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and sport pressure related to significant others
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of social and sport pressure from other
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived appearance based pressures from family
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Eating disordered behaviours in Portuguese athletes: the influence of personal, sport, and psychological variables
Authors: Gomes, A.R., Martins, C., & Silva, L.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between 14 and 30 year of age
Sport_name: Athletics; karate; swimming; taekwondo; basketball; handball; volleyball
Sporting population:
Top division (38.8%)
Regional or national levels
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and sport pressure related to significant others
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of social and sport pressure from other
Authors' conclusions: The EDE-Q global score was positively associated with weight-related coach pressure, anxiety, taske orientation, impression motivation and threat perception, and negatively associated with less satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance. Eating behaviour was predicted by lower satisfaction with body shape and physical appearance, and higher anxiety and impression motivation.
Limits: Data were based on athletes self-report, which could have resulted in under-reporting of eating disordered behaviours. A better discrimination between sports according to their requirements needs to be introduced in order to better differentiate the demands and soecific characteristics of each sport. It is vital to further explore the impact of psychological factors on eating disordered behaviours.
Perspectives: It is important to assess athletes reactions in competition, the way they perceive themselves, and the way they want others to perceive them. If there is a better comprehension of these factors, then prevention of eating problems and promotion of better experiences in sport becomes easier to achieve.

Title: Testing general sociocultural and coach-related appearance pressures as the factors associated with disordered eating in competitive female athletes participating in various sport
Authors: Jankauskiene, R., & Baceviene, M.
Inclusion criteria: Being an athlete that competed for at least two years in any competitive sport (participating in sports competitions of one sport) and being an official member of a sports school, sports club or national sports team
Sporting population: Sports school, sports clubs, national team
DEAB_measure: Lithuanian version of the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q)
Related_Factor_measure: Lithuanian version of the Sociocultural Attitudes Towards Appearance Questionnaire (SATAQ-4)
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and sport pressure related to significant others
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of social and sport pressure from other
Authors' conclusions: General sociocultural pressures (parents, peers and media) are directly associated with disordered eating, and internalization of appearance ideals and overweight preoccupation mediate these associations in female competitive athletes. Controlling for general sociocultural pressures, perceived body weight and appearance-related pressures from coaches were associated with disordered eating through appearance internationalization and overweight preoccupation.
Limits: Cross sectional desing; a full SEM to test the associations between latent variables was not conducted, only a basic path analysis. We did not assess variables such as negative affect and restrained eating that are integral parts of the original model. We assessed the aspects of negative body image (overweight preoccupation) and disordered eating as possible outcome of the general sociocultural and coach-related pressures.
Perspectives: It is important to promote resistance to sociocultural pressures (parents, peers, media) and pressures from coaches in disordered eating prevention programmes for female athletes of all ages participating in sports irrespective of sport group WS or less. Choaches must be educated to understand and recognise the associations between athletes body image, disordered eating, and physical, mental health and sports performance, as weel as their personal influence on it and to promote positive body image in sports environments.

Title: A model of relationships of teammate relations, body image, and eating behaviors among athletes
Authors: Runquist, E., Cox, M., Meyer, A., & Rodgers, R.F.
Population subgroup:
63.5% Females
35.3% Males
0.64% Other
0.64% Opted not to say
Inclusion criteria: Being a varsity or club athlete 18 years or older
Related_Factor_measure: First ten items, and an additional adapted four items of the Sociocultural Attitudes Toward Appearance Questionnaire-4 (SATAQ-4)
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of social and sport pressure from other
Authors' conclusions: Results support the importance of teammate body comparison, pressure, and relationships for muscularity oriented disordered eating and weight and shape concerns amongst collegiate athletes.
Limits: The study had varying rates of participation across varsity and club athlete groups that led to unequal representation in the final sample and inhibited group comparison. The study small sample size. The data were self-reported, cross-sectional and collecte from athletes from only one division I university.
Perspectives: Interventions such as educational programming amongst teams, compaings including on social media to promote positive repesentation of embodiment among athletes, as well as access to appropriate mental health resources are needed to protect athletes from disordered eating habits and negative body image comparisons. Future studies could utilize the model created to further explore the nunances of athlete-teammate relationships in larger, more diverse athlete populations and sporting environments.

Title: Muscle dysmorphia symptomatology in male exercisers: Associations with cognitive flexibility and appearance motivation
Authors: Abrante, D., Cano, A., Clemente, G., Diaz, M.
Inclusion criteria: Being over 18 and engaging in regular physical activity for at least three months
DEAB_measure: Spanish adaptation of the Muscle Appearance Satisfaction Scale (MASS)
Related_Factor_measure: Cuestionario de Influencia del Modelo Estetico Corporal (CIMEC-V-17)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Authors' conclusions: This study supports a dual-pathway model of muscle dysmorphia, where sociocultural pressure influences symptoms both indirectly via appearance motivation and directly, with cognitive flexibility acting as a protective moderator. It highlights the interplay between social, motivational, and cognitive factors
Limits: The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and the use of a convenience, all-male sample restricts generalizability. Additionally, the measure of sociocultural pressure was not specific to muscularity ideals
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs and more diverse samples to validate the model. Interventions enhancing cognitive flexibility and promoting non-appearance-based exercise motives appear promising avenues for prevention and treatment.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: Psychological risk indicators of disordered eating in athletes
Authors: Stoyel, H., Shanmuganathan-Felton, V., Meyer, C., & Serpell, L.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to be over 18; there was no upper cap on the age of potential participants. Participants had to consider themselves to be an athlete, and a minimum of 10 hours a week participating in their sport as well as have been actively competing, thus meaning that competitive sport-rather than zealous exercise was a significant part of their daily experience.
Sport_name: Swimming, tennis, football, basketball, volleyball, dancing, track and field, golf, boxing, equestrian, cycling, ping-pong, orienteering, rugby, rowing and race walking
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Authors' conclusions: Societal pressures mediated by internalisation, are associated with binge eating and bulimia, while body dissatisfaction leads to bulimia and binge eating, mediated by negative affect.
Limits: Cross sectional nature. None of the measurements scale were specifically designed for athletes. The scale for social media usage and modelled behaviours were purpose-built. for this study and thus were not formally validated in previous research and so had lower Cronbach alpha coefficients than would normally be acceptable. This research is limited in its ability to make sound assumptions on clinical implications.
Perspectives: Future research should use a longitudinal design to determine whether the relevant factors are able to predict future disordered eating in an athlete sample. Repeated this research with athletes younger than 18 years old would also provide additional insight as it is a high risk population for the development of eating disorders. A qualitative investigation to further understand the differences between the original etiological model and the revised model will also be undertaken.

Title: The relationship between social and disordered eating in college-aged Female gymnasts
Authors: Ausmus, J.C., Blom, L.C., Bowman, S., Lebeau, J.C.
Inclusion criteria: Participants were recruited from club gyms and colleges throughout the united states via email, social media, and word of mouth to coaches, support staff and directly to athletes; Females between 18-25 years; self identify as competitive gymnasts; must have competed within the last three years
Sporting population: 87.67% competed in varsity level gymnastics, 6.85% stated that they participated in recreational gymnastics, 5.48% competed in clubs gymnastics
Related_Factor: Severity of the comment made on social media
Related_Factor_measure: The Social Hassles Questionnaire with modifications made to identify how the participants reacted to critical comments made on social media
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Severity of the comment made on social media
Authors' conclusions: This study did not find significant correlations between criticism received on social media and disordered eating behaviors in college gymnasts. Combining variables related to social hassles, body satisfaction, usage of certain social media outlets, and years of participation could perdict disordered eating. No relationship were found between social media variables and disordered eating behaviors.
Limits: The main limitation of this study was the sample size of the participants. Although measures were exhausted in the recruitmalet of participants; it may have been beneficial to have sent the recruitmalet materials out earlier in the off season as opposed to a month before the college gymnastics season started. Another limitation was the limited reliability data for the Social Hassles Questionnaire, as it is relatively new instrument and has not been extensively tested. Furthermore this study did not account for mental health status beyond possible disordered eating behaviors.
Perspectives:
Since depression and anxiety have been linked to disordered eating patterns, future studies should also consider these pathologies, along with self-esteem. Research should aim to better understand the relationship between social media criticism and disordered eating behaviors in athletic populations. Athletes from different sports may respond differently to criticism than gymnasts, so it could be valuable to study these variables in other aesthetic sports, such as figure skating, diving, cheerleading, or even non-aesthetic sports like softball or basketball. Additionally, exploring these factors in males involved in aesthetic sports and the overall impact of social media on athletes' mental health could provide important insights.

It would also be beneficial for athletes, parents, and other significant figures in athletes' lives to be trained in recognizing the signs of disordered eating behaviors. Such training could help raise awareness of the potential dangers of social media platforms like Snapchat and offer guidance on how to support athletes if disordered eating behaviors arise.

To counter the effects of social media criticism on athletes, education initiatives should target coaches, families, friends, and athletes themselves to prevent the development of harmful eating behaviors and patterns, both now and in the future.

Title: An examination of psychosocial correlates of eating disorders among Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Reel, J.J., & Carter, J.E.
Journal: Research Quartely for Exercise and Sport
Inclusion criteria: Female collegiate athletes from three different NCAA Division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the United States.
Sport_name: Basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; field hockey; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; sport shooting; rowing; soccer; softball; swimming; synchronized swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.71, SD=1.27
M=8.89, SD=4.80
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Authors' conclusions: The pressures participants felt from general media (e.g., magazines, television/movies) rather than from sport-specific (e.g., teammates, judges) and interpersonal (e.g., boy/girlfriend, friends) sources most strongly discriminated among the three eating disorder categories. The correlations between internalization and the discriminant functin were significant but small. Athlete, relative to nonathletes, may be more satisfied with their bodies, this variable is related strongly to eating pathology. Body image, internalization, negative affect and pressures contributed similarly to the differentiation among the three eating disorder categories.
Limits: All data were self reported, which allowed for the possibility of socially desirable responding. The cross sectional design did not allow for determining temporal relationships among the variables and eating pathology.
Perspectives:
Future sudies may want to employ Petrie and Greenleaf's (2007) conceptual model using structural equation modeling and incorporate qualitative interviews to better determine how Female athletes experience and cope with the pressure from coaches, and whether these pressures change over the time they are involved in their sports. Future research should include measure of dietary restraint to determine if it assists in accurately classifying athletes into the three eating disorder groups. 
Professionals need to develop methods for screening athletes prior to each season to identify eating disorder and symptomatic groups and intervene as early as possible. Body image groups that focus on decreasing internalization and the effects of societal pressures may be an effective intervention strategy with Female athletes.

Title: A socio-sports model of disordered eating among Brazilian male athletes
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., Caputo Ferreira, M.E., Fernandes de Oliveira, S.M., Serpeloni Cyrino, E., & Sousa Almeida, S.
Inclusion criteria: Systematiccaly trained in a sport modality based on a training regimen of at least six hours of training per week (e.g., minimum of three days per week of two-hour sessions or six days per week of one hour sessions); participation in at least one regional competition in 2014 and; availability to respond to questionnaires and to participate in anthropometric evaluations.
Sport_name: Track and field; basketball; boxing; canoeing; cycling; equestrian; jiu-jitsu; judo; swimming; water polo; rowing; diving; surfing; tae-kwon-do; tennis; triathlon; sailing; volleyball
Sporting population:
30% international level
42% national level
28% regional level
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Authors' conclusions: Only the sociocultural factors and body fat dissatisfaction adhered to etiological model of DE in Brazilian male athletes. Sociocultural factors (parents, friends and the media) exhibit a direct relationship to DE. The results of the structural equation model indicate that body fat dissatisfaction mediates the relationship between sociocultural factors and DE.
Limits: Because self-reporting instruments were used as evaluative tools, the results may not reflect the reality because the responses given were subjective. The study is also limited in that it applies a doubly indirect method to evaluate fat percentages. Weight and body fat measurements can influence the survey responses about body image and disordered eating. The heterogeneity of the sample with respect to age and type of sport could have influenced the results.
Perspectives: Sport professionals may use the present study findings to intervene in factors that promote disturbed eating in athletes. Because disordered eating can cause an attenuation of anaerobic potency and resistance, prevention/intervention programs that are designed to prevent disordered eating in athletes may indirectly improve athletic performance. The construction of a socio-sports model for Female is recommaleded.

Title: The tripartite influence model of body image and disordered eating among young adult athletes
Authors: Tonsberg, E.N., Dixit, U., Henderson, R., Larsen, J., Lusich, R., Hauff, C., Ahlich, E.
Inclusion criteria: Being 18-26 years old, fluency in English and self-reporting yes to the item do you identify as an athlete ?
Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. It highlights the continued importance of both general and sport-specific influences on athletes’ eating behaviors
Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor: Perceived sociocultural pressure have a perfect body
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure related to body and appearance
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived sociocultural pressure have a perfect body
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Title: Psychological risk indicators of disordered eating in athletes
Authors: Stoyel, H., Shanmuganathan-Felton, V., Meyer, C., & Serpell, L.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to be over 18; there was no upper cap on the age of potential participants. Participants had to consider themselves to be an athlete, and a minimum of 10 hours a week participating in their sport as well as have been actively competing, thus meaning that competitive sport-rather than zealous exercise was a significant part of their daily experience.
Sport_name: Swimming, tennis, football, basketball, volleyball, dancing, track and field, golf, boxing, equestrian, cycling, ping-pong, orienteering, rugby, rowing and race walking
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure related to body and appearance
Authors' conclusions: Societal pressures mediated by internalisation, are associated with binge eating and bulimia, while body dissatisfaction leads to bulimia and binge eating, mediated by negative affect.
Limits: Cross sectional nature. None of the measurements scale were specifically designed for athletes. The scale for social media usage and modelled behaviours were purpose-built. for this study and thus were not formally validated in previous research and so had lower Cronbach alpha coefficients than would normally be acceptable. This research is limited in its ability to make sound assumptions on clinical implications.
Perspectives: Future research should use a longitudinal design to determine whether the relevant factors are able to predict future disordered eating in an athlete sample. Repeated this research with athletes younger than 18 years old would also provide additional insight as it is a high risk population for the development of eating disorders. A qualitative investigation to further understand the differences between the original etiological model and the revised model will also be undertaken.

Title: Comparing population-general and sport-specific correlates of disordered eating amongst elite athletes: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Fatt, S.J., George, E., Hay, P., Jeacocke, N., & Mitchison, D.
Inclusion criteria: Current and former athletes, who had competed at thenational, international, professional or NCAA Division I level
Related_Factor: Perceived appearance based pressures from the media
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure related to body and appearance
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Perceived appearance based pressures from the media
Authors' conclusions: Both population-general and athlete-specific factors have independent associations with disordered eating, including pressures (pressures for thinness and weight-loss from within sport) and psychological processes (drive for thinness, drive for leanness for performance, and athletic identity).
Limits: The cross sectional design ; athletes were a self-selected sample, likely leading to a bias in our sample towards participants who were interested in body image, eating and exercise ; the sample primarily included Australian female athletes ; over 2000 suspected illegitimate spam responses were removed from the study.
Perspectives: Several findings have previously indicated small but significant effects of greater risk for athletes competing in lean versus non-lean sports, this was not replicated in the present study. This challenges notions of at-risk athletes archetypes (e.g., female athletes participating in lean sport) and narrow views of eating disorder symptomatology (e.g., low BMI, vomiting) encouraging broader screening for disodered eating accross entire athlete populations. Sporting organisations should develop and implement policies for managing athletes al all levels of risk, including primary, secondary, and tertiary interventions.

Title: Psychological risk indicators of disordered eating in athletes
Authors: Stoyel, H., Shanmuganathan-Felton, V., Meyer, C., & Serpell, L.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to be over 18; there was no upper cap on the age of potential participants. Sport_name: Swimming, tennis, football, basketball, volleyball, dancing, track and field, golf, boxing, equestrian, cycling, ping-pong, orienteering, rugby, rowing and race walking
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure related to body and appearance
Authors' conclusions: Societal pressures mediated by internalisation, are associated with binge eating and bulimia, while body dissatisfaction leads to bulimia and binge eating, mediated by negative affect.
Limits: Cross sectional nature. None of the measurements scale were specifically designed for athletes. The scale for social media usage and modelled behaviours were purpose-built. for this study and thus were not formally validated in previous research and so had lower Cronbach alpha coefficients than would normally be acceptable. This research is limited in its ability to make sound assumptions on clinical implications.
Perspectives: Future research should use a longitudinal design to determine whether the relevant factors are able to predict future disordered eating in an athlete sample. Repeated this research with athletes younger than 18 years old would also provide additional insight as it is a high risk population for the development of eating disorders. A qualitative investigation to further understand the differences between the original etiological model and the revised model will also be undertaken.

Title: Bulimic symptomatology among male collegiate athletes: a test of an etiological model
Authors: Chatterton, J., Petrie, T.A., Schuler, K.L., & Ruggero, C.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure related to body and appearance
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.

Journal: Sociedade Brasileira de Medicina do Exercicio e do Esporte
Inclusion criteria: (a) present the informed consent form signed by the guardian (if she was under 18) and sign the assent form; (b) systematically train her respective modality with a minimum training regime of six hours per week (minimum frequency of three days per week and duration of two hours/training, or frequency of six days per week and duration of one hour/training; (c) have minimal participation in a regional competition in 2014; (d) be available to answer questionnaires and participate in anthropometric assessments. In addition, the following exclusion criteria were adopted (a) present a physical or intellectual disability and (b) use psychoactive medications in the last six months.
Sport_name: Athletics; Basketball; Boxing; Cycling; Football; Artistic gymnastics; Rythmic gymnastics; Handball; Jiu-Jitsu; Judo; Synchronized Swimming; Swimming; Figure skating; Water pole; Rowing; Diving; Surf; Tae-kwon-do; Tennis; Triathlon; Sailing; Volleyball and Beach volley
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure related to body and appearance
Authors' conclusions: The predictive equation is reliable to assess risk for ED in Brazilian Female athletes.
Limits: The use of questionnaires is pointed out, as researchers emphasize that athletes may omit some behaviors/feelings. In addition, another limitation was the use of a doubly indirect method to assess %F. According to some authors, using skinfolds can be limited to assess body composition.
Perspectives: The need to conduct new scientific investigations in order to assess the external validity of the created predictive equation is emphasized. In addition, it is necessary to create a risk predictive equation for eating disorders also regarding Brazilian male athletes

Title: Muscle dysmorphia symptomatology in male exercisers: Associations with cognitive flexibility and appearance motivation
Authors: Abrante, D., Cano, A., Clemente, G., Diaz, M.
Inclusion criteria: Being over 18 and engaging in regular physical activity for at least three months
DEAB_measure: Spanish adaptation of the Muscle Appearance Satisfaction Scale (MASS)
Related_Factor: Sociocultural pressure concern about being fat
Related_Factor_measure: Cuestionario de Influencia del Modelo Estetico Corporal (CIMEC-V-17)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure related to body and appearance
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Sociocultural pressure concern about being fat
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Sociocultural pressure concern about being fat
Authors' conclusions: This study supports a dual-pathway model of muscle dysmorphia, where sociocultural pressure influences symptoms both indirectly via appearance motivation and directly, with cognitive flexibility acting as a protective moderator. It highlights the interplay between social, motivational, and cognitive factors
Limits: The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and the use of a convenience, all-male sample restricts generalizability. Additionally, the measure of sociocultural pressure was not specific to muscularity ideals
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs and more diverse samples to validate the model. Interventions enhancing cognitive flexibility and promoting non-appearance-based exercise motives appear promising avenues for prevention and treatment.

Title: Correlates of eating disorders risk among Female figure skates: a profile of adolescent competitors
Authors: Monsma, E.V., & Malina, R.M.
Population subgroup:
Skaters solo
Skaters dance
Skaters pairs
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged between 12 and 22 years old; participants in four United States Figure Skating Association cluns and seven Canadian Figure Skating Association clubs
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for age and the BMI, social physique anxiety was related to the EDI accounting for 4% to 13% of the variance in five of the eight subscales. There is a positive correlation between SPA and maturity fears, bulimia and two EDI social adjustement. There is negative correlations between the EDI subscales and physical self perceptions indicated that skaters less satisfied with their physical characteristics reported higher EDI scores. Physical self perception explained a significant portion of the variance in each EDI subscale after controlling for age and body size. Satisfaction with body fat predicted both drive for thinness and body dissatisfaction.
Limits: N.A.
Perspectives: Future investigations should consider information on male partners and the potential mediating effects of SPA and self concept in the development of disordered eating. Title: Psychosocial risk factors of bulimic symptomatology among Female athletes

Bodybuilders M=6.40 hours per week
Weightlifters M=12.12 hours per week 
Controls M=3.8 hours per week
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.14 years
Weightlifters M=9.06 years
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Bodybuilding may represent a practice that encourages male to become more self-conscious of their bodies, putting them at greater risk of experiencing greater levels of monitoring of body appearance and anxiety about physical appearance. This body self consciousness is associated with a greater risk of body dissatisfaction and drive for muscularity. Weightlifting does not appear to represent an objectifying climate.
Limits: The cross sectional nature makes it possible only to speculate on the directions of causality. Unequal sample sizes of groups in our analyses, particularly with respect to fewer competitive weightlifters. Unknown selection bias that may be operating in the bodybuilder and weightlifter groups, and any subsequent influence on the interpretation of our results. The weighlifting and bodybuilder groups differed not only in the nature of their sport, but also in competitive nature of this sport, which may introduce confound for differences found between the groups.
Perspectives: Health pursuits for male should emphasize achievement and function rather than appearance if they are to avoid deleterious consesquences.

Title: Psychosocial correlates of disordered eating among male collegiate athletes
Authors: Petrie, T.A., Greenleaf, C., Carter, J.E., & Reel, J.J.
Population subgroup:
Asymptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=164)
Symptomatic group based on their QEDD responses (n=35)
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes from three different NCAA division I institutions located in the Midwest, Southwest and Mountain regions of the US
Sport_name: Football; basketball; cheerleading; cross-country; diving; fencing; golf; gymnastics; ice hockey; lacrosse; swimming; tennis; track and field; volleyball; cross-country skiing; alpine skiing
Mean_Years of experience:
College level M=1.81, SD=1.30
M=8.70, SD=5.28
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The psychosocial factors generally were unrelated to level of eating pathology. The male athletes were healthy in terms of their eating behaviors, had few negative mood concerns, were moderately satisfied with their bodies and experienced few pressures from personal and societal sources to change their weight or body size/shape.
Limits: Negative mood was represented by a single-item measures, this may have affected the relationship with disordered eating. All data are based on athlete self report and thus are subject to mono-method bias as well as underreporting that might occur when assessing sensitive areas. Only two of the male athletes were classified as having an eating disorder and both had an ED-NOS.
Perspectives: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

Title: A socio-sports model of disordered eating among Brazilian male athletes
