Sport_name: Track and field; basketball; boxing; canoeing; cycling; equestrian; jiu-jitsu; judo; swimming; water polo; rowing; diving; surfing; tae-kwon-do; tennis; triathlon; sailing; volleyball
Sporting population:
30% international level
42% national level
28% regional level
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Judgement of size, shape and weight
Authors' conclusions: Only the sociocultural factors and body fat dissatisfaction adhered to etiological model of DE in Brazilian male athletes. Sociocultural factors (parents, friends and the media) exhibit a direct relationship to DE. The results of the structural equation model indicate that body fat dissatisfaction mediates the relationship between sociocultural factors and DE.
Limits: Because self-reporting instruments were used as evaluative tools, the results may not reflect the reality because the responses given were subjective. The study is also limited in that it applies a doubly indirect method to evaluate fat percentages. Weight and body fat measurements can influence the survey responses about body image and disordered eating. The heterogeneity of the sample with respect to age and type of sport could have influenced the results.
Perspectives: Sport professionals may use the present study findings to intervene in factors that promote disturbed eating in athletes. Because disordered eating can cause an attenuation of anaerobic potency and resistance, prevention/intervention programs that are designed to prevent disordered eating in athletes may indirectly improve athletic performance. The construction of a socio-sports model for Female is recommaleded.

Title: Social and individual factors associaated with eating disorders in young athletes: effects on concentration and fatigue
Authors: Checa Olmos, J.C., Montserrat Hernandez, M., Belmonte Garcia, T., Jiminez Rodriguez, D., Rodriguez Martinez, A., Berenguel Martinez, P., & Berrio Lopez, A.M.
Inclusion criteria: The sample was selected voluntarily from the participants of a sports injury prevention and medical examination program by MasqSano for sports clubs in he Province of Almeria.
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, handball, swimming, rugby, volleyball
Related_Factor_measure: Factor 3 includes: I would like my clothes to fit better; I would like my physique to be different; I would like to be thinner
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The result of the linear regression clearly shows that the most significant explanatory weight is given by dissatisfaction with body image, despite the normal weight found. Social networks do not show a significant relationship with the risk of developing ED. We found a relationship between the risk of manifesting ED and feeling fatigued, getting little rest, and having problems concentrating. Fatigue and the risk of developing ED are not related to the hours of sports practice.
Limits: First, the sampling is not random and therefore does not offer representative data for each group of athletes. Second, there may be non-observational errors due to the impossibility of obtaining all the influencial variables, such as psychological variables. Third, although the survey were short, they were adiministered while medical examinations were conducted, meaning the subjects attitudes and cooperation could be rushed or hasty. Fourth, BMI is not a completely objective tool for diagnosing normal weight, underweight or overweight, particularly in the athletic population, since this value only considers weight and height, discarding other helpful information such as muscle mass and its ratio to fat mass. Fifht, we consider age to be a limiting factor since the subjects surveyed are at a stage in which numerous changes in body composition occur due to growth and social influence. In the absence of a longitudinal study, it is not possible to speak of a direct influence. Finally, sixth comprises the need for a non-athlete control group to compare the significance level of the variables in both populations.
Perspectives:
Its necessary and interesting for prevention to be carried out before the adolescent stage (before the age of 12 or 13). 
Implement health promotion programs where aspects of body image are also addressed in addition to working on eating and sport habits. Design interventions based on age, in addition to gender, since the data are increasingly similar between male and Female in terms of body image dissatisfaction and danger of ED. In the design of interventions, pay differentiated attention to the athlete and non-athlete population. Even within the group of athletes, it is recommaleded to differentiate according to modality for diagnosis, prevention and intervention. Finally, we would like to point out, two issues: First the young people participating in the study were not diagnosed, which shows that ecessive concern about physical appearance can lead to behavior or attitudes that affect health before the disease in diagnosed. Secondly, the results suggest the need for the development of longitudinal studies in which the variability of the different dimensions analized and their degree of influence on the risk of developing ED can be observed.

Title: Perception of eating behaviors, body image, and social pressures in Female division II college athletes and non-athletes
Authors: Gaines, S.A., & Burnett, T.B.S.
Inclusion criteria: Female college athletes and non athletes (enrolled in several general education courses) aged 18 to 42 years of age; from moderately-sized university.
Sport_name: Cross country; track and field; basketball; volleyball; softball
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Peer and romantic pressure collectively predicted Females body image, disordered eating behaviors, and self esteem, romantic pressure did not significantly contribute independently. Peer pressure positively predicted disordered eating behaviors.
Limits: The sample was primarily Hispanic, which is representative of the population where the data were collected, but reduces the generalizability of these findings. Only two sports where an emphasis is placed on the body means of the uniform were examined in the study. The athlete sample was smaller than the non-athlete sample, which made it necessary to pool data for some analyses.
Perspectives: Carefully designed education and intervention programs, peer leaders, both on athletic teams and in college counseling centers, can be a meaningful way to enrich Females body image perceptions, decrease disordered eating behaviors, and increase self-esteem. Understanding the mechanisms by which peers, as well as other significant others, influence body image perceptions, disordered eating and self-esteem will be critical in preventing the escalation of negative eating behaviors in college Females.

Title: Body image and muscle dysmorphia in competitive weightlifters: relationships across variables
Authors: Tokay, B.
Inclusion criteria: Age between 15 and 35 years, no health issues or injuries within the past six months, at least 2 years of active, licensed participation in the Olympic weightlifting discipline, participation in a minimum of three official weightlifting competitions (domestic or international) and voluntary agreement to participate in the study
Mean_Age: Females M=16.04, SD=2.22 Males M=17.53, SD=3.26
Mean_BMI: Underweight N=17 Normal weight N=124 Overweight N=41 Obese N=21
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Higher body image (BI) was associated with lower muscle dysmorphia (MD), suggesting a protective role of positive body perception in weightlifters. While overall BI and MD did not vary by most demographics, BMI and age influenced specific MD symptoms, highlighting nuanced risk patterns
Limits: The study’s cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and some findings (e.g., lack of gender differences) may be sample-specific. Additionally, focusing on total scores may overlook important variations within subdimensions
Perspectives: Future research should explore these relationships longitudinally and examine psychosocial factors such as social media and training goals. Targeted interventions promoting positive body image could help reduce MD risk and improve athletes’ well-being

Title: Testing general sociocultural and coach-related appearance pressures as the factors associated with disordered eating in competitive female athletes participating in various sport
Authors: Jankauskiene, R., & Baceviene, M.
Inclusion criteria: Being an athlete that competed for at least two years in any competitive sport (participating in sports competitions of one sport) and being an official member of a sports school, sports club or national sports team
Sporting population: Sports school, sports clubs, national team
DEAB_measure: Lithuanian version of the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q)
Related_Factor_measure: Overweight preoccupation subscale from the Lithuanian version of the Multidimensional Body-Self Relations Questionnaire-Appearance Scales (MBSRQ-AS)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Judgement of size, shape and weight
Authors' conclusions: General sociocultural pressures (parents, peers and media) are directly associated with disordered eating, and internalization of appearance ideals and overweight preoccupation mediate these associations in female competitive athletes. Controlling for general sociocultural pressures, perceived body weight and appearance-related pressures from coaches were associated with disordered eating through appearance internationalization and overweight preoccupation.
Limits: Cross sectional desing; a full SEM to test the associations between latent variables was not conducted, only a basic path analysis. We did not assess variables such as negative affect and restrained eating that are integral parts of the original model. We assessed the aspects of negative body image (overweight preoccupation) and disordered eating as possible outcome of the general sociocultural and coach-related pressures.
Perspectives: It is important to promote resistance to sociocultural pressures (parents, peers, media) and pressures from coaches in disordered eating prevention programmes for female athletes of all ages participating in sports irrespective of sport group WS or less. Choaches must be educated to understand and recognise the associations between athletes body image, disordered eating, and physical, mental health and sports performance, as weel as their personal influence on it and to promote positive body image in sports environments.

Title: Contextual body image and athletes' disordered eating: the contribution of athletic body image to disordered eating in high performance Female athletes
Authors: Karin de Bruin, A.P., Oudejans, R.R.D., Bakker, F.C., & Woertman, L.
Population subgroup:
19 athletes with eating disorders
33 without disordered eating
Inclusion criteria: High performance Female athletes with disordered eating ; competing on national or international levels ; control without disordered eating. Subjects with disordered eating meet two of the major criteria: amaleorrhoea, low BMI or low body fat, purging methods, and bulimic episodes, in addition to two of the following minor criteria: fear of weight gain, feelings of fatness, maintained low weight and increased importance of weight/shape. If participants did not meet these criteria, they were placed in the control group without disordered eating.
Mean_BMI:
Athletes with disordered eating M=20.69, SD=2.89
Athletes without disordered eating M=20.23, SD=2.23
Sport_name: Rythmic/acrobatic gymnastics and synchronized swimming, aerobic endurance training, middle and long distance running, swimming or long distance speed skating, tennis
Mean_Years of experience:
Athletes with disordered eating M=9, SD=4.27
Athletes without disordered eating M=8.36, SD=4.09
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: The athletic body image strongly contributed to ED. The athletes self-evaluations about shape, weight and fat percentage and the perceived opinions of others on these aspects appeared to be only significant factors uniquely explaining 14 and 9% of the EDE-Q variance. 64% of the variance was explained by the relevant body image components from daily life and sport.
Limits: Limitations of the present study were its sample size and consitution. Unfortunately, the number of Dutch high performance athletes is not that extensive.
Perspectives: Future studies should further explore athletes body comparisons in daliy life and sport, and possible differences between athletes with and without disordered eating in this respect. Future research should further explore body images in sport and daily life, particularly in athletes with disordered eating. We needed to extent the sample with a group of at-risk athletes who were not professionaly diagnosed in advance. Future investigation needs to take into account dynamic and contextual body image changes. It should also focus more closely on why certain athletes develop a more negative body image and how this could be prevented.

Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Sport_name: Cross country/track and field, swimming and diving, volleyball, wrestling, soccer, golf, football, lacrosse, baseball, basketball, tennis
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: The relationship between perceived stress, body image and eating behaviors in athletes

Title: Psychometric properties of the contextual body image questionnaire for athletes: a replication and extension study in Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Stewart, T., Kilpela, L., Wesley, K., & Becker, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes at each university within the ages of 17-27 years
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Authors' conclusions: Daily life thin-fat others correlated with EDE-Q global scores. Sport muscularity did not correlated with EDE-Q. All dimensions except muscularity correlated with all subscales in both contexts. Appearance dimension (perceiving others opinions of yourself) was related to higher levels of ED pathology in both daily life and sport contexts. Self evaluation and perceived other evaluation as fatter were also related to more ED pathology. Muscularity in daily life was not related to ED symptomatology. CBIQA scores related to appearance may predict future ED pathology.
Limits: Reliance on self-report data, attrition at follow-up, and that the CBIQA was delivered to participants 12 months into the FAB program as opposed to the beginning of the parent trial.
Perspectives: Further research on cntextual body images is needed to evaluate the impact of these dual body images with Female athletes not only while in sport, but while away or retiring from sport, inclusding periods of injury, between seasons and when completing sport.

Authors' conclusions: Daily life thin-fat others correlated with EDE-Q global scores. Sport muscularity did not correlated with EDE-Q. All dimensions except muscularity correlated with all subscales in both contexts. Appearance dimension (perceiving others opinions of yourself) was related to higher levels of ED pathology in both daily life and sport contexts. Self evaluation and perceived other evaluation as fatter were also related to more ED pathology. Muscularity in daily life was not related to ED symptomatology. Title: Prevalence and correlates of disordered eating in Female figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Gould, D., Reel, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged 12 to 25. Former skaters, basic skills skaters, and those in adult skating programs (e.g., age-based competitions following adult test equivalencies) were excluded
Sport_name: Figure skating (singles, multiple, synchronized, ice dancing, pairs)
Related_Factor: Self consciousness of weight and appearance
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Related Weight Pressures in Sport Scale-Females (WPS-F)
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perceptual dimension of body image and self-esteem
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Self consciousness of weight and appearance
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Self consciousness of weight and appearance
Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. Positive perfectionism made a significant contribution, but negative perfectionism did not. Self esteem may not be strongly related to disordered eating. Perspectives:
Sport psychology practiitioners should aid this effort by teaching skaters to appreciate body strengths and utilize psychological skills that may buffer the impact of negative weight pressures (e.g., utilizing positive self talk and realistic goal-setting). 
A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.

Title: Influence of perfectionism on variables associated to eating disorders in dance students
Authors: Arcelus, J., Garcia-Dantas, A., Sanchez-Martin, M., Del Rio, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female dance professionals; aged 12-20;  from two professional dance conservatories in Spain; informed consent was obtained from their parents.
Sport_name: Dance (e.g., ballet, contemporary, flamenco, spanish folk)
Authors' conclusions: Body image has been found, not only to be a risk factor for the development of an ED, but as a mediator between perfectionism and dieting, and associated to performance cognitive anxiety which mediates the relationship between perfectionism and depression.
Limits: The use of general questionnaires such as the BDI II or EAT-26 which are not validated specifically to be used within the dance population, although they are validated and highly reliable measurements. Performance anxiety was measured hypothetically and it will be best to measure it previous to an event. Performance anxiety has been retrospectively measured instead of administering the questionnaires in situ before the performance.
Perspectives: Interventions aiming at reducing concern over mistakes may required a preventative component and by doing so it will help reducing body dissatisfaction, performance cognitive anxiety and dieting which will prevent the development of eating disorders in this vulnerable group. Future research should replicate this study and include males different age range, dance levels and nationalities.

Title: Perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting in athletes: the role of gender and sport type
Authors: Prnjak, K., Jukic, I., & Tufano, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged from 18 to 29 years from the faculty of Kinesiology
Sport_name: Soccer; basketball; gymnastics; figure skating; athletics; swimming
Measure Mediator: Body Image and Body Change Inventory
Degree of relationship:
Total effect 𝛃=.005, N.S.
Direct effect 𝛃=.009, N.S.
Indirect effect 𝛃=-.003, N.S.
Adaptive perfectionism-body satisfaction 𝛃=.34, p<.01
Adaptive perfectionism-dieting 𝛃=.09, N.S.
Body satisfaction-dieting 𝛃=-.31, p<.001
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism and body satisfaction explain dieting among Female athletes. For the male athletes, none of the predictors contributed to the understanding of their dieting behaviour. In addition, age, sport type and duration of sport participation did not contribute to dieting behaviour un case of male and Female. Adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism were associated with body satisfaction among Female athletes but not with dieting behaviour directly. Satisfaction with one's body was shown to be the largest independent predictor of dieting and their relationship was negative.
Limits: The data was based on self reported measures. Cross sectional design limits the causal inference between perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting. The sample consisted of athletes who were enrolled in a university program which might limit the generalizability. PANPS should not be used as a measure of perfectionism due to a questionable factor validity of the positive perfectionism subscale. EAT-26 was shown to have a low positive predictive value due to the rarity of targeted conditions while two out of three EAT-26 subscales demonstrated low internal consistency and omitting them while investigating eating disorder may not be the best approach. The number of Female participants was lower than males, which might have affected some of the analysis were gender-split was included.
Perspectives: It would be important to further etablish the relationship between perfectionism dimensions and body satisfaction in the area of disordered eating but also take a consideration the context in which athletes perceive their body.

Title: Eating attitudes, body appreciation, perfectionism, and the risk of exercise addiction in physically active adults: a cluster analysis
Authors: Piko, B.F., Berki, T.L., Kun, O., Mellor, D.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years of age and have an active lifestyle with regular physical activity (at least once a week, for a minimum of 30min)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 1h or less/week n=72 1-2h/week n=114 3-5h/week n=16 >5h/week n=3
Mean_Years of experience: 1 year or less n=40 2-3 years n=24 3-5 years n=17 5-10 years n=37 >10 years n=87
DEAB_measure: Validated Hungarian version of the Eating Attitude Test-26 (EAT-26)
Related_Factor_measure: Hungarian version of the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale (FMPS)
Authors' conclusions: Exercise addiction (EA) can also occur in regular exercisers, not just athletes, and is often linked with disordered eating (DE) when body image concerns and perfectionism are present. These factors interact in complex ways, meaning EA is not always pathological but can signal risk when combined with unhealthy eating attitudes and excessive performance pressure
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and reliance on self-reports, a relatively small and female-biased sample, and heterogeneous sport types limit generalizability
Perspectives: Future research should use larger, more diverse samples and longitudinal designs, while exploring additional psychological variables and protective factors to better understand and prevent EA and DE

Authors: Ferrand, C., Magnan, C., Rouveix, M., & Filaire, E.

Authors' conclusions: Socially prescribed perfectionism did not explain variance in dietary restraint scores. Self esteem oriented perfectionism was associated with dietary restraint and was related to body dissatisfaction. The current findings show a mediating effect of body esteem weight satisfaction on the relationship between self-oriented perfectionism and dietary restraint. The use of both self-report measures and interview formats in longitudinal studies must be developed to gain a more precise estimate of the nature and extent of inappropriate compensatory behaviours amog synchronized swimmers.

Title: Impact of perfectionism on the risk of the female athlete triad in collegiate athletes
Authors: Brooks, S.G., Peach, H.D., Howden, R., Lowrie, J., Marino, J.S.
Journal: The Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: NCAA female student-athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 years at a Division I university
Sport_name: Cross country, soccer, softball, tennis, track throws, track sprints
Authors' conclusions: This study found significant correlations between LEA risk, DE, triad risk, perfectionism and time spent in a program for female NCAA division I athletes
Limits: Sample size of the study. The athletes came from the same institutions. Study did not collect detailed dietary information, such as macronutrient composition, we did use validated methods of interpreting athletes eating attitudes and behaviors. No causal relationship between perfectionism and our outcomes could be established because this was a cross-sectional study.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate possible interventions to hemp athletes manifest their perfectionistic tendencies in adaptive dimensions rather than maladaptive dimensions associated with an increased risk. Title: Perfectionism and learning experiences in dance class as risk factors for eating disorders in dancers
Authors: Penniment, K.J., & Egan, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Being a Female aged between 18 and 30 years, currently studying classical and/or jazz ballet
Mean_BMI: 22.5% may be classified as underweight, with a BMI under 18.5kg/m²
Sporting population: 20.4% reported that they had danced semi professionally at one time, and 23.9% reported that they had danced at a professional level at one time.
Mean_Years of experience:
Dance tuition M=6.92, SD=22
Years studying dance M=14.5, SD=5.90
Authors' conclusions: The relation between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was partially mediated by thinness related learning. The hypothesis that the relationship between thinness related learning and eating disorders symptoms were partially mediated by thiness restricting expectancies was also supported. A direct relationship between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was found.
Limits: The data was cross sectional. Although the current model fit the data well, there are multiple other risk factors for ED and it is very likely that this risk is determined by multiple factors and is not simply a function of the emphasis on thinness in the dance environment, or perfectionism. The sample was too small to split into professional and non professional dancers to examine if the model was the same in these groups. Our view of perfectionism was aligned with the construct of clinical perfectionism, and as a result we examined a selected subset of scales from the FMPS and did not use relevant scales from the HMPS.
Perspectives:
It would be useful for future research to examine the efficacy of targeting young Female involved in dance with elevated levels of perfectionism for prevention programs, as preliminary findings are positive for the ability of programs targeting perfectionism to reduce eating disorders risk in Female adolescents. 
It would be useful for clinicians to consider directly targeting perfectionism through CBT programs for perfectionism in young Female involved in dance classes as it is likely to be a factor that puts them at higher risk of developing an eating disorders within this environment.

Title: Compulsive exercise as a mediator between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology
Authors: Egan, S.J., Bodill, K., Watson, H.J., Valentine, E., Shu, C., & Hagger, M.S.
Inclusion criteria: The population was adults over the age of 18 years who participated in a diverse range of sport and exercise. The inclusion criteria of exercice twice or more per week was chosen to include people who exercised regularly but the criterion was relatively low as amount of exercise in not the defiing feature of compulsive exercise.
Sport_name: Running, triathlon, ball sports (volleyball, football, baseball, basketball, golf, rugby, squash, netball, cricket, hockey, tennis, badminton), gym, other (water polo, sailing, surf lifesaving, pilates, skateboarding, hula hooping, equestrian), cycling, dance, yoga, athletics, rowing, swimming

The sample comprised mainly of individuals who are actively involved in one particular type of athletic poursuit: individual endurance sports and particularly running. In addition, the study was cross-sectional, therefore the bidirectional relationship between eating pathology and compulsive exercise could not be assessed as this requires a longitudinal design. Indeed, Meyer et al.’s (2011) model proposed bidirectional links between eating pathology and compulsive exercise. Meyer et al. (2011) argued that dieting and exercise reinforce one another due to social reinforcers which accompany the initial weight loss from regular exercise, which then intensifies eating, shape and weight concerns.

Future research should measure perfectionism, compulsive exercise and eating pathology at two time points using a panel design and include a cross-lagged effects to determine the bidirectional relations between variables.

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Mean_Years of experience:
Dance tuition M=6.92, SD=22
Years studying dance M=14.5, SD=5.90
Authors' conclusions: The relation between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was partially mediated by thinness related learning. The hypothesis that the relationship between thinness related learning and eating disorders symptoms were partially mediated by thiness restricting expectancies was also supported. A direct relationship between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was found.
Limits: The data was cross sectional. Although the current model fit the data well, there are multiple other risk factors for ED and it is very likely that this risk is determined by multiple factors and is not simply a function of the emphasis on thinness in the dance environment, or perfectionism. The sample was too small to split into professional and non professional dancers to examine if the model was the same in these groups. Our view of perfectionism was aligned with the construct of clinical perfectionism, and as a result we examined a selected subset of scales from the FMPS and did not use relevant scales from the HMPS.
Perspectives:
It would be useful for future research to examine the efficacy of targeting young Female involved in dance with elevated levels of perfectionism for prevention programs, as preliminary findings are positive for the ability of programs targeting perfectionism to reduce eating disorders risk in Female adolescents. 
It would be useful for clinicians to consider directly targeting perfectionism through CBT programs for perfectionism in young Female involved in dance classes as it is likely to be a factor that puts them at higher risk of developing an eating disorders within this environment.

Title: Prevalence and correlates of disordered eating in Female figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Gould, D., Reel, J.J.

Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.

The associations of striving with the dimensions of eating psychopathology were both weak and one was non-significant. For each group, evaluative concerns was found to have a significant, positive association with the EAT and EDI-BD. Title: Perfectionism and eating psychopathology among dancers: the role of high standards and self-criticism
Authors: Goodwin, H., Arcelus, J., Geach, N., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female; aged 18 years or older; current member of a university recreational dance club; clubs comprised ballet, modern, tap, jazz, and/or hi hop disciplines. The participants were not screened for previous or current eating disorder treatment.
Sport_name: Dance (ballet, jazz/modern, contemporary dance, hip hop, tap, other)
Authors' conclusions: High standards and self criticism are positively associated with eating restraint, eating concern, weight concern and shape concern. The associations between self-criticism and eating pathology were not moderated by high standards. Self criticism fully mediated the relationships between high standards and restraint, eating concern, weight concern and shape concern.
Limits: The self report nature of the data means reports may be unreliable and subject to social desirability bias. The method of participants recruitlent precluded any analysis of response rate, and it was not known whether or not there was a bias to those who chose to participate versus those who did not participate. The heterogeneous nature of the sample means that underlying group differences (between dance style, competency level and hours of dance practice) may have been missed.
Perspectives: The relationships between high standards, self-criticism and eating disorder risk requires examination in more homogenous sub-groups of dancers, to further identify the risk environments for eating psychopathology.

Title: Perfectionism and eating attitudes in competitive rowers: moderating effects of body mass, weight classification and gender
Authors: Haase, A.M., Prapavessis, H., & Owens, G.
Inclusion criteria: National level heavyweight and lightweight rowers from New Zealand and Australia
Mean_Age:
Female M=20.08, SD=4.23
Male M=21.49, SD=4.67
Authors' conclusions: After controlling for social desirability effects, negative perfectionism scores were found to correlate positively with disturbed eating attitudes scores, whereas positive perfectionism scores were found to be unrelated to disturbed eating attitude scores.
Limits: Focus only on rowing sample.
Perspectives:
This would suggest that resiliency against unhealthy eating could be increased by teaching athletes how to develop and maintain high levels of positive perfectionism. Intervention with goal in mind is a worthy topic for future research. 
Do these perfectionistic tendencies change throughout an athlete's career ? How and why do these changes occur ? What implications do these changes have on eating attitude ?

Title: Prevalence and correlates of disordered eating in Female figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Gould, D., Reel, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Female figure skaters aged 12 to 25. Former skaters, basic skills skaters, and those in adult skating programs (e.g., age-based competitions following adult test equivalencies) were excluded
Sport_name: Figure skating (singles, multiple, synchronized, ice dancing, pairs)
Authors' conclusions: All sport related weight pressures were significantly related to disordered eating, however only self consciousness of weight and appearance emerged as a significant correlate in the regression model. Body dissatisfaction explained an additional 5.7% of the variance in disordered eating. Sport related body dissatisfaction also emerged as a significant predictor. Positive perfectionism made a significant contribution, but negative perfectionism did not. Self esteem may not be strongly related to disordered eating. Athletic identity did not emerge as a significant variable in the final regression model, although the bivariate correlation indicated a significant positive relationship with disordered eating.
Limits: Societal weight pressures were not exmained. Self report nature of the surveys and the willingness of athletes to honestly and accurately respond to survey items. The results are also based on a conveniance sample of skaters limited to clubs in the Midwest and Northeast. Cross sectional design, causal relationships and change over time could not be determined.
Perspectives:
Sport psychology practiitioners should aid this effort by teaching skaters to appreciate body strengths and utilize psychological skills that may buffer the impact of negative weight pressures (e.g., utilizing positive self talk and realistic goal-setting). 
A random and more representative sample of skaters nationally and internationally, inclusive of males, should be considered in future research.

Title: Disordered eating, eating attitudes and reasons for exercise among male high school cross country runners
Authors: Wadas, G.
Inclusion criteria: The runners were selected from 12 of the thirty two public high schools in the local school district sponsoring sports teams located in the USA. Participants were current members of a high shcool cross country teams, were in grades 9-12 and between the ages of 14-18.
Sporting population: Some playing time (24.2%), starter on team (29%), conference (4.8%), regional (35.5%), national (4.8%), other (1.6%)
Authors' conclusions: Factors that have a significant relationship with disordered eating are performance perfectionism and weight management. A desire to control weight is associated with disordered eating behaviors in male high school cross country runners as determined from the modest correlation coefficient for the weight management subscale and the EAT-26. There was no significant correlation for the physical appearance subscale of the EMI-2 and the EAT-26. No significant relationships were found between disordered eating behaviors and social pressure on body shape, social pressure on eating and athlete identity.
Limits: The results are generalizable only to school districts of similar size and demographic makeup. The questionnaire were completed on one occasion by runners during the sumer prior to the start of the season. The study was limited by a low number of participants relative to the number of runners on the teams and number of high schools in the school district.
Perspectives: The present study did not investigate the reasons for dissatisfaction with current weight status, future studies may seek more information relative to the reasons. For example, do male cross country runners feels a need to be more muscular ? Do the bodies of male cross country runners not fit the ideal ?

Title: Impact of perfectionism on the risk of the female athlete triad in collegiate athletes
Authors: Brooks, S.G., Peach, H.D., Howden, R., Lowrie, J., Marino, J.S.
Journal: The Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: NCAA female student-athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 years at a Division I university
Sport_name: Cross country, soccer, softball, tennis, track throws, track sprints
Authors' conclusions: This study found significant correlations between LEA risk, DE, triad risk, perfectionism and time spent in a program for female NCAA division I athletes
Limits: Sample size of the study. The athletes came from the same institutions. Study did not collect detailed dietary information, such as macronutrient composition, we did use validated methods of interpreting athletes eating attitudes and behaviors. No causal relationship between perfectionism and our outcomes could be established because this was a cross-sectional study.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate possible interventions to hemp athletes manifest their perfectionistic tendencies in adaptive dimensions rather than maladaptive dimensions associated with an increased risk. Other psychological variables (drive for thinness, self esteem) should also benefit explored to further our understanding of the role of mental health in athletes risk for adverse health conditions.

Sporting population:
51.2% national level
24.8% international level
0.4% regional
11.8% provincial
11.8% North American level
Related_Factor_measure: Multidimensional Inventory of Perfectionism in Sport
Authors' conclusions: Several factors identified in this study (e.g., athlete status, perfectionism) appear to play a role in the development of ED in this population. The study of other factors such as athletic identity and the coach-athlete relationship could provide insight into the development of ED symptoms within this group of athletes.
Limits: The study uses self-reported data; cross sectional design of the study. Athletes who were neither studying not employed exhibited more drive for thinness attitudes and behaviors than did those who were studying and/or employed yet few participants were in this situation. Perspectives: Future studies could assess whether offering athletes mental health training in their sporting environment could help reduce their ED symptoms. The development of knowledge concerning the mechanisms underlying the drive for muscularity and thinness could be the subject of future quantitative studies, providing a deeper understanding of the risk factors associated with ED.

Title: Perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting in athletes: the role of gender and sport type
Authors: Prnjak, K., Jukic, I., & Tufano, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged from 18 to 29 years from the faculty of Kinesiology
Sport_name: Soccer; basketball; gymnastics; figure skating; athletics; swimming
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism and body satisfaction explain dieting among Female athletes. For the male athletes, none of the predictors contributed to the understanding of their dieting behaviour. In addition, age, sport type and duration of sport participation did not contribute to dieting behaviour un case of male and Female. Adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism were associated with body satisfaction among Female athletes but not with dieting behaviour directly. Satisfaction with one's body was shown to be the largest independent predictor of dieting and their relationship was negative.
Limits: The data was based on self reported measures. Cross sectional design limits the causal inference between perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting. The sample consisted of athletes who were enrolled in a university program which might limit the generalizability. PANPS should not be used as a measure of perfectionism due to a questionable factor validity of the positive perfectionism subscale. EAT-26 was shown to have a low positive predictive value due to the rarity of targeted conditions while two out of three EAT-26 subscales demonstrated low internal consistency and omitting them while investigating eating disorder may not be the best approach. The number of Female participants was lower than males, which might have affected some of the analysis were gender-split was included.
Perspectives: It would be important to further etablish the relationship between perfectionism dimensions and body satisfaction in the area of disordered eating but also take a consideration the context in which athletes perceive their body.

Title: Maladaptive perfectionism as mediator among psychological control, eating disorders, and exercise dependence symptoms in habitual exerciser
Authors: Costa, S., Hausenblas, H.A., Oliva, P., Cuzzocrea, F., & Larcan, R.
Inclusion criteria: Inclusion criteria were that exerciser had trained for at least 6 consecutive months, lived at home with both parents, and were at least 18 years of age.
Authors' conclusions: There is a significant relationship between parental psychological control and both exercise dependence and eating disorder symptoms. Psychological control, both maternal and parternal, predicted maladaptive perfectionism, while maladaptive perfectionism, predicted ED symptoms and exercise dependence symptoms. Results confirmed the mediating role of maladaptive perfectionism as a full mediator for ED and exercise dependence symptoms for both male and Female habitual exercisers in the maternal data. In the paternal data, maladaptive perfectionism mediated the relationships between paternal psychological control and eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms as full mediator for the Female participants and as partial mediator for the male participants.
Limits: First, the data were collected at one time point and not across multiple time points as it should be done for a true mediational analysis. Because of the cross-sectional and self-report design of our study, we cannot etablish either the direction or causality of the effects. As weel, the self-report data may have intrinsic limitations such as social desirability, so the use of objective and multi-informant measures and experimental designs are encourages. Although, our sample consisted of habitual exercisers, this sample was deemed justified, as eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms are prevalent in this population and because psychological control is a risk factor for eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms in this population.
Perspectives: The deleterious effects of parental psychological control, both on eating disorder and on exercise dependence symptoms, require the implementation of targeted interventions to educate parents in using fewer instrusions and parental autonomy support, as opposed to psychological control. It is important to educate parents about psychological control being a universally negative parenting strategy and to help parents identify and reduce the use of such dysfunctional practices. Parent training could be used to help parents to get to practice autonomy supportive skills by taking part in various exercices from common situations in familial daily living. Results of the study suggest that the therapist and client could work together to identify and correct the client's maladaptive perfectionism thought processes that result in maladaptive eating or exercise behavior.

Title: Compulsive exercise as a mediator between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology
Authors: Egan, S.J., Bodill, K., Watson, H.J., Valentine, E., Shu, C., & Hagger, M.S.
Inclusion criteria: The population was adults over the age of 18 years who participated in a diverse range of sport and exercise. The inclusion criteria of exercice twice or more per week was chosen to include people who exercised regularly but the criterion was relatively low as amount of exercise in not the defiing feature of compulsive exercise.
Sport_name: Running, triathlon, ball sports (volleyball, football, baseball, basketball, golf, rugby, squash, netball, cricket, hockey, tennis, badminton), gym, other (water polo, sailing, surf lifesaving, pilates, skateboarding, hula hooping, equestrian), cycling, dance, yoga, athletics, rowing, swimming
Authors' conclusions: Direct and indirect effects were found between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology through compulsive exercise. Specifically, there were direct effects of clinical perfectionism on avoidance/rule driven behavior, weight control exercise, and mood improvement.
Limits: Participant recruitmalet was not random or stratified which limits generalizability. The sample comprised mainly of individuals who are actively involved in one particular type of athletic poursuit: individual endurance sports and particularly running. The sample may, therefore, not be representative of individuals involved in sport and exercise in general. In addition, the study was cross-sectional, therefore the bidirectional relationship between eating pathology and compulsive exercise could not be assessed as this requires a longitudinal design. While we hypothesized that perfectionism would affect compulsive exercise, which would impact eating pathology, it could equally be argued that perfectionism influences eating pathology, which then influences compulsive exercise (i.e., compulsive exercise is a symptom of eating pathology, rather than an antecedent). Indeed, Meyer et al.’s (2011) model proposed bidirectional links between eating pathology and compulsive exercise. Meyer et al. (2011) argued that dieting and exercise reinforce one another due to social reinforcers which accompany the initial weight loss from regular exercise, which then intensifies eating, shape and weight concerns.
Perspectives: It would be useful to determine whether interventions for both perfectionism and compulsive exercise may help to improve the efficacy of standard treatments for eating disorders, above the gain already found in efficacious treatments such as CBT-E (Fairbunr et al., 2009) where clinical perfectionism is a focus if it is elevated. Future research could also examine the efficacy of specific stand-alone treatments for perfectionism (e.g., Egan et al., 2014) for compulsive exercise and perfectionism in eating disorders. Future research should measure perfectionism, compulsive exercise and eating pathology at two time points using a panel design and include a cross-lagged effects to determine the bidirectional relations between variables.

Authors: Nordin, S., Harris, G., & Cumming, J.
Population subgroup:
Rhytmic gymnasts
Artistic gymnasts
Sport acrobats
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts who participated in one of three different forms of gymnastics: artistic, rhythmic, or sports acrobatics; training and competing for various clubs in the West Midlands, UK.
Authors' conclusions: Rhytmic gymnasts were considered to be at a greater risk for ED development than were artistic gymnasts or sport acrobats. This findings is probably due to sport-specific pressure in rhythmic gymnastics to obtain a very thin body rather than other variables such as age or perfectionist tendencies.
Limits: Sample small. Only 6 on the 9 coaches who were approached agreed to participate in the study. It is possible that only those coaches who were certain that their group was altogether healthy would be more likely to agree to take part, and vice versa. Secrecy, deception and denial are considered inherent to eating disorders, and it is generally agreed that self report measures for eating disorders tend to yield conservative estimates. Underreporting also constitues a possible limitation.
Perspectives:
The climate in training can be an important variable in eating disorder development. An investigation into motivational climates and perceived sport specific pressures would be a welcome addition to the eating disturbances literature. 
Qualitative research methologies may be used to gain a deeper insight into what pressures are present, as well as their sources, such as coaches, parents, teammates, judges, and others.

Title: Perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting in athletes: the role of gender and sport type
Authors: Prnjak, K., Jukic, I., & Tufano, J.J.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged from 18 to 29 years from the faculty of Kinesiology
Sport_name: Soccer; basketball; gymnastics; figure skating; athletics; swimming
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism and body satisfaction explain dieting among Female athletes. For the male athletes, none of the predictors contributed to the understanding of their dieting behaviour. In addition, age, sport type and duration of sport participation did not contribute to dieting behaviour un case of male and Female. Adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism were associated with body satisfaction among Female athletes but not with dieting behaviour directly. Satisfaction with one's body was shown to be the largest independent predictor of dieting and their relationship was negative.
Limits: The data was based on self reported measures. Cross sectional design limits the causal inference between perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting. The sample consisted of athletes who were enrolled in a university program which might limit the generalizability. PANPS should not be used as a measure of perfectionism due to a questionable factor validity of the positive perfectionism subscale. EAT-26 was shown to have a low positive predictive value due to the rarity of targeted conditions while two out of three EAT-26 subscales demonstrated low internal consistency and omitting them while investigating eating disorder may not be the best approach. The number of Female participants was lower than males, which might have affected some of the analysis were gender-split was included.
Perspectives: It would be important to further etablish the relationship between perfectionism dimensions and body satisfaction in the area of disordered eating but also take a consideration the context in which athletes perceive their body.

Title: Frequency and psychosocial correlates of eating disorder symptomatology in male figure skaters
Authors: Voelker, D.K., Petrie, T.A., Reel, J.J., & Gould, D.
Inclusion criteria: Male figure skaters
Sport_name: Figure skating (singles skaters, ice dancers, synchronized, multiple disciplines)
Authors' conclusions: Negative perfectionism, self esteem, and athletic identity were unrelated to ED symptomatology.
Limits: Smaller sample. Weight pressures may be experienced differently according to discipline specific performance demands. Cross sectional design.
Perspectives:
Future research should incorporate longitudinal designs to identify true risk factors of ED symptomatology and use qualitative interviews to further examine the lived experience of sport-related weight pressures. 
Practitioners may collaborate with other professionals, such as sports dieteticians, to educate skating communities on weight-performance myths and improve communication between skaters, parents, and coaches about the body. Practitioners may also assist athletes in coping with weight pressures by focusing on body appreciation and function while reinforcing that healthy training approaches can have positive effects on eating, exercise, and body image.

Title: A comprehensive model of disordered eating among aesthetic athletic girls: exploring the role of body image related cognitive fusion and perfectionistic self presentation
Authors: Paixao, C., Oliveira, S., & Ferreira, C.

Authors' conclusions: Body image related cognitive fusion was strongly associated with ED. Perspectives:

Our data seems to indicate that intervention and prevention programs for aesthetic athletes, should focus on the development of more adpative strategies related to body image, through the cultivation of a balanced and acceptance relationship with one's own body characteristics rather than on the adoption of body image related perfectionist self presentation strategies.

Title: Achievement goal theory and disordered eating: relationships of disordered eating with goal orientations and motivation climate in Female gymnasts and dancers
Authors: Karin de Bruin, A.P., Bakker, F.C., & Oudejans, R.R.D.
Inclusion criteria: Only high level aesthetic performers who did not participate in additional competitive sport activities were included.
Mean_Exercise frequency:
M=16.7 hours per week, SD=6.7
Gymnasts M=18.1, SD=7.8
Dancers M=14.4, SD=3.28
DEAB_measure: 9-point-scale running from 1(never) to 9(always) with the following item Are you trying yo lose weight ?
Related_Factor_measure: Perceived Motivational Climate in Sport Questionnaire (PMCSQ)
Authors' conclusions: Ego orientation and performance climate were related to more frequent dieting, using more pathogenic weight control methods, greater perfectionism and perceiving more weight related peer pressure. Having a high ego orientation means that a Female aesthetic performer is sgnificantly more likely to report indices of disordered eating. Non-significant correlations were found between task orientation and DE. With respect to performance climate, significant relationships were found with all DE variables. The present study also shows that a mastery climate is negatively related to disordered eating. Mastery climate explained some of the variance of dieting frequency.
Limits: A limitation in the present study was that we used a relatively crude measure for pathogenic weight control with limited reliability. Another limitation was that we had to confine ourselves to self-reported height and weight because objective measurement of body composition was perceived as too threatening form some aesthetic performers. Self-report holds the risk of both under or overstimation. Another constraint in the present study was the composition of our sample. As the number of high level competitive gymnasts in the Netherlands is limited, we also investigated a group of high level Female dancers.
Perspectives: In future studes focusing exclusively on relationships between eating disorders or disordered eating with achievement motivation, full versions of general or sport specific measures could be administered such as the Eating Disorder Inventory-2 or the Female Athlete Screening Tool for disordered eating. Future studies should continue to making an effort to include objective measurements by the researchers or recent actual data provided by medical staff members. The observed relationships of this study should be replicated in future studies using larger samples of various athletes at risk for disordered eating. Roberts (2001) stated that a high ego orientation is particularly detrimental if it is accompanied by a low task orientation. Future research should further investigate if this is also true for disordered eating. To gain a more complete understanding of the relationship between ego orientation and disordered eating, future studies could also include the more recent 2 by 2 framework which not only distinguishes between ego and task orientation but also between approach and avoidance achievmalet goals. We therefore recommaled that coaches and teachers should create a mastery climate with its emphasis on personal development and interpersonal cooperation.

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Members of various urban fitness centers aged between 18 and 60 years
Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Maladaptive personality traits for the DEAB studies available to date
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. Using self report questionnaire by collecting data at the same time from the same individuals raises the bias of common method variance. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Title: Relationships between personality traits and disordered eating among Chinese Female exercisers: the role of symptoms of exercise dependence and obsessive-compulsiveness
Authors: Yang, P., Wang, T., Herold, F., Muller, N.G., Taylor, A., Szabo, A., Granziol, U., Cook, B., Landolfi, E., Somi, M., & Zou, L.
Inclusion criteria: The Female exercises needed to be training at least three times per week for a minimum of 150 min in total, for not less than six months with respect to the recruitmalet date.
Mean_Exercise frequency:
M=4.42 times a week, SD=1.88
74.14min every session
Related_Factor_sub-class 3: Maladaptive personality traits for the DEAB studies available to date
Authors' conclusions: Only the personality traits conscientiousness, emotional stability and agreeableness are significantly associated with disordered eating. Our mediation analyses revealed the relationship between conscientiousness and disordered eating was completely mediated via the path of exercise dependence and obsessive compulsive symptoms, while the relationship of emotional stability and disordered eating was partly mediated via exercise dependence symptoms and obsessive compulsive symptoms. Moreover the relationship between agreeableness and disordered eating was only mediated by the severity of obsessive compulsive symptoms. The results of the correaltion analysis revealed that conscientiousness, emotional stability and agreeableness were negatively associated with the severity of disordered eating. In contrast, extroversion and openness to experience did not show a significant association with ED. The multiple mediation model of conscientiousness on disordered eating revaled an indirect effect of conscientiousness on disordered eating via higher exercise dependence symptoms and higher obsessive compulsive symptoms. The multiple mediation model of the effects of emotiona stability on disordered eating demonstrated an indirect effect of emotional stability via exercise dependence and obsessive compulsive symptoms. Considering the single mediation model of agreeableness on disordered eating, our results showed that the relationship between agreeableness and disordered eating can be explained through obsessive compulsive symptoms.
Limits: This cross sectional study design did not allow conclusions concerning the causal relationship. Symptoms of disordered eating were considered but we did not distinguish between different types of eating disorders, which may limit the generalizabiliy. Only Chinese Female exercisers were included. The inclusion of personality traits was operationalized by using the well etablished big five personality model. However, given that personality traits (e.g., perfectionism) were also identified as core characteristics among these disorders
Perspectives: Other personality dimensions or mechanisms should be examined in future studies to allow for more robust and nuanced conclusions.

Title: Physical self concept and disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors in French athlete and non-athlete adolescents girls: direct and indirect relations
Authors: Monthuy-Blanc, J., Maiano, C., Morin, A.J.S., & Stephan, Y.
Inclusion criteria: French adolescent girls between the ages of 12 and 16 years
Mean_Age:
Ballet M=14.6, SD=1.26
Basketball M=13.59, SD=1.32
Mean_BMI:
Ballet M=19.31, SD=2.18
Basketball M=19.42, SD=3.45
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Ballet M=4.10h/week, SD=1.16
Basketball M=4.05h/week, SD=.84
Mean_Years of experience:
Ballet M=3.78, SD=.76
Basketball M=3.93, SD=.85
Authors' conclusions: Self concept subdomains are indirectly related to disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors through their relations with global and physical self worth in non-elite athlete adolescent girls competing in different types of sports.
Limits: The cross sectional deisgn prevents causal interpretation and also precluded the consideration of inter-individual differences in rates of growth and maturation that may be involved in the development of disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors. We focused on a single leaness/aesthetic sport whereas research shows that elite athletes involved in some weight controlled, but not aesthetic sports, such as boxing or judo, may also present an elevated prevalence of disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors. This study was performed using a small convenience sample exclusively composed of non-elite adolescents girls of dubious generalizability.
Perspectives: It would be interesting to investigate similar relations in a sample of elite basketball players for whom reliance on these more extreme stretagies would likely prove counter-productive in the long term.

Inclusion criteria: French adolescent girls between the ages of 12 and 16 years
Mean_Age:
Ballet M=14.6, SD=1.26
Basketball M=13.59, SD=1.32
Mean_BMI:
Ballet M=19.31, SD=2.18
Basketball M=19.42, SD=3.45
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Ballet M=4.10h/week, SD=1.16
Basketball M=4.05h/week, SD=.84
Mean_Years of experience:
Ballet M=3.78, SD=.76
Basketball M=3.93, SD=.85
Authors' conclusions: Self concept subdomains are indirectly related to disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors through their relations with global and physical self worth in non-elite athlete adolescent girls competing in different types of sports.
Limits: The cross sectional deisgn prevents causal interpretation and also precluded the consideration of inter-individual differences in rates of growth and maturation that may be involved in the development of disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors. We focused on a single leaness/aesthetic sport whereas research shows that elite athletes involved in some weight controlled, but not aesthetic sports, such as boxing or judo, may also present an elevated prevalence of disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors. This study was performed using a small convenience sample exclusively composed of non-elite adolescents girls of dubious generalizability.
Perspectives: It would be interesting to investigate similar relations in a sample of elite basketball players for whom reliance on these more extreme stretagies would likely prove counter-productive in the long term.

Title: Eating disorders risk assessment and body esteem among elite polish contact karate athletes
Authors: Dobkowska-Szefer, D., Staskiewicz-Bartecka, W., Kiciak, A., Kardas, M.
Inclusion criteria: Consent from both the club and the athlete to participate in the study, active participation in training in contact karate clubs (defined as > 3 training sessions per week for at least the past 6 months), achievement of at least one medal-winning position in competitions at the level of the Polish championships or higher, organized by national or international sports federations, and absence of chronic diseases, including diagnosed mental health disorders, as confirmed in the demographic section of the questionnaire
Related_Factor_measure: Body Esteem Scale (BES) in the Polish adaptation by Lipowska and Lipowski
Authors' conclusions: This study identifies elite karate athletes as a high-risk group for disordered eating and orthorexia, with body image—especially in women—and weight-related pressures playing a central role. It highlights the importance of psychological factors over BMI in shaping risk.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, small and selective sample, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference and generalizability. The use of BMI and omission of key psychosocial variables further constrain interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include larger samples, longitudinal designs, and objective body composition measures. Preventive interventions focusing on body image, nutrition education, and sport-specific pressures are essential in weight-category sport

Title: Social predictors of psychological need satisfaction and well being among Female adolescent gymnasts: a longitudinal analysis
Authors: Kipp, L.E., & Weiss, M.R.
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts; aged 10 to 18; trained 15.2hr per week; competed in US gymnastics sanctioned meets, and represented the full range of competitive levels
DEAB_measure: Dieting subscale of the Children's Eating Attitude Test
Related_Factor_measure: Athletic competence subscale of Hartler's Self Perception Profile for Adolescents
Authors' conclusions: Perceptions of mastery climate, autonomy-support, and performance climate at preseason predicted higher self esteem and lower disordered eating during competitive season, through mediation of perceived competence.
Limits: We included a purposeful sample of competitive gymnasts, so our results may not generalize to other youth sport contexts. It should be noted that after removing unreliable items, performance climate in our study only tapped the unequal recognition aspect. Participants reported low lecels of performance climate. We could not examine the effect of controlling behaviors because this construct showed a poor fit in the model.
Perspectives: More theory driven longitudinal studies can determine relationships and mediation over time and inform interventions to promote well-being among youth partcicipants. Future research should continue to consider indices of physical, social, emotional, and cognitive maturity with youth samples to control for developmental differences in well-being outcomes.

Title: Social and individual factors associaated with eating disorders in young athletes: effects on concentration and fatigue
Authors: Checa Olmos, J.C., Montserrat Hernandez, M., Belmonte Garcia, T., Jiminez Rodriguez, D., Rodriguez Martinez, A., Berenguel Martinez, P., & Berrio Lopez, A.M.
Inclusion criteria: The sample was selected voluntarily from the participants of a sports injury prevention and medical examination program by MasqSano for sports clubs in he Province of Almeria.
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, handball, swimming, rugby, volleyball
Authors' conclusions: The result of the linear regression clearly shows that the most significant explanatory weight is given by dissatisfaction with body image, despite the normal weight found. Social networks do not show a significant relationship with the risk of developing ED. We found a relationship between the risk of manifesting ED and feeling fatigued, getting little rest, and having problems concentrating. Fatigue and the risk of developing ED are not related to the hours of sports practice.
Limits: First, the sampling is not random and therefore does not offer representative data for each group of athletes. Second, there may be non-observational errors due to the impossibility of obtaining all the influencial variables, such as psychological variables. Third, although the survey were short, they were adiministered while medical examinations were conducted, meaning the subjects attitudes and cooperation could be rushed or hasty. Fourth, BMI is not a completely objective tool for diagnosing normal weight, underweight or overweight, particularly in the athletic population, since this value only considers weight and height, discarding other helpful information such as muscle mass and its ratio to fat mass. Fifht, we consider age to be a limiting factor since the subjects surveyed are at a stage in which numerous changes in body composition occur due to growth and social influence. In the absence of a longitudinal study, it is not possible to speak of a direct influence. Finally, sixth comprises the need for a non-athlete control group to compare the significance level of the variables in both populations.
Perspectives:
Its necessary and interesting for prevention to be carried out before the adolescent stage (before the age of 12 or 13). 
Implement health promotion programs where aspects of body image are also addressed in addition to working on eating and sport habits. Design interventions based on age, in addition to gender, since the data are increasingly similar between male and Female in terms of body image dissatisfaction and danger of ED. In the design of interventions, pay differentiated attention to the athlete and non-athlete population. Even within the group of athletes, it is recommaleded to differentiate according to modality for diagnosis, prevention and intervention. Finally, we would like to point out, two issues: First the young people participating in the study were not diagnosed, which shows that ecessive concern about physical appearance can lead to behavior or attitudes that affect health before the disease in diagnosed. Secondly, the results suggest the need for the development of longitudinal studies in which the variability of the different dimensions analized and their degree of influence on the risk of developing ED can be observed.

Title: Personal risk factors and types of sport associated with drive for thinness and drive for muscularity in NexGen athletes
Authors: Maurin, J., Labossière, S., Pomerleau-Fontaine, L., Boudreault, V., Brassard, S., Dion, J., Durand-Bush, N., Parent, S., & Soulard, A.
Inclusion criteria: NextGen athletes aged from 14 to 25 years
Sport_name: Judo, boxing, powerlifting, karate, taekwondo, gymnastics, diving, synchronized swimming, figure skating, rowing, cycling, track and field, canoeing-kayaking, swimming, speed skating, alpine skiing, cross-country skiing, biathlon, triathlon, acrobatic skiing, tennis, equestrian, badminton, fencing, rock climbing, golf, kite surfing, snowboarding, squash, archery, table tennis, basketball, volleyball, football, softball, baseball, water polo, handball, hockey, soccer, ultimate frisbee, wheelchair basketball, rugby
Sporting population:
51.2% national level
24.8% international level
0.4% regional
11.8% provincial
11.8% North American level
Authors' conclusions: Several factors identified in this study (e.g., athlete status, perfectionism) appear to play a role in the development of ED in this population. The study of other factors such as athletic identity and the coach-athlete relationship could provide insight into the development of ED symptoms within this group of athletes.
Limits: The study uses self-reported data; cross sectional design of the study. Athletes who were neither studying not employed exhibited more drive for thinness attitudes and behaviors than did those who were studying and/or employed yet few participants were in this situation. The uniquely Francophone sample may also a limitation.
Perspectives: Future studies could assess whether offering athletes mental health training in their sporting environment could help reduce their ED symptoms. The development of knowledge concerning the mechanisms underlying the drive for muscularity and thinness could be the subject of future quantitative studies, providing a deeper understanding of the risk factors associated with ED.

Title: Eating disorders risk assessment and body esteem among elite polish contact karate athletes
Authors: Dobkowska-Szefer, D., Staskiewicz-Bartecka, W., Kiciak, A., Kardas, M.
Inclusion criteria: Consent from both the club and the athlete to participate in the study, active participation in training in contact karate clubs (defined as > 3 training sessions per week for at least the past 6 months), achievement of at least one medal-winning position in competitions at the level of the Polish championships or higher, organized by national or international sports federations, and absence of chronic diseases, including diagnosed mental health disorders, as confirmed in the demographic section of the questionnaire
Related_Factor_measure: Body Esteem Scale (BES) in the Polish adaptation by Lipowska and Lipowski
Authors' conclusions: This study identifies elite karate athletes as a high-risk group for disordered eating and orthorexia, with body image—especially in women—and weight-related pressures playing a central role. It highlights the importance of psychological factors over BMI in shaping risk.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, small and selective sample, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference and generalizability. The use of BMI and omission of key psychosocial variables further constrain interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include larger samples, longitudinal designs, and objective body composition measures. Preventive interventions focusing on body image, nutrition education, and sport-specific pressures are essential in weight-category sport
