Title: Psychosocial characteristics and eating attitudes in young elite figure skaters in Canada and France: Are there any country differences?
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Trottier, C., Marsollier, E., d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged 13 to 19 years; born in Quebec for the Canadian sample and in France for the French sample; French mother tongue and having an average of six to ten years of either national or international competitive experience at the novice, junior of senior level in figure skating
Mean_Age:
France M=15.29, SD=1.14 
Canada M=15.89, SD=2.78
Sporting population: Elite: national or international competitive experience
Authors' conclusions: The significant negative associations between relationships with significant others and disordered eating attitudes which have been observed confirmed the protective role of social environment. No significant relationship was found between perceived physical appearances and disordered eating attitudes. Perceived physical ability was negatively related to disordered eating attitudes in the Canadian sample. In the French sample, these variable were positively related.
Limits: The two samples were fairly homogenous. The results were based on only one small sample per country.
Perspectives:
Further exploration of how eating disorders are manifested in various ethnic groups and the conditions under which elite athletes are at most risk may help to clarify where and when an unhealthy athletic environment is likely to exist and how these athletes may be assisted. 
Because culture is defined as shared motives, values, beliefs, identities, and interpretations or meanings of significant events that result from common experiences of members of collectives, it would be interesting to explore the role of these constructs and norms internalization and beliefs in the context of aesthetic sport on eating attitudes.

Title: The relationship between perceived stress, body image and eating behaviors in athletes
Authors: Şentürk, G., Deliceoğlu, G., Atasoy, M., & Yıldırım, İ.G.
Journal: Research in Sport Education and Sciences
Inclusion criteria: Athletes between the ages of 13-23 who volunteered to participate
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism in athletes is linked to higher stress, eating disturbances, and body perception issues, with women showing higher stress, emotional eating, and restrictive eating behaviors. Emotional states significantly influence eating patterns, highlighting the need for psychological and nutritional support in sports contexts
Limits: Findings are partly inconsistent with previous studies (e.g., gender differences), and results may depend on specific sports or samples. The study also relies on self-reported measures, which may introduce bias
Perspectives: Future research should further explore emotional eating across different sports and genders, and develop targeted interventions. Integrating psychological support, education, and nutritional guidance could help improve athletes’ well-being and performance

Title: The relationship between psychological abuse, athlete satisfaction, eating disorder and self-harm indicators in elite athletes
Authors: Wilson, E., Buono, S., Kerr, G., & Stirling, A.
Journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
Population subgroup:
592 Current athletes
202 Retired athletes
496 Females
295 Males
Inclusion criteria: Current and retired (maximum of 10 years retired) Canadian national team athletes, including para and non-para athletes from any sex and from any sport with a national team.
Sport_name: gymnastics, volleyball, athletics, cycling, swimming, rowing, freestyle skiing, rugby
DEAB_measure: Three questions designed to gain an overall sense of athletes history with eating disorders.
Related_Factor_measure: Modified version of the Athlete Satisfaction Questionnaire (ASQ)
Authors' conclusions: This study demonstrating the detrimental effects of psychological abuse on athletes, specifically with respect to the increased risk of eating disorder and self-harm indicators.
Limits: The current methods were limited by the use of non-validated questionnaires, subsets of validated scales, and the use of a narrow population of athletes. Findings did not differentiate between maltreatment perpetrated by coaches, teammates, parents or other perpetrators?
Perspectives: Recommendations include increasing education for coaches and other sport participants, particularly on the scope of what behaviors constitute psychological abuse and the potentially harmful impacts of these behaviors on athletes. Increased awareness of the dangers of promoting adherence to the sport ethic, which emphasizes a culture that promotes self-sacrifice and accepting excessive demands, is also necessary given the potential negative impacts on athlete mental health.

Title: Social and individual factors associaated with eating disorders in young athletes: effects on concentration and fatigue
Authors: Checa Olmos, J.C., Montserrat Hernandez, M., Belmonte Garcia, T., Jiminez Rodriguez, D., Rodriguez Martinez, A., Berenguel Martinez, P., & Berrio Lopez, A.M.
Inclusion criteria: The sample was selected voluntarily from the participants of a sports injury prevention and medical examination program by MasqSano for sports clubs in he Province of Almeria.
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, handball, swimming, rugby, volleyball
Authors' conclusions: The result of the linear regression clearly shows that the most significant explanatory weight is given by dissatisfaction with body image, despite the normal weight found. Social networks do not show a significant relationship with the risk of developing ED. We found a relationship between the risk of manifesting ED and feeling fatigued, getting little rest, and having problems concentrating. Fatigue and the risk of developing ED are not related to the hours of sports practice.
Limits: First, the sampling is not random and therefore does not offer representative data for each group of athletes. Second, there may be non-observational errors due to the impossibility of obtaining all the influencial variables, such as psychological variables. Third, although the survey were short, they were adiministered while medical examinations were conducted, meaning the subjects attitudes and cooperation could be rushed or hasty. Fourth, BMI is not a completely objective tool for diagnosing normal weight, underweight or overweight, particularly in the athletic population, since this value only considers weight and height, discarding other helpful information such as muscle mass and its ratio to fat mass. Fifht, we consider age to be a limiting factor since the subjects surveyed are at a stage in which numerous changes in body composition occur due to growth and social influence. In the absence of a longitudinal study, it is not possible to speak of a direct influence. Finally, sixth comprises the need for a non-athlete control group to compare the significance level of the variables in both populations.
Perspectives:
Its necessary and interesting for prevention to be carried out before the adolescent stage (before the age of 12 or 13). 
Implement health promotion programs where aspects of body image are also addressed in addition to working on eating and sport habits. Design interventions based on age, in addition to gender, since the data are increasingly similar between male and Female in terms of body image dissatisfaction and danger of ED. In the design of interventions, pay differentiated attention to the athlete and non-athlete population. Even within the group of athletes, it is recommaleded to differentiate according to modality for diagnosis, prevention and intervention. Finally, we would like to point out, two issues: First the young people participating in the study were not diagnosed, which shows that ecessive concern about physical appearance can lead to behavior or attitudes that affect health before the disease in diagnosed. Secondly, the results suggest the need for the development of longitudinal studies in which the variability of the different dimensions analized and their degree of influence on the risk of developing ED can be observed.

Title: Social predictors of psychological need satisfaction and well being among Female adolescent gymnasts: a longitudinal analysis
Authors: Kipp, L.E., & Weiss, M.R.
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts; aged 10 to 18; trained 15.2hr per week; competed in US gymnastics sanctioned meets, and represented the full range of competitive levels
DEAB_measure: Dieting subscale of the Children's Eating Attitude Test
Related_Factor_measure: Relatedness subscale of the Basic Psychological Needs Scale
Authors' conclusions: Perceptions of mastery climate, autonomy-support, and performance climate at preseason predicted higher self esteem and lower disordered eating during competitive season, through mediation of perceived competence.
Limits: We included a purposeful sample of competitive gymnasts, so our results may not generalize to other youth sport contexts. It should be noted that after removing unreliable items, performance climate in our study only tapped the unequal recognition aspect. Participants reported low lecels of performance climate. We could not examine the effect of controlling behaviors because this construct showed a poor fit in the model.
Perspectives: More theory driven longitudinal studies can determine relationships and mediation over time and inform interventions to promote well-being among youth partcicipants. Future research should continue to consider indices of physical, social, emotional, and cognitive maturity with youth samples to control for developmental differences in well-being outcomes.

Title: mental skills as protective attributes against eating disorder risk in dancers
Authors: Estanol, E.
Inclusion criteria: The majority of participants were European American collegiate ballet dancers; however, collegiate modern and professional ballet dancers were also included in the sample. In order to ascertain a sample more less representative o the US population, the companies and universities were selected based on geographic location (east coast, midwest and western states). Selection of universities was also made by locating programs that had pre-professional or elite dance programs.
Authors' conclusions: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Negative affect partially mediated the relationship between weight pressures and ED symptoms. mental skills, specifically coping with adversity, freedom from worry, and confidence/achievement motivation, fully mediated the relationship between negative affect and ED symptoms. Total score for the athletic coping skill inventory was signficantly negatively correlated with weight pressure in dance, anxiety, depression and eating disorder risk.
Limits: One limitation of this study was that the sample was predominantly white and Female. Results from this study may therefore not be generalizable to a more ethnically diverse sample or to male dancers. Furthermore, this study lacked a comparison group of non-dancers, which would have enabled the researchers to more objectively compare the impact of the dance environment with a non-dance environment.
Perspectives: Additional studies are needed to explore how other protective factors (i.e., satisfaction with life, optimism, self-esteem, humor, and spirituality) may further explain variations in ED symptoms in dancers and contribute to this mediation model identified. Future research that looks at variables in the context of high-risk groups by providing profiles of resilient dancers vs at-risk dancers is also needed in order to further clarify the relationship between risk and resilience factors and ED outcomes. Furthermore, including demographic variables in the analyses would help us to better understand if certain subpopulations of dancers, may be more at risk or protected from pressures in the dance environment. Finally, studies should include the use of alternative methods in addition to self-report to more thoroughly explore variables relating to the dance environment.

Title: Psychosocial characteristics and eating attitudes in young elite figure skaters in Canada and France: Are there any country differences?
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Trottier, C., Marsollier, E., d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged 13 to 19 years; born in Quebec for the Canadian sample and in France for the French sample; French mother tongue and having an average of six to ten years of either national or international competitive experience at the novice, junior of senior level in figure skating
Mean_Age:
France M=15.29, SD=1.14 
Canada M=15.89, SD=2.78
Sporting population: Elite: national or international competitive experience
Related_Factor_measure: Modified version of the French SFQS in which the word friend was changed to coach
Authors' conclusions: The significant negative associations between relationships with significant others and disordered eating attitudes which have been observed confirmed the protective role of social environment. No significant relationship was found between perceived physical appearances and disordered eating attitudes. Perceived physical ability was negatively related to disordered eating attitudes in the Canadian sample. In the French sample, these variable were positively related.
Limits: The two samples were fairly homogenous. The results were based on only one small sample per country.
Perspectives:
Further exploration of how eating disorders are manifested in various ethnic groups and the conditions under which elite athletes are at most risk may help to clarify where and when an unhealthy athletic environment is likely to exist and how these athletes may be assisted. 
Because culture is defined as shared motives, values, beliefs, identities, and interpretations or meanings of significant events that result from common experiences of members of collectives, it would be interesting to explore the role of these constructs and norms internalization and beliefs in the context of aesthetic sport on eating attitudes.

Title: Application of the transdiagnostic cognitive-behavioral model of eating disorders to the athletic population
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Inclusion criteria: Males and Females British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, fencing, football, hockey, rugby
Sporting population: 31% elite athletes competing at the international or national level, 69% non elite competing for county/regional, 20% club and 30% university teams
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (SSQRI)
Authors' conclusions: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
Limits: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
Perspectives: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

Title: Interpersonal difficulties as a risk factor for athletes eating psychopathology
Authors: Shanmugam, V., Jowett, S., & Meyer, C.
Journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
Inclusion criteria: British athletes
Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, judo, rugby, football, hockey
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (SSQRI)
Authors' conclusions: Negative and positive aspects of the quality of the coach athlete and teammate athlete were related to athletes eating psychopathology after controlling for baseline eating psychopathology score. Conflict with the coach was found to be the only significant independent predictor of athletes eating psychopathology. The quality of the relationship with parents and attachmalet styles were not found to be related to athletes eating psychopathology 6 months later.
Limits: The present findings are essentially correlational, thus preventing definitive conclusions about causality. The present study only examined the direct role of interpersonal relationships in atletes eating psychopathology. Fairburn et al. (2003) noted that interpersonal difficulties interact with other core psychopathological processes (low self esteem, clinical perfectionism, and mood intolerance) to potentially elicit and maintain eating disorders.
Perspectives: Future studies should seek to examine how such processes as clinical perfectionism, self esteem, and mood intolerance interact with interpersonal difficulties to elicit eating psychopathology . And investigaite how these interpersonal variables interact with each other to predict athletes eating psychopathology.

Sport_name: Swimming, cycling, judo, rugby, football, hockey

Authors' conclusions: Negative and positive aspects of the quality of the coach athlete and teammate athlete were related to athletes eating psychopathology after controlling for baseline eating psychopathology score. The present study only examined the direct role of interpersonal relationships in atletes eating psychopathology. Fairburn et al. And investigaite how these interpersonal variables interact with each other to predict athletes eating psychopathology.

Title: Teammate influences, psychological well-being, and athletes eating and exercise psychopathology: a moderated mediation analysis
Authors: Scott, C.L., Plateau, C.R., & Haycraft, E.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes competed with a university sports team or with their club or school
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Mean_Years of experience: Member of their current team M=1.99, SD=2.61
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (SSQRI)
Authors' conclusions: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. Gender was not a significant moderator, meaning that the role of psychological wellbeing in the relationships between teammate influences and eating.
Limits: Although age and BMI were controlled for, it is acknowledged that there are a number of additional co-variates (e.g., perfectionism, athletic identity) that could have contributed to the findings of this study. The self report nature of the data collected and the context it was collected in (i.e., before/after a training session and in the company of teammates/coach) may potentially misrepresent athletes true behaviours. Employing modeeling analytic techniques to further our understanding of the complex, multi-factorial influences on athlete eating and exercise behaviours.

Title: Social predictors of psychological need satisfaction and well being among Female adolescent gymnasts: a longitudinal analysis
Authors: Kipp, L.E., & Weiss, M.R.
Inclusion criteria: Female gymnasts; aged 10 to 18; trained 15.2hr per week; competed in US gymnastics sanctioned meets, and represented the full range of competitive levels
DEAB_measure: Dieting subscale of the Children's Eating Attitude Test
Related_Factor_measure: Relatedness subscale of the Basic Psychological Needs Scale
Authors' conclusions: Perceptions of mastery climate, autonomy-support, and performance climate at preseason predicted higher self esteem and lower disordered eating during competitive season, through mediation of perceived competence.
Limits: We included a purposeful sample of competitive gymnasts, so our results may not generalize to other youth sport contexts. It should be noted that after removing unreliable items, performance climate in our study only tapped the unequal recognition aspect. Participants reported low lecels of performance climate. We could not examine the effect of controlling behaviors because this construct showed a poor fit in the model.
Perspectives: More theory driven longitudinal studies can determine relationships and mediation over time and inform interventions to promote well-being among youth partcicipants. Future research should continue to consider indices of physical, social, emotional, and cognitive maturity with youth samples to control for developmental differences in well-being outcomes.

Title: Psychosocial characteristics and eating attitudes in young elite figure skaters in Canada and France: Are there any country differences?
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Trottier, C., Marsollier, E., d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged 13 to 19 years; born in Quebec for the Canadian sample and in France for the French sample; French mother tongue and having an average of six to ten years of either national or international competitive experience at the novice, junior of senior level in figure skating
Mean_Age:
France M=15.29, SD=1.14 
Canada M=15.89, SD=2.78
Sporting population: Elite: national or international competitive experience
Authors' conclusions: The significant negative associations between relationships with significant others and disordered eating attitudes which have been observed confirmed the protective role of social environment. No significant relationship was found between perceived physical appearances and disordered eating attitudes. Perceived physical ability was negatively related to disordered eating attitudes in the Canadian sample. In the French sample, these variable were positively related.
Limits: The two samples were fairly homogenous. The results were based on only one small sample per country.
Perspectives:
Further exploration of how eating disorders are manifested in various ethnic groups and the conditions under which elite athletes are at most risk may help to clarify where and when an unhealthy athletic environment is likely to exist and how these athletes may be assisted. 
Because culture is defined as shared motives, values, beliefs, identities, and interpretations or meanings of significant events that result from common experiences of members of collectives, it would be interesting to explore the role of these constructs and norms internalization and beliefs in the context of aesthetic sport on eating attitudes.

Title: A model of relationships of teammate relations, body image, and eating behaviors among athletes
Authors: Runquist, E., Cox, M., Meyer, A., & Rodgers, R.F.

63.5% Females
35.3% Males
0.64% Other

Authors' conclusions: Results support the importance of teammate body comparison, pressure, and relationships for muscularity oriented disordered eating and weight and shape concerns amongst collegiate athletes.

Mean_Age:
Competitive M=13.89, SD=1.75
Non competitive M=13.91, SD=1.76
Mean_BMI:
Competitive M=18.63, SD=2.32
Non competitive M=19.49, SD=2.54
Sport_name: gymnastics (artistic, rhythmic, trampoline, tumbling, aerobic, acrobatic)
Sporting population:
Competitive = national/international competitions
Non competitive = local and regional events/gymnastics festival
Range_Exercise frequency:
Competitive: > 5 sessions per week (n=120); 3-4 sessions (n=23), 1-2 sessions (n=4)
Non competitive: > 5 sessions (n=14), 3-4 sessions (n=69), 1-2 session (n=38)
Range_Years of experience:
Competitive: > 8 years (n=47), 6-8 years (n=60), > 6 years (n=39) 
Non competitive: > 8 years (n=25), 6-8 years (n=39), > 6 years (n=57)
Degree of relationship:
Pressure regarding appearance and performance 𝛃=.412, p<.001
R²adjusted=.163
Authors' conclusions: A factor that significantly increases the risk of developing ED symptoms is the pressures that come from the sport environment regarding the achievement of a low weight and a lean shape.
Limits: The cross sectional design makes it impossible to demonstrate a causal relationship between the variables studied. Self reported questionnaires were used for data collection, which may have increased the risk of producing socially acceptable responses. An eating disorder diagnostic assessment was not performed. It was chosen to include athletes from different disciplines of gymnastics and not only by the more widely studied disciplines of artistic and rythmic gymnastics; it is common that artistic and rhythmic gymnastics are considered disciplines with higher training demands and weight pressures than the rest of the disciplines.
Perspectives:
Interventions should aim to improve the awareness of coaches, judges and sports officials regarding the impact that low weight pressures have on the physical and psychological health of young gymnasts. All adolescents should be offered body composition and nutritional assessment by a registered dietetian. Counseling from mental health experts is crucial in helping athletes feel confident regarding their body appearance and their performance capabilities, as well as giving psychological counseling to those who present symptoms of eating disorders. 
Future research could include males. Factors such as influence of family and social media should also be adressed. Perceptions of coaches regarding ideal weight, dieting practices and their attitudes towards athletes could also be included in future investigations.

Title: Perfectionism and learning experiences in dance class as risk factors for eating disorders in dancers
Authors: Penniment, K.J., & Egan, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Being a Female aged between 18 and 30 years, currently studying classical and/or jazz ballet
Mean_BMI: 22.5% may be classified as underweight, with a BMI under 18.5kg/m²
Sporting population: 20.4% reported that they had danced semi professionally at one time, and 23.9% reported that they had danced at a professional level at one time.
Mean_Years of experience:
Dance tuition M=6.92, SD=22
Years studying dance M=14.5, SD=5.90
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: The relation between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was partially mediated by thinness related learning. The hypothesis that the relationship between thinness related learning and eating disorders symptoms were partially mediated by thiness restricting expectancies was also supported. A direct relationship between perfectionism and eating disorders symptoms was found.
Limits: The data was cross sectional. Although the current model fit the data well, there are multiple other risk factors for ED and it is very likely that this risk is determined by multiple factors and is not simply a function of the emphasis on thinness in the dance environment, or perfectionism. The sample was too small to split into professional and non professional dancers to examine if the model was the same in these groups. Our view of perfectionism was aligned with the construct of clinical perfectionism, and as a result we examined a selected subset of scales from the FMPS and did not use relevant scales from the HMPS.
Perspectives:
It would be useful for future research to examine the efficacy of targeting young Female involved in dance with elevated levels of perfectionism for prevention programs, as preliminary findings are positive for the ability of programs targeting perfectionism to reduce eating disorders risk in Female adolescents. 
It would be useful for clinicians to consider directly targeting perfectionism through CBT programs for perfectionism in young Female involved in dance classes as it is likely to be a factor that puts them at higher risk of developing an eating disorders within this environment.

Title: Disordered eating behaviors among crossfit athletes
Authors: Franco da Cunha, M.C., Costa Pereira Junqueira, A., Berbert de Carvalho, P.H., & Laus, M.F.
Inclusion criteria: Aged between 18 and 40 years, and be enrolled in the crossfit modality in a specialized gym, with a minimum frequency of practice of 6 months. Individuals who practiced other sports that favor hypertrophy in addition to crossfit and belonging to special groups, such as pregnant or nursing Female, indidviuals with any medical condition tha could have direct or indirect influence on physical appearance, elite athletes, were excluded.
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: The predictors of disordered eating for Female were BMI, age, drive for muscularity and the general internalization of socially etablished ideals, and for male it was the muscularity-oriented behaviors.
Limits: First, the sample may not be representative of the Brazilian population, as it was carried out in a single city in a single state. Second, there is a need to study other constructs, such as body dissatisfaction, which can predict other aspects of disordered eating in this population. Third, reported weight en height may be a bias, depiste being a common finding in body image  and eating behavior studies? Finally, even though the EAT-26 is frequently used in Brazil, the measure is not validated for adults in the country. Moreover, the EAT-26 appears to be a more focused instrument for investigating the symptoms of disordered eating often seen in Female, while recent studies have shown that disordered eating among male has its own characteristics.
Perspectives: Performance is directly related to diet, some disordered nutritional strategies can impair this performance and increase the risk of eating disorders in athletes.

Title: Athlete-specific risk factors for the development of disordered eating behaviors in first-year college athletes
Authors: Palermo, M., Rancourt, D., & Juarascio, A.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years or older, an incoming first-year student, and participation in either a DI sport at the university or a fall club sport at the time of the recruitmalet.
Sport_name: Cheerleading, ice hockey, swiming, track, baseball, field hockey, golf, karate, lacrosse, rugby, sailing, soccer, softball, squash, tennis, ultimate frisbee, volleyball, water polo, crew, basketball, wrestling
Related_Factor_measure: On a scale of 1 (none) to 5 (a lot) how much pressure do you feel from the individuals listed below to lose weight or maintain a low body weight ?
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Wearing a uniform that emphasizes body concerns predicted increases in weight/shape concern during the 4-month observation period. Wearing a uniform that emphasizes body concerns did not predict increases in restrained eating behaviors. Perceived pressure for thinness from coaches predicted an increase in both weight/shape concern and restrained eating behaviors at time 2. Teammate pressure for thinness was solely predictive of restrained eating behaviors at time 2. Coach pressure for thinness was the only athlete-specific risk factor that was predictive of increases in both weight/shape concerns and restrained eating behaviors.
Limits: The study time frame was relatively short, which may have limited the ability to detect change in weight/shape concern and restrained eating behaviors. Our sample had substantial attrition, with only about 54% of participants who completed time 1 completed the follow-up survey. The director of athletics and associated staff were present for the data collection ; some athletes may have been concerned that the athletics department would have access to their data. There was a limited number of club athlete participants in the final sample, level of sport competitive could not be considered. There may be differences in competition level between club sport versus division I athletes. There are a number of measurement considerations.
Perspectives:
Future would also should assess team culture and/or group cohesion, as these may buffer against the negative impact of perceived pressure to be thin from teammates and/or coaches, as teammates can be protective against, or heighten the risk for, disordered eating. 
For athletic departments to offer training to coaches that includes learning indicators of eating disorder relapse.

Title: Social and individual factors associaated with eating disorders in young athletes: effects on concentration and fatigue
Authors: Checa Olmos, J.C., Montserrat Hernandez, M., Belmonte Garcia, T., Jiminez Rodriguez, D., Rodriguez Martinez, A., Berenguel Martinez, P., & Berrio Lopez, A.M.
Inclusion criteria: The sample was selected voluntarily from the participants of a sports injury prevention and medical examination program by MasqSano for sports clubs in he Province of Almeria.
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, handball, swimming, rugby, volleyball
Related_Factor_measure: Do you find it hard to concentrate ?
Authors' conclusions: The result of the linear regression clearly shows that the most significant explanatory weight is given by dissatisfaction with body image, despite the normal weight found. Social networks do not show a significant relationship with the risk of developing ED. We found a relationship between the risk of manifesting ED and feeling fatigued, getting little rest, and having problems concentrating. Fatigue and the risk of developing ED are not related to the hours of sports practice.
Limits: First, the sampling is not random and therefore does not offer representative data for each group of athletes. Its necessary and interesting for prevention to be carried out before the adolescent stage (before the age of 12 or 13). 
Implement health promotion programs where aspects of body image are also addressed in addition to working on eating and sport habits. Even within the group of athletes, it is recommaleded to differentiate according to modality for diagnosis, prevention and intervention. DEAB_measure: Three questions designed to gain an overall sense of athletes history with eating disorders.

Authors' conclusions: This study demonstrating the detrimental effects of psychological abuse on athletes, specifically with respect to the increased risk of eating disorder and self-harm indicators.

Title: mental skills as protective attributes against eating disorder risk in dancers
Authors: Estanol, E.
Inclusion criteria: The majority of participants were European American collegiate ballet dancers; however, collegiate modern and professional ballet dancers were also included in the sample. In order to ascertain a sample more less representative o the US population, the companies and universities were selected based on geographic location (east coast, midwest and western states). Selection of universities was also made by locating programs that had pre-professional or elite dance programs.
Authors' conclusions: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Negative affect partially mediated the relationship between weight pressures and ED symptoms. mental skills, specifically coping with adversity, freedom from worry, and confidence/achievement motivation, fully mediated the relationship between negative affect and ED symptoms. Total score for the athletic coping skill inventory was signficantly negatively correlated with weight pressure in dance, anxiety, depression and eating disorder risk.
Limits: One limitation of this study was that the sample was predominantly white and Female. Results from this study may therefore not be generalizable to a more ethnically diverse sample or to male dancers. Furthermore, this study lacked a comparison group of non-dancers, which would have enabled the researchers to more objectively compare the impact of the dance environment with a non-dance environment.
Perspectives: Additional studies are needed to explore how other protective factors (i.e., satisfaction with life, optimism, self-esteem, humor, and spirituality) may further explain variations in ED symptoms in dancers and contribute to this mediation model identified. Future research that looks at variables in the context of high-risk groups by providing profiles of resilient dancers vs at-risk dancers is also needed in order to further clarify the relationship between risk and resilience factors and ED outcomes. Furthermore, including demographic variables in the analyses would help us to better understand if certain subpopulations of dancers, may be more at risk or protected from pressures in the dance environment. Finally, studies should include the use of alternative methods in addition to self-report to more thoroughly explore variables relating to the dance environment.

Title: Emotion dysregulation mediates the relationship between psychological distress, symptoms of exercise addiction and eating disorders: a large-scale survey among fitness centers users
Authors: Kun, B., Urban, R., Szabo, A., Magi, A., Eisinger, A., & Demetrovics, Z.
Inclusion criteria: Members of various urban fitness centers aged between 18 and 60 years
Mean_Exercise frequency:
General week almost five sessions M=4.84, SD=2.80
General week was almost 7hr M=6.73, SD=4.36
Authors' conclusions: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. The difficulties in emotion regulation strongly meduated the relationship between psychological symptoms and eating disorders in Female and explained 52.7% of the total indirect effect compared to the much lower 17.3% in male.
Limits: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. Using self report questionnaire by collecting data at the same time from the same individuals raises the bias of common method variance. We used screening methods for assessing both eating disorders and exercise addiction, and these instruments are not applicable for making diagnoses. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
Perspectives: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

Title: The tripartite influence model of body image and disordered eating among young adult athletes
Authors: Tonsberg, E.N., Dixit, U., Henderson, R., Larsen, J., Lusich, R., Hauff, C., Ahlich, E.
Inclusion criteria: Being 18-26 years old, fluency in English and self-reporting yes to the item do you identify as an athlete ?
Sport_name: Cross-country, track & field, running, soccer, football, basketball, dancing, cheerleading, swimming, tennis, lacrosse, volleyball, softball, baseball, other
Mean_Years of experience: < 1 year n=2 1-5 years n=121 > 5 years n=211
Authors' conclusions: The study supports the Tripartite Model in athletes, showing that sociocultural pressures—especially media, family, and teammates—contribute to disordered eating through internalization of ideals and appearance comparison. It highlights the continued importance of both general and sport-specific influences on athletes’ eating behaviors
Limits: Key limitations include the use of non-validated measures for some pressures, reliance on self-report data, and insufficient power to test differences across gender or sport types. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents conclusions about causality
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal and more nuanced methods to explore gender, sport-specific contexts, and social dynamics. These insights could help design targeted prevention and intervention programs tailored to athletes’ unique sociocultural environments

Title: Investigation of the relationship between muscle dysmorphia disorder, orthorexia nervosa, and motivation in male individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports
Authors: Abraş, H., Erdag, D., Buran, A.
Journal: Cyprus Turkish Journal of Psychiatry & Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Volunteer male participants aged between 18 and 58 engaged in bodybuilding; registered in gyms in TRNC.
Authors' conclusions: As muscle dysmorphia increases, orthorexia nervosa increases in individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports in the TRNC.
Limits: Since this study was conducted only on male bodybuilders, the findings cannot be generalized to Female bodybuilders.
Perspectives:
It is essential to provide education on muscle dysmorphia, orthorexia nervosa, and the use of ergogenic nutritional supplements in Physical Education and Sports Schools, as well as in coach training programs. Additionally, training on athlete nutrition and sports psychology in these institutions would equip them with knowledge about both athlete motivations and the mental health disorders frequently seen in athletes. Given the rise of these mental health issues in gyms, sports psychologists should be present in these environments, and mental health assessments should be conducted alongside medical evaluations for new memberships.
Conducting similar studies across different sports and with female participants could contribute valuable new insights to the literature.

Title: Muscle dysmorphia symptomatology in male exercisers: Associations with cognitive flexibility and appearance motivation
Authors: Abrante, D., Cano, A., Clemente, G., Diaz, M.
Inclusion criteria: Being over 18 and engaging in regular physical activity for at least three months
DEAB_measure: Spanish adaptation of the Muscle Appearance Satisfaction Scale (MASS)
Related_Factor_measure: Spanish version of the Motives for Physical Activities Measure-Revised (MPAM-R)
Authors' conclusions: This study supports a dual-pathway model of muscle dysmorphia, where sociocultural pressure influences symptoms both indirectly via appearance motivation and directly, with cognitive flexibility acting as a protective moderator. It highlights the interplay between social, motivational, and cognitive factors
Limits: The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and the use of a convenience, all-male sample restricts generalizability. Additionally, the measure of sociocultural pressure was not specific to muscularity ideals
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs and more diverse samples to validate the model. Interventions enhancing cognitive flexibility and promoting non-appearance-based exercise motives appear promising avenues for prevention and treatment.

Title: Eating disorders risk assessment and body esteem among elite polish contact karate athletes
Authors: Dobkowska-Szefer, D., Staskiewicz-Bartecka, W., Kiciak, A., Kardas, M.
Inclusion criteria: Consent from both the club and the athlete to participate in the study, active participation in training in contact karate clubs (defined as > 3 training sessions per week for at least the past 6 months), achievement of at least one medal-winning position in competitions at the level of the Polish championships or higher, organized by national or international sports federations, and absence of chronic diseases, including diagnosed mental health disorders, as confirmed in the demographic section of the questionnaire
Related_Factor_measure: Body Esteem Scale (BES) in the Polish adaptation by Lipowska and Lipowski
Authors' conclusions: This study identifies elite karate athletes as a high-risk group for disordered eating and orthorexia, with body image—especially in women—and weight-related pressures playing a central role. It highlights the importance of psychological factors over BMI in shaping risk.

Perspectives: Future research should include larger samples, longitudinal designs, and objective body composition measures. Preventive interventions focusing on body image, nutrition education, and sport-specific pressures are essential in weight-category sport

Title: Understanding athletic and exercise identity in relation to disordered eating behaviors
Authors: Palermo, M., & Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate students self identifying as athletes
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, baseball, softball, football, field hockey, lacrosse, volleyball, swimming, track and field, cross country, cheerleading, dance, equestrian, gymnastics
Authors' conclusions:
Study 1 : athletic identity was not associated with global disordered eating behaviors. 
Study 2 : athletic identity appeared to be associated with less cognitive restraint and was not significantly associated with other measures of disordered eating. Only exercise identity was associated with disordered eating.
Limits: Different disordered eating measures were used across study 1 and 2. Neither study 1 nor study 2 collected data about level of sport participation. Both studies were cross-sectional. This study included a broad sample of university students and findings may not generalize to other populations.
Perspectives: Exercise identity may be an important risk factor to consider in future research related to disordered eating and exercise behaviors in college students.

Title: Self-compassion plays a role in Canadian Female athletes' body appreciation and intuitive eating: A mixed methods approach
Authors: Adam, M.E.K., Kowalski, K.C., Duckham, R.L., Ferguson, L.J., & Mosewich, A.D.
Inclusion criteria: 18-35 years; two years of sport-specific experience; had competed in the past 12 months; were currently competing at a level ranging from local to international; not currently pregnant or lactating.
Sport_name: volleyball, track and field, dance, and cheerleading
Sporting population: local (n=28), provincial (n=22), regional (n=13), national (n=19), elite for age (n=3), international (n=5)
Authors' conclusions: Protective and facilitative role of self-compassion in body appreciation, intuitive eating, disordered eating, compulsive exercise, and self-criticism for Canadian Female athletes

Title: Eating behaviors among male bodybuilders and runners: application of the Trans-Contextual Model of Motivation
Authors: Chaba, L., Scoffier-Mériaux, S., d'Arripe-Longueville, F., & Lentillon-Kaestner, V.
Inclusion criteria: Minimum of 16 years; minimum of 3 hours of physical training per week; and minimum of 3 years of bodybuilding or running.
Mean_Age:
Bodybuilders M=26.63, SD=7.38
Runners M=37.66, SD=12.20
Mean_Exercise frequency:
Bodybuilders M=6.73, SD=3.41
Runners M=6.44, SD=4.21
Mean_Years of experience:
Bodybuilders M=6.85, SD=6.71
Runners M=11.93, SD=10.12
Related_Factor_measure: French version of the Behavioral Regulation in Exercise Questionnaire (BREQ-2)
Authors' conclusions: The TCM was partially supported in the context of eating disorders in the bodybuilders and runners. Both types of motivations for sport were direct or indirect risk factors for the development of deviant behaviors, but CM seemed to indicate greater risk than autonomous motivation for the development of eating disorders.
Limits: First, our sample was composed of young male with different numbers of years of practice, hours of practice per week, and types of practices (i.e., noncompetitors, future competitors, competitors), which might infuenced their motivation and engagement. Second, the runners were older than the bodybuilders, and younger people are more at risk of developing eating disorders than older people. Third, the data were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, no model/theory on body image in male was used, although body dissatisfaction was clearly present, and drive for muscularity was not considered. Fifth, our study was correlational. Sixth, it would be useful to determine a cutoff for eating disorders in male athletes because the EAT is not adapted to measure eating disorders in male athletes desiring to gain muscle mass. Finally, the motivational mechanisms explaining the development of eating disorders in male bodybuilders and runners who desire to gain muscle mass/lean body mass need to be further investigated in terms of motivational profiles.
Perspectives:
Include the level of competition in the analyses. Another model that also takes into account sociocognitive variables, such as the Health Action Process Approach might be applied in future research. Future studies could also specifically measure body satisfaction and analyze the link between this variable, behaviors to gain muscle mass/lean body mass, and the development of eating disorders.  It would be interesting to conduct a longitudinal study to more closely examine causality in the relationships. An intraindividual approach would be more useful than an interindividual approach. 
It appears necessary to limit the deleterious effects of controlled motivation. This might be accomplished by identifying the motivational orientations of athletes and promoting the development of coaching styles and climates that support autonomy and basic needs. Given the paradoxical role of autonomous motivation observed in the present study, it also appears necessary to encourage athletes to build reasoned and healthy sports parctices, limiting muscle mass gain at all costs.

Title: Athletic identity and disordered eating in obligatory and non-obligatory runners
Authors: Gapin, J.I., & Petruzzello, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Participants were recruited from running clubs, road races, and kinesiology classes at a large Midwestern university. The only inclusion criterion was that participant be over the age of 18.
Authors' conclusions: There is relationships among obligatory exercise and DE. Athletic identity had a significant positive correlation with disordered eating attitudes and behaviours. Athletic identity correlated with both drive for thinness and perfectionism. The negative affectivity correlated with all the disordered eating measures. The hypothesis that athletic identity would mediate the effect of obligatory running on disordered eating was not supported.
Limits: All measures were self-report in nature. Not all the subscales of the Eating Disorder Inventory have been validated in athletic samples and there is some concern that the Eating disorder Inventory may not be accurate in identiying those athletes at risk for an eating disorder.
Perspectives: Obligatory and non obligatory runners were dichotomized. It is likely, however, that this form of exercise occurs on a continuum and it would be valuable to assess this. Longitudinal research of those at risk form becoming obligatory runners could determine whether th shift towards obligatory running patterns occurs immediately after adopting an exercise regimen or whether the change occurs over time as they progress in training frequency, duration, and intensity. Further research using the Athletic Identity Measurement Scale in a variety of athletic population is necessary. Future studies should examine other mediating variables related to identity (motivation to exercise are variables associated with DE and obligatory exercise). When examining obligatory runners it may be helpful to look at Deci and Ryan's (1985, 2000) self-determination theory as an explanation for obligatory exercisers motivations to engage in exercise. It would be helpful to use the regulation in exercise questionnaire in conjunction with the obligatory exercise questionnaire and eating disorder measures to evaluate in more detail why certain individuals are more susceptible to unhealthy exercise attitudes and behaviours than others.

Authors' conclusions: we determined that sport pressures and dietary restraint were highly stable over the course of a competitive season. We also found that the pressures gymnasts and swimmers/divers experienced regarding body weight, size, and appearance from their coaches and teammates predicted decreases in their body satisfaction over a 5-month period; this change occurred even though the athletes’ body mass index did not change significantly over that time.
Limits: Included only NCAA Division I Female gymnasts and swimmers.divers, who also happened to primarily be Caucasien. The authors examined the variables over only a 5-month period, which represented one competitive collegiate season for these athletes. They examined the relationships among only sport pressures, body dissatisfaction and dietary restraint, additional research is needed to examine other variables such as general sociatail pressures, internalization, and negative affect. The validity of self-report measures of dietary restraint as predictors of actual reductions in food intake has been challenged. Self report measures of dietary restraint are risk factors in the prediction of disordered eating attitudes and behaviors, the measures are poor predictors of behaviorally observed, acute dietary restriction. BMI did not vary over the course of the 5-month season, we were not able to obtain more sensitive measures of body composition due to the study's design.
Perspectives:
Health care personnel can help coaches and teammates become more aware of how, through their behaviors and comments, they create an environment that pressures athletes about their body, weight, and appearance. Sport health care professionals can target sport administrators and sport-governing bodies because they have the power to male policy changes that can improve the sport environment, maling it less toxic for athletes. Such entities, could make revealing uniforms less so, adjust judging criteria so there is less focus on aesthetic/appearance-based aspects of the performance, expand or raise weight classifications, and/or set up strict requirements regarding acceptable weight loss over specific periods of time. Preventive programming, sport health care profesionals can work directly with athletes to help them counter these sport pressures and reduce their likelihood of engaging in caloric restriction of feeling dissatisfied with their bodies. 
Future reseach should examine whether our findings are supported in other groups of Female athletes (e.g., different sports, different competitive levels, more diverse racial/ethnic groups); male athletes should also be studied and such research should include measures of drive for muscularity. Other longitudinal studies may want to examine eating disorders and other potential risk factors over a longer period of time, or a different period (e.g., from the end of the competitive season to the start of the next one).

Title: Learning Experiences in Dance Class Predict Adult Eating Disturbance
Authors: Annus, A & Smith, G.T.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate college Female who received partial course credit for participation, informed consent.
Sporting population: Ten participants reported that they had danced professionally at one time, and 47 participants reported that they had danced semi-professionally at one time.
DEAB_measure: Eating disorder inventory body dissatisfaction subscale (EDI-BD)
Related_Factor:
Time spent in dance class
Learning regarding thinness
Thinness/restricting expectancies
Related_Factor_measure:
Total time, in hours, spent in dance class
Total learning regarding thinness from all dance classes attended
Thinness and restricting expectancy inventory (TREI)
Degree of relationship:
R²=.35, p<.001
Time spent in dance class 𝛃=.01, ns
Learning regarding thinness 𝛃=.06, ns
Thinness/restricting expectancies 𝛃=.62, p<.001
Authors' conclusions: Symptom endorsement does not relate to dance involvement by itself, but rather to involvement in dance classes that teach and emphasize thinness
Limits: Sample was not a clinical sample. We did not show that dance class-related learning was related to diagnosable dysfunction. The study was cross-sectional and so does not constitute a test of the temporal or causal aspect of the proposed influences of dance class-related learning or of expectancy theory. Our measures of thinness-related learning in dance class was retrospective, so those learning reports may thus be subject to recall bis.
Perspectives: Research is needed whcich uses objective measures of thinness-related learning in dance class, such as behavioural observations of dance instructors, to begin to untangle the roles of actual learning experiences, individual perceptions and personality dispositions in the relationship between reported learning experiences and eating disorder symptoms.

Title: Sports model/sports mind: the relationship between entertainment and sports media exposure, sports participation, and body image distorsion in dividion I Female athletes
Authors: Bissel, K.L.
Inclusion criteria: Females competing in Division I athletics at a major state university in the South; competing in Female's soccer, basketball, track and field, softball, swimming and diving, and gymnastics.
Sport_name: Mixed sport (e.g., soccer, basketball, track and field, softball, swimming, diving, gymnastics).
Mean_Exercise frequency: 56% reported practicing or competing for more than 3 hours a day; 34% every day but only for a few hours; 10% every day.
DEAB_measure: Eating Attitude test (EAT-26) and Eating Disorder Inventory (EDI)
Related_Factor:
Interest in body-improvement TV content
Sports participation
Exposure to thin ideal TV
Related_Factor_measure:
Interest in body-improvement television, was measured using the question, “How interested would you be in a new 30-minute television show focused on the topics below?” The responses listed categories such as news and politics, violent crime, and dieting. The categories of dieting, sports, fitness, nutrition, and exercise were viewed as body-improvement television content. Thus, these five items were combined to create an additive score representing respondents’ interest in body-improvement television content.
Respondents were asked several questions related to their participation in sports. Respondents were asked to report the sport they competed in primarily for the university. Participants were then asked to report the total amount of time they estimated practicing their sport for competition
To measure exposure to thin ideal TV, respondents were asked to indicate how frequently they watched specific programs by using a 5-point scale ranging from 0 (never) to 4 (regularly). Forty television shows airing on six networks—NBC, ABC,
CBS, Fox, UPN, and WB—were selected from the Fall 2001 season.
Degree of relationship:
Adjusted R²=.06, p=NS
Bêta(Interest)=.23, p<.05
Bêta(Participation)=.14, p=NS
Bêta(Exposure)=.30, p<.05
Authors' conclusions: Despite great attention paid to fitness, health, conditioning and skill, participants in this study still were largely dissatisfied with their body shape and size.
Limits: Small sample size. The reliability scores for some of the dependant variables was not as robust as it could have been, and the measure for the media viewing was not as precise as it could have been.
Perspectives: Future projects should continue to examine sports media exposure and sports participation as a possibly mediating variable in the media-body image distorsion relationship.

These results indicate that the trans contextual model was partially supported in the context of bodybuiling, suggesting a complex motivational model underlying drive for muscularity in male bodybuilders.
Limits: Our data are limited because our sample was composed only of young male with different levels of expertise (i.e., non-competitors, future competitors, competitors), which might have influenced their motivation and engagement in drive for muscularity. Second, subjective norm is a questionable variable as it might indicate a measurement issue in the sense that such variables reflect greater pressure and controlling rather than supportive forms of motivation. Third, the date were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, the internal consistency of some measures was quite low and this might have been linked to our heterogeneous sample or to the psychometric quality concerning the controlled motivation scale, or the inconsistency between the external regulation and the introjected regulation.
Perspectives:
It would be interesting to conduct a longitudinal study to more closely examine the causal relationship between variables. Methodologically, an important perspective for the future would be to determine a cutoff for drive for muscularity, which might then function as a reference when using drive for muscularity as a screening instrument for disordered eating. Moreover, eating disorders are very common on male bodybuilders and it might be of value to examine the relationships between motivation for sport, drive for muscularity and other specified feeding or eating disorders such as food restriction or night eating syndrome, or binge eating. 
Preventive actions may be important for male bodybuilders, who focus on gaining muscle mass. Specifically, such actions should be directed toward helping them to avoid developing controlled motivation because, although motivation for sport of any kind can be a direct or indirect risk factor for the development of deviant behavior, controlled motivation seems to put them at greater risk. It may therefore be important to carefully keep track of the development of motivation for sport to be sure that controlled motivation stays low, with moderate and healthy practice of bodybuilding. Moreover, the motivational mechanisms explaining the development of drive for muscularity could be deepened by complementary analysis in terms of motivational profiles.

Authors' conclusions: The TCM was partially supported in the context of eating disorders in the bodybuilders and runners. Both types of motivations for sport were direct or indirect risk factors for the development of deviant behaviors, but CM seemed to indicate greater risk than autonomous motivation for the development of eating disorders.
Limits: First, our sample was composed of young male with different numbers of years of practice, hours of practice per week, and types of practices (i.e., noncompetitors, future competitors, competitors), which might infuenced their motivation and engagement. Second, the runners were older than the bodybuilders, and younger people are more at risk of developing eating disorders than older people. Third, the data were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, no model/theory on body image in male was used, although body dissatisfaction was clearly present, and drive for muscularity was not considered. Fifth, our study was correlational. Sixth, it would be useful to determine a cutoff for eating disorders in male athletes because the EAT is not adapted to measure eating disorders in male athletes desiring to gain muscle mass. Finally, the motivational mechanisms explaining the development of eating disorders in male bodybuilders and runners who desire to gain muscle mass/lean body mass need to be further investigated in terms of motivational profiles.
Perspectives:
Include the level of competition in the analyses. Another model that also takes into account sociocognitive variables, such as the Health Action Process Approach might be applied in future research. Future studies could also specifically measure body satisfaction and analyze the link between this variable, behaviors to gain muscle mass/lean body mass, and the development of eating disorders.  It would be interesting to conduct a longitudinal study to more closely examine causality in the relationships. An intraindividual approach would be more useful than an interindividual approach. 
It appears necessary to limit the deleterious effects of controlled motivation. This might be accomplished by identifying the motivational orientations of athletes and promoting the development of coaching styles and climates that support autonomy and basic needs. Given the paradoxical role of autonomous motivation observed in the present study, it also appears necessary to encourage athletes to build reasoned and healthy sports parctices, limiting muscle mass gain at all costs.

Authors' conclusions: Satisfaction of psychological need in sport was positively and significantly related to restrictive eating. The results revealed a full mediation effect of self-determination for sport in the association between frustration of psychological need in sport and restrictive eating behaviors. There is a significant negative association between self-determination for sport and restrictive eating behaviors in adolescent athletes. Being an elite athlete did not predict restrictive eating behaviors in our sample. Psychological needs frustration in sport more strongly predicts restrictive eating behaviors in girls, compared with boys. No significant moderation effect of gender was found in the association between satisfaction of psychological need and restrictive eating behaviors.
Limits: First, the associations found between variables do not demonstrate any causal link because the cross-sectional design does not permit any inference about causality. This study used a large and diverse sample, it was not representative of all adolescents in the country, limiting the generalizability of the findings. In addition, problematic eating behaviors in this study refer to restrictive eating, measured by dietary restriction subscale of the EDE-Q. Therefore, the results cannot be extrapolated to other eating behavior problems, such as compulsive eating or binge eating. Moreover, since the instruments used to measure basic psychological needs in sport and self determination for sport were adapted slightly for the sport context by the research team, further studies should replicate these findings using other measures of these contructs. Lastly, constructs were tested with self-reported measures, and therefore, the results may have been influenced by social dsirability.
Perspectives: Profesionals who guide young athletes in the regulation of their eating behaviors may benefit from more thorough consideration of self-determination and psychological needs specifically in the sport context. Moreover, both frustration and satisfaction of psychological needs in sports should be investigated because restrictive eating was associate with greater satisfaction of psychological needs in the present study. Thus, frustration of psychological needs in sport may be a better indicator of restrictive eating behaviors, especially in girls.

Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions

Inclusion criteria: People who practice physical exercise at least one day a week
Authors' conclusions: The study highlights strong links between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia, and multiple addictions, with impulsivity playing a key mediating role. These findings emphasize the importance of targeting impulsivity and emotion regulation in prevention and treatment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and the use of a homogeneous convenience sample limits generalizability. Additionally, reliance on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses may affect accuracy.

Authors' conclusions: Direct and indirect effects were found between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology through compulsive exercise. Specifically, there were direct effects of clinical perfectionism on avoidance/rule driven behavior, weight control exercise, and mood improvement. There was also a direct effect of the weight control exercise subscale on eating pathology and a negative effect of the mood improvement subscale on eating pathology.
Limits: Participant recruitmalet was not random or stratified which limits generalizability. The sample comprised mainly of individuals who are actively involved in one particular type of athletic poursuit: individual endurance sports and particularly running. The sample may, therefore, not be representative of individuals involved in sport and exercise in general. In addition, the study was cross-sectional, therefore the bidirectional relationship between eating pathology and compulsive exercise could not be assessed as this requires a longitudinal design. While we hypothesized that perfectionism would affect compulsive exercise, which would impact eating pathology, it could equally be argued that perfectionism influences eating pathology, which then influences compulsive exercise (i.e., compulsive exercise is a symptom of eating pathology, rather than an antecedent). Indeed, Meyer et al.’s (2011) model proposed bidirectional links between eating pathology and compulsive exercise. Meyer et al. (2011) argued that dieting and exercise reinforce one another due to social reinforcers which accompany the initial weight loss from regular exercise, which then intensifies eating, shape and weight concerns.
Perspectives: It would be useful to determine whether interventions for both perfectionism and compulsive exercise may help to improve the efficacy of standard treatments for eating disorders, above the gain already found in efficacious treatments such as CBT-E (Fairbunr et al., 2009) where clinical perfectionism is a focus if it is elevated. Future research could also examine the efficacy of specific stand-alone treatments for perfectionism (e.g., Egan et al., 2014) for compulsive exercise and perfectionism in eating disorders. Future research should measure perfectionism, compulsive exercise and eating pathology at two time points using a panel design and include a cross-lagged effects to determine the bidirectional relations between variables.

Authors' conclusions: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Total score for the athletic coping skill inventory was signficantly negatively correlated with weight pressure in dance, anxiety, depression and eating disorder risk.

Future research that looks at variables in the context of high-risk groups by providing profiles of resilient dancers vs at-risk dancers is also needed in order to further clarify the relationship between risk and resilience factors and ED outcomes. Furthermore, including demographic variables in the analyses would help us to better understand if certain subpopulations of dancers, may be more at risk or protected from pressures in the dance environment. Finally, studies should include the use of alternative methods in addition to self-report to more thoroughly explore variables relating to the dance environment.

Different techniques and strategies for dealing with SPA and disordered eating may be required for different sport types.

Title: The relationship between gender, type of sport, body dissatisfaction, self esteem and disordered eating behaviors in Division I athletes
Authors: Milligan, B., & Pritchard, M.
Journal: Athletic Insight The Online Journal of Sport Psychology

Authors' conclusions: Regression analyses for females revealed that body dissatisfaction was the most strongly related variable to disordered eating behaviors, followed by self esteem and type of sport. The regression analysis revealed that for males, body dissatisfaction was the only variable that related to disordered eating behavior.
Limits: Only athletes at one large public institution were examined. Only Division I athletes were examined. The athletes surveyed were primarily Caucasian and of traditional college age. This study is correlational in nature. Thus, the present study cannot say that being an athlete makes one prone to developing body dissatisfaction or eating disordered behaviors. It could be that individuals prone to those behaviors are more likely to be drawn to athletics in the first place.
Perspectives: For further research, researchers should take overall team/individual performance (wins/losses) into account for a factor associated with eating disorders because performance plays a role in self esteem, which has shown to correlate with both body dissatisfaction and disordered eating behavior.

Related_Factor_measure:
Sociodemographic information
Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q)
On a scale of 1 (none) to 5 (a lot) how much pressure do you feel from the individuals listed below to lose weight or maintain a low body weight ?
Degree of relationship:
Gender 𝛃=.09, p=.478
T1 restrained eating behaviors 𝛃=.12, p=.359
Pressure for thinness-teammes 𝛃=.29, p=.031
Authors' conclusions: Wearing a uniform that emphasizes body concerns predicted increases in weight/shape concern during the 4-month observation period. Wearing a uniform that emphasizes body concerns did not predict increases in restrained eating behaviors. Perceived pressure for thinness from coaches predicted an increase in both weight/shape concern and restrained eating behaviors at time 2. Teammate pressure for thinness was solely predictive of restrained eating behaviors at time 2. Coach pressure for thinness was the only athlete-specific risk factor that was predictive of increases in both weight/shape concerns and restrained eating behaviors.
Limits: The study time frame was relatively short, which may have limited the ability to detect change in weight/shape concern and restrained eating behaviors. Our sample had substantial attrition, with only about 54% of participants who completed time 1 completed the follow-up survey. The director of athletics and associated staff were present for the data collection ; some athletes may have been concerned that the athletics department would have access to their data. There was a limited number of club athlete participants in the final sample, level of sport competitive could not be considered. There may be differences in competition level between club sport versus division I athletes. There are a number of measurement considerations.
Perspectives:
Future would also should assess team culture and/or group cohesion, as these may buffer against the negative impact of perceived pressure to be thin from teammates and/or coaches, as teammates can be protective against, or heighten the risk for, disordered eating. 
For athletic departments to offer training to coaches that includes learning indicators of eating disorder relapse.

ED prevention programs for Female athletes should address general sociocultural pressures related to weight and appearance. Interventions could also be enhanced by strengths-based approaches that build on elements of sport participation that appear to be protective, such as the contribution of athletes positive evaluations of their physical abilities and condition to body esteem.

Degree of relationship:

Sport participation 𝛃=-.13, N.S.
Adaptive perfectionism 𝛃=-.02, N.S.
Maladaptive perfectionism 𝛃=.23, N.S.
R²=.10
Authors' conclusions: Perfectionism and body satisfaction explain dieting among Female athletes. For the male athletes, none of the predictors contributed to the understanding of their dieting behaviour. In addition, age, sport type and duration of sport participation did not contribute to dieting behaviour un case of male and Female. Adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism were associated with body satisfaction among Female athletes but not with dieting behaviour directly. Satisfaction with one's body was shown to be the largest independent predictor of dieting and their relationship was negative.
Limits: The data was based on self reported measures. Cross sectional design limits the causal inference between perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting. The sample consisted of athletes who were enrolled in a university program which might limit the generalizability. PANPS should not be used as a measure of perfectionism due to a questionable factor validity of the positive perfectionism subscale. EAT-26 was shown to have a low positive predictive value due to the rarity of targeted conditions while two out of three EAT-26 subscales demonstrated low internal consistency and omitting them while investigating eating disorder may not be the best approach. The number of Female participants was lower than males, which might have affected some of the analysis were gender-split was included.
Perspectives: It would be important to further etablish the relationship between perfectionism dimensions and body satisfaction in the area of disordered eating but also take a consideration the context in which athletes perceive their body.

This study demonstrated the influence of an internal locus of control on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in a context of social interaction and the influence of an external locus of control, attributed to the coach and sports friends on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in context of negative affect, social interaction and an absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. Limits: The data were self reported, which suggests that social desirability may have been a bias. The study used correlational and cross sectional methods, which limits the generalization of the relationships.
Perspectives:

A longitudinal study would determine the stability of this impact and an experimental study would help to etablish the direction of the causality.
