Authors' conclusions: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
Limits: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
Perspectives:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

Authors' conclusions: Negative perfectionism, self esteem, and athletic identity were unrelated to ED symptomatology.
Limits: Smaller sample. Weight pressures may be experienced differently according to discipline specific performance demands. Cross sectional design.
Perspectives:
Future research should incorporate longitudinal designs to identify true risk factors of ED symptomatology and use qualitative interviews to further examine the lived experience of sport-related weight pressures. 
Practitioners may collaborate with other professionals, such as sports dieteticians, to educate skating communities on weight-performance myths and improve communication between skaters, parents, and coaches about the body. Title: Muscle dysmorphia symptomatology in male exercisers: Associations with cognitive flexibility and appearance motivation
Authors: Abrante, D., Cano, A., Clemente, G., Diaz, M.

Title: Athletic identity and disordered eating in obligatory and non-obligatory runners
Authors: Gapin, J.I., & Petruzzello, S.J.
Inclusion criteria: Participants were recruited from running clubs, road races, and kinesiology classes at a large Midwestern university. The only inclusion criterion was that participant be over the age of 18.
Authors' conclusions: There is relationships among obligatory exercise and DE. Athletic identity had a significant positive correlation with disordered eating attitudes and behaviours. Athletic identity correlated with both drive for thinness and perfectionism. The negative affectivity correlated with all the disordered eating measures. The hypothesis that athletic identity would mediate the effect of obligatory running on disordered eating was not supported.
Limits: All measures were self-report in nature. Not all the subscales of the Eating Disorder Inventory have been validated in athletic samples and there is some concern that the Eating disorder Inventory may not be accurate in identiying those athletes at risk for an eating disorder.
Perspectives: Obligatory and non obligatory runners were dichotomized. It is likely, however, that this form of exercise occurs on a continuum and it would be valuable to assess this. Longitudinal research of those at risk form becoming obligatory runners could determine whether th shift towards obligatory running patterns occurs immediately after adopting an exercise regimen or whether the change occurs over time as they progress in training frequency, duration, and intensity. Further research using the Athletic Identity Measurement Scale in a variety of athletic population is necessary. Future studies should examine other mediating variables related to identity (motivation to exercise are variables associated with DE and obligatory exercise). When examining obligatory runners it may be helpful to look at Deci and Ryan's (1985, 2000) self-determination theory as an explanation for obligatory exercisers motivations to engage in exercise. It would be helpful to use the regulation in exercise questionnaire in conjunction with the obligatory exercise questionnaire and eating disorder measures to evaluate in more detail why certain individuals are more susceptible to unhealthy exercise attitudes and behaviours than others.

Related_Factor_measure: Motivation for Healthy Behaviors in Orthorexia Nervosa Qyestionnaire (MHBONQ)
Authors' conclusions: Health anxiety, mood modification are a strong predictor of orthorexia nervosa.
Limits: The results of the present study were based on online data gathering which questions the representative nature of the sample. Although participants were represented in a broad range of age and educational level, the highest proportion of participants were young and highly qualified Female. The participation in the research was voluntary thus the increased interest towards the topic of the examination might bias the results. The correlational desing of the present study does not allow causal inferences. Perspectives: A viable next step in orthorexia nervosa research could be the use of experience sampling method which could provide important information about the daily fluctuation of orthorexia nervosa and the related variables. It would be benefical to collect information about the type of the exercise as well, because some sport activities (category sports, aesthetic sport) can mean a higher vulnerability to orthorexia.

Title: Body-related sport and exercise motives and disturbed eating attitudes and behaviours in adolescents
Authors: Maïano, C., Morin, A.J.S., Lanfranchi, M.C., & Therme, P.
Inclusion criteria: Adolescents from educational institutions aged between 11 and 18 years ; attended regular physical education classes; exercising their main sport between one and eight times per week, for a weekly total of between 25 minutes and 12 hours.
Sport_name: 46 different sports (e.g., badminton, basketball, boxing, gymnastics, judo, soccer) and exercises (e.g., fitness, jogging, weight training), these sports were categorized into leanness (coded 1) or non-leanness (coded 0), individual (coded 1) or team (coded 0)
DEAB: Generic disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors
DEAB_sub-class 1: Generic disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors
DEAB_final_sub-class: Generic disturbed eating attitudes and behaviors
Related_Factor_measure: List of 26 possibilities then classified into four categories according to Markland and Ingledew (1997, 2008)
Authors' conclusions: There is a significant and positive relationship between body related sport and exercise motives and generic DEAB and vomiting purging behaviors. The relationship between body related motives and DEAB may be amplified when adolescents practice individual and competitive sports and exercises. Involvement in sport and exercise for body related motives predicted higher levels of vomiting purging behaviours in adolescents involved in individual sports or exercises and do not generalize to those not involved in this type of practice. Involvement in sport and exercise for body related motives predicts higher levels of vomiting purging behaviours in adolescents who compete, but not in those who do not compete.
Limits: The adolescents reporting exercising or practicing sports for at least one body related motive were coded in the category of body related motive. However for those indicating two or three motives, no information on the ranking of their motives was available. It is probable that adolescents for whom body related motives are only a minor reason for engaging in sport and exercise were still included in this category. This study relied on a cross sectional design, precluding examination of the direction of the associations between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB. Only a small proportion reported exercising and practicing sports for a body related motive. This study neglected to examine more pathogenic behaviours (i.e., dieting, vomiting, fasting, use of laxatives and/or diuretics, enemas, appetite suppressants)
Perspectives:
The relationship between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB could be moderated by the physical self perceptions (e.g., physical condition, sport competence, flexbility). This hypothesis should be the object of future research. Little is known about the beliefs of youth with body related motives regarding sport and exercises as a means to attain their goal and their reasons for engaging in DEAB. These issues should be addressed in future research, particularly in qualitative studies. It would be interesting to focus more on the role of self presentation concerns (i.e., social physique anxiety) or socio-contextual factors (parents, peers, coaches) in the relationships between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB. 
Preventive intervention should aim to encourage adolescents to become involved in sport and exercise for self-determined motives (e.g., social engagement and enjoyment) rather than for external motives (e.g., body related).

Title: Body-related sport and exercise motives and disturbed eating attitudes and behaviours in adolescents
Authors: Maïano, C., Morin, A.J.S., Lanfranchi, M.C., & Therme, P.
Inclusion criteria: Adolescents from educational institutions aged between 11 and 18 years ; attended regular physical education classes; exercising their main sport between one and eight times per week, for a weekly total of between 25 minutes and 12 hours.
Sport_name: 46 different sports (e.g., badminton, basketball, boxing, gymnastics, judo, soccer) and exercises (e.g., fitness, jogging, weight training), these sports were categorized into leanness (coded 1) or non-leanness (coded 0), individual (coded 1) or team (coded 0)
Related_Factor_measure: List of 26 possibilities then classified into four categories according to Markland and Ingledew (1997, 2008)
Authors' conclusions: There is a significant and positive relationship between body related sport and exercise motives and generic DEAB and vomiting purging behaviors. The relationship between body related motives and DEAB may be amplified when adolescents practice individual and competitive sports and exercises. Involvement in sport and exercise for body related motives predicted higher levels of vomiting purging behaviours in adolescents involved in individual sports or exercises and do not generalize to those not involved in this type of practice. Involvement in sport and exercise for body related motives predicts higher levels of vomiting purging behaviours in adolescents who compete, but not in those who do not compete.
Limits: The adolescents reporting exercising or practicing sports for at least one body related motive were coded in the category of body related motive. However for those indicating two or three motives, no information on the ranking of their motives was available. It is probable that adolescents for whom body related motives are only a minor reason for engaging in sport and exercise were still included in this category. This study relied on a cross sectional design, precluding examination of the direction of the associations between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB. Only a small proportion reported exercising and practicing sports for a body related motive. This study neglected to examine more pathogenic behaviours (i.e., dieting, vomiting, fasting, use of laxatives and/or diuretics, enemas, appetite suppressants)
Perspectives:
The relationship between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB could be moderated by the physical self perceptions (e.g., physical condition, sport competence, flexbility). This hypothesis should be the object of future research. Little is known about the beliefs of youth with body related motives regarding sport and exercises as a means to attain their goal and their reasons for engaging in DEAB. These issues should be addressed in future research, particularly in qualitative studies. It would be interesting to focus more on the role of self presentation concerns (i.e., social physique anxiety) or socio-contextual factors (parents, peers, coaches) in the relationships between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB. 
Preventive intervention should aim to encourage adolescents to become involved in sport and exercise for self-determined motives (e.g., social engagement and enjoyment) rather than for external motives (e.g., body related).

Title: Compulsive exercise as a mediator between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology
Authors: Egan, S.J., Bodill, K., Watson, H.J., Valentine, E., Shu, C., & Hagger, M.S.
Inclusion criteria: The population was adults over the age of 18 years who participated in a diverse range of sport and exercise. The inclusion criteria of exercice twice or more per week was chosen to include people who exercised regularly but the criterion was relatively low as amount of exercise in not the defiing feature of compulsive exercise.
Sport_name: Running, triathlon, ball sports (volleyball, football, baseball, basketball, golf, rugby, squash, netball, cricket, hockey, tennis, badminton), gym, other (water polo, sailing, surf lifesaving, pilates, skateboarding, hula hooping, equestrian), cycling, dance, yoga, athletics, rowing, swimming
Authors' conclusions: there were direct effects of clinical perfectionism on avoidance/rule driven behavior, weight control exercise, and mood improvement. There was also a direct effect of the weight control exercise subscale on eating pathology and a negative effect of the mood improvement subscale on eating pathology.
Limits: Participant recruitmalet was not random or stratified which limits generalizability. The sample comprised mainly of individuals who are actively involved in one particular type of athletic poursuit: individual endurance sports and particularly running. The sample may, therefore, not be representative of individuals involved in sport and exercise in general. In addition, the study was cross-sectional, therefore the bidirectional relationship between eating pathology and compulsive exercise could not be assessed as this requires a longitudinal design. While we hypothesized that perfectionism would affect compulsive exercise, which would impact eating pathology, it could equally be argued that perfectionism influences eating pathology, which then influences compulsive exercise (i.e., compulsive exercise is a symptom of eating pathology, rather than an antecedent). Indeed, Meyer et al.’s (2011) model proposed bidirectional links between eating pathology and compulsive exercise. Meyer et al. (2011) argued that dieting and exercise reinforce one another due to social reinforcers which accompany the initial weight loss from regular exercise, which then intensifies eating, shape and weight concerns.
Perspectives: It would be useful to determine whether interventions for both perfectionism and compulsive exercise may help to improve the efficacy of standard treatments for eating disorders, above the gain already found in efficacious treatments such as CBT-E (Fairbunr et al., 2009) where clinical perfectionism is a focus if it is elevated. Future research could also examine the efficacy of specific stand-alone treatments for perfectionism (e.g., Egan et al., 2014) for compulsive exercise and perfectionism in eating disorders. Future research should measure perfectionism, compulsive exercise and eating pathology at two time points using a panel design and include a cross-lagged effects to determine the bidirectional relations between variables.

Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Sport_name: Cross country/track and field, swimming and diving, volleyball, wrestling, soccer, golf, football, lacrosse, baseball, basketball, tennis
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: A longitudinal investigation of sports-related risk factors for disordered eating in aesthetic sports
Authors: Krentz, E.M., & Warschburger, P.
Journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
Inclusion criteria: Athletes from elite sports schools and olympic training centers with an emphasis on adolescent in aesthetic sports; aged between 14-22 years
Mean_Age:
M=14, SD=2.3
Female M=14, SD=2.4
Male M=14.1, SD=2.1
Mean_BMI:
M=18.1, SD=2.4
Female M=18.1, SD=2.6
Male M=18.2, SD=2
Sport_name: gymnastics, ice figure skating, diving, ballet, roller-skate figure skating, rhythmic gymnastics
Mean_Years of experience:
M=8.2, SD=2.5
Female M=8.2, SD=2.9
Male M=8.1, SD=1.9
Related_Factor: Desire to be leaner to improve sport performance
Related_Factor_measure: Athlete-Scale Drive for Thinness and Performance
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Desire to be leaner to improve sport performance
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Desire to be leaner to improve sport performance
Authors' conclusions: The desire to be leaner to improve sports performance was predictive of DE and not vice versa. Emotional distress resulting from missed exercise sessions and social pressure from the sports environment had no significant impact on DE. Sports-related body disssatisfaction is not predictive of DE when other sports-related variables are also considered.
Limits: The rather short follow-up period of 1 year. Owing to our rather small sample size, the generalization of our results is further limited. Our study focuses on only one high-risk group. High performance athletes might not report pathological eating patterns because they fear being excluded from their team sports. Inclusion of only four potential risk factors
Perspectives: It would be interesting to investigate whther the desire to be leaner to improve sports performance is a risk factor for disordered eating in other types and how this desire is related to other (also non-sports-related) risk factors. More studies with a longitudinal design are needed to deepen our knowledge of the developmental course of disordered eating in athletes.

Title: Understanding athletic and exercise identity in relation to disordered eating behaviors
Authors: Palermo, M., & Rancourt, D.
Inclusion criteria: Undergraduate students self identifying as athletes
Sport_name: Soccer, basketball, baseball, softball, football, field hockey, lacrosse, volleyball, swimming, track and field, cross country, cheerleading, dance, equestrian, gymnastics
Authors' conclusions:
Study 1 : athletic identity was not associated with global disordered eating behaviors. 
Study 2 : athletic identity appeared to be associated with less cognitive restraint and was not significantly associated with other measures of disordered eating. Only exercise identity was associated with disordered eating.
Limits: Different disordered eating measures were used across study 1 and 2. Neither study 1 nor study 2 collected data about level of sport participation. Both studies were cross-sectional. This study included a broad sample of university students and findings may not generalize to other populations.
Perspectives: Exercise identity may be an important risk factor to consider in future research related to disordered eating and exercise behaviors in college students.

Title: Disordered eating, eating attitudes and reasons for exercise among male high school cross country runners
Authors: Wadas, G.

Related_Factor: Desire to be leaner to improve sport performance
Related_Factor_sub-class 4: Desire to be leaner to improve sport performance
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Desire to be leaner to improve sport performance
Authors' conclusions: Factors that have a significant relationship with disordered eating are performance perfectionism and weight management. A desire to control weight is associated with disordered eating behaviors in male high school cross country runners as determined from the modest correlation coefficient for the weight management subscale and the EAT-26. There was no significant correlation for the physical appearance subscale of the EMI-2 and the EAT-26. No significant relationships were found between disordered eating behaviors and social pressure on body shape, social pressure on eating and athlete identity.

Perspectives: The present study did not investigate the reasons for dissatisfaction with current weight status, future studies may seek more information relative to the reasons. For example, do male cross country runners feels a need to be more muscular ? Do the bodies of male cross country runners not fit the ideal ?

Title: Investigation of the relationship between muscle dysmorphia disorder, orthorexia nervosa, and motivation in male individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports
Authors: Abraş, H., Erdag, D., Buran, A.
Journal: Cyprus Turkish Journal of Psychiatry & Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Volunteer male participants aged between 18 and 58 engaged in bodybuilding; registered in gyms in TRNC.
Authors' conclusions: As muscle dysmorphia increases, orthorexia nervosa increases in individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports in the TRNC.
Limits: Since this study was conducted only on male bodybuilders, the findings cannot be generalized to Female bodybuilders.
Perspectives:
It is essential to provide education on muscle dysmorphia, orthorexia nervosa, and the use of ergogenic nutritional supplements in Physical Education and Sports Schools, as well as in coach training programs. Additionally, training on athlete nutrition and sports psychology in these institutions would equip them with knowledge about both athlete motivations and the mental health disorders frequently seen in athletes. Given the rise of these mental health issues in gyms, sports psychologists should be present in these environments, and mental health assessments should be conducted alongside medical evaluations for new memberships.
Conducting similar studies across different sports and with female participants could contribute valuable new insights to the literature.

Title: Overweight preoccupation is associated with eating pathology in male collegiate athletes with body dissatisfaction
Authors: Murray, M.F., Perelman, H., Sandhu, D., Quinones, I.C., & Haedt-Matt, A.A.
Inclusion criteria: Collegiate athletes who identified as male and members of university-sponsored varsity athletic teams; were over age 18 years, and endorsed body dissatisfaction (i.e., scores greater than 1 on the overweight preoccupation or appearance orientation subscales of the multidimensional body self relations questionnaire, or scores greater than 5 on the appearance orientation subscales)
Sport_name: Cross country/track and field, swimming and diving, volleyball, wrestling, soccer, golf, football, lacrosse, baseball, basketball, tennis
Authors' conclusions: This studies clarifies notable correlates, particularly overweight preoccupation, of eating pathology in male athletes and highlights sport confidence as a potential prevention and intervention target.
Limits: Causality cannot be inffered from cross sectional findings and the causality of risk factors for eating pathology in male athletes remains unclear. Internal consistency of the purging subscale of the EPSI was poor. Alternately, the items composing this subscale may not adequately reflect compensatory purging behaviors or its underlying motivations in this population.
Perspectives: Future research would benefit from a larger sample without preset body dissatisfaction criteria to ensure adequate power for moderation, to allow for direct comparison across sport types, positions, and competition levels, and to avoid potential floor effects. More longitudinal and mediational designs are needed to model how sport related pressures relate to these varied correlates.

Title: Eating disorders risk assessment and body esteem among elite polish contact karate athletes
Authors: Dobkowska-Szefer, D., Staskiewicz-Bartecka, W., Kiciak, A., Kardas, M.
Inclusion criteria: Consent from both the club and the athlete to participate in the study, active participation in training in contact karate clubs (defined as > 3 training sessions per week for at least the past 6 months), achievement of at least one medal-winning position in competitions at the level of the Polish championships or higher, organized by national or international sports federations, and absence of chronic diseases, including diagnosed mental health disorders, as confirmed in the demographic section of the questionnaire
Related_Factor_measure: Body Esteem Scale (BES) in the Polish adaptation by Lipowska and Lipowski
Authors' conclusions: This study identifies elite karate athletes as a high-risk group for disordered eating and orthorexia, with body image—especially in women—and weight-related pressures playing a central role. It highlights the importance of psychological factors over BMI in shaping risk.
Limits: The cross-sectional design, small and selective sample, and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference and generalizability. The use of BMI and omission of key psychosocial variables further constrain interpretation.
Perspectives: Future research should include larger samples, longitudinal designs, and objective body composition measures. Preventive interventions focusing on body image, nutrition education, and sport-specific pressures are essential in weight-category sport

Authors: Vinkers, C.D.W., Evers, C., Adriaanse, M.A.,  & de Ridder, D.T.D.
Inclusion criteria: Women aged 17-50 years from fitness centers
Authors' conclusions: This study has extended prior work by investigating the role of exercise motives in the link between low body esteem and eating disorder symptomatology.

Title: Disordered eating, eating attitudes and reasons for exercise among male high school cross country runners
Authors: Wadas, G.
Inclusion criteria: The runners were selected from 12 of the thirty two public high schools in the local school district sponsoring sports teams located in the USA. Participants were current members of a high shcool cross country teams, were in grades 9-12 and between the ages of 14-18.
Sporting population: Some playing time (24.2%), starter on team (29%), conference (4.8%), regional (35.5%), national (4.8%), other (1.6%)
Authors' conclusions: Factors that have a significant relationship with disordered eating are performance perfectionism and weight management. A desire to control weight is associated with disordered eating behaviors in male high school cross country runners as determined from the modest correlation coefficient for the weight management subscale and the EAT-26. There was no significant correlation for the physical appearance subscale of the EMI-2 and the EAT-26. No significant relationships were found between disordered eating behaviors and social pressure on body shape, social pressure on eating and athlete identity.

For example, do male cross country runners feels a need to be more muscular ? Do the bodies of male cross country runners not fit the ideal ?

Title: Self-determination, restrictive eating, and psychological needs: challenges for young athletes
Authors: Clermont, C., Paquette, L., Lalande, D., & Dion, J.
Inclusion criteria: Participants had to meet the following inclusion criteria: (1) at least 14 years old, (2) in grade 9 or 10, and (3) attending French or English high school
Sport_name: Endurance, power/technical, ball game, weight dependent, technical, aesthetic, high mass
Sporting population: No competition (n=88); local, regional and inter-regional (n=409); provincial (n=363); national and international (n=117)
Mean_Exercise frequency: 57.8% practiced 10 hours or less, 20.1% between 11 and 15 and 22.1% 16 or more
Mean_Years of experience: M=7.89, SD=3.641 (age since they engaged in sport)
DEAB_measure: The dietary restriction subscale of the validated short form of the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q)
Related_Factor_measure: Adapted and shortened version of the Behavioral Regulation in Exercise Questionnaire-2 (BREQ-2)
Authors' conclusions: Satisfaction of psychological need in sport was positively and significantly related to restrictive eating. The results revealed a full mediation effect of self-determination for sport in the association between frustration of psychological need in sport and restrictive eating behaviors. There is a significant negative association between self-determination for sport and restrictive eating behaviors in adolescent athletes. Being an elite athlete did not predict restrictive eating behaviors in our sample. Psychological needs frustration in sport more strongly predicts restrictive eating behaviors in girls, compared with boys. No significant moderation effect of gender was found in the association between satisfaction of psychological need and restrictive eating behaviors.
Limits: First, the associations found between variables do not demonstrate any causal link because the cross-sectional design does not permit any inference about causality. This study used a large and diverse sample, it was not representative of all adolescents in the country, limiting the generalizability of the findings. In addition, problematic eating behaviors in this study refer to restrictive eating, measured by dietary restriction subscale of the EDE-Q. Therefore, the results cannot be extrapolated to other eating behavior problems, such as compulsive eating or binge eating. Moreover, since the instruments used to measure basic psychological needs in sport and self determination for sport were adapted slightly for the sport context by the research team, further studies should replicate these findings using other measures of these contructs. Lastly, constructs were tested with self-reported measures, and therefore, the results may have been influenced by social dsirability.
Perspectives: Profesionals who guide young athletes in the regulation of their eating behaviors may benefit from more thorough consideration of self-determination and psychological needs specifically in the sport context. Moreover, both frustration and satisfaction of psychological needs in sports should be investigated because restrictive eating was associate with greater satisfaction of psychological needs in the present study. Thus, frustration of psychological needs in sport may be a better indicator of restrictive eating behaviors, especially in girls.

Title: How does the level of physical activity influence eating behavior? A self-determination theory approach
Authors: Fernandes, V., Rodrigues, F., Jacinto, M., Teixeira, D., Cid, L., Autunes, R., Matos, R., Reigal, R., Hernandez-maledo, A., Morales-Sanchez, V., & Monteiro, D.
Inclusion criteria: N.A.
Sport_name: Gyms and fitness centers (i.e., cross training and weightlifting)
DEAB_measure: The Dutch Eating Behavior Questionnaire Portuguese version
Related_Factor_measure: The Regulation of Eating Behavior Scale Portuguese version
Authors' conclusions: Self determined motivation was negatively associated with external ingestion, emotional ingestion, and constraint. In constrast, non self determined motivation was associated with external ingestion, emotional ingestion, and constraint. Individuals who engage in more physical activity have a more self-determined regulation of their eating habits, whereas those who engage in less physical activity have a less determined regulation of their eating habits.
Limits: The fact that the data were self-reported and collected online is a clear limitation. In addition, due to the sample's characteritics, we were unable to explore possible differences across age groups and sex. The International Physical Activity Questionnaire shirt version is a validated and simple method for estimating physical activity levels. However, it is not an objecive assessment and only considers a limited period (only 7 days). Furthermore, only the MET was assessed, with no cinsideration given to other characteristics such as sedentary behaviors. This study is a cross-sectional, which is also a limitation due to the fact that individuals were evaluated in a single moment, which may not fully reflect their eating behaviors.
Perspectives: We suggest that future studies explore possible moderation variables (age, sex, gym facility and exercise activity) that could influence the current results. It is worth emphasizing the scarcity of longitudinal and experimental research that investigates how interventions grounded in self determination theory could enhance physical activity as a mean to increase healthy eating habits.

Title: The relationship between psychological abuse, athlete satisfaction, eating disorder and self-harm indicators in elite athletes
Authors: Wilson, E., Buono, S., Kerr, G., & Stirling, A.
Journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
Population subgroup:
592 Current athletes
202 Retired athletes
496 Females
295 Males
Inclusion criteria: Current and retired (maximum of 10 years retired) Canadian national team athletes, including para and non-para athletes from any sex and from any sport with a national team.
Sport_name: gymnastics, volleyball, athletics, cycling, swimming, rowing, freestyle skiing, rugby
DEAB_measure: Three questions designed to gain an overall sense of athletes history with eating disorders.
Related_Factor_measure: Three questions designed to gain an overall sense of athletes history with self-harm and suicidality
Authors' conclusions: This study demonstrating the detrimental effects of psychological abuse on athletes, specifically with respect to the increased risk of eating disorder and self-harm indicators.
Limits: The current methods were limited by the use of non-validated questionnaires, subsets of validated scales, and the use of a narrow population of athletes. Findings did not differentiate between maltreatment perpetrated by coaches, teammates, parents or other perpetrators?
Perspectives: Recommendations include increasing education for coaches and other sport participants, particularly on the scope of what behaviors constitute psychological abuse and the potentially harmful impacts of these behaviors on athletes. Increased awareness of the dangers of promoting adherence to the sport ethic, which emphasizes a culture that promotes self-sacrifice and accepting excessive demands, is also necessary given the potential negative impacts on athlete mental health.

Title: The self regulation of eating attitudes in sport scale: defining an optimal regulation zone
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., & Paquet, Y.
Inclusion criteria: Regular sport practitioners; were at least regional competitors; training minimum 3h per week
Mean_Exercise frequency: Trained about 8h per week on average, with 43.7% training more than 10h per week
Related_Factor_measure: Self Regulation of Eating Attitude in Sports Scale (SREASS)
Authors' conclusions: We observed an overall, negative linear relationship between self regulatory eating attitudes and disordered eating in the sports contexts. The overall relationship between self regulatory eating attitudes and disordered eating was not totally linear.
Limits: Data were self-reported and could biased by social desirability. Correlation analyses were used, which limits the generalization of the demonstrated relationshipw between variables. The ZOREAS could be compared to the individual zone of optimal functioning, and like the latter, could vary according to the sport and the indivdiual.
Perspectives: Future longitudinal studies could determine the stability and the specificity of the ZOREAS, while an experimental study would help to etablish the direction of causality suggested by our correlation analysis. This type of research would help in developing educational programs based on self-regulation of eating attitude adaptation that seek to limit the emergence of dsordere eating among athletes.

Title: Effect of locus of control on disordered eating in athletes: the mediational role of self regulation of eating attitudes
Authors: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Paquet, Y., & d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
Inclusion criteria: University students who regularly (i.e., 6h per week) practised a sport in regional and national competitions
Related_Factor: Self-regulation in context of food temptation
Related_Factor_measure: Self Regulation of Eating Attitude in Sports Scale (SREASS)
Related_Factor_final_sub-class: Self-regulation in context of food temptation
Authors' conclusions: We observed a negative influence of the locus of control attributed to the coach on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and lack of anticipation of consequences on performance. The coach and sports firends contribute to maladaptive patterns of accomplishment and function as negative predictors of the self regulation of eating attitudes in several contexts. The results showed the positive influence of an internal locus of control on the self regulation of eating attitudes in the context of social interaction. We observed a negative influence of self regulatory eating attitudes on disordered eating in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and the absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. This study demonstrated the influence of an internal locus of control on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in a context of social interaction and the influence of an external locus of control, attributed to the coach and sports friends on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in context of negative affect, social interaction and an absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. This study did not reveal a significant influence of a locus of control attributed to the family or luck on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of temptation or negative affect. The self regulation subscales were not significant in the contexts of food temptation and a lack of compensatory strategies.
Limits: The data were self reported, which suggests that social desirability may have been a bias. The study used correlational and cross sectional methods, which limits the generalization of the relationships.
Perspectives:
The social environment has a powerful impact on the development of disordered eating in athletes; the influence of these social relationship on athletes self regulatory eating attitudes merits further study, through an emphasis on locus of control and/or relationship quality. A longitudinal study would determine the stability of this impact and an experimental study would help to etablish the direction of the causality. 
The use of locus of control and self regulatory eating attitudes as concurrent variables may be useful to sports psychology practitioners in their work with athletes. They might also be used to evaluate an athlete ability to engage in new and better adapted eating strategies and to determine whether the development of new eating attitudes would benefit performance outcomes.

Title: The relationship between social and disordered eating in college-aged Female gymnasts
Authors: Ausmus, J.C., Blom, L.C., Bowman, S., Lebeau, J.C.
Inclusion criteria: Participants were recruited from club gyms and colleges throughout the united states via email, social media, and word of mouth to coaches, support staff and directly to athletes; Females between 18-25 years; self identify as competitive gymnasts; must have competed within the last three years
Sporting population: 87.67% competed in varsity level gymnastics, 6.85% stated that they participated in recreational gymnastics, 5.48% competed in clubs gymnastics
Related_Factor: Severity of critical comment about physical appearance

Title: The role of gender, type of sport practiced, and sport level on the association between experience of sexual violence in sport and symptoms of disordered eating in adolescent-athletes
Authors: Gillard, A., Labossière, S., Vaillancourt-Morel, M.P., Parent, S.
Journal: International Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology
Inclusion criteria: Students from secondary 1-5 from 483 public and private high schools in the province of Quebec
Sporting population: Low sport level n=5350 High sport level n=3567
Mean_Exercise frequency: 5h/week or less n=4138 6-10h/week n=3030 11-15h/week n=1186 16-20h/week n=459 21-25h/week n=171 >25h/week n=153
Related_Factor_measure: Violence Toward Athlete Questionnaire (VTAQ) short form
Authors' conclusions: The study shows that experiences of sexual violence, sexual harassment, and sexual abuse in sport are all positively associated with disordered eating in adolescent athletes, independent of gender, sport type, and sport level. These findings highlight the importance of screening for both disordered eating and sexual violence, as well as implementing prevention strategies targeting the broader sport environment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal inference, and the use of a convenience sample and self-reported measures limits generalizability and may introduce bias. Additionally, simplified categorizations (e.g., sport level, sport type) may not fully capture the complexity of athletes’ experiences
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify causal directions and explore additional risk, protective, and mediating factors (e.g., social support, coping). More nuanced measures (e.g., sport level, type of sport, perpetrator characteristics) and contextual influences should also be examined to better understand and prevent disordered eating in athletes

Authors' conclusions: Social pressure, social support, self esteem, body dissatisfaction was related to DE. Social support was not strongly related to DE. The use of self-report questionnaires and the fact that we have not taken into account the percentage of respondents and non respondents.
Perspectives: It is important to distinguish between pressure on Female and male aesthetic performers. These actions should focus on promoting young aesthetic performer's self-esteem and satisfaction with their activity specific body image, which is essential to reducing the impact of pressure to be thin on their eating and weight control behaviors. Title: Teammate influences and relationship quality are associated with eating and exercise psychopathology in athletes
Authors: Scott, C.L., Haycraft, E., & Plateau, C.R.
Inclusion criteria: Athletes aged 15 years and over competing in any olympic, international olympic commitee (IOC) or British universities and college sport (BUCS) recognised sport (circa 90 different sports). Had to be actively training in a group and/or competing as part of a team in a sport at local, regional, national or international level.
Sport_name: Aesthetic, endurance, weight-class, team, ball-game, power, technical
Sporting population:
22% elite level
78% county, regional, club or university/school level
Related_Factor_measure: Sport Specific Quality of Relationship Inventory (SSQRI)
Authors' conclusions: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.
Limits: Cross sectional design did not allow for cause and effect to be determined.
Perspectives: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research would benefit from assessing both teammate and coach influences in tandem to ascertain their relative strength when predicting disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

Title: Function over form: a longitudinal study of predictors and mediation pathways for disordered eating in elite athletes
Authors: Fatt, S.J., Hay, P., George, E., Jeacocke, N., Rogers, K., Mitchison, D.
Population subgroup: Males T1 N=47 Males T2 N=25 Males T3 N=22 Females T1 N=126 Females T2 N=83 Females T3 N=63 Other T1 N=1 Other T2 N=1
Inclusion criteria: Adult athletes who had competed at a national, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level
Sporting population: National, international, professional, or NCAA D1 level
Degree of relationship: Model controlling for gender T1 sport pressures-T2 disordered eating 𝛃=.10, p=.123 T1 sport pressures-T3 disordered eating 𝛃=.18, p=.046
Authors' conclusions: Disordered eating in elite athletes is predicted by sport-specific weight pressures and drive for leanness for performance, rather than societal pressures or body image concerns. This suggests that athlete-specific mechanisms differ from those in the general population
Limits: The study had a limited and somewhat biased sample (mainly female, Western athletes) and insufficient power to test moderating factors like gender. Measurement choices and attrition may also affect the robustness of findings
Perspectives: Future research should test these models in more diverse and younger athlete populations and explore additional factors like perfectionism. Interventions should focus on performance-related beliefs and sport environments rather than appearance-based concerns

Title: General and sport-specific weight pressures as risk factors for body dissatisfaction and disordered eating among female collegiate athletes
Authors: Pallotto, I.K., Sockol, L.E., Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 competing in NCAA division I programs at four-year institutions of higher education in the United States
Sport_name: Basketball, cross-country, diving, gymnastics, lacrosse, soccer, swimming and track and field
Authors' conclusions: Weight pressures from parents, peers and the media were directly associated with body dissatisfaction; moreover these pressures were indirectly associated with disordered eating via their associations with thin and muscular ideal internalization. In the full model, weight pressures specific to the sport context were not associated with body dissatisfaction or disordered eating. The degree to which athletes internalized ideals for thinness and muscularity was associated with higher levels of disordered eating. Body dissatisfaction was not associated with disordered eating after other variables in the model were taken into account.
Limits: A comprehensive understanding of sociocultural influences on disordered eating among athletes require not only greater representation of participants from marginazlied racial and ethnic groups, but also consideration of the role of intersecting marginalized identities (e.g., sexual orientation) and integration of qualitative and mixed methodological approaches that may more effectively characterizz the lived experiences of these athletes. Cross sectional design ; it is not possible to determine whether these characteristics are risk factors for disordered eating or correlates of these behaviors.
Perspectives:
There is a clear need for high-quality studies of athletes assessing weight related pressures, appearance ideal internalization, body satisfaction, and disordered eating over time. in addition to clarifying the temporal relationships among these characteristics, longitudinal designs could also address whether these relationships are stable at different stages of athletes careers or different time points throughout the athletic season. Future research sould also consider how sociocultural influences might contribute to positive eating-related outcomes, both in the sport context and more broadly. 
Interventions that specifically address the sociocultural pressures and appearance ideals most relevant to athletes, such as the Female Athlete Body Project, reduce risk for subsequent disordered eating behaviors. 
In addition to pressures and appearance ideals specific to the sports environment, eating disorder prevention programs for Female athletes should address general sociocultural pressures related to weight and appearance. These interventions should also address internalization of cultural ideals for appearance beyond thinness; for example dissonance-based interventions could challenge internalization of fit and muscular ideals and sport specific ideals for weight and shape. Interventions could also be enhanced by strengths-based approaches that build on elements of sport participation that appear to be protective, such as the contribution of athletes positive evaluations of their physical abilities and condition to body esteem.

Title: Pinning down the problems and influences: disordered eating and body satisfaction in male wrestlers
Authors: Satterfield, N.A., & Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate wrestlers; at least 18 years of age; at a college in the United States; a current mumber of a NCAA Division I wrestling team; and identified as a man.
Related_Factor_measure: The Weight Pressures in Sports Scale for Male Athletes
Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. While we did find an association between body satisfaction and restricting eating behavior, there was not a significant association among binge eating, purging, and body satisfaction. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.
Limits: The majority of participants identiied as white ; the present study sample is not representative of the racial makeup of this population. There was a relatively low response rate to the survey, which limits the generalizability of our sample. This study was cross sectional and only examined athletes in season, which limits the conclusions we can draw. The use of self report measures means it is possible that participants downplayed some of their behaviors or were unaware of the frequency of them. In addition, we did not ask specifically about frequency of binge eating.
Perspectives:
One possible intervention is by providing coaches and athletes a decision tree to plan a safe weight-cutting strategu such as consuming strategic level of carbohydrates and fluids. It is important that wrestlers evaluate their weight-cutting and recovery practices before and after competitions to assess what is working safely. 
Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies that assess these variables in season versus out of season. Body satisfaction and disordered eating should be investigated in a racially diverse sample for both generalizability and differential risk. Future studies should examine Female's wrestling and explore gender differences in body satisfaction and disordered eaating behaviors.

Title: General and sport-specific weight pressures as risk factors for body dissatisfaction and disordered eating among female collegiate athletes
Authors: Pallotto, I.K., Sockol, L.E., Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes between the ages of 18 and 24 competing in NCAA division I programs at four-year institutions of higher education in the United States
Sport_name: Basketball, cross-country, diving, gymnastics, lacrosse, soccer, swimming and track and field
Authors' conclusions: Weight pressures from parents, peers and the media were directly associated with body dissatisfaction; moreover these pressures were indirectly associated with disordered eating via their associations with thin and muscular ideal internalization. In the full model, weight pressures specific to the sport context were not associated with body dissatisfaction or disordered eating. The degree to which athletes internalized ideals for thinness and muscularity was associated with higher levels of disordered eating. Body dissatisfaction was not associated with disordered eating after other variables in the model were taken into account.
Limits: A comprehensive understanding of sociocultural influences on disordered eating among athletes require not only greater representation of participants from marginazlied racial and ethnic groups, but also consideration of the role of intersecting marginalized identities (e.g., sexual orientation) and integration of qualitative and mixed methodological approaches that may more effectively characterizz the lived experiences of these athletes. Cross sectional design ; it is not possible to determine whether these characteristics are risk factors for disordered eating or correlates of these behaviors.
Perspectives:
There is a clear need for high-quality studies of athletes assessing weight related pressures, appearance ideal internalization, body satisfaction, and disordered eating over time. in addition to clarifying the temporal relationships among these characteristics, longitudinal designs could also address whether these relationships are stable at different stages of athletes careers or different time points throughout the athletic season. Future research sould also consider how sociocultural influences might contribute to positive eating-related outcomes, both in the sport context and more broadly. 
Interventions that specifically address the sociocultural pressures and appearance ideals most relevant to athletes, such as the Female Athlete Body Project, reduce risk for subsequent disordered eating behaviors. 
In addition to pressures and appearance ideals specific to the sports environment, eating disorder prevention programs for Female athletes should address general sociocultural pressures related to weight and appearance. These interventions should also address internalization of cultural ideals for appearance beyond thinness; for example dissonance-based interventions could challenge internalization of fit and muscular ideals and sport specific ideals for weight and shape. Interventions could also be enhanced by strengths-based approaches that build on elements of sport participation that appear to be protective, such as the contribution of athletes positive evaluations of their physical abilities and condition to body esteem.

Title: The mediating role of impulsiveness in the relationship between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia and other addictions
Authors: Olave, L., Estévez, A., Momene, J., Penacoba, C., Macia, P., Macia, L., Etxaburu, N., Muniz, J.A., Iruarrizaga, I.
Inclusion criteria: People who practice physical exercise at least one day a week
Authors' conclusions: The study highlights strong links between exercise addiction, muscle dysmorphia, and multiple addictions, with impulsivity playing a key mediating role. These findings emphasize the importance of targeting impulsivity and emotion regulation in prevention and treatment
Limits: The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, and the use of a homogeneous convenience sample limits generalizability. Additionally, reliance on screening tools rather than clinical diagnoses may affect accuracy.
Perspectives: Future research should use longitudinal designs to clarify causal relationships and further explore specific dimensions of impulsivity. There is also a need to develop prevention and intervention strategies focusing on emotion regulation and impulsivity

Title: Symptoms of muscle dysmorphia, body dysmorphic disorder, and eating disorders in a nonclinical population of adulte male weightlifters in Australia
Authors: Nieuwoudt, J.E., Zhou, S., Coutts, R.A., & Booker, R.
Journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
Inclusion criteria: Adult males at least 18 years of age; individuals who are working out with weights (i.e., free weight or machines) at least 3 times per week and currently residing in Australia
Mean_Exercise frequency: At least 3 days or more per week
Authors' conclusions: Significant correlation were found between muscle dysmorphia and body dysmorphic disorder symptoms. The correlational data suggested a relationship between the symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and eating disorders. Small but significant correlations were found between the substance use subscale of the MASS and the laxatives, diuretics behavioral question of the EAT-26, between the injury risk subscale of the MASS and the vomit and exercise behavioral questions of the EAT-26, and between the muscle satisfaction subscale and the binge eating and the lost > 9kg behavioral questions of the EAT-26.
Limits: The EAT-26 may not be sensitive to muscularity oriented disordered eating and body image concerns. The current research consisted of an online survey, therefore the possibility existed that participants might have interpreted the meanings of questions or statements differently to those intended or might have perceived some of the statements or questions as vague. Self selection bias is a limitation of internet surveys. The data were exclusively based on self report which can have tendencies toward social desirability bias.
Perspectives: A better understanding and awareness of the rates and symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and body dismorphic disorder and eating disorders may help strength and conditioning professionals to identify and refer at risk individuals for help from mental health professionals.

Title: Contextual body image and athletes' disordered eating: the contribution of athletic body image to disordered eating in high performance Female athletes
Authors: Karin de Bruin, A.P., Oudejans, R.R.D., Bakker, F.C., & Woertman, L.
Population subgroup:
19 athletes with eating disorders
33 without disordered eating
Inclusion criteria: High performance Female athletes with disordered eating ; competing on national or international levels ; control without disordered eating. Subjects with disordered eating meet two of the major criteria: amaleorrhoea, low BMI or low body fat, purging methods, and bulimic episodes, in addition to two of the following minor criteria: fear of weight gain, feelings of fatness, maintained low weight and increased importance of weight/shape. If participants did not meet these criteria, they were placed in the control group without disordered eating.
Mean_BMI:
Athletes with disordered eating M=20.69, SD=2.89
Athletes without disordered eating M=20.23, SD=2.23
Sport_name: Rythmic/acrobatic gymnastics and synchronized swimming, aerobic endurance training, middle and long distance running, swimming or long distance speed skating, tennis
Mean_Years of experience:
Athletes with disordered eating M=9, SD=4.27
Athletes without disordered eating M=8.36, SD=4.09
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: The athletic body image strongly contributed to ED. The athletes self-evaluations about shape, weight and fat percentage and the perceived opinions of others on these aspects appeared to be only significant factors uniquely explaining 14 and 9% of the EDE-Q variance. 64% of the variance was explained by the relevant body image components from daily life and sport.
Limits: Limitations of the present study were its sample size and consitution. Unfortunately, the number of Dutch high performance athletes is not that extensive.
Perspectives: Future studies should further explore athletes body comparisons in daliy life and sport, and possible differences between athletes with and without disordered eating in this respect. Future research should further explore body images in sport and daily life, particularly in athletes with disordered eating. We needed to extent the sample with a group of at-risk athletes who were not professionaly diagnosed in advance. Future investigation needs to take into account dynamic and contextual body image changes. It should also focus more closely on why certain athletes develop a more negative body image and how this could be prevented.

Title: Psychometric properties of the contextual body image questionnaire for athletes: a replication and extension study in Female collegiate athletes
Authors: Stewart, T., Kilpela, L., Wesley, K., & Becker, C.
Inclusion criteria: Female athletes at each university within the ages of 17-27 years
Related_Factor_measure: Contextual Body Image Questionnaire for Athletes (CBIQA)
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Daily life thin-fat others correlated with EDE-Q global scores. Sport muscularity did not correlated with EDE-Q. All dimensions except muscularity correlated with all subscales in both contexts. Appearance dimension (perceiving others opinions of yourself) was related to higher levels of ED pathology in both daily life and sport contexts. Self evaluation and perceived other evaluation as fatter were also related to more ED pathology. Muscularity in daily life was not related to ED symptomatology. CBIQA scores related to appearance may predict future ED pathology.
Limits: Reliance on self-report data, attrition at follow-up, and that the CBIQA was delivered to participants 12 months into the FAB program as opposed to the beginning of the parent trial.
Perspectives: Further research on cntextual body images is needed to evaluate the impact of these dual body images with Female athletes not only while in sport, but while away or retiring from sport, inclusding periods of injury, between seasons and when completing sport.

Title: Athlete-specific risk factors for the development of disordered eating behaviors in first-year college athletes
Authors: Palermo, M., Rancourt, D., & Juarascio, A.
Inclusion criteria: 18 years or older, an incoming first-year student, and participation in either a DI sport at the university or a fall club sport at the time of the recruitmalet.
Sport_name: Cheerleading, ice hockey, swiming, track, baseball, field hockey, golf, karate, lacrosse, rugby, sailing, soccer, softball, squash, tennis, ultimate frisbee, volleyball, water polo, crew, basketball, wrestling
Related_Factor_measure:
1. How often does your uniform contribute to how you feel about your body ?
2. How often do you feel like you need to change anything about your body in order to look better in your uniform in front of other people ?
3. How often do you feel comfortable performing in your uniform in front of an andience of spectators ?
4. How often do you adapt your diet in order to look good in your uniform ?
Authors' conclusions: Wearing a uniform that emphasizes body concerns predicted increases in weight/shape concern during the 4-month observation period. Wearing a uniform that emphasizes body concerns did not predict increases in restrained eating behaviors. Perceived pressure for thinness from coaches predicted an increase in both weight/shape concern and restrained eating behaviors at time 2. Teammate pressure for thinness was solely predictive of restrained eating behaviors at time 2. Coach pressure for thinness was the only athlete-specific risk factor that was predictive of increases in both weight/shape concerns and restrained eating behaviors.
Limits: The study time frame was relatively short, which may have limited the ability to detect change in weight/shape concern and restrained eating behaviors. Our sample had substantial attrition, with only about 54% of participants who completed time 1 completed the follow-up survey. The director of athletics and associated staff were present for the data collection ; some athletes may have been concerned that the athletics department would have access to their data. There was a limited number of club athlete participants in the final sample, level of sport competitive could not be considered. There may be differences in competition level between club sport versus division I athletes. There are a number of measurement considerations.
Perspectives:
Future would also should assess team culture and/or group cohesion, as these may buffer against the negative impact of perceived pressure to be thin from teammates and/or coaches, as teammates can be protective against, or heighten the risk for, disordered eating. 
For athletic departments to offer training to coaches that includes learning indicators of eating disorder relapse.

Title: Pinning down the problems and influences: disordered eating and body satisfaction in male wrestlers
Authors: Satterfield, N.A., & Stutts, L.A.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate wrestlers; at least 18 years of age; at a college in the United States; a current mumber of a NCAA Division I wrestling team; and identified as a man.
Related_Factor_measure: The Weight Pressures in Sports Scale for Male Athletes
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Drive for muscularity was positively associated was associated with binge eating and restricting. While we did find an association between body satisfaction and restricting eating behavior, there was not a significant association among binge eating, purging, and body satisfaction. Coaches/teammates were only a significant predictor of restricting behavior and were the least important predictor of it compared to general pressures and sport appearance pressures.
Limits: The majority of participants identiied as white ; the present study sample is not representative of the racial makeup of this population. There was a relatively low response rate to the survey, which limits the generalizability of our sample. This study was cross sectional and only examined athletes in season, which limits the conclusions we can draw. The use of self report measures means it is possible that participants downplayed some of their behaviors or were unaware of the frequency of them. In addition, we did not ask specifically about frequency of binge eating.
Perspectives:
One possible intervention is by providing coaches and athletes a decision tree to plan a safe weight-cutting strategu such as consuming strategic level of carbohydrates and fluids. It is important that wrestlers evaluate their weight-cutting and recovery practices before and after competitions to assess what is working safely. 
Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies that assess these variables in season versus out of season. Body satisfaction and disordered eating should be investigated in a racially diverse sample for both generalizability and differential risk. Future studies should examine Female's wrestling and explore gender differences in body satisfaction and disordered eaating behaviors.

Title: A socio-sports model of disordered eating among Brazilian male athletes
Authors: De Sousa Fortes, L., Caputo Ferreira, M.E., Fernandes de Oliveira, S.M., Serpeloni Cyrino, E., & Sousa Almeida, S.
Inclusion criteria: Systematiccaly trained in a sport modality based on a training regimen of at least six hours of training per week (e.g., minimum of three days per week of two-hour sessions or six days per week of one hour sessions); participation in at least one regional competition in 2014 and; availability to respond to questionnaires and to participate in anthropometric evaluations.
Sport_name: Track and field; basketball; boxing; canoeing; cycling; equestrian; jiu-jitsu; judo; swimming; water polo; rowing; diving; surfing; tae-kwon-do; tennis; triathlon; sailing; volleyball
Sporting population:
30% international level
42% national level
28% regional level
Related_Factor_sub-class 2: Perception of sociocultural pressure from media
Degree of relationship:
Sociocultural factors-disordered eating 𝛃=.07, p<.05
Sociocultural factors-body fat dissatisfaction 𝛃=.10, p<.05
Body fat dissatisfaction-disordered eating 𝛃=.08, p<.05
R²(body fat dissatifaction)=.11, p<.001
R²(disordered eating)=.11, p<.001
Authors' conclusions: Only the sociocultural factors and body fat dissatisfaction adhered to etiological model of DE in Brazilian male athletes. Sociocultural factors (parents, friends and the media) exhibit a direct relationship to DE. The results of the structural equation model indicate that body fat dissatisfaction mediates the relationship between sociocultural factors and DE.
Limits: Because self-reporting instruments were used as evaluative tools, the results may not reflect the reality because the responses given were subjective. The study is also limited in that it applies a doubly indirect method to evaluate fat percentages. Weight and body fat measurements can influence the survey responses about body image and disordered eating. The heterogeneity of the sample with respect to age and type of sport could have influenced the results.
Perspectives: Sport professionals may use the present study findings to intervene in factors that promote disturbed eating in athletes. Because disordered eating can cause an attenuation of anaerobic potency and resistance, prevention/intervention programs that are designed to prevent disordered eating in athletes may indirectly improve athletic performance. The construction of a socio-sports model for Female is recommaleded.

Title: Effects of Sport Pressures on Female Collegiate Athletes: A Preliminary Longitudinal Investigation
Authors: Anderson, C.M., Petrie, T.A., Neumann, C.S.
Population subgroup:
Time 1: begin of the fall season (September)
Time 2: end of the season (February)
Inclusion criteria: Student athletes from 26 universities located within all regions of the United States
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Sport pressures and dietary restraint were highly stable over the course of a competitive season. Pressures gymnasts and swimmers/divers experienced regarding body weight, size, and appearance from their coaches and teammates predicted decreases in their body satisfaction over a 5-month period; this change occurred even though the athletes’ body mass index did not change significantly over that time.
Limits: Included only NCAA Division I Female gymnasts and swimmers/divers, who also happened to primarily be Caucasien. The authors examined the variables over only a 5-month period, which represented one competitive collegiate season for these athletes. They examined the relationships among only sport pressures, body dissatisfaction and dietary restraint, additional research is needed to examine other variables such as general sociatail pressures, internalization, and negative affect. The validity of self-report measures of dietary restraint as predictors of actual reductions in food intake has been challenged. Self report measures of dietary restraint are risk factors in the prediction of disordered eating attitudes and behaviors, the measures are poor predictors of behaviorally observed, acute dietary restriction. BMI did not vary over the course of the 5-month season, we were not able to obtain more sensitive measures of body composition due to the study's design.
Perspectives:
Health care personnel can help coaches and teammates become more aware of how, through their behaviors and comments, they create an environment that pressures athletes about their body, weight, and appearance. Sport health care professionals can target sport administrators and sport-governing bodies because they have the power to male policy changes that can improve the sport environment, maling it less toxic for athletes. Such entities, could make revealing uniforms less so, adjust judging criteria so there is less focus on aesthetic/appearance-based aspects of the performance, expand or raise weight classifications, and/or set up strict requirements regarding acceptable weight loss over specific periods of time. Preventive programming, sport health care profesionals can work directly with athletes to help them counter these sport pressures and reduce their likelihood of engaging in caloric restriction of feeling dissatisfied with their bodies. 
Future reseach should examine whether our findings are supported in other groups of Female athletes (e.g., different sports, different competitive levels, more diverse racial/ethnic groups); male athletes should also be studied and such research should include measures of drive for muscularity. Other longitudinal studies may want to examine eating disorders and other potential risk factors over a longer period of time, or a different period (e.g., from the end of the competitive season to the start of the next one).

Title: Bulimic symptomatology among male collegiate athletes: a test of an etiological model
Authors: Chatterton, J., Petrie, T.A., Schuler, K.L., & Ruggero, C.
Inclusion criteria: Male collegiate athletes drawn from 35 states in the United States; athletes competed at the National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels.
Sport_name: Baseball, football, track and field, swimming/diving, soccer, basketball, cross-country, tennis, wrestling, lacrosse, golf, ice hockey, crew, fencing, volleyball, skiing and squash
Sporting population: National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I, II, III and National Association of Intercollegiate Athletes levels
Related_Factor_sub-class 1: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
Authors' conclusions: Sport specific pressures played the most important role in understanding the athletes symptomatology, having effects through negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity. As the direct precursors of the athletes bulimic symptomatology, body dissatisfaction, negative affect, dietary restraint and drive for muscularity were also salient.
Limits: First due to lack of fit, we defined drive for muscularity solely by the muscularity behaviors items. Second the current study used a cross-sectional design that did not allow for a causal, or temporal, interpretation of the data. Third, although the current study used a large sample of male collegiate athletes in the United States, athletes self-selected into the study and certain sport were underrepresented. Therefore, the findings may not generalize to all sports. Finally, our measure of general societal appearance ideals was broad and did not include specific references to the body, weight and appearance pressures indivdiuals might experience through their involvmalet in social media.
Perspectives: In future studies, researchers might examine the supported relationships longitudinally, such as between sport weight pressures and dietary restraint or drive for muscularity, to determine how they change over time and which variables temporally influence others. Future research might test this model within single sports (e.g., all football players or all soccer players) or among younger athletes to determine if the influence of the sport environment remains, is heightened, or is diminished. Programs designed to educate coaches about the impact of their remarks and that highlight self-awareness regarding such comments could be implemented to help shift the focus of the athletic environment away from weight and appearance. Sport psychologist also might work directly with athletes, providing them with resources and strategies for countering the ubiquitous messages about physical and appearance ideals. Furthermore, athletic departments might develop annual screening for their athletes that could carried out by sports medicine personnel such as athletic trainers. This screening could be done to identify athletes who report high levels of body dissatisfaction, a high drive to restrict their eating and a strong focus on muscle building behaviors.
